### Saint Magnenn of Kilmainham

Before he tasted his meal or whatever he was to consume, he would perform five meditations. The first was on how he was originally born and in what a humble state <note>original: "mean estate"</note> he came from his mother’s womb. The second was how, in time, he would escape from the finality of death <note>original: "death-extremity"</note>. The third was how the soul is carried away to witness Hell. The fourth was how the soul goes to contemplate the Heavenly City so that it may avoid being pulled back <gloss>[into sin or the world]</gloss>, which increases its humility and spiritual concern <note>original: "self-distrust"</note>. The fifth was how the sinners' monument <note>original: "cairn"; a pile of stones serving as a memorial or landmark</note>—the structure of their ambition, no matter how high it is piled—is brought low <note>original: "abased"</note> in just a short time. 

He used to tell his monks that they ought to leave a path free within their inner selves for the Holy Spirit: a passage where they should not allow worldly <note>original: "secular"</note> nourishment to enter. He used to say three times at once that the world is nothing but a mass of deception. "Pay attention, my beloved people," he said, "and take notice: if you reject <note>original: "spurn"</note> God’s commandments, how can you look up to Him when making your requests? Or how will God listen to your cry and earnest prayer?"

At one time, Bishop Magnenn went to the place where Saint Moling lived. A meal of food <note>original: "victual"</note> was served to them and, according to tradition <note>original: "precept"</note>, it was blessed. A member of his monastic community <note>original: "familia"; Latin for a household or religious family</note> said, "Today, as we came here, we noticed a cross and a fresh grave, but we do not know what is buried there." 

Magnenn asked, "In what place did you see that?" 

The other answered, "On a slope <note>original: "acclivity"</note> on the side of *Berna na Gaoithe* <gloss>[Wind-gap]</gloss>." 

The bishop said, "I have never seen a cross without kneeling <note>original: "genuflection"</note> three times before it." Therefore, even though his meal had already been blessed, he left it behind. Accompanied by his twenty-seven <gloss>[thrice nine]</gloss> holy clerics, he traveled until he came to *Berna na Gaoithe*. There, he spent a long time contemplating the cross and the grave. He spoke to no one, but knelt three times before the cross. 

His people asked him why he was silent, but he did not answer them. He remained this way for three hours; then, in a mild and gentle voice, he said: "I command you to tell me who is buried in that grave, and why I never saw the cross despite having passed close by it." 

The miserable soul <gloss>[the occupant of the tomb]</gloss> answered him, saying: "I will tell you that, holy bishop, even though I gain no relief from your questioning <note>original: "interpellation"</note>. I am a pagan <note>original: "heathen"</note>, and it was never possible..."

# Saint Magnenn of Kilmainham

The next morning, Magnenn rose. He and his twenty-seven companions <note>original: "thrice nine"</note> walked all through Saturday. When the start of Sunday arrived <note>original: "Sunday’s [anterior] limit"; likely referring to Saturday evening when the liturgical Sunday begins</note>, the holy bishop happened to be on an open plain, and they camped there for the night. Throughout that cold and wet night, they endured heavy rain and harsh, shifting winds. However, Bishop Magnenn planted his four-sided pastoral staff <note>A staff carried by a bishop symbolizing his role as a shepherd</note> in the ground to stand over them; around it, each of his men also planted their own hooked staves. The holy bishop then spread his four-cornered hood over his company of clerics and performed a clear miracle for the group: despite the night’s great storm and foul weather—with every pool and hollow overflowing—not a single drop of the storm fell upon the saints. They rose on Monday, and the wonders he had performed for the saints were obvious; news of these miracles spread throughout all of Ireland.

One of Magnenn’s notable characteristics was his attitude toward wealth, for he never accepted gold, silver, or any metal designated as money <note>original: *moneta*</note>. A Culdee <term>A member of an ascetic Christian community in Ireland and Scotland known for their strict devotion</term> in Kilmainham gave this great testimony about him: “Magnenn the miracle-worker, who never sinned with a woman; Magnenn the wise, whose habit it was to weep.” Furthermore, when preaching, he never repeated a single word in the same discourse. He never finished a sermon without converting someone to the faith. He never sat beside a king or a chief (aiming thus to avoid developing a prideful spirit <note>original: "high mind"</note>), and he greatly despised the honors given by kings and mighty lords, saying, “Woe to the person who, after renouncing the world, finds satisfaction in honors granted by the powerful.”

After this, a robber came from Howth <note>original: *benn Edair*</note> and stole a cow belonging to a woman with leprosy in Kilmainham. This woman’s cow was always in milk and provided enough to support the poor, the needy, and those with paralysis. She recognized the robber and went, crying aloud as she went, to the place where Bishop Magnenn was with his gathering of saints and clerics. She bitterly told him how she had been robbed of her only cow, which had caused her to become thin and weak. At this story, the holy Bishop Magnenn and his group of clerics were angered...

"But when someone goes on a pilgrimage in body, while their mind remains at home with their children, their wife, or their land, and they prefer these things to God, then their journey is in vain. # Saint Cellach of Killala

## *The Life of Saint Cellach of Killala*

There was once a king who ruled over Connacht: Eoghan Bél, son of Cellach, son of Ailill Molt, son of Dathí, son of Fiachra, son of Eochaidh Moyvane. He used to ravage every province in Ireland and would always return victorious, bringing his plunder with him. No one was ever successful in taking back what he had stolen, for he always defeated his enemies in battle. Even if he could not catch those who attempted to raid him before they left his territory, he would raid that very same country on that very same day in retaliation. Indeed, even the people of Munster and Leinster obeyed him; because their cattle <note>original: "kine"</note> had been forcibly driven away so many times, they were eager <note>original: "fain"</note> to win his favor.

In any event, a great feud broke out between this Eoghan and the descendants of Niall <note>The Uí Néill dynasty</note>. Eventually, it was not just these families but the entire two provinces that stood opposed to one another: Connacht against Ulster. Their situations were unequal, however, because Eoghan Bél had never lost a battle, and no one had ever recovered stolen property from him. On the other hand, the number of times he took plunder and won triumphs over the people of Conall, Eoghan, and Oriel <note>The kingdoms of Cenél Conaill, Cenél Eoghain, and Airgíalla in the north</note> was beyond counting. As long as Eoghan Bél lived, there was never a day of peace with them; every quarter of a year—even every month—he raided them and put them to the sword. The descendants of Niall thought it a hard and grievous thing to constantly endure the violence of Eoghan Bél and the descendants of Fiachra, while the rest of Connacht was also against them. Therefore, the people of Ulster in general, debating what they should do, resolved to gather and prepare for a full-scale invasion, and so they fell upon the land of Connacht.

Two kings ruled Ulster at this time: Fergus and Donall, the two sons of Muirchertach mac Erca. They now took great spoils from Connacht and completely ravaged everything before them as far as the River Moy. They were a gathering "five battles" <term>a "battle" (cath) was a traditional unit of several hundred to a thousand soldiers</term> strong while driving away this plunder. The territory of the Clan Fiachra...

The warriors set out to pursue them, but not a single cow was recovered nor a sword blunted against the enemy until, at the bridge of *Martra*, Eoghan’s family and household overtook them and pressed them hard in a fierce fight. At *Sceichín na Gaoithe* <note>original: "sceichín na gaoithe," meaning "the little hawthorn of the wind"</note>, Eoghan himself caught up with them. Seeing such a vast army, he sent ambassadors—men of learning and the arts <note>likely poets and scholars who served as diplomats</note>—to Fergus, Donall, and the nobles of Ulster. They were to command them to abandon the stolen cattle <note>original: "prey"</note> in full and depart in peace, or else face an immediate challenge to battle. 

The envoys found Fergus and Donall and delivered Eoghan's message. But because they had the stolen cattle right in front of them, they were confident and eager for a fight, and they refused to return anything. The Northern forces consisted of five battalions from the Uí Néill <note>original: "clan-Neill"</note> and Ulster, along with the men of Oriel. Opposing them was one massive battalion of the Uí Fiachrach <note>original: "clan-Fiachrach"</note> and the warriors of Connacht in their own separate companies, all under the command of Eoghan Bél.

When Eoghan heard the response his poets brought back from the Uí Néill, he dismounted; they told him that war was now his only choice, and the Ulstermen declared that even if he fought, he would never win back a single cow. Then the men of Connacht armed themselves and launched a sudden, swift, and unsparing charge upon the Uí Néill. At the sight of Eoghan’s standard and the banners that had triumphed in so many raids, the Ulstermen wavered. Both sides, quivering with hatred, clashed together, and the Battle of Sligo began. 

The North of Ireland was defeated; their plunder was recaptured, and a great number of their people were slaughtered. Fergus and Donall also died there. However, Eoghan Bél was severely wounded and had to be carried away on the shafts of spears. Some say he lived for three more days; others say he lasted a week. The nobles came and went to see him, mourning him deeply during that time.

Surgeons treated King Eoghan Bél, but in the end, it was certain that he would die. The children of Fiachra sought his advice on who should be made chief in his place. Eoghan Bél said: "Your situation is difficult. I have two sons: Cellach, who is a disciple of Kieran of Cluain <note>Saint Ciarán of Clonmacnoise</note>, and Muiredach, the younger son, who is not yet old enough to be inaugurated as king. My advice to you is..."

This having been done, Eoghan prescribed the manner of his burial: in the open field on the borders of the Uí Fiachrach <note>original: clan-Fiachrach</note>, with his red spear in his hand and his face toward the North. "For," he said, "as long as my grave faces them—with my face also turned toward them—they shall not withstand Connacht in battle."

He was buried accordingly, and the rest of what he prophesied was truly accomplished; for wherever the Uí Néill <note>original: clan-Neill</note> and the men of Connacht happened to meet afterward, it was defeat that fell upon the Uí Néill and the North in general. Therefore, the descendants of Niall and the North made a plan: they would come with a great host to the fort of the Uí Fiachrach <note>original: ráth ua Fiachrach</note>, exhume Eoghan, and carry him off northwards over Sligo <note>original: Sligeach</note>. They did so, and away in the flat land of Lough Gill <note>original: loch Gile</note>, he was buried with his face downwards.

But just as Eoghan Bél had instructed them to go, the Uí Fiachrach went to Clonmacnoise and to the place where Kieran was in prayer. When they came to him, he welcomed them and settled them in a room <note>original: cubicle</note>. That night they were well provided for, and they explained their errand to Kieran afterward; but he utterly refused to give up his disciple.

Nevertheless, even though he refused their request, they stayed in Clonmacnoise <note>original: Cluain</note> a second night until Cellach came to visit them. They conferred with him and begged him to go with them; in the end, he yielded and agreed to accompany them. He departed the next morning without taking any farewell of his spiritual master at all.

Kieran was told how his disciple had been stolen away without his advice or permission. Kieran said: "If he is indeed gone, then may the choice he has made not thrive with him, but let him have a curse <note>original: malison</note> on whatever he undertakes. May it be that, at the last, a destructive grief comes upon him, and 'death by a sharp point' <note>likely referring to death by a spear or sword</note> be what removes him. I, acting for my Lord who is King of Heaven and Earth, further decree that for all time, such a 'death by point' shall be that which—beyond all help and without fail—takes whoever deserts their life as a student of the church."

# Saint Cellach of Killala

[They] conferred on him the chieftainship <note>original: chiefry</note> of the Clan Fiachrach <note>The descendants of Fiachra</note> from the River Robe <note>original: Rodhba</note> to the Codnach. He held it for a while, but when he heard that his teacher <note>Saint Kieran</note> had cursed him, he grew to dislike that way of life. At that same time, Guaire, the son of Colman, was so renowned that his fame and honor excelled throughout Ireland; the territory of the Clan Fiachrach of Aidhne <note>A region in modern County Galway</note> belonged entirely to him. 

Thus, without delay, matters concerning land ownership went poorly between the two of them, and it soon became common knowledge that they hated one another. Even so, they arranged a meeting <note>original: trysted</note> and made peace. However, Guaire acted with guile during this peace-making and treated Cellach treacherously: he killed as many of Cellach's people as he could catch, while Cellach himself escaped secretly from the camp with twenty-seven <note>original: thrice nine</note> of his followers.

For a full year, he was "under wood" <note>an idiom meaning he lived as a fugitive and outlaw in the forest</note>. He was filled with weariness and remorse for ever forsaking his life as a student, as well as for all the kindness that Kieran had shown him. He rebuked himself continually, so grieved was he by what had happened to him. 

"Woe is me!" he cried. "Why did it ever enter my head, for the sake of the material things <note>original: grossness</note> of this wretched, fleeting world, to abandon my studies and my master?" Then he said:

> "Alas for the man who forsakes the religious life <note>original: clerkly life</note> for any of this vile, crude world’s estates—woe to him who gives up the great love of a faithful God for the royalty of a passing world! 
> 
> Alas for him who takes up arms in this life, unless he performs penance for it; better for a person are the white-paged books from which the canonical psalms are chanted. 
> 
> As grand as the art of war may be, it brings little profit and is filled with heavy toil; from it, one gains only a very short life, which must in the end be exchanged for Hell. 
> 
> But of all professions, theft <note>original: stealth</note> is the worst: sneaking, perjured, and nimble thieving. He who commits it, even if he were once a good man, is from then on regarded only as a wicked person. 
> 
> A large portion of these evils has now fallen upon Cellach, son of Eoghan. As he wanders from table to table with a gang of villains, let him beware of death. 
> 
> Alas for the one who abandons Heaven, the blessed home of saints, to suffer the dark, murky slavery of Hell; O Christ, Ruler of Battles, woe to him who deserts his mighty Lord!"

After this great fit of repentance <note>original: penitence</note> came over Cellach, he decided on a plan: the nine companions who had been with him in the recent war against Guaire should seek out his former tutor, Kieran of Clonmacnoise <note>original: Cluain</note>. Cellach himself was hesitant to trust Kieran because he had previously disobeyed him. He waited outside of Clonmacnoise until he met some of his former classmates <note>original: whilom condisciples</note>.

As for Cellach, he devoted himself zealously to study, pursuing it strenuously and with careful attention. The fame of his piety spread throughout Ireland; men loved him with a universal love, and because Cellach acted in all things according to his teacher's <note>original: preceptor</note> word, Kieran was well pleased with him. From then on, he administered this greater bishopric, though he remained mostly at Clonmacnoise rather than in his own diocese. In all of Ireland, there was no one of greater renown for honor, piety, and scholarly <note>original: clerkly</note> bearing; no one whom the learned cherished more dearly, and people of all ranks and backgrounds remained loyal to him.

# Saint Cellach of Killala

The company left Cellach all alone; these four were *Maelcróin*, *Maeldálua*, *Maelsenaigh*, and *Macdeoraidh*, who were once Cellach’s fellow students <note>original: condisciples</note>. From Shrovetide until Easter, they continued performing their duties, serving God zealously. News spread throughout Ireland that the holy bishop Cellach (having abandoned his bishopric) was living the life of a hermit. When Easter arrived, his brother Muiredach (the son of Eoghan Bél) visited him often and did nothing without his advice.

When Guaire heard all of this, he was possessed by rage and felt great enmity toward Cellach. As bad as things had been between them before, they now became much worse. Guaire feared that Muiredach—prompted by his brother Cellach, and because of his own natural abilities and his awareness that he was fit to be a leader <note>original: apt matter of a chief</note>—would seize total power.

Furthermore, Guaire’s son Nar and Nemedh, the son of Ferchoga, constantly plagued Guaire with fabricated and wicked stories about the bishop. They kept insisting to Guaire that he must kill the holy bishop Cellach. Together, they devised a plan of treason: they would invite Cellach to visit them and have poison ready for him. Although Guaire hated him, the king did not want weapons to be used against Cellach in his own presence.

This is what they did: intending to kill Cellach, they prepared poison. Then they sent messengers to the island in the lake <note>original: loch</note> where he lived. They were instructed that if Cellach refused to come, they should invite his fellow students to return to Guaire instead, so they could serve as friendly messengers between the two men.

On his island, these messengers found Cellach just as he was reading his daily prayers <note>original: hours</note> and saluted him. He greeted them, and they told him they had come from Guaire to bring him to a great feast the king was holding for him, and to speak with him.

“I will go there no more,” Cellach said, “nor will I neglect my prayers for the sake of a feast or the favor of this perishing, poor world.”

“Never do what they ask,” his fellow students cried. “It is foolishness for Guaire to imagine that you could be drawn to love him through such things.”

The messengers then said, “Then allow your fellow students to come with us; Guaire will be pleased with you for that, and they can carry whatever private messages <note>original: privy errand</note> he has for you.”

He was in this state: his psalter <term>A book containing the Psalms</term> was spread before him as he recited the psalms; he never spoke to them; he finished his prayers and, looking at them, noticed their eyes were shifting and clouded with the look of a murderer <note>original: "parricide," the act of killing a parent or a person in a similar position of authority</note>.

"Young men," said Cellach, "you have a wicked look; since you left me your natures have changed, and I see that for King Guaire’s sake you have agreed to murder me." They did not deny it for a moment, and he continued: "It is an evil plan; but do not pursue your own ruin any longer, for I can give you gifts that will benefit you far more than Guaire’s promises." They replied: "By no means, Cellach, will we do as you wish, for if we did, we could not find shelter anywhere in all Ireland;" and even as they spoke, they plunged their spears into Cellach all at once; yet he managed to thrust his psalter between himself and his robe. # Saint Cellach of Killala

> “O you young men who terrify me, pride is an abomination to Heaven’s high King; as twisted as your eyes are, the secrets of your hearts are even more perverted. I have a certain One on my side, the like of whom does not exist: my cause is bound up closely with Christ, and the angels’ Heaven shall be my dwelling place. It was treason when you decided to attack me unrighteously; but in the end, death by the sword’s point shall work your destruction and, O young men, Hell awaits you!”

“Giving us further advice on this matter is useless,” they retorted; “we will not do [your bidding].”

“Well then,” he pleaded, “grant me this one night’s respite for God’s sake.”

“Reluctant as we are to grant it, we will give you that,” they said. Then they raised the swords which they had carried hidden in their clothes, and at the sight of them, a mighty fear took hold of Cellach. They searched the wood until they found a hollow oak with one narrow entrance, and Cellach was committed to this; they sat at the hole to watch him until the morning. They stayed there until the night was nearly over, when a longing for sleep came to them and a deep slumber fell upon them there. 

Cellach, in distress over his impending violent death, did not sleep at all. At that time, it was in his power to have fled (had he wished to do so), but in his heart he said that it would be a lack of faith for him to attempt to evade the designs of the living God. Moreover, he reflected that even if he were to flee, they would surely overtake him, as he was weak and feeble after the season of Lent [which had just passed]. 

Morning now shone upon them, and he (for fear of seeing the light and in terror of his death) shut the door. Yet he said: “To shirk God’s judgment is a lack of faith in me, since Kieran my teacher promised that I must meet this end.” As he spoke, he flung open the tree's door. Then the raven called, and the hooded crow <note>original: "scallcrow"</note>, the wren, and all the other birds. Though he was severely wounded in the fight, he eventually killed the beast, took its head, and carried it back to shore to Conall and his people.

Their shame shall endure for a long time, even until the arrival of the world-striking Judgment Day; their souls are with the Devil, and it was right to strangle them."

# Saint Cellach of Killala

In the territories of Tirawley and Northern Hy-Fiachrach <note>A tribal territory in modern County Mayo</note>, Cuchongeilt then and there established himself as supreme ruler. Meanwhile, in the south, Guaire was lord of Hy-Fiachrach Aidhne <note>A territory in modern County Galway</note>. A violent war immediately broke out between the two, and it would be impossible to describe all the violence and evil that Cuchongeilt inflicted upon Guaire. In short, the conflict between them nearly resulted in the total destruction of both their clans <note>original: "Irachts"</note>, and even threatened to bring the entire province to ruin.

Now, Guaire's daughter Gelghéis was deeply in love with Cuchongeilt; for the sake of this love, she had always refused to marry any other man. As the two kings grew weary of the war, Cuchongeilt pressured Guaire for his daughter’s hand in marriage. Guaire, however, absolutely refused to give her to him. Nevertheless, his people—desperate for the war to end—pleaded with Guaire so urgently that he finally consented, but only on these conditions: he himself would host the wedding feast, and Cuchongeilt must come to his house. Cuchongeilt would not agree to this under any circumstances, so they continued to wage war for a long time, until Guaire (to satisfy the majority of his people) was forced to seek peace. Exhausted by the struggle, he finally handed Gelghéis over to Cuchongeilt, and they lived together affectionately; at this time, Cuchongeilt’s reputation for generosity was highly regarded throughout Ireland.

However, although Cuchongeilt was now peaceful toward Guaire's people, he continued to desolate the churches in his own land, which Guaire considered a great evil. Therefore, Guaire practiced this treachery: he sought out the place where Kieran of Clonmacnoise <note>Saint Ciarán, founder of the famous monastery</note> was staying with his clergy. Guaire urged the saint to go and bring Cuchongeilt back with him to ensure their mutual peace and friendship. Guaire also had Kieran deliver a promise to Cuchongeilt: that if he would only come to Guaire's house, he would be allowed to rule his own country without opposition.

Kieran found Cuchongeilt and strongly encouraged him not to let the lordship of Connacht slip away, even if it meant risking a meeting with Guaire. Gelghéis also persuaded him to go, for she knew that Kieran harbored no treachery, and she could not imagine that Guaire would deal deceitfully with the saint. Against his own natural instincts, Cuchongeilt finally consented to accompany Kieran (many others also urged him to do so), and he remarked:

> "Even though I am escorted by a hundred men, I am loath to set out on this journey; but whether I return or not, it is more honorable that I go."

Until he had first denied them for a time, he did not go to Guaire's house with the company; he did not go until they had forced a fast upon him and three days of abstinence from food.

To Eoghan's most handsome son, Gelghéis of the blooming cheek said: "And would you then deal treasonably with the honor of Ireland's exalted saints? Had you only given up <term>Dúrlas</term> <note>The royal seat of King Guaire</note> and the level marshland of the Moy to Guaire, you would not have needed to enter his house under the guarantee of a saint or a <term>nemhed</term> <note>A privileged person or sacred site under Old Irish law</note>. Wit and wisdom are not equal—age and hardihood are not equal—gentleness and affection are not equal between you and the Clan Colman."

Cuchongeilt of the conventions answered: "Since you desire it, and to please you, I will go to the house of Colman's son, which is filled with many followers."

The clergy and Cuchongeilt equipped themselves in haste and, with Cuchongeilt leading, held a straight course to <term>Dúrlas</term>. Though Kieran of Cluain <note>Clonmacnoise</note> was a man prone to righteous anger, and though Brendan's miracles were potent, Guaire (Colman's son, the destroyer) never cast a single look of respect toward that perfect band of clerics. Then, in both low places and high, the people of <term>Dúrlas</term> carried out the slaughter; so it was that at the hands of the long-haired Clan Colman, Cuchongeilt perished as was ordained. Without reprieve, the saints then banned and cursed the murderous Guaire: they blighted both his life and his death, so that this spot remains empty and a desert.

### *A Story of Aedh Baclamh*

Aedh Baclamh <note>The name "Baclamh" likely refers to a physical disability or a specific way of carrying a spear; literally "lame-arm."</note>, the spear-bearer of Dermot, son of Cerbhall (the King): a fit of heavy sickness took him, and for a year he suffered from a wasting, continuous illness. However, he recovered his health and went to speak with Dermot, to whom he said: "During this past year that I have been lying down, how has the order of your discipline and peace fared?" Dermot said: "I do not perceive any decline <note>original: "imminution"</note> that it has suffered." "There is a way I will test that," said Aedh Baclamh. "I will carry your spear laid crosswise in the bend of both my arms and traverse Ireland diagonally, traveling west and south, until I reach the door of every fortified homestead <note>original: "liss," a ringfort or circular earthen dwelling</note> in Ireland. I will carry the spear transversely over their thresholds; in this way, the governance and peace of Ireland shall be proven."

From Tara, therefore, Aedh Baclamh (accompanied by the King of Ireland's herald to proclaim the peace of the land) arrived in the province of Connacht. There, he made his way to the mansion of Aedh Guaire of Kinelfechin in Hy-Many. At that time, Aedh Guaire had a stockade of red oak around his fortress <note>original: "fortalice"</note>, and a new house that had just been built for his wife's marriage feast. Now, a week before Aedh Baclamh's arrival, Aedh Guaire had heard he was coming and ordered an opening to be made for him in the outer palisade, but not in the dwelling itself.

Aedh Baclamh arrived accordingly, and Aedh Guaire welcomed him. Aedh Baclamh insisted that the house itself must be hacked open <note>to the width of the spear held crosswise</note> before him. "Give your own orders according to how you wish it to be cut," Aedh Guaire said, and even as he spoke, he struck him with a sword and cut off his head.

In those days, the law <note>original: "discipline"</note> of Ireland was such that whoever killed an innocent man could not offer cattle or any other valuable payment as compensation <note>original: "consideration"</note> for the slain. Unless the King of Ireland himself ordained or permitted a fine to be accepted, the killer had to be put to death.

<summary>Aedh Baclamh, King Dermot's spear-bearer, attempts to test the King's authority by carrying a spear horizontally through every door in Ireland, but he is killed by Aedh Guaire for demanding the destruction of his new home.</summary>
<keywords>Aedh Baclamh, King Dermot (Diarmait mac Cerbaill), Aedh Guaire, Tara, Connacht, Irish Law, blood money, sovereignty, spear-bearer</keywords>

# Aedh Baclamh

When Dermot had heard of the killing, he sent his young men and his executive officers to lay waste and plunder the lands of Aedh Guaire. Aedh fled to Bishop Senan, for they were born of the same mother. Bishop Senan then went with him to Ruadhan of Lorrha, because two of Ruadhan’s sisters—named Cael and Ruadhnait—had been the ones to nurse Bishop Senan. However, Aedh Guaire found no permanent sanctuary with Ruadhan and was banished away into Britain, where he remained for a year. Dermot’s people traveled there to demand his surrender, so he was sent back to Ruadhan once more. 

Dermot came in person to Ruadhan to demand him, but the saint had him hidden in a hole in the earth which today is called *Poll Ruadháin*, that is, "Ruadhan’s Pit." Dermot sent his servant to search Ruadhan’s kitchen to see if Aedh Guaire was there; but as soon as the servant entered the kitchen, he was immediately struck blind. When Dermot saw what had happened, he entered the kitchen himself. He did not find Aedh Guaire there and asked Ruadhan where he was (for he believed that Ruadhan would not tell a lie). Ruadhan answered: "I do not know, unless he is under that thatch over there."

Dermot began to return home; however, on the way, he remembered the cleric’s specific words and turned back again. He entered the <term>reclusorium</term> <note>original: reclusorium; a place of prayer or a cell for a hermit or monk</note> and saw a candle being carried to the place where Aedh Guaire was hidden. He sent another confidential servant named Donnan Donn to fetch him. Donnan excavated the hiding place, but the arm he reached out to grab Aedh withered up to the shoulder. At this, the servant performed an act of submission to Ruadhan. Both he and his companion who had been blinded remained with the saint, and from that time to this, they are said to be in Pollruane. Despite these miracles, Dermot seized Aedh Guaire and carried him off to Tara <note>The ancient seat of the High Kings of Ireland</note>.

Ruadhan went to the elder Brendan of Birr and to the twelve apostles of Ireland <note>A group of influential 6th-century Irish monastic saints</note>. Together, they followed Dermot to Tara and fasted against him that night <note>A traditional Irish legal custom where a person of lower status fasts at the door of a superior to compel them to settle a grievance</note>. Dermot, relying on his royal status and the perceived justice of his cause, fasted against them in return. During that night, the sons of "Tara’s Twelve Pillars" who were with the king’s steward died; but the next morning, after the steward begged him in God’s name, Ruadhan brought them back to life.

In this manner, they remained for an entire year outside Tara under Ruadhan’s tent, exposed to the wind and the rain.

# Aedh Baclamh

Both parties went without food every second night: Dermot and the clergy, who were fasting against each other <note>A traditional Irish legal practice called 'troscad', where a person fasts at the door of someone who has wronged them to compel a settlement</note>.

At that time, the other Brendan (son of Finnlogh) <note>Saint Brendan the Navigator</note> was exploring the sea in search of the Promised Land. An angel appeared and showed him that Ireland's twelve apostles were gathered before Tara, contending with the King of Ireland, who had just committed an act of violence against Ruadhan. Brendan returned from the sea and landed at *Dun Rosarach* <note>original: dún Rosarach; a fortified residence</note>, where he stayed that night and blessed the fort. However, when Dermot heard of Brendan's arrival and that he had come to help the saints and clergy, he was seized by great fear. He said to the saints, "If you were to give me fifty horses, blue-eyed and with golden bridles, I would hand Aedh Guaire over to you."

When Brendan heard this, he summoned fifty seals, transformed them into the shapes of horses, and drove them before him to the green of Tara. Then the clergy and all the people of Tara welcomed Brendan. He began to tell them of all the hardships he had faced at sea, and the people of Tara found Brendan’s speech very sweet. He asked Dermot if he would accept cattle or some other payment in exchange for Aedh Guaire. 

"I will accept those fifty blue-eyed horses," Dermot said, "but only on the condition that someone guarantees their health and service to me for a year and a quarter." 

So the horses were handed over to Dermot, and the cleric acted as security for them for that duration. When that time had passed, the horses were racing one day on the green of Tara. The riders, thinking they were not going fast enough, struck them with their riding crops. At this, the horses became frantic. No one could pull them back or control them before they—carrying their riders with them—dived into the sea. Both the men and the horses were turned into seals. 

Dermot was furious at this. He went into Tara and ordered the seven forts <note>original: lisses; enclosed farmsteads or courtyards</note> of Tara to be shut against the clergy so they could not enter, fearing they would leave behind curses or evil legacies.

Then meat and ale were given to the clergy, and people were assigned to wait on them, but also to keep a close watch over them. These guards were to stay until they had seen the clergy truly and effectively finish eating and drinking <note>to ensure they broke their fast and lost their spiritual leverage</note>. But that night, Brendan gave them this advice: they should pull their hoods over their heads and let their meat and drink pass by their lips <note>implying they should pretend to eat while continuing their fast in secret</note>.

Dermot, son of Cerbhall, lived once upon a time, and the official poets praised the king, his peace, and all his excellent ways.

### *This is the Death of Dermot, son of Fergus Cerrbeoil, as the Book of Sligo tells it.*

It happened at the time when Dermot, son of Fergus Cerrbeoil, was driven into exile on Lough Ree and the River Shannon by Tuathal Maelgarb. At that very same time, *Kieran, son of the carpenter* <note>original: Ciarán mac an tsaoir</note>, came to *Druim Tibrat* (the place where Clonmacnoise stands today) to found his monastery. Kieran traveled with eight companions on the lake, but with twelve hundred followers on land. A fire was kindled by the clergy.

Dermot was then staying in his exile at *the swimming-place of the two birds* <note>original: snámh dá én</note>. This place was named for two birds that Nar—son of Finncha, who was the son of Conall Cernach—killed there on the shoulder of Eistine the Amazon. Dermot’s wizards said to him, “The purpose for which that fire is kindled tonight is such that it will never be extinguished.” “Truly, it shall be extinguished right now,” Dermot said, as the boats arrived at *Port-grencha*, where *Finghin’s Well* <note>original: Tipra Finghin</note> is located today.

There, the cleric was in the middle of planting a church. “What is the work you are doing?” Dermot asked. “Building a little church,” Kieran answered. “That might as well be its name: *the little church* <note>original: eglais bheg</note>.” “Thrust in the foundation post with me,” Kieran said to Dermot, “and as we do it, allow my hand to be placed over yours. If you do, your hand and your royal rule shall be imposed over the men of Ireland by this time tomorrow.”

# Death of King Dermot

Dermot's foster-brother, *Maelmór son of Argat*, went [at the predicted time] to the place where Tuathal was, at *Grellach-eilte* <note>Grellach-eilte: likely located in modern County Meath</note> southeast of *Ros-ech*. He drove a spear into Tuathal’s breast so that he left him lifeless. For this deed, Maelmór himself was killed immediately afterward; hence the tale called *The Adventure of Maelmór* <note>original: "echtra Mhaeilmhóir"</note>. (Now, Maelmór was of the Hy-Conall of Murthemny, and the third foster-brother to Dermot; *Luchta* of *Ath-ferna* and *Enna son of Laighse* were the others). Consequently, before a week had ended, the men of Ireland inaugurated Dermot as king.

By Dermot and the men of Ireland, the great congregation of Usnach <note>Usnach: Uisneach, the traditional geographical center of Ireland</note> is held now at Beltane <note>Beltane: May 1st, a major Gaelic festival marking the beginning of summer</note>. At that time, Ireland’s three high gatherings were these:
*   The congregation of Usnach, at Beltane.
*   The convention of *Taillte* <note>Taillte: Teltown</note>, at Lammas <note>Lammas: August 1st, the harvest festival</note>.
*   The feast of Tara, at *Samhain* <note>Samhain: November 1st, the beginning of the dark half of the year; modern All-Hallows</note>.

Whosoever among the men of Ireland should have transgressed these—that is, whoever violated the laws of these assemblies—was guilty of death.

A message comes from Dermot to Kieran, requesting him to join the gathering. The king himself proceeds to *Cnoc-brecáin* to receive him; there he halted to wait, which is why the place is called the *Hill of Halting* <note>original: "tulach na comnaidhe"</note>. Kieran went to him accordingly. “Why, how now,” Dermot said, “since this is the first time we have met since I attained the kingdom through your blessing, let this stretch of land (with its oxen and its cattle) be made over to you as an ‘altar-sod’ <note>altar-sod: land granted to the church for its support</note>.” 

But in this same plain was a man who was an enemy to the king: Flann, son of Dima (from whom *Dima’s Hill* or *Flann’s Hill* is named). The king, finding himself in the neighborhood, has Dima’s house burned, and the owner is severely wounded within it. This warrior, seeking to escape the flames, gets into a bathing-vat inside the dwelling and there expires. 

“You have broken your covenant very quickly,” Kieran said to Dermot, “seeing as you have already committed violence upon the land you granted to us. Yet in any case,” he went on, “I will not take either Heaven or Earth from you or your children <note>meaning: I will not revoke your spiritual or temporal authority</note>...”

# Death of King Dermot

"Nay," the cleric answered, "the missile that I have delivered—by that same I may myself be hurt to death if it does not happen exactly so." The two of them, king and cleric, repaired to Usnach <note>Uisneach, the symbolic center of Ireland</note> and joined the congregation of the men of Ireland <note>original: "Erin"</note>, and there they remained for a fortnight. During this meeting, a mighty drought afflicted them, so that the people were in dire peril and their livestock perished in large numbers. Then they had recourse to Kieran <note>Saint Ciarán of Clonmacnoise</note> to find them relief. Kieran prayed, and there came a rain that, as a sign of the miracle, left twelve main streams in Ireland; because of this, Kieran is entitled to a general tax <note>original: "cess"</note> throughout Ireland. In the presence of the men of Ireland there, Dermot made obeisance to Kieran and settled on him his own service and his children's service forever.

Following this, at Lammastide <note>The harvest festival of Lughnasadh, around August 1st</note>, Kieran was at the assembly of *Taillte* <note>Teltown, the site of the ancient royal games</note>, where he worked many wonders and exceeding great miracles. There also this prodigy occurred: a man took a perjured oath, and in consequence, a running ulcer developed in his neck, causing his head to fall off. Thus, in the presence of the men of Ireland, he walked about the gathering without a head. Near them on the sward stood Dermot’s nephew, Suibne, the son of Colman More. > “Some of the young men do not calculate their accounts correctly: it was Conall who slew Aedh Slaine, because Aedh Slaine had slain Suibne.”

That is to say: Conall son of Suibne killed Aedh Slaine at Loch Sewdy. Aedh Gustan, on that same day, slew Aedh Buie, King of Teffia, and Aedh Róin, King of Offaly, in the *Hostel of Dáchoga* <note>original: bruidhen Dáchoga; a famous site in Irish literature</note>. This was the first instance of kin-slaying <term>fratricide</term> between the Clan Colman and the descendants of Aedh Slaine—namely, Aedh Slaine killing his kinsman Suibne, son of Colman, and Suibne’s son Conall killing him in retaliation.

They praised the king, his peace, and his good ways. At that time, Black Aedh, son of Suibne (the King of Dalaradia), was in the presence of Beg mac Dé. <note>Beg mac Dé was a famous Irish prophet of the 6th century.</note> It was King Dermot who had slain that Suibne and had taken his son, Aedh mac Suibne, to be raised in his own household. Beg said, "I see the gallant wolfdog that shall destroy the brilliant mansion." 

"What hound is that, Beg?" asked Aedh. 

"A *red hound* <note>original: *cú ruadh*, meaning a wolf</note>—some 'hound' or other—it might well be yourself," Beg replied. 

"How could that be?" Dermot asked. 

"It is easily said: it is truly the hand of Black Aedh that, in the house of Banbhan the hospitaller, shall cause a poisoned drink to enter your mouth. At that time, you will be wearing a shirt made from a single flax seed and a mantle produced from a single sheep. In your horn will be ale brewed from a single grain of corn; on your plate will be the bacon of a pig that was never born. Finally, it is the main beam of the house—the ridgepole—that shall fall on your head after your enemies have nearly beaten you to death." 

"Put Black Aedh to death!" everyone cried out. 

"Not so," said Dermot. "Instead, let him be removed from Ireland, and as long as I live, he shall not return." Consequently, Dermot exiled Black Aedh to Scotland, and he was not allowed back into Ireland as long as Dermot lived.

Dermot’s tribute, discipline, and law prevailed throughout Ireland. His stewards, managers, and regular soldiers in their quarters were stationed up and down the country. At this particular time, the king’s stewards and sergeants accompanied him into Connacht. They were joined by the king’s herald, who used to go before them to make a proclamation to any house where they arrived seeking hospitality. The crier’s announcement was this: that the gate of any town or castle they entered must be demolished before them so that Dermot’s spear could be carried in *sideways* <note>original: *athwartwise*</note>. Because of their fear of the king, no one dared to do anything but obey. But the Devil <note>original: *Diabolus*</note>—it was he who violently possessed the crier to urge this evil demand upon him, so that an even greater evil would result from it.

For they came once to the house of Aedh Guaire in the land of Hy-Many in Connacht. His castle had to be breached to make way for them and the king’s spear. Then anger seized Aedh; he killed "the lad of the spear" (the herald), and immediately fled to escape Dermot...

# Death of King Dermot

Aedh Guaire fled into the land of Muskerry and placed himself under the protection of Bishop Senach, for the bishop’s mother and Aedh Guaire’s mother were sisters. Subsequently, Bishop Senach brought him to Ruadhan of Lorrha and committed him to his safeguard; this was because Ruadhan had two sisters, Cael and Ruadhnait, who had raised Bishop Senach. However, Ruadhan sent Aedh Guaire away to live among the Britons <note>The people of Wales or Cornwall</note>, for because of King Dermot’s wrath, he could not safely remain anywhere in Ireland. Yet such was Dermot’s influence and power over others that, because of him, Aedh ultimately could not remain in either Scotland or with the Britons. Consequently, he returned to Ireland to Ruadhan, who hid him in a chamber underground. The place where Ruadhan was then is the same spot known as *poll Ruadháin* <note>original: "Ruadhan's Pit"</note> today. 

It was told to the king that Aedh Guaire had come to Ireland again and that Ruadhan held him concealed in the earth. Then Dermot traveled to Ruadhan and dispatched his charioteer to seize Aedh Guaire from him by force. The young man entered the sanctuary, but he was instantly struck blind. The king, now furious at this, went to Ruadhan and asked him where Aedh Guaire was (for he knew that Ruadhan would not tell a lie). Ruadhan answered: "Truly, I do not know where he is, unless he is under you, right where you are standing." 

The king then left the sanctuary and at first paid no more attention to what the cleric had said. Afterward, however, he recalled Ruadhan’s words and realized that Aedh Guaire was in the ground directly beneath where he had stood. He ordered one of his people (named Donnan) to go down to Aedh; as he began to dig away the earth over Aedh's head, his arms were suddenly paralyzed. Thereupon, he went to Ruadhan and performed an act of submission to him. The man who had previously been blinded also performed an act of submission, and from then on, they remained with Ruadhan. These are the two men who are today honored as saints at Pollruane <note>original: Poll Ruadháin</note>. 

Then Dermot himself entered the church and pulled Aedh Guaire out of the hole in the ground, which today is called Pollruane. Aedh was brought in chains by the king to Tara, where Dermot intended to have him hanged as punishment for all his schemes.

# Death of King Dermot

With the purpose of taking him with him to retrieve his protégé <note>original: "protégé," referring to Aed Guaire, who had sought sanctuary with the saint</note>, the pair went on to Tara. There they demanded that the king release the man whose safety Ruadhan had guaranteed. However, Dermot answered that the Church had no right to extend immunity to someone who had broken royal law; he argued that doing so was an inherent violation of both human and divine justice.

The clerics then chanted psalms of commination <note>psalms intended to invoke divine vengeance or cursing</note> and rang their bells against the king. That night, at the exact same moment, twelve sons of chiefs who were being raised as wards of the king died in Tara. Their respective guardians came to the clergy and persistently urged them to bring the youths back to life. The saints prayed, and the boys were restored to life.

For a full year after this, they excommunicated <note>original: "anathematised"</note> Dermot and directed miracles against him, while he matched them wonder for wonder. But in the end, they gained no advantage over him until they promised Heaven to the king's house-steward in exchange for a deception. They convinced the steward to tell the king that the clergy had finally broken their fast and shared a meal. The house-steward went to Dermot and told him the clergy were eating, so that in this way—though it was not actually true—they gained a spiritual advantage over him in their fasting contest. 

That night, Dermot had a dream: he saw a great tree in Tara, the top of which reached the clouds of heaven and whose shade covered all of Ireland. He saw fifty foreigners (including two leading strangers) chopping down the tree, but every chip they cut from it was immediately restored. Eventually, they drove him away from the tree and leveled it; it was the crash of the falling tree that woke him. "Even so," Dermot said, "I am the tree. The foreigners chopping it are the clergy cutting short my life, and it is by them that I have fallen."

The next morning, the king rose and went to the place where the clergy were. "You have done an evil thing," he said, "to destroy my kingdom simply because I upheld a righteous cause. At any rate," he continued, "may your diocese be the first one ruined in Ireland, and Ruadhan, may your monks desert you!" 

The saint retorted: "May your kingdom wither quickly!" 

Dermot said: "Your seat of power shall be empty, and swine shall root up your churchyards." 

"Tara shall be desolate," Ruadhan replied, "and no one shall dwell there forever."

The clergy (with their prisoner) started for home toward Pollruane; but first they saw thirty dark-grey horses, of excellent shape, which came out of the sea toward them. These they presented to the king. Their speed was tested against his other horses and they proved to be faster; but the horses then returned to the same form they had held in the sea and went back to the place from which they first came. After this, Dermot and the clergy were at peace.

# Death of King Dermot

One night, while Dermot was sleeping, he saw two men draw near him. One man, he believed, had the appearance of a clergyman; the other appeared to be a layman. They came up to him, took off his royal crown, and made two crowns out of it—each man taking one half, for that is how they divided it between them—and then they departed from him. Dermot started out of his sleep and told his vision.

"Just so," said Beg mac Dé <note>A famous Irish prophet and seer</note> and Cairidh son of Finnchaemh (Dermot’s poet). "We have the interpretation of your dream for you: Your kingdom is decided, your reign has reached its end, and from now on your princely grip on Ireland is cast off. Specifically, there shall now be a division between the Church and the Laity. The partitioning of your royal crown foretells a similar dividing of Ireland’s sovereignty between the Church and the State."

He continued: "A time will come when the Church shall be enslaved by the State, and when the privileges of church lands shall no longer exist; instead, they shall be subject to 'free quartering' <note>The forced housing and feeding of soldiers</note> by everyone. In exchange for this, however, evil shall overtake the State: so that son, father, and kinsman—of whatever degree—shall kill each other, and every man’s weapon shall be red with another’s blood. Because of the treachery of all men, the fruits of the earth shall perish, as well as the nuts of the trees and the produce of the waters."

The Festival of Tara was then held by Dermot. During the actual banquet, Curnan—the son of Aedh, son of Eochaid Tirmcharna, from whom the *descendants of Maeilruain* <note>original: síol Maeilruain</note> in Connacht are descended—killed a man. Curnan placed himself under the protection of Muirchertach mac Erca’s two sons, Fergus and Donall, who in turn placed him under the guarantee of Columbkill <note>Saint Columba</note>. 

The King had Curnan executed to pay for his crime, and the people of Connacht turned against Dermot, accusing him of the wrongful slaughter of their king’s son, Curnan. Dermot proceeded to ravage Connacht and reached *Cúil Sibrinne* near *Cúil Dreimne*. In order to avenge the violation of his guarantee, Columbkill gathered the northern O'Neill clan <note>original: clan-Neill</note>. Along with him, Fergus and Donall (the two sons of Muirchertach mac Erca), Ainmire son of Sedna (King of Kinel-connell), Muiredach mac Duach, and Aedh (son of Eochaid Tirmcharna) marched into Connacht. 

Between the two armies, Frechan son of Tenesan (Dermot’s wizard) set up a "magic barrier." It was then that Columbkill spoke:

> "Why, O God, do You not ward off from us . . . ."

# Death of King Dermot

Dermot went with Banbhan (who had invited him) to Rathbeg. When they had sat down in the house, they saw a graceful young woman enter, wearing exceptionally fine clothing. "Where does this woman come from?" Dermot asked. Banbhan answered: "She is a daughter of mine; and to spite Mughain <note>Dermot's queen</note> because she did not come with me, the girl shall be your wife tonight." "I am well pleased," said the king.

While the food was being prepared, a bed was made for them. When the meal was ready, Banbhan said: "Well, girl, have you brought clothing for the king?" "I have," she said, and handed him a shirt and a mantle, which the king took and put on. "It is a good shirt," everyone remarked. "It is one worthy of you," said Banbhan, "being a shirt made from a single flax-seed. That girl there is quite imaginative; she sowed a single seed of flax and harvested a handful from it, which then grew to fill an entire ridge of land." "It is a good mantle," everyone cried. "It is indeed," said Banbhan, "it is made from the wool of a single sheep."

Then food and drink were served to them, and Banbhan said: "This bacon from a pig that was never farrowed <note>born naturally</note> is good." "How can that be?" asked Dermot. "There were sows with young; they were cut open with knives so that their piglets were extracted while still alive, and then fattened afterward." "It is good ale!" everyone said. "It is indeed," said Banbhan, "ale brewed from a single grain of corn. One day I went out to inspect my plowed land and killed a ringdove; in its crop was found one grain, though we did not know what kind of cereal it was. It was planted in a ridge, however, and its yield was a sickle-full. This was sown again, and this ale is the result of its harvest."

After this, Dermot looked upward and said: "The lower part of the house is new, but its upper-work is not recent." Banbhan answered: "Once upon a time, we went out in <term>currachs</term> <note>traditional Irish boats made of a wicker frame covered in hide</note> to catch fish, and we saw the ridgebeam of a house floating toward us on the sea. ### Birth of Aedh Sláine

Tara of the Kings: she was the private estate belonging to all the kings who successively ruled Ireland. It was a universal custom that all of Ireland's taxes, prescribed dues, and rents had to be brought to the kings there. It was also common for the men of Ireland to travel from all directions <note>original: "airts"</note> to Tara to hold the Feast of Tara at the time of *Samhain* <note>The festival marking the beginning of winter and the new year in the Gaelic calendar.</note>. These were the two principal gatherings they held: the Feast of Tara at every *Samhain* (which was the pagans' equivalent of Easter); and at every *Lughnasa* <note>The harvest festival beginning in August.</note>, or "Lammas-tide," the Convention of *Taillte*. No person was allowed to break any laws or enactments ordained by the men of Ireland during either of these festivals for the entire following year.

# Aedh Sláine

At a regular great convention, the man who was King of Ireland at that time was Dermot, son of Fergus Cerrbeol. The men of Ireland were arranged along the benches of the assembly ground, all of them according to their precedence of rank, their profession, and their legitimate claims—essentially following the established customs and traditions of the past.

Now the women, including the king’s two wives, had a separate seating area. The queens accompanying Dermot on this occasion were Mairenn (surnamed *Mael*, meaning "the bald") and Mughain, daughter of Conchraid, son of Duach (of the men of Munster). Mughain felt a great jealousy toward Mairenn. She told a certain female jester that she could name her own price if she would remove the golden headgear from the other queen’s head. This was because Mairenn was completely bald, and she habitually wore a queen’s headdress to conceal this defect.

The jester approached Mairenn and began to beg her for some gift or favor. The queen declared she had nothing to give. "You shall have this, at any rate!" the jester cried, as she tore the golden helmet from the queen’s head. Mairenn cried out, "May God and Saint Kieran <note>Saint Kieran of Clonmacnoise, a major Irish saint</note> help me in this moment of need!" Before a single person in the crowd could even turn their eyes toward her, a mass of flossy, wavy, golden-shining hair—which grew through Kieran’s miraculous power—fell down to her very shoulders. The entire host was astonished by the miracle and pleased that the queen was not shamed. "I pray to God," cried Mairenn, "that you will be disgraced for this in the presence of the men of Ireland!"—which later came true.

After this, Dermot continued to visit Mughain, but she was barren. This made her unhappy, as the king considered abandoning her entirely. The king's other wives were also a source of grief to her because they bore children: specifically Eithne, daughter of Brenann Dall of the *Conmaicne Cúile Talad* <note>A tribal territory in County Mayo</note> and mother of Colman the Great; and Breo, daughter of Colman mac Neman from *Dún* Suane, mother of Colman the Small. Mughain was deeply saddened by this—both by her lack of a son or daughter and by the king's intention to dismiss her.

For "a golden wand laid across a plate of white bronze"—that is what the descendants of Aedh Sláine are across the plain of Bregia.

## *The Wooing of Becfola.*

It was once upon a time, when Dermot, the son of Aedh Sláine, enjoyed the royal rule of Ireland, that his foster-son Crimthann, son of Aedh, was with him as a hostage from the people of Leinster. One day, he and Crimthann his student, taking with them their various weapons and a single servant boy, went to *Ath Truim* <note>modern: Trim, County Meath</note>. They saw a lone woman in a chariot coming out of the west and across the ford. She was fairer than any other woman in the whole world. Dermot inquired: "Where have you come from, woman?" "Not from far," she answered. "What causes you to be alone?" "I am in search of wheaten grain," she said. "You shall find such with me," said Dermot. "We do not refuse it," said the woman. Thereupon he escorted her to Tara, and she shared his comfortable bed. Everyone in general inquired: "Where is this woman from, Dermot?" "I will not tell," he replied. Everyone said then: "*Bec a fhola*" <note>original: "bec a fhola"; meaning "small is her bride-gift" or "little value"</note>, that is, his bride-gift to her is but small." "Let 그 that be her name," said the magicians, "namely, *Becfola*."

Subsequently, the woman set her love on Crimthann, son of Aedh, the king's pupil, instead of Dermot, and for a long time she persisted in soliciting him. The young man indeed said that at the hour of <term>tierce</term> <note>the third hour of the day, approximately 9:00 AM</note> on Sunday, he would go to *Cluain Dá Chaillech* <note>The Meadow of the Two Nuns</note> to meet her for the purpose of carrying her off secretly; however, his people dissuaded him from eloping with the wife of the King of Ireland.

As soon as he had finished roasting the pig, he washed his hands and went down from the fire to the lake. 

She followed after him. The young man got into his boat, and she went with him. They rowed until they reached a high, pleasant island, and there they entered a vast and beautiful palace where they found no one else. Next, they ate various meats and drank delicious mead. Then the eight fought a manly and vigorous fight, four on each side. He and his three companions defeated the other four, but all of them—except for him alone—fell side by side, lifeless and dead. He then returned to the fort.

Instead, let that gold and silver be used to fashion a reliquary <term>shrine for holy relics</term> and sacred emblems with expert craftsmanship." This was exactly what was done; for from that gold, the Shrine of Molasius and his pastoral staff <term>crosier</term> were made.

The young clerics then told the King that the Queen had been present at the battle and the slaying of the warriors. By this time, the King had finished dressing, and he commanded Becfola to return to Flann, the descendant of Fedach. She rose eagerly and traveled back to Flann, and after that, the two were never parted again.

### *The Disappearance of Caenchomrac*

There was a certain noble bishop in Clonmacnoise named Caenchomrac, whose original name had been Mochta. He was a man of pure character and a <term>coarb</term> <note>original: "coarb"; a Gaelic term for a spiritual successor to a founding saint</note> of God. He came to Cluain <note>Clonmacnoise</note> on a pilgrimage, where he was held in great reverence and consideration. This was because he could learn from God whether those who died from time to time would receive a heavenly reward or suffer torment. Furthermore, he could announce to anyone who desired to know, during the final quarter of the preceding year, the exact year in which they would die. However, he eventually felt that the deference shown to him in Cluain was excessive. Therefore, he went to *Inis Aendaimh* <note>modern: Devenish Island</note> in Lough Ree to continue his pilgrimage, for he considered it a suitably lonely place for performing the canonical hours, the Mass, and his prayers.

A prayerful community of monks lived with him on the island. They used to travel across the mainland to gather alms and firstfruits in Teffia, for the men of Teffia were very devoted to him. They gave him one hundred piglets, a hundred calves, a hundred lambs, a cake of bread from every kneading trough, and a <term>screpall</term> <note>an ancient Irish silver coin or unit of value</note> from every <term>cathair</term> <note>a stone fortress or settlement</note>. They yielded these gifts on the condition that—provided they paid him this tribute—the number of their men killed in any single battle would never exceed nine. As he once said after a battle:

> "I thank my King <note>meaning God</note> that the men of Teffia remain in their land; not one of them has been killed. I declare to you—and this is no false promise of friendship—that if you only call upon my name, your losses in battle shall be no more than nine men."

He added: "Furthermore, even if those who attack you are many and you are but few, if you only think of me, you shall return home safely:

> "Though nine men in the land of Teffia face a hundred thousand thousands, let them only meditate on Caenchomrac, and they shall return to their own countries safe and sound. The armies of this world shall not achieve victory over them—provided they render me their service, just as my service is directed toward God."

For a while, then, he remained in both Cluain and the island...

Caenchomrac answered, "I will go."

On the next morning, he returned to his house, completely covered in lake-weed <note>original: "lacustrine wrack"</note>. He made a frequent practice of visiting the areas beneath the lake; from that time forward, as long as he lived, the monastery was never hidden from him.

### *Here is the Panegyric of Conn's son Cormac and the Death of Finn son of Cumhall.*

There was a monarch, noble and honorable, who attained the rule of Ireland: Cormac, son of Art, son of Conn of the Hundred Battles. Subsequently, he reigned over her for forty years, excepting the two years during which Ulster usurped the throne: that is to say, Fergus Black-knee for one year, and Eochaid Gonnat for another. Twice, in fact, the Ulidians <note>The people of Ulster</note> deposed Cormac. This same Cormac was also missing from among his people for four months; until he himself came back and told of his adventures, it was not known in what direction he had gone.

To proceed: except for David's son Solomon, there never was a king in the world who could be compared to Cormac for the brilliance of his intellect or the wealth of his reign. For he never gave a judgment unless he had the three judicial requisites: a mind gifted with sagacity, judicial precedent, and...

# Cormac and Finn

As a result of the wisdom and knowledge of these judgments, it was said that in Cormac's time, calves were commonly born after only three months' gestation. In his day, a sack of wheat was produced from every ridge of land; in his day, the *colpach*-heifers <note>original: "colpach"; a young heifer or bullock, usually in its second year</note> were already fully grown, calved cows. In any river that was only knee-deep, a salmon was caught in every single mesh of the net. In his time, every cow had an udder full of colostrum <note>original: "biestings"; the first milk produced after giving birth, rich in nutrients</note>. In his time, men could gather honey with their fingertips <insert>as they walked</insert>, because it rained down from Heaven due to the righteousness of Cormac's governance. In his time, enough vessels could not be found to hold all the milk, for the cattle produced milk without ceasing.

That king was also comparable to Octavius Augustus: for just as everyone paid the Caesarian (that is, imperial) tribute to Augustus for their paternal inheritance, so too did all men pay the royal rent to Cormac from their own districts; for Cormac never deprived anyone of what rightfully belonged to them.

In all the world, there was no king like Cormac. He excelled in form, figure, and clothing; in stature, justice, and equity. This was true even of his eyes, in each of which were seven pupils, as Senuath the poet tells us when he says:

> "Beautiful was the difference between that variegated pair of eyes: for in the man's head, fourteen pupils existed."

He was the most vigorous man of his time in terms of sagacity, wisdom, eloquence, action, and valor; in royal influence, domination, splendor, ambition, ethics, and lineage. He made Ireland into a "land of promise." At that time, the country was free from theft, robbery, and violence. It was exempt from the need for constant watching or herding, and no man suffered any anxiety regarding food or clothing.

But <insert>what we have said</insert> in praise of Cormac is far too little; for unless an angel were to instruct him, a man could not declare it all. Great were his power and control over the men of Ireland, seeing that—unless they were performing military service for Cormac—none of them dared to remain idle.

Now, the man whom Cormac appointed as his chief of the household and his paid master of the hounds was Finn, son of Cumhall <note>Finn mac Cumhaill, the legendary leader of the Fianna</note>; for the finest leader the King of Ireland had was always his master of the hounds.

# Cormac and Finn

A warrior better than Finn never struck his hand into a chief's. In terms of service, he was a soldier; in hospitality, he was a host; and in heroism, he was a hero. In his duties in battle, he was a fighting man, and in strength, he was a champion worthy of a king. Ever since that time, and until this day, every such great man is compared to Finn. Besides all this, Finn and the king's special bands <note>The Fianna, the elite standing army of ancient Ireland</note> enjoyed the general right to hunt and pursue game throughout all of Ireland.

Finn lived mostly in *Almha* <note>modern: Allen</note> in Leinster. However, when the weakness of old age weighed on him (King Cormac also being dead by then), he lived in *Almha* permanently, unless he had a reason to make a brief trip away from it. Finn's wife was Smirgat, the daughter of Fatha Canann. She was a prophetess and a wise woman, and she had told him that whenever he should drink from a horn, that act would end his life. Because of this, he never again drank from a horn, but used *cuachs* <note>original: "cuachs" [Scottish: "quaighs"]; shallow, two-handled drinking bowls</note> instead.

One day, Finn set out from *Almha* and eventually found himself in the place called *Adharca Iuchbadh* in Offaly. There, on a hillside, he came upon a well and took a drink from it. He then put his thumb under his "knowledge-tooth" <note>A legendary ritual where Finn gained prophetic insight by sucking his thumb</note> and performed the incantation of *teinm laeghda* <note>original: "teinm laeghda"; a traditional Irish mantic or prophetic ritual</note>, through which it was revealed to him that the end of his time and his life had come. He then sang these following verses:

->The prophecy has befallen Finn . . .<-

Then he traveled on until he reached *Druim Bregh* <note>original: "druim Bregh"; the Ridge of Bregia in County Meath</note>. In that country, there were many reasons for people to hate Finn and the Fianna; for it was by Finn's hand that Uirgrenn, of the tribe called the *Luaighne* of Tara, had once fallen. These people now gathered together, including Uirgrenn's three sons and Aichlech the Great—the son of Duibrenn, who was the third of Uirgrenn's sons. Between them, an extraordinary and ruthless battle was fought—manly, fierce, and violent—in which every person remembered their grievances against one another, whether they were old grudges or more recent injuries. This battle took place at *Brea* upon the River Boyne. They fought hand-to-hand for a long time, until both sides had suffered many casualties. The battle was won against Finn, and he perished in it. It was by Aichlech, the son of Duibrenn, that—

# Finn's People

Finn fell, and it was he <note>referring to a specific warrior mentioned in the preceding text</note> who beheaded him. Therefore, to commemorate the deed and to lead the unlearned toward knowledge, the <term>sennachie</term> <note>original: "sennachie"; a traditional Gaelic historian or storyteller</note> sang these verses:

> *Brea's great battle of bright exploits . . .*

This, then, according to archaeological truth and as the experts relate it, is the manner of Finn's death. However, they give various accounts of his origin. Some say that he was of the *Corca-Oiche* in *Ua Fidhgeinte*; others assert (and this is the truth of the matter) that he was of the *Ui Tairrsigh* of Offaly, who were of the Attacotti, as Maelmura said in the chronicle: "There are six stocks that shall have territorial settlements but are not of Breogan's people, namely: the *Garbraighe* of the *Suca*; the *Ui Tairrsigh*; the *Galeoin* of Leinster [and others]."

The people of Leinster, however, state that Finn was the great-grandson of Nuada Necht, and that his pedigree is as follows: Finn, son of Cumhall, son of Sualtach, son of Baeiscne, son of Nuada Necht.

## The Enumeration of Finn's People

This is the enumeration and description of Finn's people. Their strength consisted of seven score and ten officers <note>150 officers</note>, each of whom commanded twenty-seven warriors. Every one of these was bound to certain conditions of service (just as Cuchulainn was in his time). These conditions were:
*   That they must not accept material compensation <note>original: "eric" or blood-money</note> for the violation of their honor or guarantees.
*   That they must never deny any person a request for valuables or food.
*   That no single individual among them should flee before nine enemy warriors.

No man was accepted into the <term>Fianna</term> <note>original: "Fianna"; the semi-independent warrior bands of ancient Ireland</note>, nor admitted to the great Gathering of Usnach, the Convention of Taillte, or the Feast of Tara, until both his paternal and maternal relatives, his <term>tuatha</term> <note>original: "tuatha"; tribes or people-groups</note> and kindreds, had given legal securities for him. These securities guaranteed that even if the man were killed, his family would urge no claim for compensation. This was required so that the warriors would look to no one for protection or redress but to themselves alone.

# Finn's People

<margin>The laws of the Fianna</margin>
The community should look to avenge them. On the other hand, if it were they who inflicted great mischief upon others, reprisals were not to be made upon their respective people.

Of all these candidates, not a man was accepted until he was a prime poet, well-versed in the twelve books of poesy <note>original: "poesy"; refers to the traditional Irish poetic arts required of a warrior-elite</note>. No man was accepted until a large hole had been made in the ground (deep enough to reach the waist-fold of his belt) and he was placed into it with his shield and a hazel stick the length of a forearm. Then, nine warriors with nine spears, standing ten furrows' width away from him, would assail him and let fly their spears at him all at once. If he were wounded despite his guard, he was not received into <term>Fianship</term> <note>The status or profession of being a member of the Fianna</note>.

Not a man of them was accepted until his hair had been interwoven into braids and he started at a run through the woods of Ireland. While he ran, the others followed in his wake seeking to wound him, with only the distance of a single forest bough between them at the start. Should he be overtaken, he was wounded and not received into the <term>Fianna</term> <note>The legendary semi-independent bands of warriors in Irish mythology</note> afterward. If his weapons had quivered in his hand, he was not accepted. Should a branch in the wood have disturbed any of his hair out of its braiding, he was not accepted. If he had cracked a dry stick under his foot as he ran, he was not accepted. Unless, at his full speed, he had both jumped over a stick level with his brow and stooped to pass under one level with his knee, he was not accepted. Also, unless he could extract a thorn from his foot with his fingernail without slackening his pace, he was not taken into <term>Fianship</term>. But if he performed all this, he was one of Finn's people.

He who led those <term>Fianna</term> was a good man indeed, for he was the seventh king ruling Ireland. That is to say, there were five kings of the provinces and the High King of Ireland; he himself was the seventh, ruling in conjunction with the High King of all Ireland.

Finn's two head-guards <note>original: "poll-wards"; guardians of the head or perhaps personal bodyguards</note> were Noenalach and Raer, grandson of Garb. The two stewards of his hounds were Crimthann and Connla Cas. His dispenser was Cathluan, son of Crimthann. His master of the banquet was Corc, son of Suan. His three cupbearers were Dermot, grandson of Duibhne; Faillin; and Colla, son of Caeilte. The two overseers of his hearth were Caeilte and Glanna. His two bed-makers were Admoll and Mac Neri. His twelve musicians were Fergus True-mouth, Fianu, Bran, the two Reidhes, Nuada, Aithirne Aghmar, and... Flann, Aedh, and Cobthach of...

## The Colloquy with the Ancients.
<note>original: "Acallam na Senórach." This is a famous Middle Irish narrative where the last survivors of the Fianna meet Saint Patrick and recount the legends of Ireland's landscape.</note>

When the battle of Comar, the battle of Gowra, and the battle of Ollarba had been fought, and after the <term>Fianna</term><note>The Fianna were semi-independent bands of warriors in Irish mythology, led most famously by Finn mac Cumhaill.</note> were for the most part extinguished, the survivors had dispersed in small bands and companies throughout all Ireland. At the point in time which concerns us, there remained only two good warriors of the last of the Fianna: Ossian son of Finn, and Caeilte son of Crunnchu son of Ronan (whose youthful vigor and power of spear-throwing were now diminished), along with enough fighting men to make eighteen in total. These eighteen came out of the flowery-soiled, wooded borders of Slievefuad <margin>County Armagh</margin> and into the *white gardens*, at this present called Louth. There, at the falling of the evening clouds that night, they were melancholy and dispirited.

Caeilte then said to Ossian: “Well now, Ossian, before the day ends, what path shall we take to find lodging for the night?” 

Ossian answered: “I do not know, seeing that of the elders of the Fianna and of Finn’s people, only three survive: I and yourself, Caeilte, along with *Cámha*, the female chief and guardian. From the time he was a boy until the day he died, she kept Finn son of Cumall safe.” 

Caeilte said: “We are entitled to this night’s lodging and food from her; for it is impossible to describe or show the great amount of wealth and goods she received from Finn and the Fianna.”
