# The Colloquy

Finn, captain of the Fianna <note>The legendary band of Irish warriors</note>, bestowed on her many precious things and treasures, including the third best valuable item that Finn ever acquired: namely, the *Anghalach*, a drinking-horn which Moriath, daughter of the King of Greece, gave to Finn, and Finn in turn gave to Camha.

With Camha, therefore, they received hospitality for that night. She asked them for their names and, at the sound of them, wept vehement showers of tears; then she and they sought news from one another. Next, they entered the guest house prepared for them, and Camha, the female chief, ordered their meal: she commanded that the freshest of all kinds of meat and the oldest of all sorts of drink be given to them, for she knew the manner in which men like them were accustomed to be fed. She also knew exactly how much had, many times before, constituted a sufficient portion for Ossian and for Caeilte. Languidly and feebly she arose and spoke at length about the Fianna and about Finn mac Cumall; she also spoke of Ossian’s son, Oscar, of *Mac Lugach*, of the Battle of Gowra <note>The catastrophic final battle of the Fianna</note>, and other matters. Because of this, a great silence eventually settled over them all.

Then Caeilte said: "We find such memories no more painful than the fact that we—the eighteen of us who remain of that great and noble fellowship—must now by necessity part and go our separate ways." Ossian answered him: "Now that they are gone, I swear by my word that there is truly no more fight or strength left in me." Valiant as these warriors were, they nevertheless wept in gloom, sadness, and dejection there with the female chief, Camha. Their full allowance of food and drink was given to them; they stayed there for three days and three nights, then bade Camha farewell, and Ossian said:

> "Camha today is sorrowful: she has reached the point where she must struggle to stay afloat; Camha is without either son or grandson: it has befallen her to be old and withered."

They came out of the town then and onto the green. There they made a resolution, which was this: to separate. This parting of theirs felt like the sundering of soul from body. And so they did: Ossian went to the *sidhe* <note>original: *sídh*; a fairy mound or otherworldly dwelling</note> of *Ucht Cleitigh*, where his mother lived: Blái, daughter of Derc, surnamed *Dianscothach* <note>original: *dianscothach*; meaning 'of the forcible language' or 'eloquent'</note>; while Caeilte took his way to *Inbher Bic Loingsigh*, which is currently called *Mainistir Droichid* <note>The Monastery of the Bridge, likely Mellifont Abbey</note>.

# The Colloquy

*Átha* <note>original: "the Monastery of Drogheda"</note> was named after *Beg Loingsech*, the son of Arist, who was drowned there. He was the son of the King of the Romans who came to invade Ireland, but a tidal wave drowned him there in his *inbher* <term>inver: an Old Irish term for an estuary or river mouth</term>. Caeilte then went on to *Linn Féic* <note>Fiac’s Pool</note> on the bright-streaming River Boyne, southwards over the Old Plain of Bregia, and finally to the earthen fort of Drumderg where Patrick, son of Calpurn, was staying.

Just then, Patrick chanted the Lord’s order of the canon <note>the Mass</note>, praised the Creator, and pronounced a blessing on the fort where Finn mac Cumall <note>the legendary leader of the Fianna</note> had once lived: the fort of Drumderg. The clerics saw Caeilte and his band drawing near to them. Fear fell upon the priests at the sight of these tall men accompanied by their huge wolf-dogs, for they were not people of the same era or time as the clergy.

Then Heaven’s distinguished one, that pillar of dignity and angel on earth—Patrick, son of Calpurn and apostle of the Irish—rose and took the *aspergillum* <term>a brush or branch used for sprinkling holy water</term> to sprinkle holy water on the great men. Floating over them until that day there had been a thousand legions of demons. Into the hills and "skalps" <note>rocky clefts or caves</note>, and into the outer borders of the region and the country, the demons immediately fled in all directions. After this, the enormous men sat down.

"Tell me now," Patrick said to Caeilte, "what is your name?" 

"I am Caeilte, son of Crunnchu, son of Ronan." 

For a long while, the clergy marveled greatly as they gazed at them; for the tallest man among the clergy reached only to the waist, or perhaps the shoulder, of the visitors even while the giants were sitting down. 

Patrick spoke again: "Caeilte, I desire to ask a favor of you." 

He answered: "If I have the strength or power, you shall have it; in any case, please name it." 

"I wish to have a well of pure water nearby, from which we might baptize the *tuatha* <term>tribes or people-groups</term> of Bregia, Meath, and Usnach." 

"Noble and righteous one," said Caeilte, "I have that for you." 

Crossing the fort's ramparts, they came outside. Caeilte took Patrick’s hand, and in a short time, they saw a spring-well right in front of them, sparkling and clear. The size and thickness of the watercress and the *fothlacht* <note>brooklime, a medicinal water plant</note> growing in it was a wonder to them. Then Caeilte began to describe its fame and qualities, saying:

> "If only the brown leaf shed by the wood were gold—if only the white wave were silver—Finn would have given it all away."

> "Finn had three hundred and twelve drinking-horns made of gold; whenever they were filled for the pouring, the quantity of liquor they held was immense."

"If it were not a distraction from the devout life, an occasion for neglecting prayer, and for abandoning our conversation with God, we would feel the time pass quickly as we talked with you, warrior." > "It was like counting branches on a tree to number Finn's full-grown hounds and his sleek, melodious pack of young dogs: there were three hundred of the first, and two hundred puppies."

...without a whitened shield, nor a right fist that did not grasp two great and lengthy spears. At that moment, Goll son of Morna <note>Goll mac Morna: a leader of the Connacht Fianna and sometimes a rival to Finn</note>, looking about him, saw an iron-grey horse, flecked with spots and wearing a bridle decorated with wrought gold. With another glance to his left, he spotted a bay horse—one not easy to catch—which had a woven bridle of double-refined silver and a golden bit. Goll son of Morna seized this second horse as well and placed it in the hand of Ossian <note>Finn's son and a famous poet-warrior</note>, who passed it on to Dermot *grandson of Duibhne* <note>Dermot ua Duibhne: the famous lover and warrior of the Fianna</note>. We returned to where Finn was: in the old *Plain of the Flocks* <note>original: magh nelta; modern: Moynalty</note> at Edar. We reached his tent, and Caeilte said, "We have brought Arthur." Arthur entered into a bond of service with Finn and remained Finn’s follower until the day he died. 

<margin>The origin of horses in the Fianna.</margin>
We gave the two horses to Finn: a stallion and a mare. From their offspring came all the horses of the Fianna, who until that time had not used any. The mare gave birth eight times, producing eight foals at each birth. These were distributed among the various detachments and noblemen of the Fianna, who subsequently had chariots built for them.

"Success and a blessing be upon you, Caeilte," said Patrick, "now tell us the names of the chiefs and mighty men who owned those horses." Then Caeilte, telling the story, said:

"Success and a blessing, Caeilte! All of this is a recreation for our spirits and minds—if only it were not a distraction from our devotion and a neglect of our prayers."

They remained there until the following morning, when Patrick dressed in his robes and went out onto the green, accompanied by his sixty priests, sixty psalm-singers, and holy bishops.

There were sixty others as well who, along with him, disseminated faith and piety throughout Ireland. Patrick’s two guardian angels came to him now: *Aibellán* and *Solusbrethach*. He asked them whether, in God’s sight, it was appropriate for him to be listening to the stories of the Fianna <note>The Fianna were a legendary band of warriors in Irish mythology, led by Finn Mac Cumhaill</note>. With equal emphasis and in total agreement, the angels answered him: “Holy cleric, those ancient warriors tell no more than a third of their stories because of forgetfulness and a lack of memory. However, let these stories—such as they are—be written by you on the writing tablets of poets and in the words of *ollaves* <note>term: ollaves; high-ranking learned men or master poets in ancient Ireland</note>; for it will be a pastime for the companies and nobles of future times to listen to these stories.” Having said this, the angels departed.

Messengers were then dispatched from Patrick to fetch Caeilte. He, along with the nine companions who made up his group, was brought to the saint. Their names were these: Failbhe son of Flann; Eoghan Red-weapon, the son of the king of Ulidia <note>modern: Ulster</note>; Flann, son of Fergus, king of Kinelconnell; Conall the Slaughterer, son of Angus, king of Connacht; Scannlan, son of Ailell, king of Ossory; Baedan, son of Garb, king of Corcaguiney; Luaimnech Linn, son of the king of the *Erna* of Munster; Failbhe and Uainchenn, the sons of the king of Dalaradia from the north; and Fulartach, son of Finghin, king of the *tuatha* <note>term: tuatha; territories or tribal lands</note> of Bregia and of Meath.

Patrick said: “Do you know why you have been brought to speak with me?” 

“In truth, we do not know,” they answered. 

“So that you should show obedience and conform to the gospel of the King of Heaven and Earth: the True and most Glorious God.” Then and there, the water of Christ’s Baptism was sprinkled on them by Patrick, as a preparation for the baptism and conversion of all Ireland.

Then, with his right hand, Caeilte reached across himself to the rim of his shield and gave Patrick a ridged mass of gold taken from there, which contained one hundred and fifty ounces. This was a fee for the baptism of the nine men with him. He said: “That was the last wage given to me by Finn, the chief; and Patrick, you shall have it for the sake of my soul’s health and the soul of my commander.” The size of this mass of gold reached from Patrick’s middle fingertip to the highest point of his shoulder, while in width and thickness it measured a man’s cubit <note>A cubit is an ancient measurement roughly the length of a forearm</note>. This gold was then bestowed upon the *Táilchenn*’s <note>term: Táilchenn; "Adze-head," an archaic Irish nickname for Saint Patrick, referring to his tonsure</note> canonical hand-bells, on psalters, and on missals <note>A missal is a book containing the texts for the celebration of the Mass</note>.

Patrick said again: “It is well, Caeilte; what was the best...”

"...hunting that the Fianna <note>The Fianna were a legendary band of semi-independent warriors in early Ireland</note> ever had, whether in Ireland or in Scotland?" "The hunting of Arran." > "Arran of the many stags—the sea beats against her very shoulders! An island where whole companies were fed—and with ridges where blue spears are stained red in battle! Skittish deer are on her peaks, soft blackberries on her waving heather; there is cool water in her rivers, and acorns upon her reddish oaks! Greyhounds were there, and beagles; blueberries and sloes <note>The small, sour fruit of the blackthorn</note> of the dark blackthorn; houses were built with their backs against her woods, and the deer grazed scattered by her oak thickets! Her level ground was smooth—her wild swines were fat; her fields were cheerful (this is a story that can be believed), her nuts hung on the boughs of the forest hazels, and long ships sailed past her! Their condition was truly pleasant when the fair weather set in: trout lie under the banks of her rivers; the seagulls circling her grand cliffs answer one another—at every season, Arran is delightful!"

To Mac Lugach then the chief <note>Finn mac Cumhaill</note> gave counsel, and his counsel had great virtue in it, and remained lastingly with Mac Lugach; and Finn said:

"Mac Lugach! If armed service is your design, be quiet in a great man’s household, but be formidable in the rugged mountain pass. Do not beat your hound without a fault of its own; do not bring a charge against your wife until you ascertain her guilt; in battle, do not meddle with a buffoon, for, O Mac Lugach, he is but a fool. Do not censure anyone if he is of grave repute; do not stand up to take part in a brawl; neither have anything at all to do with either a madman or a wicked one. 

Show two-thirds of your gentleness to women and to those who creep on the floor <note>i.e., little children</note>, likewise to men of art who compose the poems <note>original: "duans"</note>; and do not be violent toward the common people. With your close friends, and those who are of your counsel, do not hasten to be the first into bed; shun perverse alliances and all that is prohibited; do not yield your reverence to everyone. 

Do not utter swaggering speech, nor say that you will not provide what is right; for it is a shameful thing to speak too stiffly unless it is feasible to carry out your words. So long as you exist in the universe, do not forsake your lord; neither for gold nor for any other valuable in the earthly world abandon your guarantee <note>original: "guarantee"; referring to one who has placed himself under your protection</note>. 

To a chief, do not utter strenuous criticism of his people; for it is not a gentleman’s occupation to abuse a great lord’s people to their chief. Do not be a continually tattling tale-bearer, nor a false one; do not be loquacious, nor rashly censorious; no matter how many chivalrous qualities you possess, do not let the assemblies <note>original: "Irachts"; tribal gatherings or districts</note> be hostilely inclined toward you. 

Do not be a frequenter of the drinking-house, nor given to mocking an elderly man; the conduct you hear recommended, that is what is appropriate <note>original: "τὸ πρέπον"</note>: do not meddle with a man of mean estate. Do not make a habit of refusing to share your food, and do not have any penurious person as a close friend; do not force yourself upon a chief, nor give a chief lord occasion to speak ill of you. Stick to your clothing, hold fast to your armor, until the stern fight with its glittering weapons is well ended; never renounce your luck, yet follow after gentleness, Mac Lugach!"

"Success and benediction!" said Patrick. "It is a good story that you have told us there; and where is Brogan the scribe?" 

Brogan answered, "Here, holy Cleric." 

"Let that tale be written by you"; and Brogan performed the task on the spot.

Then Patrick questioned Caeilte: "Did you have musicians among the Fianna?" 

And he answered, "We did indeed, the finest musician that was in either Ireland or Scotland." 

"What was his name?" 

"*Cnú dheireoil*" <note>meaning "diminutive nut"</note>. 

"Where was he found?" 

"Between the Harps of Cliu <note>original: "crota cliach"</note> and the Mound of the Fair-Haired Women <note>original: "sídh na mban fionn"; anglicized as Slievenaman</note>..."

The chief <note>Finn mac Cumhaill</note> said that he would bestow both gold and silver on anyone in Ireland who could discover such a thing: a woman who was his dwarf’s counterpart. *Scí mac Eoghain*—a warrior with the nature of a lion—spoke up: "I will name a place (and my story is full of good fortune) where there is one who shall match him exactly."

In all haste then, we and the chief of the Fianna—who was skilled in the use of all bladed weapons—took our journey to "Donn’s House" to seek the woman; a journey that greatly raised our spirits. We found Bláthnait within the *sídh* <note>original: 'sídh'; a fairy mound or hollow hill</note> and truly brought her away. Then, in the great house yonder, Bláthnait and *Cnú Deireoil* <note>meaning 'Little Nut'; Finn's beloved dwarf musician</note> slept as man and wife. Every man of us among the Fianna gave an ounce of gold as a dowry for the blameless woman who was given to the dwarf. 

The man’s stature was four fists high, I say, and his smooth white harp was three fists; the wife was taller than the husband, and they made a lovely, white-handed couple! The wife possessed all the mysteries of the embroidering art, with the skill to work both silver and gold. The man’s gift—and it was a stupendous one—was to delight the crowds of the whole world at once with his minstrelsy. Among the Fianna, there was not a queen, a leader, nor a wise chief who did not give their love and various precious gifts to the couple, who were so childlike in size. 

Whenever hard, foul weather came upon the Fianna, Finn—a man of kingly mind—would keep them both under his mantle: Bláthnait and the little man. When good fortune was coming to the Fianna, Bláthnait would wisely reveal it; and when evil awaited them, the dwarf would not hide it from them. There is no melody on Earth that a man’s soul might desire that did not seem insignificant in the banquet hall compared to the music *Cnú Deireoil* used to make. These were the three best windfalls that Finn, the most generous chief of the Fianna, ever received: his faultless deerhounds, Bran and Sceolan, and Bláthnait together with the dwarf.

After this, it was not long before they saw seven tall young men coming toward them. Patrick asked, "Where do you come from, young men, and who are you?" 

"We have come from *Eoghan Lethderg*, son of Angus and king of both provinces of Munster, to fetch you, holy Patrick." 

The saint said, "We will indeed go there; for wherever gifts and support may be found, it is a duty to accept them." 

"And what shall we nine warriors do?" asked Caeilte. 

"You have a welcome to stay with me for a month, a quarter, and a year," Patrick replied.

We used to gain some eminence in a level land, and there we would have beautiful blackberries, haws of the hawthorn, and nuts from the hazels of Kintyre. We ate tender twigs of the thorny bramble-bush and sprigs of the beneficial gentian; and every Beltane <note>The Gaelic May Day festival marking the beginning of summer.</note> we used to consume both the smooth shoots and the heads of the watercress. Birds from trackless oaken woods would find their way into the Fianna's <note>The legendary band of warriors led by Finn mac Cumhaill.</note> cooking pit; we had multi-colored squirrels from Berramain and variegated nests from mountain pinnacles. 

We caught rapid salmon out of *Linnmhuine*, eels from the noble Shannon, woodcocks from Fidhrinn, and otters out of the hidden places of the River Deel. Truly, a great calamity occurred on the last day of the battle: namely, the drowning of Cael. There were other creatures of the animal kind that had lives of equal length to his—that is, they perished at the same time. When he drowned, the outer swell of the sea washed him ashore. The women and the nobles of the Fianna came to find him; they raised him up and carried him to the southern shore (that is, to the south of Ventry), so that the shore has been called <term>trágh Chaeil</term> or “Cael’s Strand” ever since, and his burial place <term>fert Chaeil</term> or “Cael’s Grave.”

A sorrowful melody, and oh, a melody of sorrow, is that which the heavy surge of Tullachleish emits! As for me: the calamity that has fallen upon me has shattered me; for me, happiness exists no more. Since the son of Crimthann is now drowned, there is no one left in existence for me to love; many a chief fell by his hand, and in battle, his shield never cried out in retreat!”

“Then the young woman stretched herself out by Cael’s side and died of grief because he was gone. They were both buried there in the same grave; and it was I myself who raised the stone that stands over their resting place, which is why it is called ‘the tomb of Cael and of Credhe.’”

# The Colloquy

<margin>A description of the warriors' equipment.</margin>
They arrived with shields locked together, carrying at their shoulders a virtual forest of lofty spears with gold sockets. Some of them entered the tent where Patrick was staying. Their leader laid his head in the saint's lap while the others knelt before him in respect. Patrick asked, "Who are you, young man?" He answered, "I am Bran, son of Derg, King of Munster." Patrick continued, "Why have you come here?" "It is the art and discipline of the Fianna <note>original: "Fianry"; the lifestyle and military training of the ancient Irish warrior bands</note> that I am eager to learn, holy cleric. I have heard that in your company is a warrior of Finn’s people, and I desire to study the *war-cry of the Fianna* <note>original: "dord fiansa"; a rhythmic, low-toned musical chant or war-cry used by the Fianna</note> with him."

"Caeilte, my soul, you hear that," said Patrick. "I hear it," Caeilte replied. "Now then, Bran, how do you usually manage a hunt?" Bran answered, "We surround some hill <note>original: "tulach"</note>, cairn, or mountain woods rising from a plain, and we pursue the game there for the entire day. Sometimes we kill a deer; other times he escapes us." In Patrick’s presence, Caeilte wept then, tearfully and in such sadness that his very breast and chest were wet.

Then Patrick and Caeilte, along with their entire company, went up to *Cenn Febhrat* <note>a mountain pass in the Ballyhoura Mountains</note> of Slieveriach. The layout of the particular spot they reached was this: there were three glens around the mountain and a lake between them called *Loch Bó* ("Lake of the Cow"). The mountain itself was named *Osmetal*. 

Caeilte said: "West of the lake is *Cnoc na Haeire*, and *Finninis* is the name of the easternmost hill. But the name of this hill is *Cnoc Máine*. Here lived a famous, cunning stag called *Liath na dTrí mBenn*, or 'The Grey One of the Three Antlers.' For twenty-seven years, he had eluded the Fianna, both men and deerhounds alike. Eventually, a warrior of the Fianna killed him—and I am that warrior."

Caeilte rose then. He stationed his people to the east, west, south, and north of the lake. Patrick sat down, which is why that place in *Cenn Febhrat* of Slieveriach is called *Suidhe Pátraic*, or 'Patrick’s Seat.' Then Caeilte raised his waving signal for the chase and for the hunt in the manner of the Fianna. He let out three mighty and terrifying whoops. Because of this, there was not a single free-roaming stag nearby—whether on the plain, the moor, the mountain, or in the woods—that did not come running at headlong speed. To cool themselves after their race, they all plunged into the water.

# The Colloquy

Before the hunters' faces, the animals fled into the great Lake of the Cow <note>original: *loch bó*</note>. At that rushing noise and mighty resonance, horror, fear, and apprehension seized the men. I speak of the wild stags, the frenzied roe deer, and the heavy-sided boars; they were so exhausted by the length of the chase and the distress of their breathing that they nearly all perished on the spot. The huntsmen spread themselves around the lake, and not a single beast from the quarry escaped alive. They divided the fruits of the chase, with eight hundred head of game to be apportioned. Benignus <note>A disciple of Saint Patrick</note> said, "Let a tithe <note>A tenth part</note> of the hunt be given to us." But Bran mac Derg was not at all pleased to share what had fallen to his own portion—that is, the proceeds of the hunt he had started and his men had carried out.

At this, an inward disorder <note>likely a digestive ailment or flux</note> seized the son of the King of Munster, who cried out, "Holy cleric, lay your hand on this!" Caeilte said, "By my word, he shall not go to help you until you pay the fee." Bran asked, "What fee?" Caeilte replied, "Since the ailment is in your stomach, let the belly of every cow, every swine, and every sheep slaughtered in your country be yielded by you to Patrick for the Church’s use forever." Bran said, "I will grant that, and my son shall do so after me." From that time forward, this became a continuous practice throughout all Ireland. Then Patrick placed his hand on Bran mac Derg’s stomach, and he was healed instantly.

"We must be going now," Caeilte said. Patrick asked, "And which way is that?" Caeilte replied, "I remember, saintly Patrick, that for fear of the *Tuatha Dé Danann* <note>The 'People of the Goddess Danu,' a supernatural race in Irish mythology</note>, no crowd or host dared to sit upon these three mounds <note>original: *tulachs*</note>."

> "Three mounds I bear in mind that do not age or fade away, over which the 'Grey One of Three Antlers' used to run from one border to the other. When we had to cross the glen, we never halted. When Finn the Fian-chief was alive, he would not endure the sound of a flighty young buck with sprouting horns belling over his spacious camp. I and Flann, son of Failbhe, used to 'redden' <note>To draw blood or wound</note> many heroes of the men of Leinster; I affirm on my conscience that I remember many a battle."

# The Colloquy

And so the company, laden with the spoils of the hunt, departed.

With a look that Caeilte cast around the mountain on his left hand, he saw a fort—a beautiful town. He said, "On my conscience, we never knew a fort to exist over there; let us go toward the town."

They made their way to the dwelling accordingly, but it was a wonder to them that they saw neither a crowd nor a throng there. Instead, they found only nine female slaves and three male slaves. They entered a private chamber apart from the rest of the town, where they found two women weeping and mourning. Here, Caeilte and his men were fed and cared for; their traveling and wayfaring gear was taken from them, and Caeilte asked the women what fort this might be. 

"It belongs to the two sons of the Chief of Fermoy," they replied. "Their names are Lochan and Eoghan." 

"And why are you so gloomy and melancholy?" 

"We have good cause," they said. "We are two sisters married to two brothers. Our husbands have gone tonight to bring home other wives. Therefore, our time in this fort lasts only until our husbands return with their new brides."

With a glance that Caeilte threw around him into the inner part of the fort, he noticed a huge mass of stone. This stone had once belonged to Senach mac Maeilchró, a trusted warrior and one of Finn mac Cumall’s <note>Finn mac Cumall: The legendary leader of the Fianna; Caeilte’s former commander.</note> original people. This stone was significant because all the wages Finn had ever given to Senach—one hundred and fifty ounces of gold, one hundred and fifty ounces of silver, and one hundred and fifty ounces of white bronze <note>original: "findruine"; a precious alloy of copper and tin or silver used in ancient Irish metalwork.</note>—were sealed up tightly beneath it.

Caeilte then said to the women, "If I were to help and relieve you, and bring your husbands back to you, what payment would you give me?" 

They replied, "If we had anything in the whole world that would please you, we would give it to you." 

"Truly, you have such a thing," Caeilte said. "That vast lump of stone at the far side of the fort." 

"Alas that you should say so!" they cried. "For it took the multitude of the entire country to move it to where it sits, and setting it properly took all their effort. Yet you seem to think you can manage it alone!" 

"It is I who will be proven wrong," said Caeilte, "if I am not able to do it." 

"Then it is granted from us to you, and with our blessing," said the women.

They passed *Ráth Ghlais*, which men now call *Ráth Brénainn* <note>Brendan’s Fort</note>. There, the King of Connacht’s tent was pitched. Then Muiredach mac Finnachta questioned Caeilte: "Why is the name *Ráth Ghlais* <note>The Fort of Glas</note> applied to this place?" 

"I will tell you," Caeilte said. "It was Glas, son of Drecan, King of Lochlann <note>The Gaelic term for Scandinavia, particularly Norway</note>, who came with a force of twenty-five battalions to win the royal power of Ireland. The place where they arrived was the stone fort of *Damh Dilenn*, now called *Dún Rosarach*. At that particular time, Finn mac Cumall was in *Almha* <note>The Hill of Allen</note> in Leinster." 

Here, Muiredach asked Caeilte: "Why was that place named *Almha*?" 

Caeilte replied: "There was a warrior of the *Tuatha Dé Danann* <note>The "People of the Goddess Danu," a supernatural race in Irish mythology</note> who lived in the teeming, glittering *Brugh* <note>Newgrange/The Boyne mound</note>; his name was Bracan. He had a daughter who was a virgin named *Almha*. Cumall, son of Trénmór, took her as his wife. She died while bearing him a son, and this green-surfaced hill was closed over her. It is named after her now; whereas until then, it had been called *Tulach na Faircsena*, meaning 'the Look-out Hill.' 

Alternatively, it is said that *Almha* was the name of the man who owned it in the time of Nemed <note>A legendary early colonizer of Ireland</note>. Or yet again, it is said that Nuada the Magician built a fort and stronghold there, and from that fortress he produced an *almha*—meaning a 'herd of cattle'—from which the name *Almha* is derived." 

And Caeilte said:

> "Leinster’s *Almha*—the fortress of the Fianna—the town which the

It was from her that all the countries they occupied extended far and wide in the course of time. *Carmann* lived in *Carmann's* rough land, where bards stayed for a season; *Trega's* wife lived in his powerful house. . . . . . Liffey's golden-hued plain was the share of that skilled, fair, and tall young woman (as I believe this is no false tradition), and the fifth daughter was *Almha*, who was seated here. *Nuada* the wizard <note>original: "druid"</note> was a harsh man; he built a strong, high *fort* <note>original: "dún"</note> in *Almha*, using bright crystal for the stockade of his spacious fortress. The fort was pure white all over, as if it had been coated with all the lime in Ireland. It was named after the *almha* or "herd" that he brought from his mansion; from that, I say, the name of *Almha* sticks to it.

"You have told that tale well, Caeilte," said Muiredach son of Finnachta.

Caeilte resumed: "Where we were then—at the point where you interrupted me—was in this same *Almha* of Leinster. News of that invading fleet reached us there. The one who brought the news was *Spré aithinne*, or 'Firebrand-spark,' the daughter of *Mughna mucraesach* and the King of Ireland's female messenger <note>original: "she-runner"</note>. Finn summoned his own messenger to gather and muster the Fianna <note>The legendary band of semi-independent warriors</note> of both Ireland and Scotland. King Cormac, the grandson of Conn, gathered the tribes of Tara, the bands of Bregia, and the great general army of all Ireland. They came here to this place, twenty-five battalions strong. Lots were cast between the Fianna and the settled people to determine who should engage the *foreigners* <note>original: "allmarachs" or "over-sea men"</note>; it fell to the Fianna to open the battle. 

A fight was fought every day for a week. Fifteen hundred foreigners and Irishmen <note>original: "éirennachs"</note> were killed, and then the main battle took place. In that battle, Glas fell at the hands of Finn son of Cumall, and his seven sons were killed by the Fianna. We marched with Finn to that battle one hundred and fifty warriors strong, and each one of us killed fifty fighting men. Three of us from the Fianna entered the tent where Glas son of Drecan was; there we found nine columns of gold, the smallest of which was as thick as a yoke for three oxen. We hid these in this red moor north of the circular fort <note>original: "rath"</note>, and here Glas son of Drecan was buried. Therefore, this fort is called *Ráth Ghlais* <note>The Fort of Glas</note>."

Patrick exclaimed: "Victory and a blessing to you, Caeilte! That is a good story you have told us. Brogan, let this be written down." And Brogan wrote it. They stayed there for that night and rose early the next morning. They traveled to the *Arena of Fergus's Chariot* <note>original: "roe carpait Fergusa"</note>.

(As is common in an ancient legend) a situation arose in which nearly all of them were slaughtered because of a quarrel born from a certain match. Guaire, Finn’s *gilla* <note>original: gilla; a servant, attendant, or youth</note>, and Bresal’s son, Finn Bane, held a skillful match at the chess-board, from which a contention sprang. As a player, Finn Bane was better than Guaire from *Glas Bemann*; Finn Bane won four games, and Guaire won only a single one. 

Great anger now grew in Guaire against Bresal’s green-mantled son; he said evil things to him in earnest, all because of his opponent's fair and honorable play. Finn Bane’s shame was very great, and he quickly lifted his hand; thus, from Bresal’s winning son, a fist landed on Guaire’s mouth. 

The splendid Fianna <note>The legendary band of warriors led by Finn mac Cumhaill</note> rose up—the generous, the famous, the all-valorous. It was a vexation to them to have the Chief’s servant stricken for such a paltry cause. They rose up, I say, with one accord: Finn Bane’s Fianna and Finn mac Cumhaill’s; Caeilte’s Fianna and Conan’s, Ossian’s and Ferdoman’s. 

Then it was that Finn himself said: "See outside, my stalwart, powerful son, why the Fianna’s anger kindles—what may be the cause of their uprising." 

[But here a man of Finn’s comes in and cries:] "Guaire your servant, O Finn, a young man who was the bearer of your chess-board: it is for no valid cause that his slaughter by the son of Bresal has been carried out!"

"Let the son of Bresal be seized," said Finn, "and let no ransom-gift be accepted in his place; neither let Ossian, Dermot, nor Caeilte act as a protection for him in this matter."

Ossian spoke then: "By your hand, O glorious Finn—by your nobility and by your honor—the son of Bresal shall not be slain because he happened to be involved in a brawl. If it were we who lacked self-restraint, it is from you that our correction should come. We came away from the son of Cumhaill (the man of tender honor) to find Finn Bane; and so we brought Bresal’s son to the Chief of Ireland’s Fianna. The first Finn—Finn mac Cumhaill of *Almha*—then questioned the other Finn: why it was that he assaulted Guaire, who was now gone and passed away.

Finn Bane answered: "Finn! Guaire your servant, a fellow who carried your chess-board, came at early morning and defied me to play a single game. I tell nothing but a truthful tale."

It would be wrongful now if you persisted in refusing to listen to us. He sheared the right hand and the left foot from the vehement Dithramach; but it was Dithramach's own head that stern Caeilte left upon the north side of Drumcliff."

From there they proceeded to *Coill na mBuidhen* or "wood of the companies," now called *Coill Muadnatan* or "Muadnait’s wood"; over the peak of Muiredach’s son Gulban, or "Benbulbin"; to *Garbhros* or "rough-grove," now *Daire na Damhraidhe*, "the deer-herd’s oak-grove." There they made a spacious hunting booth for cooking; they roofed it in with sedge that was green at the top and pale towards the bottom...

# The Colloquy

"Derg, your hunting party consists of only a few; you are separated from your Fianna <note>The Fianna were semi-independent warrior bands in Irish mythology, led by Finn mac Cumhaill.</note>, the companions of your chase. But are you well-versed in the various violent deaths they suffered?"

At that time, there was a great war between Lir of *sídh Finnachaidh* and Ilbhrec of Assaroe. A bird with an iron beak and a tail of fire used to come and perch at a golden window in the *sídh*. Every evening, it would shake itself until it knocked every sword from its pillow, every shield from its peg, and every spear from its rack, bringing them all down upon the heads of the people in the *sídh*. The residents used to hurl missiles at the bird, but every shot would instead strike the head of one of their own boys, women, or foster-children. 

On the night of Caeilte’s arrival, while their banquet hall was being prepared, the same bird arrived and caused the same destructive mischief. The people of the *sídh* began throwing at it, but they could not do anything to stop it. Caeilte asked, "How long has the bird been acting this way?" Derg answered, "For a year now, ever since we and the people of the other *sídh* went to war."

Then Caeilte reached his hand inside the rim of his shield and pulled out a copper rod. He threw it at the bird, knocking it down so that it fell onto the floor of the *sídh*. "Did anyone ever throw better than that?" asked Ilbhrec. Aedh *minbhrec* of Assaroe asked, "Was there anyone among the Fianna <note>term: Fianna; the legendary band of warriors led by Fionn mac Cumhaill</note> who was as good at throwing as you?" 

"I give my word," Caeilte answered, "that no one among them had any right to brag over another; for every man of them possessed a full and sufficient measure of martial strength and marksmanship, and I was the same." <insert>✓</insert>

<margin>✓</margin>However, no one could count all the stories the ancient men told about what they and the other chiefs of the Fianna <note>The Fianna were a legendary band of semi-independent warrior-hunters</note> had achieved through great valor and mastery of arms. This was in addition to the legendary lore of every hill and all the lands about which the men of Ireland questioned them.

Then Trenbrugaid, son of Treon, arrived. He was a principal <term>brughaid cétach</term> <note>A wealthy landowner and "hospitaller of a hundred," responsible for providing food and shelter to the king's company</note> to the king of Ireland, and a man of great ambition. He was accompanied by one hundred and fifty tall men. Every man wore a deep blue cloak and a beautiful shirt of pure white. In their hands, they carried one hundred and fifty forked spears. They saluted the king of Ireland, and he answered them. "King," they said, "we have a great banquet for you: one hundred and eighty vats of mead and two hundred vats of clear fermented ale, along with a sufficient proportion of various meats." They had brought these provisions <note>original: "provant"</note> and liquors with them for the king. The king asked Ossian: "Will you, like the others, join the nobles of Ireland in the hall of drinking and pleasure?" 

<note>Text in pencil brackets:</note>Ossian answered: "Let our share of food and drink be given to us separately, for those of the present day are not of our generation or our time." "How many of you are there?" asked the king. Ossian said: "Eighteen men; nine for me, and nine for my comrade, Caeilte." "You shall have twenty vats, with their sufficient share of meat," said the king. "Now, King," Caeilte objected, "do not put us on the same footing regarding food or drink; for where I am given ten vats, it is only right that Ossian should receive thirty." Thus, they spent that night joyfully and in good cheer, with no shortage of either food or drink.

The next morning they all rose, and the king of Ireland's tent was spread over him on a <term>tulach</term> <note>a small hill or ceremonial mound</note>. No one was admitted into that tent except for a chief or a chief’s heir-apparent. Patrick and his clergy were lodged in the other half of the tent, where in turn no one was permitted to enter except a bishop, a priest, or those specially devoted to the King of Heaven and Earth. Ossian sat before Patrick, and Caeilte sat before the king of Ireland, who asked: "Which of you is the elder?" "I am," Caeilte answered, "for when Ossian was born I had already completed thirty years; for now seventeen

Then the king questioned them further: "What was the number of Ireland’s kings by whom lands were granted to the Fianna?" Caeilte (for he knew the answer) replied: "It was a king who rose to rule Ireland named Feradach Fechtnach <note>Feradach the Righteous, a legendary High King of Ireland</note>, and he had two sons: Tuathal and Fiacha. When Feradach died, his two sons divided Ireland between them. To the one went her precious things, her various wealth and treasures, her cattle and herds, her <term>dúns</term> <note>fortified hills or residences</note> and hill-forts. To the other went her cliffs and her estuaries, her mast <note>forest nuts used for animal feed</note> and her 'sea-harvest' <note>original: 'sea-fruit,' likely referring to shellfish and seaweed</note>, her salmon beautiful in their varied colors, her hunting, and her sport."

Dermot asked: "Where did they make this partition?" 

"At this very hill upon which we sit now." 

"That was not an equal division," said the noblemen of Ireland. 

Ossian asked: "Which of the portions would you yourselves have preferred over the other?" 

"The feasts, the dwelling-houses, and all the rest of her good things," they replied. 

"The portion which they despise," said Caeilte, "that is the very one which in our eyes was the better part."

Five physicians, a wondrous group! The best that ever came to the land of Banba <note>Banba is a poetic name for Ireland</note>. Five poets, a noble company! The best that ever came to the land of Erin <note>Erin: Ireland</note>: my memory accurately allows me to detail them and their bardic skill. Cairbre, the poet whom Amergin of the Gaels' island brought across the seas; **Fercheirtne** along with **Labraidh Lorc**, **Moghruith** again, and Finn of the naked sword.

# The Colloquy.

The gentle, marriageable, yellow-haired young women and the small green-cloaked boys of the residence came out to give Caeilte welcome. The company remained at the festive banqueting until the sun, rising from its fiery pillow, flooded the cliffs, waterfalls, and estuaries of the Earth.

Caeilte and Conall, along with the noblemen of his people, left the town. Conall asked, “Why was the name *Artrach’s Fort* <note>original: *ráth Artrach*</note> given to that fort, *Mongach’s Fort* <note>original: *ráth Mongaigh*</note> to that one to the north, and *the Poets’ Enclosure* <note>original: *lios na néices*</note> to this enclosure south of us?” 

Caeilte answered: “Bodhb Derg <note>original: *Bodb Derg*; a king of the Tuatha Dé Danann</note>, son of the Dagda <note>the 'Good God' of Irish myth</note>, had three sons in the many-windowed grand hall <note>original: *brugh*</note> on the Boyne: Artrach, Aedh (surnamed ‘the Handsome’), and Angus. A disagreement broke out between these sons and their own father. 

‘Come now, my sons,’ said Bodhb, ‘leave the People of the Goddess Danu <note>original: *tuatha dé danann*; a supernatural race in Irish mythology</note> and go to the King of Ireland, Cormac, grandson of Conn. There is a good reason why it is right for you to leave them: the People of the Goddess Danu do not have enough country or land to support both themselves and all the wealth in cattle that Artrach possesses. Angus alone has more attendants <note>original: *gillas*</note> and young warriors <note>original: *óglaechs*</note> than the entire *Tuatha Dé Danann*, and in his multitude of poets, the handsome Aedh exceeds the bardic brotherhoods of both Ireland and Scotland.’

“Accordingly, Bodhb’s three sons went to Cormac, who asked what had brought them there. ‘Our own father has ordered us to clear out from the *Tuatha Dé Danann*,’ they said, ‘and we have come to seek land from you.’ 

‘You shall have it,’ Cormac answered. ‘I will grant you four districts <note>original: *triuchas*; a land division similar to a barony</note> of the rough land which today is called the Land of Conall <note>original: *tír Conaill*, or Tirconnell</note>.’ 

Now the eldest son, Artrach, had a great hall <note>original: *bruidhen*</note> with seven doors, offering a free welcome to all travelers. Angus, called ‘the many-skilled’ <note>original: *ilchlesach*</note>, lived in *Mongach’s Fort* and hosted the sons of the kings of Ireland and Scotland, who came to learn the art and craft of throwing weapons. Handsome Aedh lived in the *Poets’ Enclosure* with the bardic troupes of Ireland and Scotland surrounding him. 

They spent thirty years there during Cormac’s reign, until he died at *Spelán’s Fort* <note>original: *ráth Speláin*</note> in Bregia <note>an ancient kingdom in East Ireland</note>. Then they returned back again to the *Tuatha Dé Danann*. At that time, because of the smooth, crimson-tipped nuts of the forest and the beautiful golden-yellow apples, this enclosure was colorful and diverse...”

On that day, he traveled eastward to *Loch an Daimh Dheirg* <note>original: *loch an daimh dheirg*; 'The Lake of the Red Stag'</note> in Dalaradia, where there were two eminent priests of Patrick’s <term>community</term> <note>original: *familia*; the Latin term for a religious household or followers</note>: Colman of Ela and Eoghanan. Then three young clerics from the priests' community came out and launched their <term>currach</term> <note>original: *currach*; a traditional Irish boat made of a wooden frame covered in hide</note> to catch fish, reciting their prescribed <term>Hours</term> <note>original: *Hours*; the set of prayers recited at specific times of the day</note> as they worked. Caeilte saw them, listened to them, and said:

> "It was always a rare thing for my ears to listen to such sweet-sounding reading; there was a time when I more often listened to the songs of <term>high-born ladies</term> <gloss>[noblewomen]</gloss>. Whoever owned a pen would be occupied for a long time in writing about them; for as miserable as I am here now, I have experienced many wonders. My journey from Tralee was slow, and I have waited a long time for it; as for listening to the reading of <gloss>[clerical]</gloss> books, that was a rare occurrence for me."

Then Colman of Ela and Eoghanan came out and saw the large men with the giant wolf-dogs <gloss>[on leashes]</gloss> in their hands. He and his companions were brought in accordingly and settled in a private house, where they were given the oldest of every liquor and the freshest of every meat.

When they had finished their supper and meal, Colman asked Caeilte: "Why was the name *Loch an Daimh Dheirg*, or 'the lake of the red stag,' given to this place?" 

Caeilte answered: "It was a red stag that lived in the open lands of lush Luachra in the south. Four times a year, he managed to escape from the hounds and men of the Fianna, but at last they followed him to this spot. Finn set the base of it on one of his feet, and the highest point reached the crown of his head; and Finn was the tallest man of the Fianna. I placed the other antler in the lake close to this island, and I believe that if the light were better, I could find my way to it." And he said:

The young lady and her thirty women used to come every morning, and in this blue-surfaced water they would wash their faces and their hands.

The fact that his daughter was stolen away by Ossian weighed very heavily on the king of Munster. He gathered the armies of both provinces of Munster: five hardy battalions <note>original: "battles"</note> of equal size, and they came here in pursuit of the Fianna. Just then, Niamh was washing herself at the well, and she saw the five battalions on the hill <note>original: *tulach*</note> right above her. 'Woe is me!' the young woman cried. 'Happy is she who had died, or been killed, before her protector, her father, her three brothers, and the nobles of Munster had seen her like this!' She laid her face to the ground and, along with her thirty companions, she died. As for her, her heart passed from her mouth as a lump of black blood, and that is why, from that time until now, the name of this hill is *cnoc an áir* or 'the hill of slaughter' <note>original: *cnoc an áir*</note>." Then Caeilte spoke:

A separate blood-fine was to be paid for every chief or chieftain’s daughter who had perished there. "Fianna of Ireland, how shall we divide such a fine?" asked Finn. They answered: "One-third from Clan-Baeiscne; and from us, the rest of the Fianna, two-thirds." "And this, Colman," Caeilte ended, "is the only blood-fine that Finn ever divided among the Fianna."

At this point, Eochaid "Red-edge" sent a message from *Ráth Áine* to the "Lake of the Red Stag" to fetch Caeilte. Caeilte then bid Colman and Eoganan farewell; the saints promised him eternal happiness, promised to listen to his grievances, and promised to pray to the King of Heaven and Earth for his welfare. Then Caeilte journeyed away in the chariot of the King of Ulster <note>original: "Ulidia"</note>.

Patrick, Caeilte, and everyone with them in the dwelling went out onto the green; soon they saw a solitary <term>óglaech</term> <note>young warrior</note> coming toward them, who looked like this: he wore a shirt of yellow silk next to his skin, a handsome green cloak around him, and a gold brooch fastened upon his chest. “Who are you, young man?” Caeilte asked. “Aedh, son of *Aedh na Nabasach* from *Cnoc Árdmhulla* out in the sea, which is currently called *Rachlainn* or *Rachrainn*—that is, Rathlin or Raghery Island. I am a leader among the youth of the <term>Tuatha Dé Danann</term> in general, and I have come now to ask you something.” “Young man, what would you ask me?” Caeilte replied. “There is nothing I would rather ask you than the reason why this place is called *Carn Manannáin*, or ‘Manannan’s Cairn.’” Then Caeilte began:

> “There was a warrior of the <term>Tuatha Dé Danann</term> named *Aillén mac Eogabail* who fell in love with the wife of Manannan mac Lir. Meanwhile, Aillen’s sister, Aine, the daughter of Eogabal, fell in love with Manannan, to whom she, in turn, was dearer than all the rest of humanity. Aine then asked her brother, Aillen, ‘What is it that has wasted <note>literally "made to ebb"</note> the kingly, stately form you once had?’ ‘By my word and in truth, young woman,’ Aillen said, ‘except for you alone, there is no one of the human race to whom I would reveal this.’ Then he told her, ‘It is that I am in love with *Uchtdelbh* <note>meaning "Breast-shape" or "of the shapely bosom"</note>, the daughter of Angus Finn and wife of Manannan.’ ‘The remedy for that lies in my hand!’”

The company, together with Saint Patrick, came out onto the fort's green.

Then Coscrach asked Caeilte: “Why was the name *cloch na narm* [the stone of arms] given to this solid block of stone?”

“*That*,” Caeilte answered, “is the stone on which the Fianna used to sharpen their weapons every year at *Samhain*-tide; and on that stone was displayed the best official proof of the peace [prevailing in the land] that existed during the reigns of Conn, Art, Cormac, and Cairbre Lifechair in either Ireland or Scotland: an arm-ring of red gold. Because there was a hole in the pillar-stone, the ring was passed through it, and the rule of those kings was so excellent that no one dared to take it away. Furthermore, the magicians' divination was so sharp that, because of it and the discipline of those kings, no one ventured even to touch it. However, those former kings passed away one after another until Cairbre Lifechair arose, who fell in the Battle of Gowra; then we (the few of us who remained of the Fianna) retreated to this ford, and by turning what had been the top part downward, I inverted the stone so that it is as you see it now.”

The company said: “If we could only see the hole and the token, we would believe it.”

“Give me a short moment—for the Gael is a passionate being—until I lift the bottom and make it the top,” said Caeilte; from which comes the proverb: ‘The Gael is a passionate being.’

Then all of them together went at it immediately, yet even so, they could not move it at all. Then Caeilte came forward and embraced it with his two arms, heaved it out of the earth, and it was revealed: the gold bangle was through a hole at the lower end, so that everyone saw it. Caeilte took the bracelet and divided it in two: he gave one half to Patrick and the other to the people of the town where they were, and its name from that time until now is *cluain fhalach*, that is, the ‘meadow of the *fail* or armlet’; the stone's name being *lia na narm* or ‘the monolith of arms.’”

Whereupon Caeilte uttered a quatrain:—

> “Many a spear of the kind that causes grief, and many an accomplished hero’s sword, was sharpened by us here upon the pillar-stone, O Coscrach, on every recurring *Samhain*-day.”

“Success and blessings be with you, Caeilte; that is excellent ancient lore you have shared with us!” said Patrick.

Here the fawn ‘put its head into the earth’ <note>meaning it vanished underground</note>, and we did not know in what direction it went afterward. Heavy snow began to fall now, making the forest’s branches look like woven wicker; the severity of the foul weather and the storm that came robbed us of our strength and our resourcefulness. Finn said to me: ‘Caeilte, can you find us protection against tonight's tempest?’ I limbered up and set off over the shoulder of the mountain to the south where, when I took a look around, I saw a well-lit *sídh* <note>a fairy mound or dwelling</note> furnished with a great variety of *cuachs* <note>cups or bowls</note>, horns, and cups. For a time I stood in front of the *sídh* considering it, and wondered how I might manage to enter the place to inquire about it, or whether I should go back to Finn and his few *Fianna*. They arrived at *eas na finghaile* or "the falls of fratricide," now called "the falls of Cronan son of Balbh." "Well then," said the host, "I have another thing to ask you: why was this liss called 'of women'?"

"It was nine sisters of the <term>Tuatha Dé Danann</term> women who came here to meet nine warriors of the <term>Fianna</term>; but when they had come this far, the children of Morna spied them out as they kept their meeting and killed them. From them, this spot has the name *lios na mban*." They spent that night there; the next morning they took their leave and left a blessing.

They reached *carn na finghaile* or "the cairn of fratricide," now called *dumha na con* or "the mound of wolf-dogs," where, as they stepped up the <term>tulach</term> <note>mound</note>, they saw nine lovely women with a queen of excellent form in their midst waiting for them. She wore a smock of royal silk next to her skin; over that was an outer tunic of soft silk, and around her was a hooded crimson mantle fastened at her breast with a golden brooch. Upon seeing Caeilte, the lady rose and gave him three kisses; then he asked: "Maiden, who are you?" She replied: "I am Echna, daughter of Muiredach mac Finnachta—that is to say, the daughter of the king of Connacht." Now, the group of them had a chessboard on which they played, and also a can of delicious mead which they drank, in which floated a beautiful polished horn. Every time a game was won and ended, they took a drink; in fact, they caroused and made merry. The lady's character was this: she had three perfections; for she was one of the wise women of the whole world, and anyone she counseled would gain both wealth and respect as a result. "Caeilte, my soul," she said, "where were you last night?" "In the house of Blathmac the stock-owner, at *cúil radhairc* below, in Leyney of Connacht." "All hail to you! It is your own way you have come!" cried the girl. She took one end of the chessboard and Caeilte took the other in his lap, saying: "It has been a long time since I played chess."

### This is the death of Eochaid son of Mairid.

There was a good king who ruled over Munster: *Mairid*, son of *Cairid*. He had two sons: *Eochaid* and *Ribh*. Guaire's daughter *Eibhliu*, from the dwelling <note>brugh</note> of the Young Son <note>mac óg</note>, was the wife of Mairid. She set her fancy upon his son, Eochaid (it is from this Eibhliu that *Sliabh Eibhlinne*, or 'Eibhliu's mountain,' is named). For a long time she solicited the young man, and at last pressed him so hard that he should secretly fly with her. Ribh told his brother that, rather than disgrace himself, he ought to carry the woman off, and that he himself would leave the country with him.

Therefore, Eochaid eloped with Eibhliu, and Ribh went with them. Their company consisted of a thousand <note>ten hundred</note> men, and they traveled by bringing their flocks and herds with them. Their soothsayers told them that they were not fated to establish a settlement in the same place, and they parted accordingly at *Bealach Dá Liag*, or 'the way of the two flagstones.'

Ribh went westwards to 'the country of Midir's game with the Young Son <note>mac óg</note>,' otherwise known as *Magh Finn*, or 'the white plain.' Here Midir—who had previously killed their horses—came to them, leading by the halter a horse that carried a pack-saddle. On him they

Eochaid, on the other hand, traveled until he reached the dwelling <note>brugh</note> of the Young Son <note>mac óg</note>. A tall man came to them and tried to turn them out of the country, but they would not leave for him. That night, the man killed all their horses. On the morrow he returned to them and said: "Unless you leave the land on which you stand, tonight I will slay all your people." Eochaid answered: "Great mischief you have already wrought us by killing all our horses; without them, we could not depart even if we desired to." Angus <note>or the Young Son, for it was he</note> gave them a great horse, and they threw all their gear upon him; he furthermore commanded them not to unload the horse on the way, nor at any time to let him halt, lest where he stood something should happen that would cause their deaths. Upon a Sunday in the 'mid-harvest month,' or September, they set out and came to *Liathmuine* or 'Grey Bramble-bush' in Ulidia, where they all gathered around the horse and with one movement relieved him of all their baggage; but not one of them turned his head back the way they had come. The animal remained with them there, and in that place there was also a spring well. Over this, Eochaid had a house built, with a lid to cover the well and a woman to tend it constantly; and later, against Muiredach, son of Fiacha, he successfully established his claim to the half-rule of Ulidia.

But once, when the woman had not shut the lid of the well, *Linn Muine* or 'the bramble-bush water' rose and covered *Liathmuine*; there Eochaid was drowned with his children, except for Liban and Conaing, and Curnan the half-wit (from whom the *Dál mBuain* and the *Dál Sailne* are descended). Curnan, indeed, had frequently foretold to them that the lake would overrun them, saying:—

> “Come, come, grasp edged tools and carve out vessels for yourselves: with a gray flood *Linn Muine* shall overwhelm *Liathmuine*; in the broad water, Aire and Conaing shall be drowned; swim east and west and up and down through every sea!”

And this was true for him; for for the space of three hundred years Liban ranged the sea, with her lap-dog in the form of an otter close after her whichever way she went, never parting from her at all. It was she herself who, when Beoan son of Innle caught her in his nets, told him her whole story, at which time she sang these words which follow:—

> "Beneath *loch nEchach* I have my dwelling now: high above me is the once solid surface which troops of horses trod; under ships' rounded hulls is my appointed place; the wave is my roof, the shore my wall . . ."

This, then, was what most contributed to scattering the Ulidians throughout Ireland: namely, the eruption of *loch nEchach* or 'Loch Neagh.' After her baptism, another name was given to Liban: *muirghein* or 'sea-birth,' that is to say, *gein mara* or 'birth of the sea.' As for her, one half of her was a salmon, while the other was human; and it was for her that the *sennachie* <note>a traditional historian or storyteller</note> sang these verses:—

> "A sea-birth, which is a birth filled with special virtues, the daughter of haughty Eochaid is . . ."

Liban and Airiu were the two daughters of Eochaid Finn; Airiu, the wife of Curnan, was drowned there, and he died of grief for her: hence *carn Curnáin* or 'Curnan's cairn' has its name, and that is 'the invention of Curnan.'

Now for a full year Liban had been in her bower beneath the lake with her lap-dog, God preserving her the while from the waters of Loch Neagh, when she said one day: "O Lord, happy is the one who could be in the shape of a salmon, traversing the sea and swimming just as they do!" Then she was turned into a salmon's form, and her lap-dog into an otter's; so that whatever course she took, and into whatever direction, he was immediately in her wake under the waters and the seas. In this way she continued from the time of Eochaid, son of Mairid, to that of Comgall of *Bennachar* or 'Bangor.'

Then the clergy gave her a choice: whether to be baptized and then and there immediately go to Heaven; or to be continued in life for that same length of time again <note>300 years</note>, and so go to Heaven after a life prolonged beyond many ages. The choice she made was to depart then. Comgall baptized her, and the name that he conferred on her was Muirghein or “sea-birth,” as before; or perhaps Muirgheilt, that is, “sea-prodigy,” which is to say *geilt in mhara* or “the prodigy of the sea.” *Fuinche* was also another name for her.

In that place, wonders and miracles are performed through her, and there she (after the manner of every other sainted virgin) enjoys honor and reverence just as God has bestowed them on her in Heaven.

To Esirt, who asked, "What do you see?" Aedh answered, "I see a russet-clad hare." But Esirt said, "Not so—rather it is Iubhdan's horse coming to fetch you." The appearance of that horse was this: he had two fierce flashing eyes, an exquisite pure crimson mane, four green legs, and a long tail that floated in wavy curls. His general color was like that of a master artisan's gold-work, and he wore a gold-encrusted bridle as well. Esirt, mounting him, said, "Come up beside me, Aedh." But Aedh objected again, "No, poet, his capacity is all too small to serve as a boat for even you alone." "Aedh, stop finding fault; for as heavy as the wisdom in you may be, yet he will carry us both."

Now, both being mounted on the horse, they traversed the breaking seas, the expanse of the mighty main, and the great depths of the ocean, until in the end they reached *magh faithlenn* safely and without mishap. There, the Luchra people were gathered before them in assembly. "Esirt approaches," they cried, "and a giant keeps him company!" Then Iubhdan went to meet Esirt and gave him a kiss. "But poet," he said, "why do you bring this giant to destroy us?" 

"He is no giant," Esirt replied, "but Ulster's poet and man of science, and the king's dwarf. In the land where he comes from, he is the smallest, so that he lies down in their great men's laps and stands on the palms of their hands like an infant. For all that, he is still such a man that you would do well to be careful of yourselves in his presence." When they asked further, "What is his name?" they were told that he was called "Poet Aedh." "Alas, man," they cried to Esirt, "your giant is huge indeed!"

Next, Esirt addressed Iubhdan and said, "On you, Iubhdan, I lay bonds <note>geasa</note> which true warriors may not refuse: that you go in your own person to see the region we have come from, and that you be the first man to taste the 'lord's porridge' that is made for the King of Ulster tonight."

"I will do that," she said: "but you acted unjustly when Esirt was cast into prison." "Iubhdan," said Bebo, "search the town for the porridge spoken of by Esirt, and let us depart again before the people of the place shall rise."

They gained the inside of the palace and there found Emania’s great cauldron, having in it the remnant of the "people’s porridge." Iubhdan drew near, but could by no means reach it from the ground. "Get upon your horse," said Bebo, "and from the horse onto the cauldron’s rim." This he did but, the porridge being too far down and his arm too short, he could not touch the handle of the silver ladle that was in the cauldron; whereupon as he made a downward effort, his foot slipped, and he fell into the cauldron up to his very navel; in which, as though every existing iron shackle had been upon him, he now found himself fettered and tethered both hand and foot. "You tarry long, dark man!" Bebo cried to him (for Iubhdan was thus: he had jet-black and curled hair, his skin being whiter than the foam of a wave and his cheeks redder than the forest’s scarlet berry: whereas—except for him only—all the Luchra people had hair that was ringleted indeed, but of a fair and yellow hue; hence then he was styled "dark man"). Bebo sang now, and Iubhdan answered her:—

> *She.* "O dark man, and O dark man! Dire is the strait in which you are: today it is that the white horse must be saddled, for the sea is angry and the tide is at flood." *He.* "O fair-haired woman, and O woman with fair hair! Shackles hold me captive in a viscous mass nor, until gold be given for my ransom, shall I ever be released. O Bebo, and O Bebo! Then he was conducted into a fine and private chamber that Fergus had, where a trusted servant of the king was assigned to attend to him. “This is an excellent retreat indeed,” he said, “yet my own retreat is more excellent than it”; and he composed a song:

> “In the land that lies far to the north, I have a retreat whose ceiling is of red gold and whose floor is all of silver. Its lintel is of white bronze, and its threshold of copper; I believe the thatch on it is made of light-yellow bird feathers. Its candelabra are golden, holding candles of bright light and studded with rare gems, in the lovely center of the house. Except for myself and my queen, no one who belongs there feels sorrow now; there is a retinue there that does not age, wearing wavy yellow hair. Every man there is a chess player, and there is good company that knows no limit: the retreat is never closed against any man or woman who seeks to enter it.”

> “O man who kindles fire for Fergus of the feasts, whether at sea or on shore, never burn the king of woods. The woodbine is the monarch of Innisfail’s forests, whom none may hold captive; it is no effort for a weak sovereign to hug all tough trees in its embrace. If you burn the pliant woodbine, wails for misfortune will abound; dire extremity at weapons’ points or drowning in great waves will follow. Do not burn the precious apple tree with its spreading and low-sweeping boughs: a tree always decked in white bloom, against whose fair head all men reach out their hands. The surly blackthorn is a wanderer, and a wood that the craftsman does not burn; throughout its body, though it is thin, birds warble in their flocks. Do not burn the noble willow, a tree sacred to poems; bees suck within its bloom, and everyone loves the little cage. Burn the rowan, the graceful tree with berries, the wizards’ tree; but spare the limber tree: do not burn the slender hazel. Dark is the color of the ash: timber that makes the wheels turn; he furnishes rods for horsemen’s hands, and his form turns battle into flight. The spiteful briar is a tenterhook among woods; by all means burn him, he who is so sharp and green; he cuts, he flays the foot, and forcibly drags backward anyone who would advance. The green oak is the fiercest heat-giver of all timber; from him none may escape unhurt: by favoring him the head is set to aching, and by his acrid embers the eye is made sore. Alder, the very battle-witch of all woods, the tree that is hottest in the fight—undoubtedly burn both the alder and the whitethorn as you see fit. Holly, burn it green; holly, burn it dry: of all trees whatsoever, holly is the very best. The elder that has tough bark, a tree that in truth hurts sorely: burn him—the one who furnishes horses to the armies from the *sídh* <note>the fairy mounds</note>—until he is charred. The birch as well, if he is laid low, promises lasting fortune: burn up most surely and certainly the stalks that bear the constant pods. If it please you, let the russet aspen come headlong down: burn, whether late or early, the tree with the shaking branch. The yew is the patriarch of long-lasting woods, sacred to feasts as is well known: from him now build dark-red vats of a good size. Ferdedh, you faithful one, if you would only do my bidding: it would be an advantage, O man, to your soul as well as your body!”

In this manner then, and free of all supervision, Iubhdan lived in the town; while for the people of Ulster, it was recreation for both mind and body to look at him and to listen to his words.

Yet another day the household argued about all sorts of things, how they would do this or that, but never said: "if it so please God." Then Iubhdan laughed and recited a poem:

> "Man talks, but God shows the outcome; to men all things are but confusion, and they must leave them as God knows them to be. All that which You, Monarch of the elements, have ordained must be right; He, the King of kings, knows all that I crave of you, Fergus. No man's life, however bold he may be, is more than the twinkling of an eye; even if he were a king’s son, he does not know whether what he speaks of the future is the truth."

Iubhdan now remained in Emania until such time as the Luchra-folk, who were seven battalions strong, came to Emania's green in search of him; and among them, no single person exceeded another in height or in bulk. Then they said to Fergus and to Ulster's nobles who came out to confer with them: "Bring us our king so that we may redeem him, and we will pay a good ransom for him." Fergus asked: "What ransom?" "Every year, without any ploughing or sowing, we will cover this vast plain with a harvest of corn." "I will not give up Iubhdan," said the king. "Tonight we will do you a mischief." "What mischief?" asked the king. "We will let all of Ulster's calves in to their mothers, so that by morning time there shall not be found in the whole province enough milk for even a single infant." "You will have gained that much," said Fergus, "but not Iubhdan."

Accordingly, they caused this damage that night; then in the morning they returned to the green of Macha and, promising to make good everything they had spoiled, they again demanded Iubhdan. However, when Fergus refused them, they said: "Tonight we will perform another deed of vengeance: we will defile the wells, the rapids, and the river-mouths of the entire province." But the king answered: "That is but a puny mischief" (from which comes the old saying 'dirt in a well') "and you shall not have Iubhdan."

Having done this, they came again to Emania on the third day and demanded Iubhdan. Fergus said: "I will not give him."

> "We proclaim a raid upon you this night, O Fergus, owner of many strong places! From your standing corn we will snip the ears, so that your tables will not benefit. In this matter we have already burnt your kilns; your mill-beams, too, we have all consumed; we have very precisely and completely let your calves reach their mothers. We will crop your men's hair, and all the locks of your young women: it shall be a disfigurement to your land, and that shall be the completion of our mischief. Were it not for Iubhdan here, whom Fergus holds at his mercy, the way we carried out our raids would have been such that the disgrace Fergus suffered would have shown his refusal to be an evil one."

“And now go from here,” said Iubhdan: “for Esirt has prophesied of me that I may not return until I have left behind the choicest of all my precious things.”

So for nearly a full year he lived in Emania, and then he said to Fergus: “Choose one of all my treasures now, for you are permitted to do so. My treasures are also excellent”; and in a song he proceeded to list them:—

> “Take my spear, oh take my spear, you, Fergus, who have many enemies! In battle it is a match for a hundred, and a king who holds it will have good fortune among enemy weapons. Take my shield, oh take my shield; it is a good price for me, Fergus! Whether it be a youth or a greybeard, no one can be wounded behind its shelter. My sword, oh my sword! Regarding a battle-sword, there is no more excellent or valuable thing in a prince’s hand throughout all Innisfail <note>An ancient name for Ireland</note>. Take my cloak, oh take my cloak, which if you take it will be always new! My mantle is good, Fergus, and will endure for your son and grandson. My shirt, oh my shirt! Whoever he may be who in time to come may wear its weave—it was the wife of my great-grandfather whose hands spun it. Take my belt, oh take my belt! Gold and silver are part of its craftsmanship; sickness will not seize him who is encircled by it, nor will it touch the skin encompassed by my girdle. My helmet, oh my helmet, there is no prize more admirable! No man who places it upon his head will ever be subject to the shame of baldness. Take my tunic, oh take my tunic, a well-fitting silken garment! Even if it were on someone for a hundred years, its crimson would be no worse. My cauldron, oh my cauldron, a rare and special thing for its practical use! Though they were stones that went into my cauldron, it would turn them into meat fit for princes. My vat, oh my vat! Compared to other vats of the best, anyone who bathes in it will live through three lifetimes. Take my mace, oh take my mace, you can choose no better treasure! In time of war, in a sharp skirmish, it will protect nine heads besides your own. Take my horse-rod, oh take my horse-rod: the rod of the yellow horse so fair to see! Let all the women of the world but look at you [with that rod in your hand] and all their deepest love will focus on you. My timpan <note>A stringed instrument</note>, oh my timpan, endowed with sweet strings from the borders of the Red Sea! Within its wires resides music enough to delight all the women of the universe. Whoever might be suddenly tested in tuning my timpan, even if he had never before been a man of art, the instrument would perform the minstrel’s role by itself. Ah, how melodious is its warlike strain, and how sweet its low cadence! It even plays all by itself, without a finger on any of its strings. My shears, oh my shears, that Barran’s smith made! Every man who takes them into his hands will secure a sweetheart. My needle, oh my needle, that is made of the *eanach’s* gold! . . . . Of my swine, take two porkers! They will last you until your dying day; every night they may be killed, yet within the watch they will live again. My halter, oh my halter! Whoever goes intent on plunder—even if he put a black cow into it, she would immediately become a white one.”

But this was now the time and the hour when the poet Aedh returned from his adventure; and the learned men immediately questioned him regarding Iubhdan's house, his household, and the region of the Luchra. Concerning all of this, Aedh immediately began to tell them, composing a poem:

> "It was a wondrous enterprise that took me away from you, our poets, to a populous fairy palace with a great company of princes and tiny men. There are twelve doors to that house with spacious beds and window-lighted sides; it is made of vast marble blocks, and in every doorway are doors of gold. Its bedclothes are of red, yellow and green, azure and blue; its authority is ancient: it includes cooking-places for warriors, and baths. Its terraces are smooth, made of the eggshells of Iruath; there are pillars of crystal, and columns of silver and copper too. Silk and satin, silk and satin, bridles . . . . . . . . . . ; its authority is ancient: it includes warriors' cooking-places and chessboards. Every day there was the reciting of romances and of the Fian-lore; the singing of poems, instrumental music, the mellow blast of horns, and orchestrated minstrelsy. He is a noble king: Iubhdan son of Abhdaein, owner of the yellow horse; he is one whose form never changes, and who does not need to strive for wisdom. Women are there, who play in pure, clear lakes: their clothing is satin, and each one has a gold chain. As for the king’s men-at-arms, they wear long tresses of curly and glossy hair: men of the ordinary size of the Luchra can stand upon the palms of those soldiers. Bebo—Iubhdan's blooming queen, an object of desire—the white-skinned beauty is never without three hundred women in her train. Bebo's women—they chatter little of evil or arrogance; their bodies are pure white, and their hair reaches to their ankles. The king’s chief poet, Esirt son of Beg son of Buaidghen: his eye is blue and gentle, and that man of poems is smaller than a clenched fist. The poet’s wife—she was inclined toward all good things; a lovely and wonderful woman: she could sleep in my curved glove. The king’s cupbearer—a trusty and true man in the banquet hall: I well loved Feror, who could lie within my sleeve. The king’s strong man—Glomhar son of Glomradh’s son Glas, a stern doer of brave deeds: he could knock down a thistle with one sweep. Of those who are the king’s confidants, seventeen 'swans' <note>Pretty girls</note> lay in my bosom; four of the men in my belt, and another would be in my beard without me even knowing it. They (both the fighting men and the scholars of that *sídh* <note>Fairy mound or palace</note>) would say to me, and the public cry was always: 'Enormous Aedh, oh what a giant!' Such, oh son of Leide of vast forests, such is my adventure: truly, a wondrous thing has happened to me."
