...made a choice, and his choice was Iubhdan’s shoes. This latter, therefore, leaving them his blessing and receiving theirs, said farewell to Fergus and the nobles of Ulster (with Ulster grieving for his departure), and the story has no more to do with him from this point on.

Regarding Fergus, however, this is why he picked out Iubhdan’s shoes: while he and a young man of his people were walking one day near Lochrury, they entered the lake to bathe; and the monster that lived in the lake—the *sinech* of Lochrury—became aware of them. Then, shaking herself until the whole lake was in a great and stormy commotion, she reared herself up high as if she were a hideous solid arch, so large that she equaled the size of a rainbow in the sky. Both of them, seeing her coming toward them, swam for the shore, while she followed in pursuit with mighty strokes that sent the water spouting from her sides in a bursting deluge. Fergus allowed his attendant to reach the land before himself, which resulted in the monster’s breath hitting the king and turning him into a crooked and distorted, squint-eyed being, with his mouth twisted around to the very back of his head. But he did not know that he looked this way; neither did anyone dare to ask him what it might be that had caused this change in him, nor did anyone venture to leave a mirror in the same house as him.

The young man, however, told the whole matter to his wife, and the woman revealed it to Fergus’s wife, the queen. Therefore, when there was a falling-out between the king and queen concerning priority in using the bath-stone, the king struck her with his fist and broke a tooth in her head. At this, anger seized the queen, and she said: "It would suit you better to avenge yourself on the *sinech* of Lochrury that dragged your mouth around to the back of your head than to win bloodless victories over women." Then she brought a mirror to Fergus, and as he looked upon his image, he said: "The woman’s words are true, and it is indeed the *sinech* of Lochrury that has brought me to this appearance." And this was why, above all of Iubhdan’s other precious wares, Fergus had taken his shoes.

In their ships and in their galleys, the whole province of Ulster accompanied Fergus and now gathered at Lochrury. Entering the lake, they reached its center; the monster rose and shook herself in such a way that she smashed all the vessels into small pieces.

<header>Death of Fergus.</header>

...and, like withered twigs under horses’ feet, they were each crushed to pieces and, before they could even reach the shore, all were swamped.

Fergus said to the people of Ulster: “Stay here and all of you sit down, so that you may witness how the monster and I shall deal with one another.” Then, wearing Iubhdan’s shoes, he leaped into the lake, standing tall, brilliant, and brave, heading toward the monster. At the sound of the hero’s approach, she bared her teeth like a wolf-dog threatened with a club; her eyes blazed like two great lit torches. Suddenly she extended her jagged array of sharp claws, bowed her neck into an arch, and clenched her glittering tusks, pulling back <note>that is, throwing back</note> her ears hideously, until her entire appearance was one of gloomy, cruel fury. Alas for anyone in this world fated to battle that monster: what a huge-headed, long-fanged omen she was! The fearsome and colossal creature’s form was this: she had a crest and mane of coarse hair, a yawning mouth, and deep-sunken eyes; on each side she had one hundred and fifty flippers, each armed with as many curved claws; her body was impregnable. Her height when extended was one hundred and fifty feet; she was as round as an apple when contracted, but in bulk she equaled a prominent hill in its rough covering of furze.

When the king sighted her, he charged, instant and impetuous, and as he went he composed this <term>rosg</term> or ‘<term>rhapsody</term>’:—

> “The evil that was foretold is upon me . . . ”

Then both of them, seeking the middle of the lake, thrashed the water so much that the many-colored salmon leaped and flung themselves out onto the shore, because they could find no resting place in the water, for the white sand from the bottom was churned up to the surface. At one moment the lake was whiter than new milk; soon after, it all turned to a crimson froth of blood. At last the beast, shaped like a vast royal oak, rose on the lake and fled before Fergus. The hero-king pressed his attack, dealing blows so stalwart and deadly that she died; and with the sword in his hand—the <term>caladcholg</term>, the best blade in Ireland at that time—he hewed her into pieces. To the shore of the lake where the men of Ulster sat, he brought her heart; but though he did, his own wounds were just as numerous <note>as hers</note>, and his skin was more full of holes than a sieve. Truly, the beast had bitten him to such a degree that he

<header>Death of Fergus.</header>

...brought up his very heart’s red blood and could hardly speak, but groaned aloud.

As for the men of Ulster, they took no pleasure in watching the fight, but said meanwhile that if the king and the beast had fought upon land, they would have helped him, and done so right valiantly. Then Fergus composed a poem:

> “My soul tonight is full of sadness, my body is cruelly mangled; red Lochrury’s beast has pushed painfully through my heart. Iubhdan’s shoes have brought me through without drowning; with a shining spear and with the *caladcholg* I have fought a hardy fight. I have avenged my deformity upon the *sinech*—this is a notable victory. Man! I would rather death should snatch me than to live on misshapen. It is Great Eochaid’s daughter Ailinn who forced me into the lists of mortal combat; and it is I, assuredly, who have good reason to grieve for the shape imposed on me by Iubhdan.”

He went on: “Ulster! I have met my death; but lay aside and preserve this sword until there comes after me one of Ulidia who shall be a fitting lord for it, whose name shall also be Fergus: Fergus, the son of Ros Rua.”

Then, lamenting and in tears, the men of Ulster stood over Fergus; the poet Aedh, the king’s bard, also came and, standing over him, mourned for Fergus with this quatrain:

> “Let Fergus’s grave be dug by you now—the great monarch’s grave, the grave of Leide’s son; it is a most dire calamity that he is put to death by a foolish, petty woman’s words!”

Answering him, Fergus said:

> “Let this sword, with which ‘the iron-death’ is performed, be stored away by you; here after me shall arise one with the name of Fergus. Let this sword be treasured by you, so that no one else takes it from you; my part in this matter for all time shall be this: that men shall retell the story of the sword.”

So Fergus’s soul departed from his body. His grave was dug, his name was written in the Ogham, and his lamentation ceremony was performed. From the monumental stones [*uladh*] piled by the men of Ulster, the name of *Uladh* [Ulster] had its origin.

Thus ends the Death of Fergus and the doings of the Luchra-people.

->*This that follows is the Birth of Cormac, grandson of Conn.*<-

Art, son of Conn of the Hundred Battles, went to fight the battle of *magh mucramha* against Maccon. Westwards over the Shannon he marched with the general army of all Ireland, and the night before the battle he stayed as a guest in the house of Olc Acha the smith. That night they had unpleasant conversation and harsh words: Olc Acha said to Art that there was no better or more fitting reason for him to give battle to Maccon than there had been for his engaging Eoghan, son of Olioll Olom; furthermore, he said Art's cause was poor, because Lughaid [surnamed Maccon] had certain rightful claims against him. "How many children do you leave behind?" the smith asked Art, who answered: "I know of only one son." "That is too few," the smith said. "Tonight, marry my daughter, for it is prophesied for me that from my lineage some great dignity must arise." This was proven true, for Cormac, son of Art, son of Conn of the Hundred Battles, was indeed a person of great dignity.

That night the king mated with Olc Acha's daughter Etan, and it was then that Cormac was conceived. Art told her that she would bear a son and that he would be king over Ireland. Then also he gave her all secret instructions for the boy's benefit and declared to her that on the morrow he would be killed. [In the morning] he bade her farewell, saying: "Take your son to his friend in Connacht, to Lughna in Corann, to be fostered there"; and as he had predicted, the king was later killed in the battle.

Accordingly, Etan was found to be with child, and [in due time] she decided to travel to Lughna's house so that she might give birth to the child she carried there. But as soon as she arrived within that country, her labor pains began; she stepped down from her chariot and gave birth to a son. Her maid went and pulled twigs, which she scattered under

Once upon a time, Cormac and Lughna’s sons, Ochomon and Nathnach, were at play. He struck one of them, and “Oh dear,” cried the boy who was struck, “a fellow whose clan and race are unknown has struck me—except that he is a gentleman without a father!” At this, Cormac, in great dejection, sought out Lughna and told him how he had been insulted. “That is not true,” his guardian said. “You are the very prince’s son, son of Art, son of Conn of the Hundred Battles, and it is foretold that you will hold your father's helm. Then the two went their way: Lughna and Cormac, accompanied by his wolves. He also had a bodyguard of Kerns who, from the time of Eochaid Airemh until that present day, had been in Corann; for it was they who slew Eochaid because of an excessively heavy rent that had been imposed on them. They are the *firchúl Bregh* of today, <note>and are there</note> because they came there with Cormac out of comradeship.

So they continued until they reached Tara, where they were welcomed, and Cormac was received on the footing of a <term>dalta</term> <note>that is, a protégé and pupil</note>. At that time, there was a female hospitaller in Tara named Bennaidh, whose roaming sheep came and ate the queen’s crop of woad. The case was referred to Lughaid Maccon <note>the king</note> for judgment, and his ruling was that the queen should have the sheep in place of the woad. “No,” Cormac said, “the shearing of the sheep is a sufficient compensation for the cropping of the woad, for both the one and the other will grow again.” “That is the true judgment!” everyone exclaimed. “It is a true prince’s son who has pronounced it!” One half of the house in which the false judgment had been given slid down the steep slope <note>on which it stood</note> and will remain that way forever; from this comes <term>claenfherta Temrach</term>, or ‘the sloping mounds of Tara.’

Maccon’s rule, in truth, was not good; therefore, the men of Ireland drove him away and bestowed the kingship upon Cormac. After

As long as Cormac lived, the world was full of all good things. Cormac also continued to keep his wolves with him; the reason for the great esteem he held for wolves was that they had raised him.

He carried out the renovation and decoration of Tara as it had never been seen before, regarding both houses and ramparts and all other structures: both *laech*-houses <note>warrior houses</note> and ladies' chambers, and 'houses of the earth' <note>underground storehouses, cellars, etc.</note>. Ireland was also very prosperous during that king's time: because of the abundance of fish, the rivers could not be forded, nor could her woods be easily crossed due to the profusion of forest mast; while because of the quantity of honey granted from heaven on account of his righteous rule, traveling across the plains was no easy task. The number of wild animals for the hunt was also so great that, even if the people had neither cultivation nor harvest, they would have been provided with plenty of meat.

Thus, Cormac continued to reign in Tara, and in time, he constructed the noblest building ever erected there. Although he was opposed by Ulster, he was never removed from his kingdom; however, he died in the house of *Spelán* the hospitaller when a salmon bone, which had been kneaded into the wheat bread given to him, stuck in his throat. This was the cause of his death.

What Cormac bequeathed to his confidants, and commanded of them, was this: not to bury him in the *Brugh* <note>Brú na Bóinne</note>, because he and those buried there did not worship the same god. Instead, he ordered his burial in Ros-naree, with his face turned eastward toward the rising sun.

### *Laeghaire mac Crimthann's visit to the fairy realm of Magh meall or 'the Plains of Pleasure.'*

Once upon a time, when Crimthann Cas was their king, the people of Connacht held a convention by *énloch* or 'Bird Lake' in *magh nAei* or 'the Plain of Aei.' They remained assembled through the night in question, and when they rose early the next morning, they saw a man coming toward them through the mist. He wore a five-folded mantle, and in his hand were two five-barbed darts; a gold-rimmed shield was slung across him, a gold-hilted sword was at his belt, and golden-yellow hair streamed behind him.

"Give a welcome to him who comes to you!" cried *Laeghaire Libhán* son of Crimthann, who was the noblest young man in Connacht. "A welcome to the warrior whom we do not know!" he said to the stranger, who answered, "I thank you all."

"Why do you come?" Laeghaire asked, and the other said, "To ask for a force of men."

"Where are you from?"

He replied, "I am of the men of the <term>sídhe</term>; *Fiachna mac Retach* is my name. The matter is that my wife has been taken from my head <note>meaning from his pillow</note>, for Eochaid son of Sál has carried her away. After I killed him in a pitched battle, she went to his nephew: Goll son of Dalbh, who rules the fort of *magh meall*. I have fought seven battles against him, but all have gone against me; for this very day another one has been declared by us, and I have come to solicit help. Furthermore, to every man who desires it, I will give a fair sum of gold and an equal amount of silver in exchange for coming with me." With that, he turned and left them.

"It would be a shameful thing not to help that man," Laeghaire said, and along with fifty fighting men, he stepped out after the stranger. Still preceding them, the stranger dived down into the lake, and they followed him. There they saw a strong fortress before them, and an army drawn up for battle that stood face to face with them. *Fiachna mac Retach* continued on in front of them and to his

<header>The Gilla decair.</header>

### *This is the pursuit of the Gilla decair and his Horse.*

A noble and excellent king once held royal rule and supreme authority over Ireland: Cormac, son of Art, son of Conn of the Hundred Battles. During this strong sovereign's reign, Ireland was disciplined, prosperous, peaceful, happy, rich, and full of all good things. It was no wonder she was so, for in his practice of hospitality, Cormac was a provider; in poetry, he was a poet; and in martial worthiness, he was a true king.

In the time of this same sturdy king, Finn—son of Cumall, son of Trenmor’s grandson Baeiscne—was the commander-in-chief of Ireland’s Fianna. That is to say, Cormac was the monarch over all; after him came the five provincial kings and then the royal captains. Finn, as the leader of these captains, was considered the seventh king in the order of those who ruled Ireland at that time.

The profits and wages of Finn and the Fianna were abundant: a townland in every <term>tuath</term>, a <term>cartron</term> of land in every townland, and in every house, a wolf-dog whelp or a beagle pup to be raised from All-hallows to Beltane, along with many other privileges not mentioned here. However great these privileges were, the pains and hardships that Finn and his followers, the Fianna, faced in return were far greater: to fend off and repel foreign invaders and overseas aggressors, to stop the thefts and schemes of outlaws, and to prevent all other villainy. As is described here, the Fianna performed much exhausting work to safeguard Ireland.

One day, while Finn and the Fianna were in Leinster's spacious Almhain enjoying the exhilarating and cheerful banquet of All-hallowtide, Finn—who had the gentlemen and chief nobles close beside him—asked if they thought it was time to go out and hunt. This was how they spent the year: from Beltane to All-hallows, they spent their time hunting and in acts of <term>venery</term>; from All-hallows to Beltane, they were tasked with the prescribed protection of all Ireland.

At any rate, they then resolved to proceed with the arrangement of that noble hunt, and the ground they went to for that purpose was Munster’s two proud provinces [namely, Thomond and Desmond]. Accordingly, they set out from Almhain by the nearest paths until they reached *tuath ó mBuilc*, the center of Fircall, and the Brosna river in Slievebloom; then on to Eibhliu’s twelve mountains (or ‘Slievephelim’), to *cnámhchoill* (or ‘Cleghile’ of *mac Raighne*), and to *drom collchoille*, which is now called *Aine cliach* or ‘Knockany.’

The hunt was spread out and extended by them along the borders of that forest which men today call *magh Breogain*; through blind and trackless places and the broken lands; over fair and open level regions and Desmond’s lofty hills, called at this day *luachair Deghaid* or ‘Slievelogher’; in among beautiful and pleasant Slievecrot, *sliabh na muc’s* lovely smooth *tulachs*, and the even banks of the azure-streaming Suir; across the green-grassed, verdure-coated plain of Femen, and Eithne’s high-lying rugged Decies, on to dark-wooded Ballachgowran.

In short: there was no wood, plain, or hill-country in both provinces of Munster where a chief of nine did not hunt and practice woodcraft, deploying and distributing the chase. Finn sat on his hunting-mound, and certain of the good warriors stayed with him: his own son Ossian, Ossian’s son Oscar; Goll mac Morna, Art ‘of the great strokes’ mac Morna; Dathchain’s son Sciathbreac, bearer of Finn’s shield; the three Balbhs; the three sons of the ‘caird of Berra’; Caeilte son of Ronan, Duibhne’s grandson Dermot of the glittering teeth, Liathan *luath* (or ‘the swift’) from *luachair Deghaid*; Conan mac Morna, the Fianna’s man of scurrilous and abusive speech, along with Finn Bane son of Bresal. In the forests and waste places around him, Finn and his accompanying Fianna thought it sweet to hear the hounds’ cry and their baying, the youths’ hurried calls, the strong men’s noise and din, and the whistling and joyful shouting of the Fianna.

Finn asked of those who were with him who would go watch and guard the hill [on the side of which the mound of his seat was made], and Finn Bane, son of Baeiscne’s grandson Bresal, answered the chief captain that he would go. Now the sea rose, turning into a wondrous and loudly roaring thing of awe, in a fierce and varied-sounding, wild-racing, heavy mass; in restless peaks, curving and grim-topped; in gloomy, dark, impenetrable surfaces; in wide-jawed, white-capped waves; in mighty, foam-crested hills that seemed frenzied and devoid of reason in their motion; in dire currents fed by many smaller streams; and in heavily laden, wide-reaching, broken green waters. To Finn and his people, it was both a lullaby and an early morning wake-up call to hear the broad ocean’s concert as it purred against the ship’s sides one moment and then loudly boomed, accompanying her always.

Dermot followed the wizard. They journeyed long and far from that spot until they found a towering fortress ahead of them. Inside were one hundred and fifty high-spirited men-at-arms with an appropriate number of noble women, as well as a white-toothed, rosy-cheeked, delicate-handed, and black-eyebrowed maiden sitting against the castle wall. She wore a silken mantle and a tunic woven with golden threads, and on her head, a queen’s proper decorated wimple. 

Dermot was given a most friendly welcome by his name and surname. He was placed in an infirmary, where valuable and potent herbs were applied to his wounds, and he was healed completely—made "whole" again. Now the castle’s tables and benches were set. No commoner was placed in a noble's seat, nor a noble in a commoner’s; rather, at these tables, everyone was in their proper place according to their rank, inheritance, or skill. Excellent, delicious foods were brought to them, along with well-flavored strong drinks. They spent the first part of the night banqueting, the second in intellectual and mental recreation, and the third they concluded with the soundest sleep, lasting until the sun’s fiery orb rose over the physical world the next morning.

For three days and three nights, Dermot stayed in the fort, served with the best feast he had ever had. At the end of that time, he inquired what this castle and country were where he found himself, and who ruled over it. The wizard told him that this was *tír fó thuinn*, or "the submerged land" <note>literally "the land under the wave"</note>. The man who had fought with him was the king of that realm, and his title in chivalry was "the Wizard of the Well." With that, the king glanced at Finn, who understood within himself that the king was seeking help and partnership from him; he therefore said: "I take upon myself the holding and the defense of this land until I leave it."

The King of the Greeks had an unmarried daughter named Taise (called *taebghel* or ‘white-sided’). Just as the sea surpasses all torrents, the Shannon other rivers, and the eagle all other birds, she transcended all the women of the world in form, beauty, and appearance. Because of his fame and wide renown, she loved Finn even though she had never seen him. Therefore, she begged her father for the favor of allowing her to watch the combat arranged between Finn and her brother. The king granted her this permission, and she brought with her the handmaid who was assigned to accompany her.

The Greek prince approached the tent where Finn and his friend the king were, whereupon Finn said: “I see it all—he wants single combat with me, and one of my people to fight with each of his men.” Like two most formidable lions, he and the Greek confronted each other; in their hostility, they were like a pair of venomous snakes, or again, in their swift-footed rushes, like two taloned griffins. The heavy soil of the earth shook beneath their tread. With the speed and fervor of those good warriors' strikes, they actually knocked the straight swords from their hands, the sound echoing among the crags and distant recesses. At last, Finn dealt the prince a heavy blow of mighty impact and sent his head flying far from his graceful neck and body. A shout of victory and triumph was raised by Finn and his people; while from the Grecian fleet came a cry of gloom and discouragement. A monumental stone was raised over the grave of the fallen, and their names were written in <term>Ogham</term> above them all. As great as the love was that white-bodied Taise had first felt for Finn, she felt seven times more as he slaughtered her brother. Therefore, she secretly sent him a message, offering herself to him—a proposal that gave Finn great joy and to which he was completely inclined.

That night, Taise stole away to join him. In the morning, the monarch awoke, and he was told how Taise had fled to Finn. He did not lament the loss of his people now, but only the loss of white-bodied Taise. He declared that he would bestow many precious things and great wealth upon anyone who could recover her from Finn.

Without stopping for either rest or recreation, Cathal traveled until he reached Sligo at the very moment when—in order to avenge the Connacht crone’s basket upon the Munster crone—O’Conor-Sligo was about to set forth. Just as he was ready to march, he saw a kern coming toward him who wore clothes with narrow stripes, and who said: “God save you, O’Conor!” “And you too,” O’Conor answered: “where have you been just now?” “Last night I was in the Lagan of Leinster, in M’Keogh’s house; the night before, twelve miles outside of Limerick in the house of *Shane mac an iarla* of Desmond; the night before that again in O’Donnell’s mansion at Ballyshannon; and in *dún monaidh*, in the king of Scotland’s house, the night before. In Ellach of the kings I was born. I am in Islay one day, in Cantyre another; a day in Man, a day in Rathlin, and another on Finncharn in Slievefuad; for I am a poor, rambling, shambling, flighty fellow.” “What name do you bear?” the Chief inquired. “My name is *Gilla dé*; and what is it that takes you all away from home?” O’Conor answered: “I am setting out for the purpose of giving battle to Munster.” “If you would only hire me, I would go with you,” said the Kern; but one of O’Conor’s own kerns spoke up and called out: “By my faith, it is not just that we would not hire you, but we wouldn’t take any bribe or reward if it meant having you with us at all!” “It is not with you I seek to go, but with O’Conor,” returned *Gilla dé*: “and it might well happen that by having me with him, O’Conor should in the end be none the worse.” The Chief then questioned him: “How much will it take to hire you, *Gilla dé*?” “I ask for nothing except that while I remain with you, nothing unfair be done to me,” he said; and O’Conor promised him that he should have those terms.

The men of Connacht marched and, crossing over the Shannon to the west, carried out a three-day raid into Munster. O'Conor handed the cattle over to the Connacht crone. But they had not been driving the captured livestock for long when they saw the brave men of both Munster provinces [Thomond and Desmond] following closely after their cattle. *Gilla dé* presented himself before O'Conor and gave him a choice: whether he wanted the cattle driven onward or the pursuers held back. The Chief said that he would rather the pursuit be stopped, so *Gilla dé*, with a bow and twenty-four arrows, turned on the pursuers. He never fired without striking down eighty-one of the Munster men, so that within bow-shot of him, no one could stand his ground without being hit. On the other hand, although all the Connacht men had [during this time] focused their efforts on just twenty of the captured cattle, they had not managed to drive them even the distance of an arrow's flight.

O'Conor sent for *Gilla dé* and now ordered him to drive the cattle. With immediate agreement and with the speed of a swallow, the *gilla* swept around the cattle to herd them and drove them all until, by virtue of hard running, they were far beyond Munster’s sight. But the pursuers, noticing *Gilla dé* turn his back on them, hurried after the Connacht men and slaughtered them so unmercifully that he was forced to turn back and stop the pursuit again.

In this manner, he was kept running back and forth between the cattle and the pursuers until they recrossed the Shannon from the west and returned home to Sligo and O'Conor's dwelling-place.

The Chief entered before everyone else, and when a drink was put into his hand, he drained it without a thought for *Gilla dé*. The *gilla* arrived instantly in O'Conor's presence and announced that he was taking his leave of him. This was unwelcome to the leader, and he said that to make up for the insult regarding the drink, the Kern should name his own reward. But the *gilla* declined the offer and refused to stay with him any longer, saying that he had composed certain verses regarding the matter:

> "An injustice to *Gilla dé* is shameful for the one who commits it; what I tell the Chief is that the judgment he has made is poor. It was certainly I who went to Tralee to fetch the cattle; it is not fair that the one who could stop the pursuit should be the only one to receive nothing. Even if I had been with Brian's son Murrough, taking hostages and cows along with all other spoils—even if we had seized the rents of the whole world—I would never have given him more than half of the total."

O'Conor looked around once, but he never knew into which direction of the world *Gilla dé* had vanished.

Then he left their presence and did not stop or stay until he came to Shane O’Donnellan’s house; a <term>mether</term> <note>a square wooden drinking vessel</note> of bonnyrowar <note>thick milk</note> and a dish of crab apples were served to him, and of these he ate his full share. He left their presence as well without taking leave or saying farewell, and afterward, by running with great speed, he moved ahead in such a way that they did not know which direction in the whole wide world he had taken—only that he had departed and was heard of no more. And so there you have the Journey of Manannan mac Lir of the *tuatha dé danann*, who used to wander about in the character of a magician and a master of various arts—one who played tricks of wizardry on everyone—until now at last he has vanished from among us, leaving nothing behind but the report of him; just as all other magicians and artists who have ever lived have vanished, so too have the Fianna and all classes of people who have appeared since that time or shall appear for all time, and in the end, we will vanish along with them.

*Here is the visit of Cael an iarainn, the son of the King of Thessaly, to Ireland, and how unfortunately his walking-match turned out for him; or according to some authorities, the Adventure of the Carle of the Drab Coat.*

It was a day of gathering and conference held by Finn, son of Cumall, son of Art, son of Trenmor, grandson of Baeiscne, with the seven battalions of the reserve and seven of the regular Fianna, at the Hill of Edar, son of Edgaeth. As they looked out over the sea and the great ocean, they saw a large and grand ship that was heading straight toward them from the east under full sail. She was fitted out as if for war and battle; and they did not have to wait long before they noticed a tall, warlike, and impetuously brave <term>óglaech</term> vault by means of his javelin staves or his spear shafts, so that both his feet landed on the white-sanded beach. He wore a polished and very handsome <term>lorica</term>; solid and unbreakable armor surrounded him; his handsome red shield was on his shoulder, and a hard helmet was on his head. At his left side was a straight-bladed, wide-grooved sword; in his two fists he held a pair of thick-shafted spears, unpolished but sharp. A fitting scarlet cloak hung on his shoulders, with a brooch of refined gold on his broad chest.

Thus equipped then, and in this manner, he came into the presence of Finn and the Fianna; and Finn spoke to him, saying, "Of all the world's bloodlines, noble or low-born, who are you, warrior; or from which of the four directions have you come to us?"

"*Cael an iarainn* is my name, the King of Thessaly’s son; and in all the parts of the globe that I have traveled (since I left my own land until this moment), I have not left any island or isle that I have not brought under the tribute of my sword and under my own power. "Conan," Cael answered, "in your words I find nothing but those of a fool or a simpleton; for if all those of the Fianna who have died during these past seven years were added to those who still live, I would in a single day subject them all to the sorrow of death and a shortened life. "Let it be done so," Cael agreed.

"So let it be done," Finn agreed: "but what is your name?" and he answered: "my name is *bodach an chóta lachtna* or 'the carle of the drab coat.'"

Then Finn and the Carle returned back again, and nothing is told of their travel or journeying until they reached Ben-Edar.

There, the Fianna of Ireland gathered in great numbers around the big man, for they had never before seen anyone like him; *Cael an iarainn* also arrived on the scene and asked whether Finn had brought a man to race against him. Finn replied that he had, and showed his man; but when Cael had seen the Carle, he protested that he would never race against such a greasy *bodach*. Hearing this, the latter let out a coarse burst of horse-laughter, saying: "Regarding me, you are mistaken, warrior; inform me, therefore, of the length of the course you would run. If I do not run it with you—and more besides, if that is your pleasure—then the stakes shall be yours to take." "I do not care," Cael replied, "to have a course before me of less than sixty miles." "It is well as it happens," said the Carle: "it is exactly sixty miles from Ben-Edar to Slieveluachra in Munster." "So let it be done," Cael agreed. "Well then," the *bodach* suggested, "the right thing for us to do is to head west to Slieveluachra to begin with, and stay there tonight, so that tomorrow we may be ready for our start and our walk."

Those two good <term>laechs</term> <note>warriors</note> (*Cael an iarainn*, namely the King of Thessaly's son, and the Carle of the drab coat) set out accordingly, and of their journey there is no record until, as the sun went down, they reached Slieveluachra in Munster. "Cael," the other said then, "it is necessary for us to put together some kind of dwelling, whether a house or a hut, to have over our heads." But Cael retorted: "By all that is certain, I will never set about building a house on Slieveluachra for the sake of passing one night there, considering that I have no desire at all to ever return here during the whole course of my life." "So be it," said the *bodach*: "but if I manage to build one, anyone who did not help to make it will be kept far outside."

The Carle then entered the nearest dark and intricate wood, where he never stopped or rested until he had tied up twenty-four pairs of thick timbers; and these, along with a full set of rafters from the same wood and fresh mountain rushes, he brought in a single load and so built a house, long and wide, completely thatched and warm. Using the forest’s sticks, both green and dry, he built a vast bonfire on the floor of that lodging and addressed Cael a second time: "If you are man enough to come with me and seek some game or other in these woods—" "I know nothing about it," Cael answered: "and even if I did, I would not go as a helper to the likes of you."

Again the *bodach* sought the depths of the nearest wood, and he had not gone far into it when he flushed out a herd of wild swine; he cut off the stoutest boar he saw from the rest and followed it along every track and through every thicket until, by tireless running and great effort, he overcame and struck it to the ground. Neatly and quickly, he prepared the boar and set it down to roast before that same great fire, using a mechanical spit that would keep it turning on its own. Then the Carle set off and never stopped until he reached the Baron of Inchiquin’s house (which was thirty miles from Slieveluachra); he took away two barrels of wine, two pewter dishes, all the bread that was ready in the house, a table, and a chair, all of which he carried in a single load back to Slieveluachra. There he found his meat roasted; he set aside half of the boar, half of the bread, and one barrel of wine for the morning; the other half of each he served to himself on the table and sat down comfortably and luxuriously. Then the *bodach* takes him by his fingertips, leads him to his ship, and places him in a sitting position within it; he gave the ship's stern a kick, and with that same kick sent her seven leagues out to sea. This is the way in which the expedition of the king of Thessaly’s son, *Cael an iarainn*, turned out for him: to be sent home in the condition of a fool or simpleton, without the power ever again, as long as he lived, to strike a blow in battle or in a tough single combat. The *bodach* came back to Finn and the Fianna, and told them that he was the fairy chief of *ráth Chruachan* or ‘Rathcroghan,’ who came to release them from the bonds in which they had been <note>that is, to help them in their time of need</note>. For the fairy chief, Finn then prepared a feast and banquet that lasted a year and a day.

So far then are the adventures of *Cael an iarainn*, the king of Thessaly’s son, and of the Carle of the Drab Coat.

## *How the Leg of Cian son of Maelmuaidh son of Bran was healed.*

One day, when the stewards of Brian of the Tribute went to collect his rent and taxes in West Munster, they came to the house of O'Cronagan of *Coirell*. However, O'Cronagan himself (who was a dependent of *Cian, son of Maelmuaidh*) was not at home. His wife asked who they might be, and they answered, "We are the king of Ireland's stewards." "And who is king over Ireland?" the woman asked again. "Brian, son of Kennedy; we are here to collect his tribute." "We have never paid rent to any man, nor will we pay any to him." So the stewards went away and returned to Kincora, where Brian was with the nobles of the Dalcassians; at that time, he was also holding a great festival for the men of Ireland. The stewards reported the insult that O'Cronagan's wife had given them, and Brian said, "I well know how that will be settled; for before the men of Ireland depart from me, I will set out and avenge this dishonor upon O'Cronagan." "That is the proper thing to do," the nobles of the Dalcassians said, and they all went away to the Coirell of O'Cronagan. There they burned the *triucha céd* immediately adjoining him, but once again he was not at home.

Therefore, his wife followed them as they retreated and found Brian and the chieftains of the Dalcassians at the rear of the plunder; she greeted them, and Brian responded to her. Then she began: "You have unjustly taken this plunder from us, because we have never yet paid rent to any man; the one who is lord over us has never demanded any such thing." "And who is he?" "Cian, son of Maelmuaidh, who is a dependent of your own; and, Brian, grant me a favor now!" "I will," said the king. "Well then, return my little greyhound and my sheep to me." "That, on my conscience, is a lady's request, and you shall have it. You, therefore, Cian son of Mahon, go and give her as much of the plunder as you are able to overtake as a reward for her wise speech; as for O'Cronagan, let him follow me to

She answered that, although she was reluctant, she would do as he asked. However, the elderly couple said they were displeased by the matter, as they did not know if this was all a plot orchestrated by Brian for some purpose.

The next morning O'Cronagan and the young woman rose and traveled to Coirell-O'Cronagan; and as they drew near to the town, a young man met them and told them that O'Cronagan's wife was missing. In this way O'Cronagan sat at the table, while Cian and the wife were together <note>waiting on the company</note>; and he told her that he felt a great love for her and longed for her companionship. She, however, declaring to him that she would never be his, Cian proceeded to knock her down; whereupon she was immediately changed into a large brood mare and rushed for the door. Cian indeed caught her by one hind leg; but she, raising the other, struck him in the leg and broke it, after which she managed to escape.

<header>The Cave of Keshcorran.</header>

### *Here follows the Enchanted Cave of Keshcorran.*

It was a great and general hunting match that was held by Finn son of Cumall son of Art son of Trenmor, grandson of Baeiscne, with the brave and handsome Fianna of the Gael, which was convened throughout the fair borders of Corran; among the beautiful <term>*tuatha*</term> of Leyny; within the borders of Brefny; in the trackless wilderness of Glendallan; in the nut- and mast-abundant regions of Carbury; in the thick coverts of Kyleconor’s woods, and over the wide, flat expanse of Moyconall.

Then Finn sat upon his hunting mound on the top of high Keshcorran; at which moment no one stayed with him but his two wolf-dogs, *Bran* and *Sceolaing*, and Conan Mael mac Morna. Now it was sweet for Finn to look on; to listen to the hounds’ music, to the young men’s clear joyous cheering, to the voices of athletic warriors and the deep tones of mighty men, to the various whistling of the Fianna in all the wild and desert forests of the land. For even in the bordering countries, those hunting cries which they let out were freely heard; these were such that deer were roused out of their wilds, badgers <note>brocks</note> banished from their holes, and birds driven to take wing. At this point, every angry and fiercely eager wolf-dog was slipped from its leash to course the <term>*tulach*</term>.

However, the ruler who held sway in Keshcorran at that time was Conaran son of Imidel, a chief of the <term>*tuatha dé danann*</term>; and as soon as he perceived that the hounds’ cry now sounded scattered, he ordered his three daughters (who were full of sorcery) to go and take vengeance on Finn for his hunting. The women sought the entrance of the cave that was in the <term>*tulach*</term>, and there sat beside each other. Upon three crooked and twisted sticks of holly, they hung as many pagan, bewitched skeins of yarn, which they began to reel off counter-clockwise in front of the cave. ### *Here follows the origin of the Battle of Magh Mucramha, and the occasion of Lughaid mac Con’s death.*

Olioll Olom, son of Mogh Nuadat, of the lineage of Heber, son of Milesius of Spain: this Olioll was king of Munster; and with him was Sabia, daughter of Conn of the Hundred Battles.

Three sons of hers—<term>Eoghan</term>, <term>Cian</term>, and <term>Cormac Cas</term>, sons of Olioll—were the ancestors from whom are descended the <term>Eoghanacht</term>, the <term>Cianacht</term>, and the <term>dáil gCais</term>, i.e., ‘the Dalcassian race’ or ‘the Tribes of Thomond.’ A foster-son to Olioll and Sabia was <term>Lughaid</term>, surnamed <term>mac con</term> (or ‘wolf-dog’s son’), who was of the <term>corca Luighe</term>, and was nursed on the same knee and at the same breast as Olioll’s son Eoghan.

To wreak his vengeance on the men of Ireland, Maccon then went with this great army, with this massive host; and truly, it was no loving son of Ireland who brought them. They harried the land, and great multitudes submitted to them there; but until they reached *magh mucramha* on the borders of *óg Bethra*, namely northwards from *áth cliath*, they encountered no resistance.

(Now *magh mucramha*, or "the plain of *mucramh*," is derived thus: It was certain pagan pigs that once upon a time emerged from the Cave of Cruachan—that is to say, the Hell’s Gate of Ireland, out of which the *ellén trechenn* came and ravaged Ireland until, in the presence of all Ulidia, Amergin, the father of Conall Cernach, destroyed it in single combat. From this cave also came a flock of white birds that, throughout Ireland, withered up whatever their breath touched, until such time as the men of Ulidia killed them with their slings. Out of this cave, I say, those same swine emerged; and they were such that in any spot they trod, neither corn, nor grass, nor leaf would sprout before the end of seven years. In any place where they were counted, they did not stay; if the counting of them was even attempted, they would migrate into another country. Nor was it possible to count them so that <note>even with several people doing it</note> they should arrive at the same total: “There are three there!” one would say; “Seven, rather!” another would cry; “Eleven pigs!” “Thirteen pigs!” and so their count would be lost. The swine could not be wounded <note>killed</note> either; for when they were attacked with missiles, they would disappear. Once, however, Meave of Cruachan and Ailill <note>her husband</note> proceeded to count them on the plain of *mucramh*, and the pigs were numbered by them <note>that is, the attempt was made</note>; but, while Meave was in her chariot, one hog among them cleared it in a single leap. Everyone cried out: “There goes a pig over you, Meave!” “Not at all!” said the queen as she caught the pig's leg <note>as it passed</note>; but at the beast’s forehead the skin opened, so that in Meave’s hand he left his hide <note>entire</note> with the leg <note>and so sped on his way</note>; nor from that time to this has it been known where they all went. Hence, it is called *magh mucrímha*, or "the plain of swine-counting.")

The plundering of Ireland was permitted to Maccon until he reached this same *magh mucramha* in the eastern part of Connacht;

(*Fiacha* was only a nickname for him, being essentially the same as *fer dá liach*, that is, the "man of two sorrows" or the "man of two pitiable things." As for the epithet *muillethan* or "broad-crown," the reason he was called that was this: at *áth Nemthenn* on the Suir <note>as she drove the wizard's chariot</note>, the pains of labor struck Dil's daughter Moncha. The night before the battle, *Olcacha* (a smith of Connacht) hosted him, and his speech was something like this: "A heavy company are these that Maccon brings against you—this herd of oxen of Alba's and Britain's men will bellow and will press you hard; their minds are not set on flight, for flight would be too far for some of them, even to *sliabh Ealpa* <note>The Alps</note>. And this came true; it was a great honor indeed: Cormac mac Art mac Conn. Art told her that she would bear a son who would be king of Ireland; and he shared with her every secret and every most hidden thing to be used for that son's well-being. He also informed her that he would be killed on the following day; he instructed her to take his son to his friend in Connacht to be fostered, and so he said farewell to her. Then, on the next day, he went duly to the battle.

Lughaid *mac con*, for his part, had his plans already prepared: half of his people were stationed underground, which means that a pit was made for his advanced guard and hurdles were laid over them; their spears were broken off at the bulge, and the tips just protruded through the hurdles. This was done at the point where the finest of the men of all Ireland were. Besides this, to ensure they would not desert, every Gael among those who had joined the invaders either had one leg fastened to that of an Albanach, or two Britons were assigned to one Gael. Immediately the air above them turned black with demons that waited for the miserable souls to drag them away to Hell. Except for two, there were no angels; yet whichever direction Art moved throughout the army, those two always stayed over his head (because of the true prince’s righteous nature).

The two lines advanced on one another, and they played a stern part on either side; there were grim sights: white dust of chalk and lime rose like a cloud from shields and targets battered by the edges of swords and the points of spears and javelins, well-given and well-taken by the warriors; the pounding and splintering of bucklers hammered with sword-blades and stones; the whirring sound made by the flight of missiles; the spouting and dripping of blood and gore from the limbs of commoners and through the sides of nobles. The manner of both Lughaids <note>*mac con* and *lágha*</note> up and down the battle was like bears among piglets; in that style, they dashed aside all men in turn. A crested helmet was on the head of each; around him, iron mail; in his hand, a great sword; and they charged the opposing host so that they laid low many hundreds of them. Eoghan and Corbchacht, sons of Olioll, were of the same likeness on the other side. This was a competitive contest, one worthy of honorable men, which the men of Erin and Alba fought together; and it was nearly the case that, in the process of their mutual pounding, every man had to trample on his fellow’s very feet. But as they were thus locked together, one man <note>then another</note> would be wounded from the ground at both his right and left rear and flung prostrate; then out of their pits, the men of Alba rose up and surrounded them. The purpose of holding the Feast of Tara was for a fortnight before Samhain—that is to say, on Samhain day itself—and for a fortnight after. And the reason for which they made it a practice to gather together at every *Samhain* season was this: because at such a season, the mast and other products were the best matured. Here too is the reason for which the Feast of Tara was held at all: the body of law which all of Ireland enacted then, during the interval between that and their next convention at a year’s end, no one might dare to violate; and he who by chance did so was outlawed from the men of Ireland.

Now the Ulidians, with a great army, set out to take part in the Feast, and they sent messengers ahead of themselves to examine their own house there, and also to scout Tara. The condition in which these messengers found their lodging was: no thatch, no means of warmth, walls gapping open, and all fouled by the royal town’s cattle and dogs. The emissaries returned and said that the house was not fit to be entered, and that in Tara, Cormac had only a small force. Then, to determine what they should do, the Ulidians assembled in a general council; and their decision was to throw themselves into battle order and to march on Cormac. Whereupon they sent him word to come and meet them in line, face to face, with their weapons between them. But Cormac’s strength was not sufficient to give them battle; what he did, therefore, was to evade them. Westwards he departed out of Tara; his trusted advisors joined him, and he questioned them on what plan they should adopt, and from what quarter they should seek reinforcements. Then it was that Cesarann, Cormac’s poet, said:—

> "O Cormac, unless you have some battle-winning friend closer at hand, then seek a champion from Munster—mighty and hard-hitting; a lord that may relieve you of all fear of enemies . . ."

So Cormac went to Olioll Olom’s house, and there a great welcome was given to him. “The reason for which we have come here,” he said, “is to entreat your good will.” “Which you shall have,” they answered: namely Cormac Cas, son of Olioll Olom, and Fiacha Broadcrown, son of Eoghan, and Olioll himself. Cormac and Fiacha were at this time Olioll’s representatives; and his country was divided between them, for he was not able to govern it himself: from the one *áth cliath* to the other every second subdivision of the land was allotted to Cormac, and the rest to Fiacha, with Teigue standing as next heir to either.

They—Olioll Olom, Cormac Cas, and Fiacha—then took counsel together; and what they planned was to lead Cormac to the place where he should find Lughaid *lágha*, with a view to him accompanying him northwards to fight the battle. Accordingly, they sought the spot where Lughaid was, and where should that be but in the glen of Aherlach: there they caught him bathing himself, and consequently unarmed. In order to hem him in on all sides, they divided themselves into three parties; Cormac approached him, held his naked sword over his head, and cried: “Death hangs over you, Lughaid!” “A death from me instead of my own!” Lughaid answered. “I will not accept it,” said Cormac, “unless it is a king’s head taken in battle.” “It shall be given to you.” “I will not accept it,” Cormac continued, “unless it is the head of Fergus Blacktooth, king of Ulidia.” “You shall have it.” “Pledge your honor to it,” insisted Cormac. “I do so.” Then Lughaid raised his head and said: “May he never thrive who prompted you! This is the old counselor’s advice that has been put into action here; and as its beginning has been bad for us, so too will its end be an ill one.”

Afterward they reached Crinna, and Teigue said to Cormac: “You come as well, with a strong force, to fight the battle, because I have come from my country with only a small number: fifty good warriors and thirty chieftains, *Lughaid lágha*, and myself.” “I will by no means bring an army with you for the battle. This was contrary to the custom that had prevailed in Ireland until then, which was: their elders in front, their prime men in the center, and their youths <note>striplings</note> in the rear. The reason for the traditional custom was that every man should face opponents of his own age. Now the

Then the armies proceeded to clash: Ulidia charged with reckless bounds, so that the earth shook again under the warriors’ feet; on both sides, their mindless horses of strange appearance were routed, distracted, and driven into a frenzy by the chaos of the bloody points and gold-encrusted edges of the weapons; by the blows on blood-red war-shields, by the hurling of sharp-headed javelins, long and thick, and by the rattle of glittering, proven mail. Then, falling at the same time, the old men of Ulidia and the young men of Munster killed each other.

Lughaid, venting his fury on the common soldiers until he reached him, finally got to Fergus through the crowd, and in doing so was badly wounded; however, he dragged Fergus’s head toward him and hacked it off. He went with it to where Cormac was and said to him: “Here, Cormac, is a king’s head taken in battle, just as I promised you; that is, Fergus’s head.” “A blessing on your bravery and your skill in arms, Lughaid,” said Cormac. “If the head of the true king had been brought to me, I would not have valued it more than this head of his own brother!” “Is that what it is then?” asked Lughaid. Cormac answered: “Indeed it is” (for on the spot, the men of Ulidia made Fergus Longhair their king; they set the king’s helmet on his head, he was saluted by them with the title of king, and they continued to fight for their own cause). “Very well, Lughaid,” Cormac continued: “recollect what you promised me—that I should receive a king’s head in battle from your hands—if it is now plain to you that this is not the king’s head; for I still see the king, with his helmet on his head.” “It is evident,” said Lughaid. “Now, stuff dry wads into my wounds to see whether I can manage anything against that other Fergus.”

After that, Ulidia was routed; and the ill-informed claim that Lughaid killed *Eochaid gunnat* in this battle, but it is not true. Against Ulidia on that day, seven battles "were broken" <note>won</note>: the battles of Crinna, of *Ráth chró*, of *Aircetros*, of *Conachadh*, of *Sithbe*, of *Ath an inathair*, and of *druim Fuaid*.

## The Story of *Eochaidh Muighmedóin’s* Sons.

Over Ireland was an admirable and eminent king: Eochaid, called *Muighmedóin*; and he had five sons: Brian, Ailill, Fiachra, Fergus, and Niall. *Mongfhionn*, or ‘Long-fair-haired,’ daughter of Fidach, was the mother of Brian, Fiachra, Fergus, and Ailill. *Cairenn*, called *Casdubh* or ‘the curly-black,’ daughter of Saxall, called *Balbh* or ‘the stutterer,’ king of the Saxons, was the mother of Niall. To the queen, this last son was an object of malice; for it was to her disgrace that the king had fathered him by Cairenn, whom the queen therefore kept in a state of great hardship. It was so great indeed that on one hand, she had to draw water for Tara, while on the other, all the rest of the female slaves were set against her alone, and they depended on her service [to keep them

## *Death of Crimthann son of Fidach, and of Eochaidh Muighmedóin's three sons: Brian, Ailill, Fiachra.*

A noble and revered king once ruled Ireland: *Eochaidh Muighmedóin*. He had a spouse worthy of him: Mongfhionn, daughter of Fidach, and she bore him four sons: Brian and Fiachra, Ailill and Fergus were their names. She had a dream concerning them, and it was this: that they were transformed into four carnivores. Brian took a lion's shape, Fiachra a greyhound's, Ailill a beagle's, and Fergus the shape of a common dog. Then they carried on with wrestling and tearing at one another. In the beginning, at every other bout the greyhound would defeat the lion; but finally, the lion prevails against all three who—meekly, submissively, and without a sign of rebellion—give in to him <note>acknowledge his superiority</note>. 

Mongfhionn tells this dream to the magician Sithchenn, and he says: "Just so; Brian will be an aggressive and a raging lion, and his descendants after him will be the same. Against the fury of all other men, they shall be a fiercely combative phalanx, steadfast in enduring the onslaughts of others. After them, Fiachra and his lineage will be given to war and excursions: he shall hack and hew at Brian's race, and Brian at his. Between them both there shall be armed strife and mutual mischief, and the rule shall be divided between the posterity of each alternately. In the end, however, the descendants of Brian will prevail over the children of all the other sons, and the pre-eminence shall be theirs. Ailill will be a hound of the chase, seeking out and striving for lands to provide for his brothers. As for Fergus, his descendants will be only a sorry set of commoners, and it is hardly likely that his race will be recognized at all."

Then there was dire contention for his land: Niall by himself on the one side, and Mongfhionn’s four sons on the other. What she decided upon, now that she had failed to get the kingdom for her son Brian alone (who was her favorite child), was this: through persuasion and magical practices (for she was an expert in all sorcery and witchcraft), she would entice the men of Ireland to confer the royal power upon his brothers, so that she might send him overseas to learn the art of war. Thus, he would later become an eminent hero fit to make the kingdom his own.

Accordingly, Brian crossed the sea and, with Senach son of Onga in the north of Scotland, learned warlike accomplishments until he was vigorously competent in all feats of arms and valor. When his training was perfected at the end of seven years, he returned from the east: a brown-haired, powerful, and bull-like man, with solid limbs, the strength of nine men, and endowed with equal weapon-skill in each hand—such was Brian.

Crimthann still reigned over Ireland, and it was a great vexation to Mongfhionn that Brian was not king. But Crimthann went on a royal progress into Scotland—for this was how the king of Tara always proceeded on his grand visitation: from Tara into the Galianic province <note>Leinster</note>; then into both provinces of Munster <note>Thomond and Desmond</note>; afterwards into the province of Olnegmacht <note>Connacht</note>, then again into the province of Ulster, and so into Scotland—whereupon Mongfhionn’s sons took forcible and violent hold of Crimthann’s domain. Upon hearing of this, he returned from the east; he brought a great host that he had mustered into Connacht to expel his sister’s sons from his kingdom. He marched and pitched camp on the Moy among the Connachtmen. Mongfhionn debated with herself, and what she imagined was that she should offer a banquet to Brian’s brothers on the Moy in Tirawley, and invite her own brother there as if to make peace with her sons. Lughaid *Menn*, son of Angus (called *Tíreach* or "landgrabber"), son of Fercorb, was the one who first and violently seized the land of Thomond. For this reason, it is called "Lughaid Red-hand's cruel sword-land"; seeing that the territories which the men of Munster acquired by main force were two: that of Ossory as an *eric* for *Edirsceol* (whom the people of Leinster killed), and Thomond as an *eric* for Crimthann son of Fidach. However, they do not possess it because they have any legitimate title to it; because, according to the legal right of provincial partition, such ground in Thomond belongs to the province of Connacht, which properly speaking extends from *Luimneach* [the lower Shannon] to the river Drowes.

Immediately and promptly, a crier stood up and, to restrain the servants and thieves, rattled a coarse iron chain; he shook a long one of antique silver to silence the gentlemen and chief nobles of the Fianna, as well as their professional scholars, and everyone listened in hushed silence. Fergus Truelips, the poet of Finn and the Fianna, rose and sang the songs, lays, and sweet poems of Finn’s ancestors and forefathers before Finn, son of Cumall. "By your own hand," said Goll, "if you were to dishonor me as your father did, I would deal you the very same treatment that I gave to Cumall." 

"Goll," Finn answered, "I have enough power not to let you get away with that; for against every one man in your household, I have a hundred warriors." 

"Your father was the same," said Goll, "and I avenged my dishonor on him; I would do the same to you, if you only deserved it of me."

Cairell Whiteskin, grandson of Baeiscne, spoke <note>mockingly</note>, saying, "Many a man, Goll, you have quelled in Finn mac Cumall's household!" 

Conan *mael* <note>the bald</note> mac Morna, a man of curses, spoke and said, "I swear by my weapons that, however few men he might have with him, Goll was never without a hundred and one men in his household, every one of whom would have quelled you!" 

"And are you one of them, you crooked-speaking, bald-headed Conan?" Cairell asked. 

"One of them exactly, you comb-wearing, nail-scratching, rough-skinned Cairell of little strength; and I would undertake to prove on your person that Finn <note>when he spoke</note> was in the wrong."

With that, Cairell stood up and struck Conan a furious blow; this was not responded to tamely by the victim, but right across his forehead and his teeth <note>over his whole face</note> he dealt Cairell another. In any case, they then delivered to each other's skin and entire bodies a series of rapid blows...

   Triumphantly now, Finn vented his battle-cry or "forest-shout," and enjoined all of Ireland's Fianna to utterly quench and unsparingly kill the sons of Morna <note>that is, all Clan Morna</note>.
   Then the Fianna made close, solid palisades of their shields around themselves; Finn put himself at the head of those men of might, and the two parties fell unrelentingly to splitting each other's bones. A ferment of anger took hold of Goll, and to shelter his people he turned himself into a massive, unbreakable shield; the various bands and their chieftains grew furious; the champions became reckless; the combatants increased in number, and from the tough, hostile battle they fought together, the martial men were full of injuries. Blood was plentiful there, flowing in streams down the sides of free-born offspring; deep and incurable gashes covered those destructive and inseparable phalanxes. It would have been a bad place for a feeble invalid, a delicate, taper-fingered woman, or an aged elder of long standing to be: the "little brawl" at Almhain on that night, listening to the groans of young and old, of high and low, as they lay maimed, faint, and infirm, or were struck down and cut up. At this game, then, they endured from the beginning of the night until the rising of the next day's sun, and never gave each other quarter.
   Then rose the wise and sharp-worded poet—the richly rewarded good man of verse—Fergus Truelips and, together with him, all the Fianna’s men of science, and they chanted their <term>duans</term>, their skilled rhymes, and eloquent panegyrics to those companies of men-at-arms, with a view to check and soothe them.
   Thereupon, with the poets' music, they ceased their hacking and hewing and allowed their weapons to fall to the ground; the poets picked up these arms and effected a reconciliation between their owners. ### *This that follows is the Adventure of Teigue, son of Cian.*

Once upon a time, Teigue—son of Cian, who was the son of Olioll Olom—was on his <term>next heir's circuit</term> into the west of Munster, and his own dear brothers, *Airnelach* and *Eoghan*, were with him. That was the very time and hour in which *Cathmann*, son of *Tabarn*—a man who was king of the beautiful land of Fresen, a country lying opposite Spain to the southeast—came out from the coasts of Fresen. This same Cathmann (with a force of nine first-rate ships' crews) came on a roving expedition, scouring the sea to make discoveries, until they reached land in the western part of Munster. There, near Berehaven (to be precise), they caught the country off guard and slipped ashore with the whole fleet; by whom the country was

Cathmann claimed Teigue's wife for himself, for his own bed and most private chamber; he relegated the two kinsmen to servitude and hardship. Eoghan was forced to work a common ferry across a fjord on the coast, and Airnelach was made to gather firewood and keep up fires for the people at large. For their support, they were given only barley seed and muddy, turbid water.

Teigue's situation must now be told: he was overcome by grief and discouragement for the sake of his brothers and his wife, who had been snatched from him by the Allmarachs. However, forty warriors of his people had also escaped being killed by them; on the contrary, they had each killed one of the attackers, and they had captured one of the seafaring men. This man told them the details of the land from which they had been attacked. As a result, the project Teigue formed was to build and equip (suitably for a long voyage) a swift, strongly constructed <term>currach</term> of twenty-five thwarts, which required forty ox-hides of hard, bark-soaked red leather. Then he provided all the necessary items for his currach: thick tall masts, broad-bladed oars, fully qualified pilots, and thwarts solidly laid and fitted in their places, so that in all respects this currach was exactly as it should be, and thoroughly watertight.

With a mighty effort, they now ran the craft down and bravely launched it. Some strong hands were in her, all standing by to meet the huge green billows and to deal with the high rising of the salmon-bearing, strong-crested sea and the rough, broken race of the spring tide. ...good clothing. The young men then being ready in every way, Teigue said: "Men! Take your <term>currach</term> to sea, and let us be off in search of our people who have been away from us for some time now"; and he recited a song:—

> "Take your currach out upon the high and stormy sea . . . "

Accordingly, they drove their vessel out onto the vast, limitless abyss, over the mass of the powerful and tremendous deluge, until at last they could see no land at all, neither ahead of them nor behind, but only the surface of the colossal ocean. Further on, they heard all around them the chorus of various unknown birds and the hoarse booming of the sea; shimmering, white-bellied salmon leaping all around the currach; in their wake followed thick and dark bull seals that constantly cut through the flashing spray of the oars as they pursued them; and following these again were great whales of the deep. Because of the incredible nature of their form, movement, and variety, the young men found it a festive thing to examine and watch them all, for until then they were not accustomed to seeing the various oceanic creatures and the bulky marine monsters. For twenty days and twenty nights they continued rowing on the sea in this way, and then they sighted a prominent land with a fair and favorable coast. They held a straight course toward it until they reached it, then everyone landed and they beached their currach there; they lit fires, their provisions were passed out to them, and the warriors ate them heartily. On the beautiful green grass, they made their beds, and from that moment until the bright hour of sunrise the next day, they enjoyed their sleep. Next day, Teigue rose early and prepared to walk through and search out the land, to make a circuit and find out whether there were any inhabitants, either men or beasts, on the island. He put on his battle armor, and thirty fully armed warriors of his people set out with him; they went straight ahead and explored the whole island, but they found no signs of human habitation whatsoever, nor anything else except for flocks of sheep. The size of these creatures was beyond words: they were no smaller than the largest horses, and the entire island was full of their wool. They found one especially remarkable flock of gigantic rams, among which one in particular exceeded all the others: nine horns decorated him, and he charged at our heroes, butting violently. Some of the sailors ate part of these eggs, and instantly a covering of feathers sprouted all over everyone who fed on them; however, when they bathed, this plumage would drop from them just as quickly. Now the <term>Allmarach</term> they had with them was the one who had set this course, for on a former occasion while cruising, he had followed this same track of theirs.

Again they pull away for six weeks (during which time they never made a landfall), until the Allmarach said: “We are all adrift and carried into the deep, illimitable ocean of the great abyss!” Then the wind rose with a rough roar; a great uproar was created in the sea, so that it turned into heaving hills and into great mountains difficult to climb. At the encounter of all this foul weather and these heavy squalls—things which until now they were not accustomed to enduring—great fear gripped the people of Cian’s son Teigue. To the end of a fortnight they stayed in that fort, and as a result of it all Eochaid Redweapon was made king over the fair realms of Fresen. To Teigue they yielded pledges and hostages. Then he urged his people that they should depart, telling them to face the sea cheerily; out of the strong place he carried away precious things, treasures, and other good booty, besides Liban his wedded wife and his two brothers: Eoghan and Airnelach. He reached Ireland bringing with him victory and spoils and, to wind up the story, Teigue made a poem:—

> “Time it is for us to seek our home, my fair and dear people.”

By him, Elim son of Conrach was slain in the battle of Acaill by Tara; he “won” twenty-five battles against those of Ulster, another twenty-five against Leinster, thirty-one against the men of Munster, and twenty-five against Connacht. All this was to avenge the murder of his father and of his grandfather, whom the Plebeian Tribes of Ireland had killed; it was against these Plebeians that Tuathal won all these battles. 

Then he sat down in Tara, and the Feast of Tara was held by him. All of Ireland flocked there to him: both men and women, both lads and lasses, and by all the elements they pledged themselves that they would never, for all eternity, strive for the sovereignty of Ireland against himself or against his descendants. The provincial kings present at that festival were these: Fergus of *Febhal*, king of Ulster; Eoghan son of Ailill *érann*, king of *Cúrói's* province or “West Munster”; Daire's son Eocho, king of the province of Eochaid son of Luchta or “Thomond”; Conrach son of Derg, king of Connacht; and Eocho son of Eochaid *doimhlén*, who ruled Leinster.

Now Tuathal had two daughters, loving and beloved: *Fithir* and *Dáirine* were their names. Because it was not the custom or practice in Ireland at that time that the younger should “be married before her elder sister’s face” (that is, be married before her), the son of Eochaid *doimhlén* took the elder daughter to wife and brought her home to *ráth imil* in Leinster. This daughter of Tuathal's was also the dear foster-child of the king of Connacht mentioned above. 

However, the people of Leinster said to their king: “You have left behind the better one.” Therefore, he went north to Tara again and said to Tuathal: “The girl that I took away is dead, and now I wish to take your other daughter.” 

Tuathal answered: “Had I fifty-one daughters, they would all be given to you so that you might enjoy a wife from among them.” 

Therefore, the other maiden, Dáirine (who was the foster-child of the king of Ulster), was given to him, and he carried her also to *ráth imil*, where the first sister was still living. When Fithir saw Dáirine, she died immediately of shame; when Dáirine witnessed her sister's death, she likewise died of grief.

What Connacht said then was that they would accept nothing from Leinster but battle; Ulster pronounced the same; but the King of Ireland said: “I indeed do not care to give battle to Leinster; nevertheless, if it is your resolve, let everyone in general march directly upon them.” Together they numbered twelve thousand, and Connacht took their way over *Guala* to Naas, where they camped; Tara’s host, with the King of Ireland, set out over *Buaidghen*, over *Righe*, and over *magh Nuadhat* (or Maynooth) to Naas, and there made camp; over *Esa*, over *Odhba*, over *Fithart*, and over *Faendruim*, Ulster set out and on to *Lethduma*, where they pitched their tents. In this engagement, Eocho, son of Eochaid *doimhlén* and King of Leinster, was slain, along with twenty other kings <note>prominent chiefs</note>. After this, the Boromha was not collected from Leinster until thirty royal maidens, each accompanied by a hundred young women, were slain at Tara by Dunlaing, son of Enna Nia. This event resulted in the *claenfherta*, or ‘sloping mounds,’ at that site, and because of it, the Boromha was once again imposed on Leinster. From that time forward, Leinster fought many battles over the matter of the tribute, until Laeghaire, son of Niall, acquired the sovereignty of Ireland. These battles and the most notable deaths were as follows: the battle of Maynooth, won by Bresal *bélach*; the battle of Cruachan *claenta*, won by Labradh against Eochaid *muighmedóin*; twelve battles that Enna won against Niall of the Nine Hostages; and Niall’s death at the hands of Enna’s son, Eochaid, at the Iccian Sea.

Then Niall’s son, Laeghaire, reigned over Ireland. He gathered the North with him to levy the Boromha and entered Leinster on a military campaign. At that period, the king of the province was Enna *cinnselach*, also known as ‘the quarrelsome,’ who was the son of Labradh and grandson of Bresal *bélach*. The people of Leinster rallied around Enna and gave battle to Laeghaire at the battle of *áth dara*, or ‘Adare,’ upon the River Barrow. There, Laeghaire was defeated, and a ‘red slaughter’ was made of Conn’s Half; their heads were collected into a cairn at *magh Ailbhe*, or ‘Moyalvy,’ on the side of the Barrow. Laeghaire himself was captured. He promised that he would never again collect the Boromha for as long as he lived if they would spare him. Furthermore, he pledged himself by an oath to the Elements that he would never again enter Leinster to levy it for all eternity. However, he did not fulfill any of these promises, for at the end of two and a half years, he returned and seized cattle at *sídh Nechtain*. For this reason, on the bank of the stream called *cas*, or ‘the crooked,’ the Elements delivered death to Laeghaire: the Earth swallowed him, the Sun scorched him, and the Wind [his breath] passed away from him. Then Finnachta *fledhach* or ‘the festive,’ son of Dunchadh, held Ireland for twenty years and twice carried off the Boromha *sine renitentia* <note>without resistance</note>; the third time that he came to collect it, Leinster rose against him. Intelligence of this reaches Bran son of Conall <note>king of Leinster</note>, by whom the province is summoned, and they travel (both laity and clergy) to Dunallen. However, Molling did not come with them, so they sent to fetch him; and where he was just then was at *ros broc* (which at this present time is called *tech Molling*, that is, ‘Molling’s house’ or ‘St. Mullen’s’), for from the time when he first came from *sruthair Guaire*, that is, ‘Guaire’s stream’ or ‘Shrule,’ until he reached *ros broc*, he had not found a place of habitation: *unde Molling cecinit* <note>from where Molling sang</note>:—

As soon as that summons reached Molling, he assembled his *familia* <note>community or household</note> and made a song:—

So Molling took his way to Dunallen, where the men of Leinster were; by all, a very gentle welcome was extended to him, and he sat down at the king of Leinster’s side.

A.D. 615 . . . *Suibhne menn* (being a very young man at that time) was in his own house one day, and perhaps said to his wife: “I marvel to see how small the measure of Kinelowen’s superiority over the rest of the tribes is at this hour.” To which the woman, answering with a kind of mockery: “And what hinders you from showing some bravery, from leading them to war against others and always having victory over them?” He said again: “Even so shall it be.”

Therefore, with his weapons about him, he went out on the next morning, and a young man of the local people, who was also armed, met him; Suibhne fought with him, forcing him into ‘submission at the point of a spear.’ In the same way <note>eventually</note>, he gathered an army for himself, by which he finally seized the sovereignty of Ireland.

A time came when he returned to his father’s and his mother’s house; but because of his sullenness, and because of his mother’s nature that was in him, his father did not love him. She, therefore, taking him away, placed him in a little dwelling apart, where he was raised together with a guardian he had. One day the boy came out, carrying in his hand for some other boys a spit on which were the remains of his meat, and so he came to the royal dwelling in which his father was. But the father, seeing him approach, released a savage hound of his and set it upon his son. At that very instant, and intending to snatch the meat, a hawk swooped down upon the young boy; who, nevertheless, skillfully dealt with both the hawk and the hound, like this: with the spit that still had the meat upon it, he thrust it down the hound's gaping throat to its heart; the hawk he grasped and held in his other hand. Then his mother, seeing the hawk on one side of her son and the hound on the other, was so startled—a start so great that from then on she never again bore a child.

Regarding the great war that was between the two previously mentioned Fiachnas, it was Baetan’s son who always had the victory; not only over Fiachna, son of Deman, but over all other kings whatsoever who opposed him. Also, the famous Mongan was the son of that same Fiachna, son of Baetan; for although certain tellers of ancient fables suggest that he was the son of Manannan and used to take various shapes at his pleasure, yet we cannot believe this. Instead, we choose to take Mongan as one who was but a man of extraordinary knowledge, and gifted with an intelligence that was clear, subtle, and keen.
