649. During the time of those kings, *Raghallach mac Fuatach*, king of Connacht, was killed—that is, *in the sixth year*. Raghallach's nature was this: he was self-willed and full of malice. For he had a nephew who was a young man, whom he intensely desired to kill, yet he could never lay hands on him. Therefore, he schemed to make himself look thin and miserable, and he ate no food other than sheep's legs, saying all the while that a sickness ailed him. And it was indeed a very sore distress that truly afflicted him then: namely Envy—Envy, the greatest torment that has any place in this world, seeing as it leads one brother to kill the other.

So Raghallach, through the working of envy and by abstaining from food, grew thinner and weaker until death was at hand; then he sent a message to his kinsman that he should come and speak with him, for he lay at death’s door. But the nephew, knowing his uncle's guile well, did not go at once when he was summoned; rather, he waited to gather a strong company for himself, and so entered the house where Raghallach lay. His band also carried their swords drawn under their clothing and closely surrounded their lord on all sides.

As for Raghallach, though he was also well-provided with retainers, he nevertheless did not trust in them but in his own craftiness; following this, he said: “Alas! How evil and pitiable is my plight when my own kinsman—he whom I would have be king after me and whom I love above all men—will not venture to approach me without a troop to guard him. Yet even so, I offer thanks to God that you, being of my race, are of sufficient age and vigor to reign in my place. But how grievous it is that you bring a company to protect yourself against me, who now lies at the point of death, with my flesh and my body all shrunken and wasted away!” When the young kinsman heard those words, his heart yearned greatly for his elder, and he shed many tears.

On the next day, he came to visit him with fewer people; on the third day, he appeared all alone, and it was then that Raghallach’s people leaped out upon him and killed him. Raghallach rose immediately, as though he had been healthy and sound; however, far from being so, that was the very time at which he who

Next, Raghallach's wife Mairenn questioned her magician, who was one that had knowledge of the future, saying: "How stands this great prosperity which Raghallach—his foes all fallen by his hand—now enjoys with a sense of contentment so surpassing?" And that which moved her query was a premonition she had that Raghallach must indeed perish by some enemy; but who that enemy should be, she could not tell. The seer answered and said: "A king who has slaughtered all his own brothers—by his own offspring shall the downfall of such a one be brought, though as yet he has no hint of such a thing. Also for yourself—your luck will soon have an end, and by your own womb's fruit you shall be undone." <insert>When all this was told to him,</insert> Raghallach ordered her that secretly and at its very birth she should kill whatever child she might bear, so that the prophesied event should not come upon them through their own offspring.

It was not long after when Mairenn had a daughter, whom she ordered her swineherd to take away and kill. The swineherd, for his part, looking upon the tiny baby's face, felt his heart go out to her; therefore, putting her again into the same pouch and carrying her to the house-door of a certain pious woman who was his neighbor, he left her hanging upon a cross near the church. At early morning, the devout widow came forth and, finding the pouch on an arm of the cross, peeped to see what might be in it. When she saw the tiny baby girl, she loved her immediately and took her in; and in the ordinances of the Church, she nurtured her until there was no one in all Ireland fairer than she. Raghallach heard of her fame and sent messengers to the girl's nurse demanding the girl from her; but she did not give her up, and men took her forcibly to the king from the sanctuary in which she was. When he saw her, he loved her passionately, not knowing she was his own daughter; because of this, Mairenn, in her jealousy, swam across the Shannon and fled to *ailech Mairinne* to seek out *Diarmaid ruanaidh*, king of Ireland. From this Mairenn, in truth, this Ailech has its name.

This strange thing, being reported throughout all Ireland, soon became a matter of indignation to the saints of Ireland. *Féichín*

643. The saints prayed that before *Beltane*, and at the hands of common people, he should perish in a foul pit by dishonorable weapons. Seeing the deer approach, he took his spear and pierced it from one side to the other with a thrust; yet the deer escaped by swimming. Raghallach got into a boat and pursued the deer, which ran a long way from the lake until it came upon certain laborers who were cutting turf. These men killed the stag and divided it. The king, arriving then, loudly threatened them because they had butchered the deer, commanding them to surrender the venison to him. But the laborers decided among themselves to slay King Raghallach rather than be forced to give up the meat. They truly carried out this plan with the turf-spades they held in their hands, striking him on the head until he was lifeless, exactly as the saints had promised. Guaire now sent *Cuimín fada* (who was Fiachna’s son and the <term>coarb</term> <note>successor</note> of St. Brendan), requesting from the king a twenty-four-hour truce before he should cross westward over the Shannon. Dermot met Cuimin on a raft in the middle of the Shannon, and there Cuimin explained his mission. Cheerfully and kindly, Dermot answered: “It is only a small thing you ask; and if the favor were a greater one, in truth it would be yours.” “If that is so,” said Cuimin, “then go back to the same bank from which you came.” Dermot answered: “As you are the head of Ireland’s piety, I give my word that until either peace or war is granted to me, I may not retreat [a step].” “Come on then to this nearer bank,” said Cuimin. “I swear to Heaven,” cried Dermot, “that for the duration of the truce you ask, I never would have disobeyed your command if you had only met me further to the east.”

So these two, the cleric and the king, stayed there until morning, when Cuimin said to Dermot: “O king, observing as I do the small number and the sorry appearance of your army, I am amazed at your triumphs in raids and in battles. For as great as your force may seem to some, those who are arrayed against you are far greater in number and, since they are better equipped in every way, they make a more impressive appearance.” “Cleric,” answered Dermot, “do you not know that a battle is won neither by numbers nor by outward appearance, but according to God’s will? And while you say that our army is but humble to look at, it is not handsome appearances but hardy hearts that win the fight. This truth holds good not only for men, but for other animals as well: for though a wolf is but one, he will drive a flock of many sheep before him with slaughter—and not just that, but he will put to flight and destroy many of the larger cattle; the hawk and the falcon also pursue other birds that are larger and more beautiful than they are.” “Why then, O king,” asked Cuimin, “did you say that the battle is won according to God’s will?” “Well now, Cleric,” the king replied, “is it not true that one who has Truth on his side prevails against a man of lies? Yes, consider how Christ, as you tell us, though he was alone against the Devil and the Jews, nevertheless prevailed in spite of everything, because Truth was with him.”

Then Guaire and the men of Connacht met Dermot *ruanaidh* and his army, and a hard, painful, and wrathful battle was fought between them. A slaughter of the Connacht men took place there, as well as a slaughter of the men of Munster and their two leaders, both named Cuan, who had joined the Connacht army. It was because of the word of *St. Cáimín* of *Inis Cealtra* (or ‘Innishcaltra’ in Lough Derg) that the battle went against Guaire. The Saint had fasted against him for three cycles of the canonical hours and for this reason said: "If it is right in the sight of God, may the man who is stubborn enough to stand against me be unable to stand firm against his enemies." At that time, an Angel also spoke with *Cáimín*, saying:

> "In the battle at *Innishcaltra* where the lowly shall fight against the powerful, it is the weak who shall prove strong, and the strong who shall be subdued."

Therefore, before the battle, Guaire had sought out *Cáimín* and, kneeling, offered to do whatever he wished; but the Saint had said: "It is no longer in my power to prevent your enemies from triumphing over you; yet I may arrange this: once that is done, they in turn shall submit to you." At that point, *Cáimín* uttered:

> "When sword edge meets sword edge, and spear point encounters spear point, then the humble cleric to whom you have been stubborn will be a cause of repentance for you, O *Guaire*! The Son of God has ordained that in an hour’s change of fortune, *Guaire's* heart shall be subject to the stronger men, and they, in turn, shall be subject to *Guaire*."

His people having been destroyed, Guaire fled from the battle and came all alone to a small monastery where there was a pious woman; she began to question him about who he was. The king presented himself as a trusted follower belonging to Guaire. "Woe is me!" she cried, "for the king who is foremost in all Ireland for his generosity in giving alms—after the red havoc made of his people, he is now a fugitive before his enemies!" So Guaire made his submission to Dermot at the sword’s point, the manner of which is this: the point of a sword or spear is placed between the teeth and in the mouth of the one making the submission, while he lies on the ground on his back. In due time, Guaire went to the great gathering of Taillte, and with him a large sack of silver to distribute to the men of Ireland; but Dermot had commanded them that neither high nor low among them should dare to ask anything of Guaire in the Assembly. Then in the convention, Guaire sat beside Dermot, in the company of the High King of Ireland himself. In this fashion, two days passed; on the third, Guaire said to the king: “Let a bishop be fetched; I wish to make confession and receive extreme unction!” “Why is this?” asked Dermot. Guaire answered: “For my death, which is at hand;” and on being further questioned how he knew it to be so, he went on: “That is easily told—it is because, with all Ireland gathered together in one place, not a single poor wretch among them has yet begged for alms from me!” “From now on, no prohibition shall be placed on anyone to prevent them from asking of you,” said Dermot, “and here I bestow on you a sack of silver to distribute.” “Not so,” was the answer, “for I myself have a sufficient store of silver.”

Finnachta *fledhach*, or "the festive," son of Dunchadh, reigned next for the space of twenty years. At the end of those years, in *Grellach Dolluid*, he was slain by Conghalach and Aedh, the son of Dluthach.

And regarding this world's goods, this same Finnachta was poorly endowed at first: he possessed only a wife and a house and, except for one ox and one cow only, no livestock at all. One night, near to his cottage, the king of the *fir Rois* (or "the men of Ross"), who had lost his way, wandered up and down. No night that ever preceded it had been worse than this because of the storm, darkness, and snow; so that because of the magnitude of the tempest and the gloom obstructing them, they could by no means reach the dwelling to which the king, with his wife and people, intended to go. Therefore, they even deliberated about resting under a tree.

Finnachta (whose cottage, as stated before, was at no great distance) overheard this debate and, when he had sought them out, he said it was fitting that they take recourse in his own poor man's shelter rather than travel throughout the murky night, especially as the weather was so foul. The king and his people answered:
> "Your words are just, and we are right glad to hear them spoken."
So they accompanied him to his house, the size of which certainly exceeded its furnishings, and there Finnachta dealt his ox one blow in the head and his cow another. The king’s own party most speedily and heartily prepared these with spit and cauldron; which being done, they ate of them until they were full and so slept until morning’s dawn.

At daybreak the king said to his wife:
> "Do you not know that, as poor as this house has always been, it is even poorer now that its only cow has been slaughtered for us?"

> "You speak well," said the chief of the men of Ross.

Nevertheless, even though the horses traveled swiftly, Adamnan’s speed was no less than theirs, as he sorrowfully and in grief carried the fragments of his pitcher along with him.

Finnachta, noticing him, laughed aloud and said, “I will make you a cheerful boy again, for I am very helpful in all times of trouble and distress; you shall have my protection, my young student.” In this manner, he told Adamnan to cast off his gloom, but the lad answered him: “I have good cause for it, fair sir; for there are three worthy students of theology who live in one house, to whom I and two others are servants. It is our custom that one servant among us (each in his turn) must go out seeking provisions for the other five. What I had gathered is now spilled upon the ground; but most of all I grieve for the borrowed pitcher that is broken, because I own nothing with which to make restitution.”

Shortly after this, Finnachta, accompanied by his close friend the king of the *Fir Rois*, went to his uncle, Cennfaela, begging that he might be put in charge of a territory. Cennfaela then assigned him the high stewardship of Meath, from the Shannon to the sea; for a time, Finnachta remained in that position. But it happened that one day, as he consulted with his close friend the king of the *Fir Rois*, he asked him what he should do, for in his own eyes, his current status was no longer sufficient. Then that chief gave him stern and daring advice, saying: "Is it not true that the *Slighe Asail* divides Meath evenly in two? Therefore, manage one half of Meath so that it stays loyal to you and devoted to your cause. Then, after arranging a meeting with the other half, kill their leaders and the pillars of their army. In this way, you will win not only the sovereignty of Meath, but if it pleases you, the royal power of Tara itself may truly be yours."

This plan was carried out by Finnachta, and he provoked his uncle Cennfaela to battle. When Cennfaela's wife heard of it, she began rebuking her husband for the stewardship he had granted to Finnachta, and the woman spoke this poem: —

> "The fighting men of the western country are rallied around Finnachta; Cennfaela is stripped of his royal dignity—how much of this is his own doing!"

675. A fierce battle was then fought between Finnachta and Cennfaela, in which the latter was killed along with a great many others. After this, Finnachta held the monarchy of Ireland for twenty years.

It was this same Finnachta who cancelled the Boromean Tribute for Molling; before his time, the tribute had been collected by forty successive kings, namely from *Tuathal Techtmhar* down to Finnachta himself. 702. In Loingsech's seventh year <note>Read: sixth, i.e., 701</note>, there was a falling out between Conaing's son Irghalach and Adamnan. Irghalach had outraged Adamnan by killing his kinsman Niall, who had taken sanctuary with the Saint. Then Adamnan, so that Irghalach's life would be cut short, began fasting through the night: remaining sleepless and immersed in a cold stream. Irghalach, for his part, used to question Adamnan, asking: “And what will you do tonight, Cleric?” To this, the latter, being loath to tell a lie, would reply that he would fast until morning, remaining sleepless and immersed in cold water. Then Irghalach would do these same things, for the purpose of shielding himself from Adamnan's curse. Yet despite all that, the Saint still trapped him in the end; for he instructed a cleric of his <term>familia</term>: “At evening, be here in my likeness, wearing my robes; should Irghalach then come to ask what you are doing tonight, tell him that you will both feast and sleep, and so persuade him to do the same.” For Adamnan could more easily endure that a man of his <term>familia</term>, and not he himself, should tell a lie.

Irghalach in due course came and found the cleric; believing him to be Adamnan, he asked: “Cleric, what are you doing tonight?” “I banquet and I sleep,” he answered; therefore, that night Irghalach also both feasted and slept. But Adamnan kept his fast and vigil, and stayed in the river until dawn.

702. In the next year (that being the seventh of Loingsech's reign), this Irghalach was killed, after having seen the manner of his own death on the night before he was slain. On the morning after this vision, Irghalach went out and, standing upon a high rock, heard a loud voice cry: "Spread yourselves over the surrounding country, and burn, and scorch, and harry it!" Then he saw great bands and companies despoiling the land; and he came and stood beside *Inis mac Nesain* or "Ireland's Eye," where at that very hour a British fleet had been forced to take refuge by a great storm. One of these British warriors had likewise had a dream the previous night: it was as if a herd of wild boars grunted around him, and he had killed the largest boar with a javelin strike. This omen was verified exactly: for that boar represented Irghalach, and the rest of the herd his retinue of sinners; and with a single javelin throw, Irghalach was killed there and then by that warrior.

703. In the aforementioned Loingsech's eighth year, a great army was gathered by him to plunder and waste Connacht. 704. Next in order, and for one year, *Fuagartach* son of Niall held the sovereignty of Ireland; that is to say, for a second term. It was in this year that all Ireland adopted one discipline and one rule from Adamnan; for in Ireland until then, there had been one party which followed Columbkill regarding the celebration of Easter on the fourteenth day of the April moon and the 'tonsure of Simon Magus'; another group followed Patrick in keeping Easter on the fourteenth of April when that day happened to be a Sunday, while yet a third faction took a middle course between the other two. 705. Then Conghal of Kinnaweer, son of Fergus of Fanait and grandson of Donall (the son of Aedh mac Ainmirech), assumed the royal power of Ireland.

707. In his second year, he led a hosting into Connacht, which he plundered and burned as far as the plain of Murrisk. In his third year, he also gathered a great army for the purpose of completely uprooting Leinster. He marched the general muster of the North, and thus they entered *úi Faeláin*. Now, the man who was actually king of Leinster at that time was Faelan; as soon as he heard that Conghal had pitched camp in his territory, he decided that in order to secure peace, envoys must be sent with a great store of precious gifts for presentation. But when Conghal was told that the King of Leinster’s messengers were on their way, he used deception regarding himself, his brother, and his army. For it is the custom of kings (who prefer to conquer by subtlety rather than by main strength) to devise ruses and plausible deceits for their enemy’s overthrow, even if their own force is sufficient to crush the foe. Conghal now laid just such a plot: he ordered the chiefs of his army to leave the camp until sunrise the next morning, and by no means to be present when the King of Leinster’s messengers arrived. He also had certain men of low status take the places of those chiefs and serve as his companions; various men of despicable and ragged appearance were dispersed throughout the entire camp, and he himself was dressed in tatters. Then he sent his own horseboy to meet the messengers with this command: “Use all your diligence to disparage me, speaking of me with contempt and claiming that I am nothing; perhaps then the men of Leinster will despise us and consider us of no account.” Whereupon the horseboy went his way and did as Conghal commanded.

As for Conghal, once the messengers were gone, he gathered his chiefs and, after deliberation, they decreed to execute his design, which was: to harry Leinster, to kindle fires, to burn, and to kill. This they did accordingly: burning up the entire plain of Leinster and wreaking bloody havoc on its people. Nor did their king once show himself to check them, which was for two reasons: because of his messengers’ report, and because of the defeat which he had inflicted on Fuagartach last Martinmas [so that now he rested on his laurels]. In the long run, however, he gave more credit to the burnings which he witnessed with his own eyes than to all his ambassadors’ discourses.

With fire and otherwise, Conghal distressed Leinster for the space of half a year, yet Faelan never offered him battle; therefore Conghal, greatly blaming him, composed:—

"...promised you?" and he answered: "their clergy have promised me Heaven; their king, the freedom of my descendants to the end of time." "You shall be my retainer," the king replied, "and Leinster shall make good those promised gifts nonetheless."

The king happened to be at the foot of an oak tree at that moment. A heavy snow was falling, and the tree was laden with ripe mast <note>acorns or forest nuts</note>. Because the man of Leinster was standing there [to guard the king], and because of the trusted position granted to him, some of the warriors were filled with envy. One of Conghal's men said, "It would be well to test that favored henchman of the king’s—I will throw this acorn at the king’s head; for if it passes the guard and hits the king, then a spear or a stone could just as easily have reached him." With that, he aimed the acorn at Conghal’s head. But the Leinster guard, deflecting it with his sword, cut the acorn in two and [with the same motion] struck the man who threw it in the head, killing him.

Finally, the king returned to his own house with victory and spoils; he had also taken vengeance on Leinster to satisfy the death of his grandfather [who had been killed by them].

† 706. Seven years after this, Conghal died of the plague.

->*The End.*<-

### *The story of the fate of a certain wicked Greek girl.*

Once, in a castle, there was a certain admirable king of the Greeks. In the East, kings always have a castle, while outside [on the outskirts], the queens are accustomed to eat and drink. A message was brought to him: "Dignity to you, honor to you, O king! This past night a daughter was born to you." The king said, "May she thrive happily, and may there be a blessing upon the womb that bore her!" Then a soldier standing nearby said, "O king, dignity to you! A son was born to me this past night." The prince replied: "Therefore, let the daughter be betrothed to him." For they spoke in this way because it was their constant custom that if a son were born on the same night as a daughter, they should be bound to one another, the one...

But when her husband said, "This is no concern of yours," she immediately offered herself as his companion in bed, and she later followed him when he returned to his own country. 

Consequently, the woman's father died, and her husband also passed away. A new king took power over the kingdom; his dignity was great, and that of the widow was also very great. Therefore, the woman was summoned to the king so that he might grant her gifts; when she visited him, she was received very pleasantly and from then on lived as his companion during banquets. 

After a short time, the lady asked, "Do you have a confessor <term>confessor</term>?" The king replied, "Certainly; a truly admirable man." She said, "He shall be my spiritual guide <term>director</term> as well." Without delay, she went to make use of the guide's ministry and, setting aside all concealment, made her confession <term>confessionem</term>. 

But when the ordained man heard that the penitent <term>pœnitentem</term> had committed such folly <note>original: "insipientiam," often used in a religious context to denote grave sin</note>, and noticed her extremely beautiful form, he worked hard to seduce the woman. The man did not continue further in hearing confessions, and she said goodbye to the king. He explains it. The prince said, "This matter is going poorly," and having summoned the woman again, he asked, "Have you made a confession?" When she answered, "Yes," he asked, "Did the cleric solicit you?" But she said, "I am not the kind of person who would declare such a thing." "But this too is wrong," the prince said. "Therefore, you, cleric, go away to some place where I shall not hear even a mention of your name."

The prince then saw to it that the woman was led to an oak house that had no door for entry, lacking any other opening except for some small little windows, and located at a crossroads. Afterward, there were holy men who reached small scraps of food inside to her. After seven years had passed in that condition, she finally became a mournful, miserable, and thin creature. Then it was reported to the king that she was still living such a life; the prison is opened, and the prince carries her away with him, still enclosed, to be cared for. Immediate effort was given to her restoration, and soon she became by far the most beautiful of all women.

He said, "This woman is suitable for a king to choose," and addressing her, he said, "Come to him, and I will be under your direction." But the woman said, "I have already given myself to a King than whom no other more excellent could exist to whom one might go <note>or "to whom I might go"</note>, and from whom I shall never turn away as long as I am alive. But you, see that a hermitage <term>desertum</term> and a church are built for me."

It was done as she asked: the hermitage <term>desertum</term> was filled with cows, oxen, horses, gold, and silver. The king said, "Come now, woman, enter your building." But she replied, "Let the cleric, namely my director, go before me." "Who is he?" "The very one whom I once rejected." Because he had shown himself to be holy during this time through the power of the great penance he had performed in the meanwhile, he approached her. Thus they lived in their hermitage <term>desertum</term>; eventually, they departed to heaven. Through their grace <note>or "through their intercession"</note>, so many miracles were performed that the city founded around them became the greatest place of prayer among the Greeks. Such, therefore, was the outcome which the wicked Greek maiden obtained.

<header>Ambacuc.</header>

### *Here follows an account of one of the wonders of the Assembly of Taillte.*

The Assembly of Taillte is held by Dermot, son of Cerbhall; Saint Kieran, the carpenter's son and his confessor, was also there beside him. The assembly's games are played and its races are run. There, a certain woman accosts her husband and accuses him of an affair with another woman. He persisted in denying the fact, and the wife said, "I will accept his sworn statement made under Kieran's hand." The husband accordingly swore under Kieran’s hand that he was innocent of the charge his wife had laid against him; but he was lying. Therefore, upon his neck, exactly where the cleric's hand had rested, an ulcerous tumor afflicted him and his head fell off, so that in the presence of all Ireland there, he walked about in the gathering without a head: a miracle by which the names of God and Kieran were magnified.

Kieran subsequently brought the headless man to Clonmacnoise, to be cared for there for as long as God should grant him life. For seven years after Kieran’s time, he lived on with the monks; then a woman was brought to him, he coupled with her, and in due course she bore a son, from whom, as some say, the *Soghain* in Meath are descended. However, shortly after his marriage was consummated, the man died and was laid by the clergy at the east end of *iomaire Chomgaill*, or "Comgall's Ridge," where *cros Comgaill* or "Comgall's Cross" stands today. There, Ambacuc's stone and final resting place remain as a commemoration of his story for all men, and this is one of the wonders of the Assembly of Taillte.

Here too is another of the same assembly's marvels: namely, the sighting of three ships that navigated the air over their heads when the men of Ireland celebrated the assembly with Donall, son of Murrough.

->*Finis.*<-

<summary>This text describes miraculous events at the Assembly of Taillte, primarily the story of Ambacuc, who lost his head after swearing a false oath but continued to live and father a child. It also records a sighting of three ships flying in the air during another assembly.</summary>

# Irish Text of Extracts.

I. PAGE 1:—(i) Ciarán of Saigir, son of Luaigne, son of Ruanann, son of Conall, son of Coirpre Nia, son of Buan, son of Dimbuan, son of Echu Lámdóit, son of Amalgaid, son of Loegaire Birn the Victorious, son of Oengus Osrithe. (ii) The 5th of March. Ciarán, *bishop and confessor*. He is of the descent of Oengus of Ossory, who is of the descent of Labraid Loingsech, from whom the Leinstermen come; and Ciarán is of the seed of Eiremón. A very ancient vellum manuscript says—as we said regarding Brigid on February 1st—that Ciarán of Saigir was similar in character and life to *Pope Clemens*. (iii) *Here begins the genealogy of the seed of Birn, that is, the people of Ossory.* Those are the Ossory of the seed of Bresal Brec. Bresal Brec was the son of Fiacha Fobrec, son of Ailill Glas, and others, *as we have written in the genealogies of the Leinstermen*. [Bresal Brec, then, was the son of Fiacha Fobrec, son of Ailill Glas, son of Feradach Foglas, son of Nuadu Fullón, son of Allót, son of Art, son of Mog Art, son of Crimthann Coscrach, son of Feradach Finnfechtnaid, son of Fedlimid Fortriun, son of Fergus Fortamail, son of Oengus Ollamh, son of Ailill Bécán, son of Labraid Loingsech, son of Ailill Áine, son of Loegaire Lorc, son of Ugaine the Great]. Now Bresal Brec had two sons: Lugaid, the ancestor of the Leinstermen, and Connla the Fair, the ancestor of the people of Ossory; and the name "Leinstermen" belongs no more rightfully to the descendants of Lugaid than to the descendants of Connla. In the time of that Bresal Brec, the first cattle plague came to Ireland, and it left only three red heifers in all Ireland: a heifer in Cliu, a heifer in Line, and a heifer in Cooley. From this comes [the name] *Imbliuch Fir Oendarta* (the Navel of the One-Heifer Man). From the cattle tribute that Bresal brought into Ireland, the name of Comgall's Bangor (*Bennchur*) is derived, *as some say*... Loegaire Birn the Victorious was the son of the daughter of Delbáeth the Druid, brother of Mog Ruith, and son of Oengus Osrithe—that is, he was found among wild deer—son of Crimthann the Great. Cennait, daughter of Daire son of Det, was the one who was with Crimthann the Great, and she is the mother of Oengus Osrithe... son of Ier, son of Faelreg, son of Sétna, son of Ailill, son of Lugaid, son of Labraid, son of Carthach, son of Nuadu, son of Connla, son of Bresal Brec, and others. (iv) *Oraighi*, that is, *os-éirghi* (deer-rising); that is, rising like a deer while fleeing before the Déisi when they left the land where the Déisi are today. Or *Osraighi*, that is, *os-fríthi* (deer-found); that is, Oengus Osraige (the elder of Ossory) was found among wild deer. (v) *Laigin* (Leinster), from what was it named? Not difficult. *Laigin* is like *lagain*, that is, from the broad spears (*lágna*) which the "dark foreigners" brought with them across the sea from where they came together with Labraid Loingsech. Ernoll, son of the king of Denmark, was their leader. It is from this Labraid onwards that there is horror, valor, fear, and great dread upon the Leinstermen. *Whence the poet said*: Labraid the Exile, his following was sufficient, with whom he destroyed Cobthach at Dinn Ríg; with a Leinsterman host across the sea’s surface, from them were the Leinstermen named. *Tuaim Tenba* was its name before that; the hill where the massacre was performed; it has been Dinn Ríg from then until now, from the killing of the kings. Twenty-two hundred foreigners with broad spears came over with them; from the spears brought there, the Leinstermen are called Leinstermen. (vi) *Gailíon* and *Domnann* are names for the Leinstermen, as is recounted in the *Táin Bó Cúailnge*. A band of foreigners came one day as followers of Labraid the Exile to Ireland, so that they destroyed Dinn Ríg and so forth. *Thence they are named Gailíon, as if from Gall-líon* (foreign host). And their descendants remained for a long time in the land, *as in the "Fort of the Gailíon" by the Dál Meisi Corb*. Baiscinn and Duibne crossed over to Munster in the time of the sons of Ailill Olum, namely Cairpre Músc, son of Mug Láma, and Ailill Bascháin—another name for him was also Cairpre, son of Oengus, son of Mug Láma. Though others say the three Cairpres were brothers, they were born of different fathers. Their origin, however, is the same further back, *as we have said before*. Others say, however, that Oengus Músc, Ailill Bascháin, and Eochaid Riata were brothers, namely, the three sons of Cairpre, son of Conaire, son of Mess Búachalla. (xxii) A.M. 3503: the second year of the reign of Érimón over Ireland. The eruption of the nine Brosnas—namely, the rivers of Éile; the nine Riges—the rivers of Leinster; and the three Unshins of the Uí nOilella in the same year.

PAGE 9:—(xxiii) The genealogy of the Uí Cheinnselaig. Why are they called the Uí Cheinnselaig from the seed of Labraid Laidech, son of Bresal Belach? It is not difficult. The battle of Cruachan Cloenta was won by the Leinstermen against Eochaid Mugmedón, King of Ireland, where Cétnadach, the poet of Eochaid Mugmedón, was captured. Then, while he was being protected above on the shields of the men, Énna came into the battle and thrust a spear into Cétnadach, and Énna laughed. Then Cétnadach said: "That laugh is foul, O Énna, and your name shall be Énna of the Foul Laugh (Gen Salach) until the end of time." *Hence the name Uí Cheinnselaig* . . . . Now, Énna Ceinnselach had eight sons: Crimthann and Feidlimid, Eochu, Erc, Trien, Conall, and Cairpre. It was Crimthann who believed in Patrick at Ráith Bilech, and Patrick left a blessing upon him forever . . . Eithne Uathach, daughter of Crimthann and wife of Oengus son of Nad Fraích, was the mother of Bresal and Senach, the two sons of Oengus son of Nad Fraích, King of Munster. It was this Eithne and Oengus her husband who went with the Uí Cheinnselaig to contest the kingship of Leinster against Illann son of Dúnlang <insert>son of Enna Niadh, the brother of the father of Enna Ceinnselach</insert>. Then Illann and Muirchertach mac Erca came with the men of the north of Ireland against the men of Munster and the Uí Cheinnselaig, so that they met in the battle of Ceann Losnada in Mag Fea—that is, the "fragments" (losnad) of the pig of Mac Dá Thó were divided there—where Eithne and Oengus her husband fell, along with a slaughter of the rest of the army. Meld, Beloc, and Cinniu were the three daughters of Ernbrainn of the Déisi and the three wives of Crimthann son of Énna . . . Cinniu, however, had no children except for one daughter, namely Eithne Uathach. She was called "Uathach" (the Horrible) because the flesh of children was given to her so that she might grow more quickly, and so that children conceived a hatred (fuath) for her. The reason she was given the flesh of children to make her grow faster was because their prophets had told the Déisi—the people who reared her—that they would obtain land as her bride-price (tinnscra). (xxiv) A.D. 527. After being twenty-four years in the kingship of Ireland, Muirchertach son of Muiredach, son of Eogan, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages, was burned in the house of Cletech above the Boyne on Samhain night, after being drowned in wine.

PAGE 11:—(xxv) 11th of *August*. Liadain the widow, mother of Ciarán of Saigir and first abbess of the holy virgins of Ireland. (xxvi) Odrán the Master in Leitir in Uí Daigri, and Medrán of Saigir, were the two sons of Meiccraith, son of Trochall, son of Esamain Daigre, son of Nuadu Neimnech from the woods of Cenn Febrat. (xxvii) *a*. 2nd of *October*. Odrán of Leitir; and he is Odrán the Master who is of the descent of Conaire <insert>the Comely</insert> son of Mug Láma, and brother to Medrán, *etcetera*. It was Odrán the Master and Mac Cuilinn of Lusk who told Ciarán of Clonmacnoise that his life would be cut short. *b*. 26th of *November*. Odrán of the Leitirs of Odrán in Múscraige Tíre. *c*. 6th of *July*. Medrán; this may be the Medrán of Saigir who is of the descent of Conaire son of Mug Láma, high king of Ireland, who is of the seed of Íth son of Breogan. (xxviii) Ciarán son of the Carpenter at Clonmacnoise; Ciarán son of Luaigne and Carthach at Saigir. (xxix) 5th of *March*. Bishop Carthach, the pupil of Ciarán of Saigir. Druim Fertáin was among his homesteads, and Druim Fertáin is in Cairbre Ua gCiardha.

After completing thirty years, he went to heaven in A.D. 563. There was an eclipse of the sun on the third day of May. (v) Féichín of Fore, son of Cuilcharna, son of Killíne, son of Killíne, son of Cael, son of Aed, son of Saini, son of Art Corb, son of Niadh Corb, son of Cormac Mór, son of Eochaid Finn Fuath nAirt, son of Feidlimid Rechtmar, son of Tuathal Techtmar. Dairinis was his from the beginning, as is understood from these verses: Aedh was his name . . .
Bishop Mac Cairthinn was the strongman of Patrick, and he used to carry him across every uneven place. The genealogy of Bishop Mac Cairthinn is found from Clogher to Eochaid son of Muiredach, and from Eochaid to Eiremón. *6th of October*. Aedh; and this may be Bishop Mac Cairthinn of Clogher, i.e., Patrick’s strongman. He is of the seed of Eiremón, from the lineage of Eochaid son of Muiredach. Or it may be that Aedh son of Aedh, who is of the lineage of Fiachra son of Eochaid Muighmedhóin, belongs to this day. (xiii) *19th of August*. Mochta, Bishop of Louth; three hundred years was his age when he went to heaven, A.D. 534. And he never spoke a word that was false or ignorant, and he did not eat a fat morsel or anything that contained seasonal juice during that time. Therefore, this account was given of him, also revealing that there were sixty elders in his house, or that they did no labor at all except for saying psalms and prayers:

Mochta's tooth had good habits,
three hundred years was the long tribute:
without a straying word from it,
without a morsel of fat within it.
Sixty psalmist elders,
his royal household in its ranks:
without plowing, reaping, or drying,
without any labor but study.
A man of sixty, a man of three hundred,
*Arco fuin* <note>A prayer formula, often meaning "I pray for fiveness"</note> is that old tooth:
no more is the love of a youth under valor,
than is found in that old tooth.

Cuimín of Connor says in the poem that begins: *Patrick loved . . .* that Mochta was a hundred years without eating a morsel of condiment or anything fat. Here is what he says:

My Mochta of Louth loved,
through law and through rule:
without a morsel of condiment in his body,
in poverty for the span of a hundred years.

This Mochta prophesied Colum Cille 200 years before his birth. (xiv) *a.* Tigernach, Bishop of Cluain Eois, son of Coirpre, son of Fergus, son of Enna, son of Labraid, son of Brion, son of Eochaid, son of Dáire Barraig, son of Cathaoir Mór. *b.* Tigernach, Bishop of Cluain Eois, son of Coirpre, son of Fergus, son of Enna, son of Laebán, son of Bran, son of Dáire Barraig, son of Cathaoir Mór. *c. 4th of April*. Tigernach, Bishop of Cluain Eois in Fermanagh; or perhaps Cluain Eois is between Fermanagh and Oriel. Tigernach was of the lineage of Cathaoir Mór, High King of Ireland, of the Leinstermen. Derfraoich, daughter of Eochaid son of Crimthann, King of Oriel, was his mother. A.D. 548. (xv) *a.* Bécán of Cluain Ard, son of Murchad, son of Muiredach, son of Diarmait, son of Eogan, son of Oilill Ólum. *b. 5th of April*. Bécán son of Cula in Imlech Fiaich in the territory of Fir Cúl Breagh; he may be of the seed of Eogan Mór son of Oilill Ólum. When Colum Cille and the King of Ireland, Diarmait son of Fergus Cerrbeóil, came there after the killing of Bresal, his son, where Bécán was, they found him building a stone wall with a wet cloak around him and he was praying, so that it was said of him:

Building a wall and cross-vigil,
prostrations and pure prayer:
his tears falling without gain,
the victory of Bécán without a portion of sin.
A hand on a stone, a hand raised,
a knee bent against the corner of a rock:
an eye shedding tears of another holiness,
and a mouth at prayer.

Bécán looked behind him and when he saw Diarmait, he said: "Into the ground, you kinslayer!" and he went up to his knees into the ground. "I have come to you under my protection," said Colum Cille, "to resuscitate his son for him." Bécán resurrected Bresal, the king’s son, from the dead. PAGE 29:—(xvi) *a.* Moedóc of Ferns, son of Setna, son of Erc, son of Feradach, son of Amalgaid, son of Muiredach, son of Colla Uais. *b.* Moedóc, son of Setna, son of Erc, son of Feradach, son of Amalgaid, son of Muiredach, son of Carthenn, son of Erc, son of Eochaid, son of Colla Uais. *c. 31st of January*. Maedhóg, Bishop of Ferns; Aedh was his first name. He was of the seed of Colla Uais, High King of Ireland. Eithne was his mother's name, of the seed of Amalgaid son of Fiachra, son of Eochaid Muighmedhóin. Among his first miracles was the flagstone on which he was born to be baptized; everyone used to be ferried out and in upon it like any other vessel.

...another to the island that was on the lake where he was born. It was also among his miracles that a weaver's shuttle, which was in the hand of Eithne, Maedóg's mother, while she was giving birth to him, and which was a withered, hard stick of hazel, sprouted leaves and good flowers and good fruit afterward. That hazel still survives as a fresh tree without decay or withering, bearing nuts every year in Inis Brechmaighe, etc. A.D. 624 was the time he sent his spirit to heaven. A very ancient vellum book says that Maedóg of Ferns was similar in habits and in life to Pope Cornelius.

# PAGE 32:—(xvii) 
### The genealogical branch of the men of Bréifne follows here. 

Fergus son of Muiredach Mál, son of Eogan Srem, son of Daui Galach, son of Brian, son of Eochaid Muighmedhóin. He had three sons: namely, Eochaid Tirmcharna, the ancestor of the Síl Muiredaig; and Daui Tenga Uma, the ancestor of the Clann Choscraig and Muintir Murchada; and Fergna, the third son, the ancestor of the Uí Briúin. 

# (xviii) 
The Airgialla, moreover, are those who are nearest to the Uí Néill after the Connachta. Fiacha Sraibtine, son of Cairbre Lifechar, is the ancestor of the Uí Néill and the Airgialla. Namely, Muiredach Tírech, son of Fiacha Sraibtine, is he from whom the Uí Néill descend; and Eochaid Doimlén, son of Cairbre Lifechar, is the ancestor of the Airgialla. [Eochaid] had three sons: namely, the three Collas. From them are the Uí Meic Uais, the Uí Chrimthainn, the Mugdorna, and the Airgialla. Fiacha Sraibtine and Eochaid Doimlén were the two sons of Cairbre Lifechar. 

It was against Fiacha that the three sons of his brother—namely, the three Collas—committed the kin-slaying <term>fingal</term>, so that it was that kin-slaying which separated the kingship of Ireland from the descendants of Eochaid Doimlén. This is how the kin-slaying happened: Fiacha Sraibtine was king in Tara, as we have said. He had a wonderful son, namely, Muiredach Tírech. He was the commander <term>tuarcnid flatha</term> for Fiacha; for it was the custom at that time that the king himself did not go into battle, but his commander went in his stead. 

Then Muiredach Tírech went once on behalf of his father with great armies around him into Munster, and the men of Munster gave him battle. He was victorious and took the hostages of Munster. Fiacha Sraibtine remained meanwhile at Dub Commair, south of Taltiu. He had an army with him in the fortress where he was. The three sons of his brother, the three Collas, had another army on a hill; yet they were all with Fiacha. When the news came—namely, of the victory of Muiredach—what was on everyone's lips was that Muiredach Tírech was the heir-apparent of Ireland. 

Then the three Collas said: "What shall we do? King Fiacha has taken the sovereignty, but everyone says that it will be his son who will be king after him. It is better for us to give battle to this old king; this army will flee from around him and come to us before Muiredach arrives, and we will give battle to him as soon as he comes." 

They went from one hill to the other to Fiacha, their father's brother, and battle was proclaimed against him by them—that is, by the sons of his brother. Fiacha had a druid; Dub Commair was his name. He said to Fiacha: "I can grant you victory, but there is this condition. If you are victorious, you will commit kin-slaying against the sons of your brother; you will be king then, but none of your children will ever be king. If you are defeated, kin-slaying will be committed against you, but the sovereignty of Ireland will belong to your descendants forever, and the three Collas will never have the sovereignty. Choose from that," said the druid. 

Fiacha said: "Defeat for me, and kingship for my seed." 

"I shall fall along with you," said the druid, "and it will be my name that will be on the battle forever." The Battle of Dub Commair is the name of that battle. Fiacha was then killed in the battle. The Collas, with three hundred men, went into Scotland fleeing from Muiredach, who took the kingship of Ireland. The king of Scotland gave great honor to the Collas because of their heroism. They were three years in Scotland. They planned to return to Ireland so that Muiredach might commit kin-slaying against them, and so that the burden that was upon them—namely, the kin-slaying—might be taken from them. The three Collas came as a trio, without a dog or a servant, until they were at Tara. The doorkeeper said to Muiredach: "The three Collas are on the green. What shall be done with them?" 

"Open the court," said Muiredach, "to see what they will do." The three of them came in...

...so that they were in the middle of the royal house at Tara. "Do you have news?" asked Muiredach. One of them answered him: "There is no news more difficult for you than what we have done: namely, the slaying of your father." "We already know that news," Muiredach replied. "However, it is not for that reason that we have come," said the Collas. "It is all the same to you," said Muiredach; "it shall not be avenged upon you. If you have come for your own slaying, it will not happen. As for the territory you have taken, I will not take it from you." "That is a good excuse for a bad warrior," said the Collas. Muiredach said: "Let there be no fear upon you; you shall have welcome and kindness."

They lived in great brotherhood for a long time, and the three Collas were the leaders in battle for Muiredach Tírech, and there was great love between them and the king. Afterward, Muiredach said to the Collas: "I see that your descendants have multiplied. Perhaps they will not be peaceful after us. Let each of us move away from the other, and take a single territory during my lifetime." The Collas said: "What land would you prefer to give us from your power so that we may make it a 'sword-land' <note>land won by conquest</note>?" For there were no warriors better than the Collas. Muiredach said: "Go against the Ulstermen; they are not loyal to us."

The Collas then had a great <term>fianlaech</term> <note>warrior-band</note>. After that, the Collas went to the men of Connacht, for they were their foster-sons, and the Connachtmen received them. Then the men of Connacht came with seven battalions and joined the Collas against the Ulstermen at the cairn of Achad Lethderg in Fernmag. They fought seven battles from that cairn against the Ulstermen, one battle every day for a week. Six battles were fought by the men of Connacht, and the seventh battle was led by the Collas. The Ulstermen were defeated every single day. The battle of the Collas was on the final day; there was no failure of prowess there. The battle was joined by day and by night until blood reached the belts. Near the cairn is the hazel tree <note>of the wounded</note>.

Afterward, the Ulstermen were defeated at the beginning of the second day. The slaughter extended to Glen Righe. For a week after that, they continued plundering the Ulaid, until they had made a 'sword-land' of the territory where the Mugdorna, the Uí Chrimthainn, the Airthir, and the Uí Meic Uais are now located. This constitutes the 'Half of Conn': the southern Uí Néill, the northern Uí Néill, the three Connachts, the Airgialla, and others.

# (xix)
Cairbre Lifechar was so named because of the greatness of his love for the Liffey; or because Liffey was his mother; or because he was fostered by the Liffey. As the poet said: "Three sons of his family, without being cast aside, belonged to Cairbre who loved the Liffey: Fiacha Sraibtine of the omens, Eochaid, and Eochaid Doimlén."

Colla Uais <note>the stag</note> was fostered by a wild stag; from him descend the Uí Meic Uais and the Uí Thuirtri. Colla Menn, from whom the Mugdorna descend, was fostered by Mennet the Pict and Mugdorndub of the Ulstermen. Mennet, from whom the Dál Mennet among the Mugdorna come <note>but the origin of Mugdorn is unknown, though they are assigned to the Ulstermen</note>. 

Colla Fochrích (or Fochrí, or Ochre) was the son of Eochaid Doimlén. Elige, the wife of Crinden the smith, was impregnated by Eochaid behind her husband's back, and she bore Colla. She hid this from her husband, and the child remained in fosterage for twenty years. Eochaid Doimlén paid fifty cows to Crinden for his fosterage according to the rule of Cormac grandson of Conn: for every woman's son belongs to her husband unless he is purchased from him. Because of this, his name is Connla Fochrith <note>purchased</note>. Or he is called Colla Fochridaig, because his mother put clay <note>cré</note> under his bones to disguise him among the smith's sons. Or Connla Ochrae, because Ochrae was the name of the foster-mother who reared him. From this Colla descend the Uí Chrimthannáin, the Airthir, and the Uí Méith.

# (xx)
*a*. **Collaidh**: meaning 'sinful' because of the act by which they killed Fiacha Sraibtine. 

**Colla Uais**: that is, Cairell. He was called 'Uais' <note>the stag</note> for his swiftness; or because a wild stag fostered him; or because he was a 'stag-slayer'—for <term>segh</term> is said to mean a wild deer. Or he was called Colla Uais for his nobility <note>uaisle</note>, for it was he who took the kingship of Ireland over the other Collas. 

**Colla Menn**: that is, Aed. Mennet the Pict fostered him; or perhaps it was a stammer <note>menn</note> that he had, from which the name was given. 

**Colla Fochrích**: that is, Muiredach. Eochaid begot him with Ailech, daughter of the King of Alba, under the roof of Crinden the smith. Or **Fochri**, from 'under clay' <note>fo chriaidh</note>, because the smith's wife put clay around him to disguise him. Or **Ochrae** was the name of the fosterer who reared him. Or **Connla Forcraid** <note>the excess</note>, because he was attributed to the wife of Crinden the smith. 

*b*. Cairbre Lifechar had three sons: namely, Fiacha Sraibtine, from whom descends Eochaid...

(xxvi) *a.* Genealogy of the <term>Delbna Bethra</term>. Trén son of Sige, son of Aindiled, son of Bic, son of Baetán, son of Delbáith, son of Tál, son of Conall Echluath, son of Lugaid Menn, son of Aengus Tírech, son of Fer Corb, son of Cormac Cas, son of Ailill Olum. 

*b.* Genealogy of the <term>Delbna Móire</term>. Blat son of Sige, son of Aindiled [as before]. 

*c.* The thirteen sons of Cas, son of Conall Echluath; and this is why Cas was called <term>Tál</term>, because he was the fosterling of a craftsman. These are his children: Lugaid the second; Sedna; Aengus "Serpent-Head"; Blad, from whom the Uí Blaid descend; Caisen; Lugaid Delbaeth, from whom the Delbna descend; Cormac; Carthann; Cainnech; Aengus "Furze-Head"; Aedh; Loiscen; and Noe. 

It is Delbaeth the Bold who is the second Lugaid mentioned here, from whom the seven <term>Delbna</term> descend. 

*d.* <term>Delbaeth</term>, that is, <term>doilbaeth</term>, which means "enchanted fire" which he made; or <term>delb aeda</term>, meaning "shape of fire." For when his own son-in-law, Trat son of Tassach, expelled him by means of druidry from the land where the <term>Tratraige</term> are, he fled into the territory of the Uí Néill. He went to Carn Fiachach, and there he kindled a druidic fire from which five streams of fire burst forth. He placed a son of his at each of those fire-streams, so that from them the five Delbna are named. From this the name Delbaeth stuck to him—that is, "shape of fire"—for his name was Lugaid until that time. Or he was called "shape of fire" because of his beauty, for his form was very radiant.

(xxvii) <term>Connachta</term>, that is, <term>coin-échta</term> (dog-slaughters); it was from when they killed Ailbe, the dog of Mac Datho, that they were named <term>Connachta</term>. 

Or <term>coinn-ichta</term>, that is, the "tribes of Conn" (the children of Conn), for <term>icht</term> means children or kindred. 

Or <term>Connachta</term>, that is, <term>achta Chuinn</term> (the deeds of Conn), for it was he who gained the territory by the sword through force, and <term>acht</term> and <term>gním</term> (deed) are the same. 

Furthermore, they are called the Province of <term>Olnégmacht</term> because of this: a feast was prepared for them and for the Clanna Degaid in the house of Doma the Druid. The Connachta arrived first and did not wait for the Clanna Degaid, but they divided the ale and drank two-thirds of it. The druid said, "This drinking is unequal (<term>égmacht</term>)," and from that the name "Province of Olnégmacht" stayed with them.

*November.* Finnchú, son of Finnlog, of Brí Gobhann in Fermoy, in Munster; he was of the lineage of Brian, son of Eochaid Muigmedón—that is, Finnlog, son of Sétna. Idnait, daughter of Flann Lethderg of the Ciannachta of Glengiven, was his mother, as the *Book of MacCarthy Reagh* says. Ailbe of Emly baptized him. Finnchú was seven years in the abbacy after Comgall; he was a pupil of Comgall, and it was with him that he performed his studies. It is this Finnchú who used to be frequently in a stone cell that was higher than his own height, with a stone above his head and a stone under his feet, and two iron hooks on each side of the cell; he would rest his two armpits on those hooks so that his head would not touch the stone above nor his feet the stone below. Comgall of Bangor came to him at another time and ordered him to come out of that cell, though he was reluctant to do so. It was he who would lie in the same grave with every dead person who was buried in his church on the first night.

(vi) *a.* Maelruain of Tallaght, son of Colmán, son of Senán, son of Agnide, son of Mochta, son of Cuinneda, son of Fiacca, son of Máel. *b. 7th of July.* Maelruain, bishop of Tallaght in Leinster; Tallaght is between Dublin and Kildare. Maelruain is of the lineage of Eochaid, son of Muiredach, of the seed of Eremón. Broicsech was his mother’s name. Mainnsena, the mother of Brendan of Birr, came to Saighir and wished to go to the Island of Doimhle. "Do not go," said Ciarán, "for it is in Tallaght that your own resurrection and the resurrection of your son, Brendan, shall be." A.D. 787.

(vii) *a.* Enda of Aran, son of Conall, son of Daimine, son of Coirpre Dam Argait, son of Crimthann. *b. 21st of March.* Enda, abbot of Aran. Conall Derg, son of Coirpre Dam Argait, was his father, specifically of the seed of Colla Fochrith. Aeibfionn, daughter of Ainmire, son of Rónán, king of the Ards, was his mother and the mother of Libba. He renounced the inheritance of the kingdom and the great wealth of his father’s house for God, so that he built a church in Aran and afterwards took up its abbacy. Three times fifty was the number of his community. This was the test and proof he would put upon them every evening to free them from sins: each man of them, in turn, was placed in a coracle without a skin <note>a boat frame without the leather covering</note> out upon the sea. The salt water would enter the coracle if there were guilt or sin upon the person who was in it; it would not enter if he were pure from sins. Enda was the last abbot to go into the coracle. Not one man of those three times fifty was found who did not come out of the coracle without being wet, except for Gigniat, Enda's cook, alone. "What have you done, Gigniat?" said Enda. He said that he had done nothing except add a small amount of his own portion to the portion of Ciarán <term>mac an tSaoir</term> <note>son of the craftsman</note>. Enda ordered him to leave the island and said: "A thief does not belong there." I have not permitted that otherwise.

PAGE 43:—(viii) *a.* Molling of Luachair, son of Faelán, son of Feradach, son of Erc, son of Fiachna, son of Eogan, son of Deg, son of Labraid, son of Bresal Belach, son of Fiacha Baiceda, son of Catháir Mór. *b. 17th of June.* Molling of Luachair, bishop *and confessor* of Tech Moling; he was of the lineage of Catháir Mór, high king of Ireland, of the Leinstermen. Nemhnat of Kerry was his mother, or Emhnat according to his *Life*, chapter 2. It is he who leaped over Luachair Degaid in three leaps when the specters were after him, so that for that reason he was called Molling <note>Molling means "the leaper"</note> of Luachair, though Tairchell was his first name. His miracles are too numerous to tell. Dairchell, then, was his first name. One night, Molling sent his fishermen to catch fish, and they caught a large salmon in the nets. When it was split open, an ingot of gold was found inside it. Molling divided the gold into three parts: a third for the poor, a third for the decoration of reliquaries, and the other third for the performance of labor and works. A.D. 696.

He was of the seed of Eremón *b.* for the Dál Fiatach are of the children of Oengus Tuirbech, while the Ulaid and the Dál Araide are of the children of Ollam Fótla; for those are the true Ulaid *c.* The four sons of Fiacc, son of Imchad, son of Bresal, son of Sirchad, son of Fiatach Finn *from whom* the Dál Fiatach [descend]: Trichem, *from whom* the Ui Thrichim; Trian, *from whom* the Ui Thréna; Brian, *from whom* the Ui Briuin; and Eochaid Gunnat, *whose mother was called Máthair-chaem, and from whom* descend the Ui Echach of the Ards. Finnbarr, that is, Finnia of Moville, son of Coirpre, son of Ailill, son of Trichem, *whose son was Díchú* (x) *a.* Colmán Elo, son of Beodgna, son of Mochta, son of Cuinneda, son of Lairine . . . [son of Eochaid], son of Maired . . . son of Ethriel, son of Iriel, son of Eremón *b. 26th of September.* Colmán Elo of Lann Ela <note>Lynally</note> in Fir Cell in western Meath; he was of the seed of Eremón on his father’s side, and his mother was the sister of Columb Cille, namely Mór, daughter of Fedlimid, son of Fergus Cennfada, son of Conall Gulban, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages, as the Life of Colmán himself says *c. i.* He was 50 years of age when he sent his spirit to heaven, A.D. 610. (xi) *a.* Comgall of Bangor, son of Sétna, son of Eochaid, son of Broen, son of Forgo, son of Ernaine, son of Crimthann, son of Eochaid, son of Lugaid, son of Ross, son of Imchad, son of Fedlimid, son of Cas, son of Fiacha Araide, *who was previously called Darerca b. 10th of May.* Comgall, abbot of Bangor in Ulster, was of the seed of Iriel, son of Conall Cernach. This man was full of the grace of God and of His love; a man who nurtured and improved many other saints, in whom he kindled and lit an unquenchable fire of God's love in their hearts and in their minds, as is evident in the ancient books of Ireland. Cuimín of Conor says that Comgall ate food only on Sundays. The Life of Ciarán says that the Rule of Comgall was one of the eight orders that were in Ireland. An extremely ancient vellum book says that Comgall of Bangor had a similarity in habits and life to the Apostle *James*. (xii) *a.* Duilech, son of Malach, son of Sinell, son of Nadfráech, son of Fiachna, son of Alla, son of Conmáel Glas, son of Fergus, son of Ross. Mobái also was a son of Sinell, son of Nadfráech; and Malán was a son of Sinell, *and* Curnán son of Sinell, *and* Crónán son of Sinell, *and* Mániu son of Sinell. (xiii) A.D. 631. The eighth year of Domnall [son of Aed, son of Ainmire]. Carthach, also known as Mochuda, son of Findall, was expelled from Rahan. 636. The thirteenth year of Domnall. St. Mochuda, bishop of Lismore and abbot of Rahan, died on the 14th of May. 750. The twelfth year of Domnall [son of Murchad, son of Diarmait]. Fidmhuine O Suanaigh, anchorite of Rahan, died. 758. Fidhairle O Suanaigh, abbot of Rahan, died on the first day of October. 1153. A hosting by Muirchertach, son of Niall Mac Lochlainn, and by the north of Ireland to aid Tairrdelbach Ua Briain, to restore him to the kingship of Munster again, until he reached Craeb Teine. Tairrdelbach O Conchobair gathered the men of Connacht until he reached the plain of Lici Pátraic against the north. Then Tadg O Briain came with his army to Rahan of the O Suanaighs to aid the Connachtmen. (xiv) *a.* Tlachtga—from what was it named? Not difficult. Tlachtga, daughter of Mogh Roith, whom the three sons of Simon the Druid <note>Simon Magus</note> raped when she went with her father to learn druidry in the East of the world. For it was she who made [<gloss>Manuscript: doroighne</gloss>] the "Rowing Wheel" for Trian, and the stone in Forcharthain, and the cauldron in Cnamchoill. She returned afterward from the East with those two things until she reached the Hill of Tlachtga. She was then delivered of three sons: Doirb, from whom is Mag nDoirbi; and Cuma, from whom is Mag Cuma; and Muach, from whom is Mag Muich. As long as those names shall be in the memory of the men of Ireland, no foreign vengeance shall come to Ireland. And she died after her labor, and the fort was built over her. *Wherefore* it is called Tlachtga. Tlachtga, daughter of Mogh Mór, the sons of Simon raped her; from the hour she came across the beautiful sea, from her it is [named].

Not difficult. The hounds of Manannán son of Ler and the pack of Mod, from whom the islands of Mod are named, met around the pig that laid waste to the land about them, that is, the islands of Mod. If the dogs had not intercepted the pig, it would have been a wasteland as far as Scotland. The pig leaped into the lake before the dogs; the dogs followed after it. It fought against them on that lake, and not a single dog escaped alive without being cut or drowned. Tailltiu, daughter of Magmór and wife of Eochaid Garb son of Duach Temen. It was by him that the Mound of the Hostages at Tara was built, and she was the foster-mother of Lugh son of Scal Balb. She requested of her husband that the forest of Cuan be cleared by him so that it might be a place of assembly around her grave. She died on the Calends of August after that, and her lamentation and her games were performed by Lugh; *whence* we say *Lugnasad*. This was three thousand five hundred years before the birth of Christ, and that assembly was held by every king who took Ireland until Patrick came. And there were four hundred assemblies in Tailltiu from the time of Patrick until the "Black Assembly" of Donnchad son of Flann son of Maelshechlainn. (vi) Temuir <note>Tara</note>, *from where is it named*. Not difficult. Temuir, that is, *Tea-múr*, the wall of Tea daughter of Lugaid son of Ith <note>son of Breogan</note> and wife of Eiremón son of Míl; it was there she was buried. Whence the poet sang:

->The first woman who went into a cold grave,<-
->of the company from the tower of fair Breogan:<-
->Tea of Brega, the wife of the king,<-
->from whom Tara is called the "Land of Fál."<-

*Or* "temuir" comes from the Greek verb *TEMORO*, meaning *I behold*; for *temair* is the name for every place from which a view is easy and pleasant; *whence it is said* "the *temair* of the countryside" and "the *temair* of the house." Cormac mac Cuilennáin.

(x) *a.* Bec mac Dé the druid, son of Gnoei, son of Lughaidh, son of Dallán, son of Bresal, son of Máine, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages. Or Bec mac Dé the druid, son of Noei, son of Conall Echluath, son of Lughaidh Minn Dimmain.

(xi) Genealogy of the Dál Araide.

*a.* Fiacha Araide, son of Oengus Goibnenn, son of Fergus Gallini, son of Tipraiti, who killed Conn of the Hundred Battles, son of Bresal Láig, who entered Loch Láig, son of Bresal, son of Feirb, son of Mál, who killed Tuathal Techtmar, son of Rochride.

*b.* Araide Bibre, the satirist of the Munstermen, was the steward to Cormac grandson of Conn. Cairech was his wife; it was she who protected Fiacha son of Oengus. From this, he is called Fiacha Araide, from whom the Dál Araide are named.

*c.* Dál, that is, the "portion" of Araide; that is, the *airial* <note>bedchamber or designated lands</note> of the king of Ireland. That is his lawful residence because it was the inheritance of heroes that they took, or because they are of the family of heroes. It was also a distinction for them to be "under the knee" of the king, for the "chief hero" of Ireland in the time when he lived was Conall Cernach son of Amergin. Alternatively, and more truly: Dál Araide, that is, Fiacha Araide is the name of the man from whom they are named.

PAGE 76:—(xii) 15th of April. Ruadán son of Fergus, Abbot of Lorrha. One hundred and fifty were in his congregation, and they always received their sufficiency without human labor, being sustained continually while praying and praising the Lord of creation. He was of the seed of Eogan Mór son of Oilill Olum. A very ancient vellum book says that Ruadán of Lorrha was like Matthew the Apostle in his habits and life.

This was the cause of the Battle of Cúl Dreimne.

555. The seventeenth year of Diarmait. The battle of Cúl Dreimne was won against Diarmait son of Cerball by Fergus and Domnall, the two sons of Muirchertach son of Erc; by Ainmire son of Sétna; and by Aindid son of Duach; and by Aedh son of Eochaid Tirmcharna, king of Connacht. In revenge for the killing of Curnán son of Aedh son of Eochaid Tirmcharna while under the protection of Columba, the clans of Niall of the North and the Connachtmen gave that battle of Cúl Dreimne to the king, Diarmait. And also because of the false judgment that Diarmait gave against Columba concerning the book of Finnian, which Columba wrote without Finnian noticing; when they went to the judgment of Diarmait, Diarmait uttered the famous judgment: "To every cow its calf, etc."

Fraochán son of Tenusán is he who made the druid's fence for Diarmait. Tuathán son of Dimman son of Sárán son of Cormac son of Eogan is he who threw the druid's fence over his head. Three thousand men of Diarmait's people fell there; only one man fell on the other side. Maghláim was his name, for it was he who leaped over the druid's fence.

Gulban, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages. A.D. 564: the first year of Ainmire, son of Sédna, son of Fergus Cennfota, in the kingship of Ireland. 566: after being three years in the kingship of Ireland, Ainmire son of Sédna fell by the hand of Fergus, son of Neilline.

(xvi) *a.* Here follows the genealogy of the men of Bréifne: Fergus, son of Muiredach Máel, son of Eogan Srem <note>that is, a small contortion that was in his mouth</note>, son of Duach Galach, son of Brian, son of Eochaid Mugmedón. He had three sons: Eochaid Tirmcharna, ancestor of the Síl Muiredaig; Duach Tenga Uma, ancestor of the Clann Choscraig and Muintir Murchada; and Fergna, the third son, ancestor of the Uí Briuin. 

*b.* Eogan Srem: <note>that is, a distortion that was in his mouth or in his eye</note>. 

Duach Galach: <note>that is, "valor and sighing" was his lot; meaning the other sons of Brian used to raid and attack him when he was a young youth</note>. 

Duach Tenga Uma: <note>that is, "Brazen Tongue," because of the excellence of his eloquence and the sweet resonance of his speech</note>. 

Eochaid Tirmcharna: <note>that is, "Dry Meat," because his brother, Duach Tenga Uma, King of Connacht, would give him no food but dry meat</note>. 

*c.* A.D. 557: the Battle of Móin Doire Lothair [was won] over the Cruithne <note>the Picts</note> by the Northern Uí Néill, namely the Cenél Conaill and Cenél Eogain. In this place, seven chieftains of the Cruithne fell, including Aodh Brec. It was on that occasion that the territories of the Lee and Carn Eolairg were won again by the Northern Uí Néill. Cennfaoladh said this:

> The blades were extended, the men advanced, at the great bog of Doire Lothair: the cause of an unjust division was the seven kings of the Cruithne around Aodh Brec. The battle of all the Cruithne is fought, and Eilne is burned: the battle of Gabra Liffe is fought, and the battle of Cúil Dreimne. They took hostages after the conflict, from there westward around the fresh harvest: Fergus, Domnall, Ainmire, and Nainnid son of Duach. The two sons of Mac Erca returned for the head of the same battle; and the king Ainmire returned into the possessions of Sédna. 

567: after being one year in the kingship of Ireland, Baodán, son of Ninnidh, son of Fergus Cennfota, was killed at the Horse-leap in a skirmish by the two Comaoines, namely Comaoine son of Colmán Beg, son of Cerball, and Comaoine son of Librene, son of Illadhan, son of Cerball. It was by the advice of Colmán Beg that they performed that deed. 

*d.* A.D. 499: the Battle of Segas [was won] by Muirchertach mac Erca over Duach Tenga Uma, King of Connacht. This is the cause of the battle: Muirchertach had been a guarantor between the king and his brother Eochaid Tirmcharna, until Eochaid was seized despite being under Muirchertach's protection. Cennfaoladh spoke to prove this:

> The Battle of Segas, a woman was the cause of it. There was red blood over the spear-rank with Duísech, daughter of Duach: the Battle of Delga, the Battle of Mucrama, and the Battle of Tuaim Drubha, along with the Battle of Segas in which Duach Tenga Uma fell.

<insert>PAGE 81:---</insert>(xvii) *a.* A.D. 965: the Battle of Formaoil at Ráith Beg [was won] by the Cenél Eogain over the Cenél Conaill. In this place, Maolísa O Canannáin, lord of Cenél Conaill, fell, along with Muirchertach O Taidhg, royal heir of Connacht, and many others with them. 

*b.* Ráth Mór in Magh Line: from where was it named? It is not difficult: Ráth Rogin was its name at first, until the reign of Bresal Brec, son of Brian, King of Ulster, who went on an adventure under Loch Láig and remained there for fifty years. Mór, daughter of Rithir, son of Derlam, was in the fort during that time, and she said:

> Long to me is the adventure of Bresal.

And a woman said:

> It will be long for you, for Bresal shall not return until Judgment Day from his adventure to his home, until the dead return to everyone.

Mór then died immediately, and her name stayed with the fort; hence "Ráth Mór" <note>Mór's Fort</note>. And Bresal Brec arrived that very evening, as is told in the "Adventure of Bresal."

VII. <insert>PAGE 82:---</insert>(i) A.D. 558: after being twenty years over Ireland in the kingship, Diarmait son of Fergus Cerrbeol fell by the hand of Aodh Dubh, son of Suibne, King of Dál nAraide, at Ráith Beg in Magh Line. His head was brought to Clonmacnoise and buried there, and his body was buried in Connor. 

(ii) *a.* Corbach, daughter of Maine of the Leinstermen and wife of Fergus Cerrbeol, was the mother of Diarmait son of Fergus. Mugain, daughter of Concraid, son of Duach of the Connachtmen, was the wife of Diarmait.

[He was the son] of Duach Cliach, son of Maine Muncháin, son of Coirpre, son of Corc, son of Lugaid, son of Ailill Flann Bec, son of Fiachu Muillethan, son of Eogan Mór, son of Ailill Olomm. *c.* Flann sang: "Mugain, daughter of fair Concraid, son of Duach from southern Munster: the noble and generous one bought [fame] without deceit, the wife of Diarmait son of Cerball. This is she, without any boastful word of betrayal; the opinion of another historian: with her great, faultless wealth, Mugain was of the Connachta."

PAGE 84:—(iii) *a.* The Plain of Breg (*Mag mBreg*), from what was it named? Not difficult: The Plain of Breg, indeed, is named after Breg, the name of the ox of Dil. Dil, daughter of Lugmannrach, came from the land of Uí Failge with Tulchainne the druid, the druid of Conaire son of Meisi Buachalla. In the same hour, this girl was born and the cow gave birth to this calf, ahead of the other cattle; the girl loved the calf because of their simultaneous birth. Tulchainne refused to bring her until his ox was brought with her; and it was the destiny of the great queen <note>the Morrígan</note> that he went to bring that prize with him so that it would be in the Plain of Eolgaide—the first name of the plain—so that from it, the Plain of Breg (*Mag mBreg*) is named. Or, it may be from Breogan that the plain was cleared and named, as was said: "The Plain of Breogan, a peak of our origin, with a prudent house and every equipment; we, following after him across the seas, Breg took possession of Bregia."

*b.* Essa, daughter of Eochaid Aireman and Étaín, was the mother of Mesbuachalla. That Mesbuachalla was the wife of Eterscél and the mother of Conaire. That Mesbuachalla was also the wife of Conchobar son of Ness, so that she was the mother of Cormac Condloinges; or else Clothra, daughter of Eochaid Feidlech, was his mother.

VIII. PAGE 85:—(i) *a.* A.D. 630. The Battle of Cúil Chaoláin was won by Diarmait son of Aed Sláine, where the two sons of Aongus son of Colmán Mór were killed: namely Maoluma and Colga, and others along with them. *b.* Temair, daughter of Aed Bolc son of Finghin—the King of the Déisi—was the wife of Diarmait Ruanaid son of Aed Sláine and the mother of Cernach Sotal. He was called Cernach Sotal <note>the Proud</note> because of his pride and the greatness of his spirit.

(ii) A.D. 628. The fifth year of Domnall [son of Aed son of Ainmire]. The Battle of Áth Goan in western Liffey was won by Faolán son of Colmán, Conall son of Suibne (the leader of Meath), and Failbe Flann (the King of Munster); there, Crimthann son of Aed son of Senach, the King of Leinster, was killed along with a great many others.

(iii) Dubthur, from where is it named? Not difficult: from the "dark land" (*dub-thír*) of Guaire son of the Blind (*mac in Daill*). That was after he committed kin-slaying against his brother at Devenish against Dáirine the Dubchestach, son of the Blind; that is, he killed him out of envy and treachery, until the woods and thickets spread over his land. From which the poet sang: "Guaire killed brown-haired Dáire, without shame it was no mistake: his father's son, a great deed, he was killed through evil jealousy."

IX. PAGE 87:—(i) *a.* 30th of July. Caenchomrac of Inis Éndaim on Lough Ree; he was first a bishop in Clonmacnoise, of the Uí Dega by kin. He left Clonmacnoise because of the great reverence shown to him there, for those nearby worshipped him as a prophet; so he went to seek solitude on Lough Ree afterward. *b.* The King of the Uí Dega: Dub dá Críoch son of Conamhal, son of Aed, son of Oengus, son of Dega, son of Enna Cennselach.

(ii) *a.* Tefftha, daughter of Eochaid Aireman, was the wife of Naoise son of Nechtan. As for Eochaid Airemh: it was by him that a yoke was first placed on the necks of oxen; or else [his name comes] from a cave (*uamh*), for it was by him that the earth was first dug to make a cave. Bé Bindía, daughter of Cremthann, was the wife of Finn son of Finntan and the mother of Eochaid Finnleith and Eochaid Aireman. *b.* A.M. 5084. After spending fifteen years in the kingship of Ireland, Eochaid Airemh was burned by Sigmall in Fremhain. *c.* Tethba...
