From where was **Tebtha** named? Not difficult. Tebtha was the daughter of Eochaid Aireman until Nóisiu, son of Nechtan of the fair shoulders, from Loch Léin, carried her away. Her foster-mother was Eitech, daughter of Lennghlas son of Luan of the Glomraide of Turvey Strand. She went along with her foster-child. When Tebtha reached the Height of Nóisiu—which was called the Height of the Sanctuary until then—she said: "It will be a loss (*tesbaid*) to the adornment of this land that I am leaving it." "That is not true," said Nóisiu. "Your name shall not be missing (*teiséba*) from this land; that is what is intended." "It is a plague upon one to share the words you leave upon this land," she said, "and may it follow my journey on our migration." And it was true; for her foster-mother died while going southward, so that from this come Cenn Eitig and Tebtha. *Concerning which it is said*:

    Tebtha gave to the northern land,
    May there be no departing from the great victory;
    Her namesake Cleitech she loved,
    The daughter of Eochaid Aireman.
    She came with Nóisiu from afar,
    With [the son] of Nechtan of the fair shoulders:
    Tebtha enriched every house,
    And her foster-mother, great Eitech.
    Eitech, daughter of swift Lennghlas,
    Parted from her lifelong struggle:
    In the place where she left the darkness of her face,
    Eitech was the end of her journey.
    Their names remain after them,
    As we find them in the narrative:
    Of the women of power and fame,
    Each chose a land for her fruit.

**Turvey Strand** (*Tráig Tuirbi*), from what was it named? Not difficult. Tuirbe Trágmar, the father of Gobán the Smith, is the one who owned it. From that inheritance, he used to cast a throw of his axe onto the shore-hill in the face of the flood-tide, so that he forbade the sea, and it would not come past it. His specific genealogy is not known, unless he was one of the missing [craftsmen] who fled from Tara before the "multi-skilled master" <note>Lugh Lamfada</note> who is in the secret places of Bregia.

**X. PAGE 89** :—(i) *a.* A.D. 157. After being thirty-five years in the kingship of Ireland, **Conn of the Hundred Battles** fell by the hand of Tibraide Tírech, son of Mál, son of Rochraide, King of Ulster, in the district of Amros. *b.* Conn of the Hundred Battles: that is, he won a hundred battles over Munster, a hundred battles over the Ulstermen, and sixty battles over the Leinstermen. As was said:

    A hundred battles over great Munster,
    Brave Conn broke immediately:
    A hundred over the Ulstermen along with them,
    And sixty battles over the Leinstermen.

*c.* Una the very-beautiful, daughter of the King of Lochlann, was the wife of Feidlimid the Lawgiver and mother of Conn of the Hundred Battles. Lennabair, daughter of Cathair Mór, was the wife of Conn of the Hundred Battles. Aife, daughter of Alpin, was another wife of Conn and mother of Art the Solitary, Connla the Red, and Sadb; she was also the mother of Lughna Fertrí later on. Lann, daughter of Cremthann Cas, was another wife of Conn. Main, Sadb, and Sáraid were the three daughters of Conn. Sadb was the mother of Mac Con and the seven sons of Ailill Olomm, and Ainel (*sic*), daughter of Eogabal, was another wife for him. Main was the mother of the three Ferguses: namely, Fergus Black-Tooth (*Duibdédach*), Fergus Long-Hair (*Foiltlebar*), and Fergus Bód over Bregia, and all three of them fell in the Battle of Crinna by the hand of Cormac. Sáraid was the mother of the three Coirbres: namely, Coirbre Rigfhodae, Coirbre Musc, and Coirbre Bascháin, the three sons of Conaire son of Mug Láma. (ii) Fergus Black-Tooth: that is, he had black teeth. Or he was black and had large teeth; that is, "black-toothed." (iii) *a.* A.D. 267. One year for **Eochaid Gonnat** in the kingship of Ireland until he fell by the hand of Lugaid Menn, son of Aongus of the Ulstermen. *b.* Eochaid Gonnat: that is, he was a very small man; that is, he was "stumpy" (*gunnataig*); that is, he was "fragmented"; it was by him that the Conaille were scattered throughout Ireland. Or Eochaid Gonnat: that is, Eochaid "Long-Neck," *for "gunnat" means a throat or neck.* **PAGE 90** :—(iv) *a.* Bresal Brec had two sons: Connla, ancestor of the Ossory, and Lugaid, ancestor of the Leinstermen. A son of that Lugaid was Sétna Sithbac. Sétna had four sons. Nuadu Necht was the fourth son of Sétna Sithbac; from him is the origin of the Leinstermen. He was King of Tara, and it was by him that Etirscél Mór, son of Eogan, King of Munster, fell. It was for the sake of Lugaid Reo nDerg that Nuadu performed [that deed], and it was after that that Lugaid took the kingship of Ireland. Nuadu Necht was the grandfather of Finn ua Báiscné and Cáilte. *As Senchán Torpéist sang in the "Cóir Anmann"*: Finn of the hills...

The host of the company... they shook the belt of battle <note>the *cres mbodbae* or "belt of the war-goddess"</note>... the three victorious descendants of Báiscne, namely: Finn, Oisín son of Finn, and Cáilte. A company whose graves will endure are the three descendants of Nuada Necht, so that their sons are... Finn, then, was the son of Cumall, son of Trénmór, son of Suaelt, son of Eltan, son of Baiscne, son of Nuada Necht. **Baine**, daughter of Scál Balb and wife of Tuathal Techtmar, was the mother of Fedlimid Rechtmar and of Cumall son of Trénmór. **Muirne Muncháem**, daughter of Tadg son of Nuada, was the mother of Finn mac Cumaill. **Gráinne**, daughter of Cormac grandson of Conn, was the wife of Finn grandson of Báiscne, and she was later the wife of Diarmait. **Aillbe of the Freckled Cheek**, daughter of Cormac, was another wife of Finn. Another wife was **Moingfionn**, daughter of Dubán, mother of Ulach son of Finn. Another wife was **Bodomar**, daughter of Lugar the fisherman, and it was she who killed Currach of the Liffey, son of Catháir, so that in revenge for this Finn killed Currach. Another wife of Finn was **Smirgad**, daughter of Fothad Canann. **Áine**, daughter of Finn mac Cumaill, was the mother of Eochaid Doimlén. (iv) **Sédna Sithbac**, that is, "peace-hinderer," for he was always preventing peace and bringing about war for the sake of honor.

PAGE 91:—(v) **Fothad Canann**: Canann was the name of a dog he had; he was named after it. (vi) **Adarca** <note>the "Horns"</note>, from which it is named: that is, in Uí Failge. **Iuchna Horse-mouth** was a royal hospitaller who lived at Faffainn, northeast in the slope of the hospitaller's land, in the place called the Field of Brigit today. It was his custom that whatever was born in his house each year would be reared and sheltered there until the Beltane of every year, so that his cattle loved him. When he died, all his cattle came to that hill and remained there for three days and three nights contending on that hill while mourning Iuchna, until their horns fell off and mounds were made around them. From those hills they called them the Horns of Iuchna. Afterward, they went to quench their thirst at the Boyne, from which comes the "Ford of Almain" at the mouth of the Boyne. (vii) *a.* **Bóand**, from what is it named? Not difficult. Bóand, wife of Nechtan son of Labraid, went to the secret well that was in the courtyard of Nechtan’s fairy mound (*sidhe*). No one could visit it without their two eyes bursting, unless it were Nechtan and his three cupbearers, whose names were Flesc, Lesc, and Luam. Once, Bóand went there out of pride to test the power of the well, and she said that there was no secret power that could mar the beauty of her form. She walked counter-clockwise around the well three times, and three waves burst over her from the well, breaking her thigh, her hand, and one of her eyes. She then turned to flee from her shame toward the sea, with the water following behind her to the mouth of the Boyne. She was the mother of Aengus, son of the Dagda. Or else "Bó" is the name of the stream and "Finn" the river of Slieve Guaire, and from their meeting together comes the name "Bóand." **Dabhilla** was the name of her lapdog, from which comes Cnoc Davilla—it is called the Mountain of the Covenant today. *b.* Bóand, daughter of Delbaeth, was the mother of Aengus of the Brug, and she was the wife of Nechtan son of Labraid the Freckled. *c.* Three landmarks of Ireland without blemish: the Mound of the Hostages at Tara; the Brug of the son of the Óc <note>Brug na Bóinne</note>, a beautiful place to visit; and the Fort of Cremthann at Howth. (viii) *a. A.D.* 283. The sixteenth year of Cairbre. Finn grandson of Báiscne fell at the hands of Aichlech son of Duibdrenn and the sons of Uirgrenn of the Luaigni of Tara, at the Ford of Brea on the Boyne, of which it was said: Finn was killed by spears <note>or "fishing spears"</note>, that is, he was wounded by spears. *b.* Finn was beheaded, though he was a strong man, by the warrior son of Duibdrenn; and his head was taken from him by the fierce sons of Uirgrenn.

PAGE 92:—(ix) The genealogy of the **Uí Fidgentid**. Conall (from whom the Uí Chonaill Gabra descend), son of Intat, son of Dáire, son of Brión, son of Fiacha Fidgenid, son of Dáire Cerba, son of Ailill Flann Bec, son of Ailill Flann Mór. *From the putting of a ship into a wood he was named "Fidgenid" (wood-maker), and it was he who made a wooden horse to be moved in the circus of Colmán in Liffey.* [Others say that Maine Muncháin, son of Ailill Flann Bec, son of Fiacha Muillethan, was the "Fidgenid."] (x) *A.D.* 884. **Maelmura**, the accomplished poet, truly learned historian, and master of the Scotic language, died.

It is for him this testimony was given:
The chosen earth did not cover,
There shall not come to many-towered Tara,
The vastness of Ireland does not conceal,
A man like the smooth, pure Maol Mura.
He did not drink death without delay;
He did not reach the state of the dead <note>literally "the custom of the dead"</note> [until his time];
The earth of the husbandman was never closed
Over a historian more wonderful than he.

### XI. *ibid.*:—
(i) <term>fianna</term> from *uenatione* <note>hunting</note>, that is, from the hunt they used to perform they were called "fianna." Or "fianna," that is, <term>finedha</term> [kindreds], because it was in their kindreds and in their tribes they used to be. Or "fianna," that is, they were the warriors of the king. 
(ii) <term>Mide</term>, from where was it named? Not difficult. Mide son of Brat son of Det was the first who kindled a fire for the children of Nemed in Ireland, and it was burning for seven years; so it was from that fire that every chief fire in Ireland was kindled. For this reason, his successor is entitled to a sack of grain and a pig for every single roof-tree <note>or hearth</note> in Ireland. Then the druids of Ireland said: "This fire is a 'middle' (*mide*) to us that has been kindled in the land." Then the druids of Ireland were gathered into one house, and their tongues were cut out of their heads by the counsel of Mide; he buried them in the earth of <term>Uisnech</term>, and Mide, the chief druid and chief historian of Ireland, sat above them. Gaire daughter of Gumor, the foster-mother of Mide, said: "Noble is the person who is quenched <note>or "buried"</note> here tonight." *Unde* [from which comes] Uisnech and Mide.

### XII. PAGE 94:—
(i) A.D. 284. After being seventeen years in the kingship of Ireland, **Cairbre Lifechair** fell in the battle of Gabra Aichle by the hand of Sémeon son of Cerb of the Fothairt, after the <term>fianna</term> had been brought by Fearchorb son of Cormac Cas with him against the king to contest Leth Mogha [the southern half of Ireland] against him. 
285. One year for the two **Fothads** over Ireland until Fothad the Charioteer fell by Fothad the Wealthy. Fothad the Wealthy fell after that in the battle of Ollarba in Line by **Caoilte**. 
(ii) **Ossín** *cecinit* [sang]: in the battle of Gabra, **Oscar** and Cairbre Lifechair were killed:
An <term>ogham</term> on a stone, a stone over a grave,
In the place where men used to go once;
The son of the king of Ireland was slain there,
By a slender spear above bright Gabair.
Cairbre threw a difficult cast...
Oscar, his right hand struck him.
Oscar threw a great cast,
Angrily and fiercely like a lion,
So that he killed Cairbre, grandson of Conn,
Before those who gave battle could shout.
The great feats of the youths,
They met their death from the fight;
Before their weapons could meet,
There were more dead than living.
I myself was in the fight,
On the south side of green Gabair;
I killed fifty warriors twice over,
It was I who struck them to their deaths.
A chariot-rider entertains for a fee,
In the time when my strength was at its peak;
I would kill a boar in a holy wood,
I would overpower a swift bird over its egg.
That <term>ogham</term> which is on the stone,
Around which the doomed men fell:
If Finn of the twenty deeds were alive,
Long would that <term>ogham</term> be remembered.

(iii) **Sliab Fuait**, from where was it named? Not difficult. Fuat son of Bile son of Brige son of Breogan visited an island on the sea while they were coming to Ireland, that is, the "island of the maiden" or "my young god" (*id est* [that is] *morogdiada*). Whoever would set his sole upon it would not speak a lie as long as he remained on it. Fuat then brought a sod from it with him, and it was upon it that judgment and its correction were settled; when a lie was told, its bottom turned upwards and its grass toward the sun, and when truth was spoken, its grass turned upwards. And that sod is still in the mountain, and it is upon it that the grain fell from Patrick’s gelding; so that it has been a sacred place from then until now for the preservation of truth there. *Aliter* [Otherwise], it may be from Fuat son of Breogan specifically that it was named. *Unde* [From which] Sliab Fuait *nominatur* [is named].

PAGE 96:—
(iv) A.D. 447. The nineteenth year of **Laogaire** [son of Niall of the Nine Hostages]. ***Secundinus***, that is, Sechnall son of Ua Baird, the son of Patrick’s sister, namely Darerca, bishop of Armagh; seventy-five years was his age when he sent forth his spirit, that is, the 27th of November.

PAGE 98:—
(v) a. **Benn Edair** [*etc.*] Etar wife of Gann son of Dela, the fifth king of the Fir Bolg; she was the first woman who died here of grief for her husband *prius* [formerly], and it was there she was buried at Benn Edair [Howth]. *Aliter* [Otherwise], Etar, that is, from Etur son of Edgáth, who was in the service of Manannán; it is he who died for the love of Áine, so that his burial mound was built on that peak.

### XII. *ibid.*:—
(vi) a. A.M. 4875. After being sixty years in the kingship of Ireland, Aenghus Tuirmech of Tara died at Tara. He was called Aenghus Tuirmech because to him are enumerated <note>Irish *tuirmigter*</note> the noble clans of the seed of Eiremón. b. Oengus Tuirbech, that is, he felt "shame" <note>Irish *tuirbech*</note>, because of the son he had by his own daughter, namely, Fiachaid Fer Mara. Or else it is to him the noble clans of Ireland are enumerated, and that is why he was called Aenghus Tuirmech. 
c. Twelve primary tribes of the Ernaí and twenty-four additional families <note>Irish *forshlointe*</note>, that is, two additional families for every tribe.

(vii) The mother of Diarmait from the Dál was the daughter of Currach son of Catháir. It is Blai Derg from vigorous Banba who was the mother of fierce Ossine. She used to come in the shape of a doe to the assembly of the reavers; so that Ossine was born of her, from Blai Derg in the shape of a doe.

(viii) A.D. 2550. Parthalón died on the old plain of the flocks <note>Irish *elta*</note> of Edair in this year. In the time of Parthalón's arrival, these plains were cleared, but it is not known in what year they were cleared: Mag nEithrige in Connacht; Mag nIthe in Leinster; Mag Lii in the territory of the Uí mac Uais of Brega; Mag Latharna in Dál nAraidi. 
2820. Nine thousand of Parthalón's people died in one week on the old plain of the flocks of Edair—namely, five thousand men and four thousand women—so that from that event comes the name <term>Táimlecht</term> <note>Tallaght, meaning "plague-grave"</note> of Parthalón's people. They spent three hundred years in Ireland.

PAGE 102:—(ix) a. Now Eochaid Ollathair—that is, the Great Dagda son of Elathan—was eighty years in the kingship of Ireland. He had three sons: Aenghus, Aedh, and fair Cermad. It was for them, as a group of four, that the men of Ireland made the mound <note>Irish *síd*</note> of the Brug. 
b. Eochaid Ollathair: that is, he was "greater" <note>Irish *uille*</note> than his father; or "Ollathair," meaning "Great Father" <note>Irish *uille*</note> of the Tuatha Dé Danann. 
Dagda: that is, "good god" <note>Irish *daigh dé*</note>, for he was an excellent god among the heathens. 
c. Tuatha Dé Danann: that is, the "gods" <note>Irish *dee*</note> were the people of arts and "un-gods" <note>Irish *andé*</note> were the people of husbandry.

PAGE 103:—(x) a. Dagda, Ogma, Alloth, Bres, and Delbaeth were the five sons of Elathan son of Delbaeth son of Néd. 
b. Oengus the Young, Aedh the Fair, and Cermad Honey-mouth were the three sons of the Dagda son of Elathan. 
c. Midir of Brí Léith was the son of Indúi son of Echtach son of Edarlám. 
d. Nuada Silver-hand was the son of Echtach son of Edarlám. 
e. Bodhb of the mound of the men of Femen was the son of Eochaid Garb son of Duach Temin son of Bres son of Elathan son of Delbaeth son of Néd.

(xi) a. Brí Léith [etc.] Liath son of Celtchair was a prince’s son who lived in the mound-dwellings; he loved Brí of the speckled eyebrows, the daughter of Midir of the great deeds, son of Indúi son of Echtach. Now Brí went with her maidens to the Mound of the Maidens beside Tara. Liath went with his troop of youths until he was at the hill of the after-grief. They were unable to come any closer because of the slingers of Midir's mound, for they were as numerous as a swarm of bees on a beautiful day, answering each other's casting. Consequently, Cochlán, Liath's servant, was struck by them and died. The girl turned back to Brí Léith until her heart broke within her, and she said: "Though Liath does not come, and though this girl does not grow old, it is my name that shall be upon it"—that is, Brí Léith, meaning "the Hill <note>Irish *Brí*</note> that belongs to Liath." So from that it is called Brí Léith and the Grave of Cochlán. 

b. Mag Femin, from what is it named? Not difficult. Femen and Fera were two brothers—the two sons of Mogab son of Dachair of the family of Brath son of Deth. They had one spade and one iron shovel between them both. When Femen was digging, Fera was shoveling, and vice versa. From this comes Mag Femin and Mag Fera. As the poet said:
>Femen and Fera, men of [prophetic?] skill,
>Of the clear-formed seed of Death;
>It is they who cleared the plains,
>Femen and Fera, from the forest.

PAGE 104:—(xii) Fid nGaibli [etc.] Gabul Glas son of Ethadón son of Nuada Silver-hand stole a bundle of twigs from Ainge daughter of the Dagda, which she had gathered to make a vat <note>Irish *drochtai*</note> for herself; for the vat the Dagda made would never stop dripping as long as the tide was rising, and not a drop would come out while it was ebbing. Gabul then made a cast of that bundle from the Pass of Fualascach, so that it took root and the wood grew on every side. From this comes Fid nGaibli <note>the Wood of Gabul</note>. Or it may be that Gabul the Laughing, daughter of Goll Glas and wife of Orc son of Ingas, was drowned in that river.

...after her husband was killed by Ailill son of Aed Rón at Áth Orc. *Whence* Gabul and Áth Orc *are named*. *Or* the river Gabul is so named because of the forking (*gablugud*) it makes at the tips of its two meadows, namely Cluain Sasta and Cluain Mór.

PAGE 106:— (xiii) *a.* **Temair Luachra** [*etc.*] Temair, daughter of Lugaid son of Íth and wife of Eiremón; from her Temair Luachra, Temair Breg, and every other Temair in Ireland are named. Luachair itself, however, was a flowery plain until the time of the sons of Ugaine, or until the birth of Conn, *as others say*, because from it gushed the Suir, the Nore, the Barrow, Loch Riach, and Loch Léin in Luachair; and a fruitful tree and Eoron were seen. 

*b.* **Loch Léin** [*etc.*] Léin of the scale-teeth, son of Bán Bolgaid son of Bannach son of Glammach son of Gomir; he was the smith of Bodb. He lived in the lake making the shining vessels of Fainne daughter of Flidais. After finishing his work each night, he would cast his anvil eastward to the anvil of the Déise at the burial mound; and he would cast three showers: a shower of water, a shower of fire, and a shower of purple-bright pearls. Nemandach did the same while shaping the cup of Conchobar in the north; *whence* Loch Léin *is named*.

PAGE 107:— (xiv) **Crota Cliach** [*etc.*] Cliach was the harper of Smirduib son of Smál, king of the three *narus* from the fairy mound of Baine. He went to woo Conchinne daughter of Bodb from the fairy mound on Femen—or perhaps her name was Baine. Cliach was then a full year playing music on that hill, but he did not reach Bodb’s fairy mound—which was not near—because of the great power of the mound; and he could do nothing for the maidens. But he struck his harp until the earth broke under him, so that from there the dragon burst forth. From this comes Loch Bél Dracon <note>Lake of the Dragon’s Mouth</note>. A fiery dragon was found by the nurse of Ternog there in the shape of a salmon, and it is Fursa who confined it in the lake. And that is the dragon prophesied to rise over Ireland on the feast of St. John at the end of the world to destroy Ireland; and from that come the Crota <note>The "Harps" of Cliach</note>.

PAGE 109:— (xv) *a.* **Berba** <note>The River Barrow</note> *whence it is named*. The Berba is where the three snakes were cast that were in the heart of Méiche son of the Morrígan, after he was killed by Diancecht in Mag Méichi. Mag Fertaige was the original name of that plain. The shapes of three snake-heads were on the three hearts that were in Méiche; and if their killing had not been achieved, those snakes would have grown in his breast until they left no living creatures in Ireland. So Diancecht burned them after the killing and threw their ashes into that stream, so that it boiled (*romberb*) and dissolved every living thing within it. *Whence* Mag Luadat, Mag Méichi, and the Berba:
> The heart of Méiche, harsh the wound; in the Berba it was drowned.
> Its ashes, after you burned them; the son of Cecht, the hundred-yoker, cast them.

*b.* **Slige Dala** <note>Dala's Way</note> *whence it is named*. Not difficult. Dalo Glas of the Greeks of Scythia—it is from him that Slige Dala is called. Créa, daughter of Feidlech, his wife—it is from her that Ros Cré <note>Roscrea</note> is named. Cannan son of Eidlech, moreover—it is from him that Cluain Cannan is called. Carmun the hundred-landowner was brother to Dalo, and he came after Dalo's death to travel from Ireland until he reached Carmun Liphi, where he died of grief for his brother. Dala, indeed, and Carmun, and Imteng (*according to some*), and Gláire, and Brea, and Grea, and Cairiu were the seven prophets, sons of Tait son of Ogamun son of Beamun son of Srú son of Esrú son of Gaedel Glas; and Rafann was their sister. They were dispersed upon the death of Dalo, for Dalo was their leader. Inteng, then, at Dún Inteing; *here according to some* [Carmun died]; Gláire over Dún Gláire in Éile; Brea at Dún Brea in Uí Briuin Cualann; Grea in Dún Grea in Uí Garrchon above Sliab Airgiall; Cairiu at Dún Cairenn; Rafann, their sister, at Ráirinn in Uí Muiredaig. In that way the seven prophets were dispersed, and those places are named after them:
> Dalo, Inteng, bright Gláire; Brea, Grea, Cairiu, and Cannan:
> And crooked, warlike Carmun; they were the vast offspring of one father.

*c.* **Cenn Febrat** *where does it come from* [*etc.*] Not difficult. Febra son of Sin, brother of Old Dedaid son of Sin, whom Cáin son of Derg Dualach killed; and he brought his head to that mountain yonder; *whence* Cenn Febrat <note>Febrat's Head</note> *is said*. Then Garbán went...

...son of Dedad, to avenge himself on Cáin son of Derg "of the long hair," so that he killed him on Mount Cáin and took his head to Cenn Febrat. Many heroes and heroines were buried there by them: Lughaid Loighde, and Dodera son of Urmor the poet, and Eithne, and Maer, and Mugain, and others. *d.* Maer and Modar were the two daughters of Fergus Cnae, son of Ugaine. Maer was the mother of Eochaid son of Luchta. Maer was the daughter of Buide son of Buan and wife of Ardán. PAGE 110:—(xvi) The genealogy of Ciarraige Luachra: Ussalach son of Astuman, son of Ciar, son of Fergus, son of Róig, son of Ros, son of Rudraige.

PAGE 116:—(xvii) *a.* **Luimnech** [etc.] A meeting took place between Munster and Connacht, where the two kings brought their champions with them: the two sons of Smucaille son of Bacdub, named Rinn and Faebar. One of them took protection from Bodb of the fairy mound of Femen; the other took protection from Ochaill of the fairy mound of Cruachan. Then the champions brought their swineherd-craft forward, and each went to compete in the stream, wearing grey-blue cloaks (*odarluimni*) around the host of the two parties. Then a flood came into it, and because of the size of the gathering, they did not notice until the stream swept all their cloaks (*luimne*) from them. Then the watchers said: "This estuary is cloak-ful (*luimnechda*) today." Or, *Luman* was the name of the shield; and while the battle was occurring, the stream snatched the cloaks—that is, the shields—from the heroes, so that the kings said from the edge of the waves: "This estuary is cloak-ful today." *From this*, Luimnech *is named*.

*b.* **Echtga** *whence it is named*. . . It is not difficult. Echtga the Horrible, daughter of Urscothach son of Juinni the Stout, of the Tuatha Dé Danann. She was reared in a remote corner beside Nenta by Moach "Bald-head." The swineherds of Gann and Sen-Gann were seeking her: namely, Fergus son of Ruide the "maimed-beast"—a beast that was reared in his hollow (*lusca*), that is, in his infancy within him. Then the girl agreed to sleep with him for the sake of the land of the swineherds and cupbearers which was in his hand from the King of Olnécmacht <note>Connacht</note>: that is, from Maenmag to the sea. He had no wealth, but he had land. So that mountain was given to her as a bride-price. Two cows were brought there: a cow from the north and a cow from the south; and the cow from the north produced a third more milk than the cow from the south. *Whence the poet said*:

> Echtga the Horrible above all fame, the illustrious daughter of Urscothach: she it was who requested the mountain without plunder from Fergus of the land-grant.

*c.* **Moenmag** *whence it is named*. . . It is not difficult. Moen "of the great deeds," a barber and son of Míl; he was the first man to perform a shaving in Ireland after the arrival of the sons of Míl. Also, the first fee for shaving ever given in Ireland was Berramain: that is, *main* (wealth) in exchange for (*i commáin*) shaving (*berrtha*). Moen then died in Moenmag. *Whence the poet said*:

> Moen of the gentle valor died on the Plain of Moen (*Mag Moein*), as we have heard; he found it without the strife of settlement as a reward for the shaving of Berramain.

PAGE 119:—(xviii) A.D. 241. The fifteenth year of Cormac. These are the battles of Cormac against Munster in this year: the battle of Beirre, the battle of Loch Léin, the battle of Luimnech, the battle of Grian, the battle of Clasach, the battle of Muirisc, the battle of Ferta (where Eochaid "Long-side" son of Ailill Ólomm fell), the battle of Samhain (where Cian son of Ailill Ólomm fell), and the battle of Ard Cam.

PAGE 120:—(xix) A.D. 746. Saint Comán, the saint of Ros Comáin, and from him Ros Comáin is named. He is missing from this year or the following year, and it is written of him that he was two hundred years of age. There is a dispute between the annals as to which year he died in.

PAGE 122:—(xx) A.D. 76. After being twenty years in the kingship over Ireland, Elim son of Conrach fell in the battle of Aichill by Tuathal Techtmar.

PAGE 126:—(xxi) *a.* **Mag Luirg** [etc.] When Conall Cernach was being cared for in Cruachan, he wounded Ailill, King of Connacht, at the urging of Medb; for that reason, he fled from Cruachan. The youths of Connacht went after him, and the "three red hounds of Martine" went on his track. From there they took up his track: that is, from Mag Luirg to Mag Slecht of Bréifne.

# XII. xxii—xxiv Text of Extracts.

...so that the three red hounds of the Feine killed him at the ford of the mines at Maigen, and they took his head with them to the territory of Beirre in Corcu Laigde in retaliation for the head of Cú Roí son of Dáire. So that is "Conall’s shout" in Cruachain, and *from this* comes Mag Luirg.

*b.* A.D. 748. Fursa, son of Eirc, died. Eirc’s son was at the Buill—the waterfall of the descendants of Flann today.

*c.* Es Ruaid [etc.]. Aed the Red, son of Badurn of the Ulaid, King of Ireland, drowned there while looking at his own image while swimming in the waterfall, and *from him* Es Ruaid is named. His fairy mound is Síd nAeda on the bank of the waterfall. *Alternatively*, Ruad daughter of Máine Milscothach chose Aed son of Labraid Leisbric, son of Roga the Great. From there she came from the many-islands of the plain of Maen; she came in the boat of Abhcán the poet, keeping her left hand toward Ireland as she went with Geth, son of Geth the Pure, to the assembly of the men of Fidga. The girl raised a bronze sail upon her boat and went alone into the estuary until she saw Aed from the seat where he was. The girl did not know which land she was in until she heard the sound of the mermaid-strain <note>Original: *samghuba*</note> in the estuary, which no one had ever heard before, and she said: "This is the estuary that shall be the most famous in Ireland." Then she fell into a deep sleep and fell over the prow of her ship so that she was drowned. From this it is called Es Ruaid.

PAGE 127:—(xxii) **Druim cliab** [etc.]. It was there that the baskets <note>Original: *cléib*</note> of the boat of Curnán Black-foot were made when he went to destroy Dún Bárc against Ainle son of Lóat Long-hand, where he stayed for a year and a half [until Ainle fell there with his queens and the rest of his family]. It was then that Curnán Black-foot, son of Réa the Dark, said after the destruction: "It is a thing that men come to do." *Whence the poet said*: The son of Réa the Dark, the pleasant Curnán the hardy and long-headed; he made baskets long ago—as was heard—in Druim Cliab where the forest was.

PAGE 153:—(xxiii) *a.* **Liamain**, why is it so named? Not difficult. Liamain of the beautiful cloak, Fercharthen, Mianach, and Truistiu were the four daughters of Dubthach Dubthaire, son of Fergna, King of the Déisi of Bregia. The four sons of Aicher the Bent, son of Eochaid Ondot of the Érainn of Munster—of the seed of Mug Láma, son of Lugaid, son of Cairbre Croimchenn—separated from them. The four sons of [Aicher] came from the west to the house of Dubthach; their names were Fer Dub, Fer Nocht, Roimper, and Fomu. They made a contract to serve Dubthach for a year. Afterward, they were demanding their sick-maintenance <note>Or wages; original: *nothor*</note>, but Dubthach would not give it unless they stayed a month beyond the year; for it was Dubthach who earned a month for preparation along with the year's companionship. 

Then Dubthach went on a raid into Leinster. The men feigned illness so that they would not have to go with him. Dubthach left, and they escaped after he was gone, taking the four daughters of Dubthach with them. Dubthach encountered them in Leinster and killed all eight of them: Fomu, the husband of Liamain; Roimper, the husband of Fercharthen; Fer Nocht, the husband of Mianach; and Fer Dub with Truistiu. They were all killed then: Fer Dub at the black-fords of Maistiu; Fer Nocht at Fornocht; Roimper at Glais Rompair; Fomu at Fomain; Liamain upon Liamain; Mianach in Achall; Ferchartain in Forchartain; and Truistiu upon the ford of [Truistiu]. 

Then their mother came from the west; her name was Luachair Boirennach, and she was from Boirenn Corcomruad. When she found out the truth of the killing of her four sons, her heart broke within her. From her is named Luachair Bairnig. Aicher came until he died at the hill of the mound of Aicher in Uí Felmeda.

*b.* The genealogy of Uí Fheilmeda: the three sons of Muiredach, son of Oengus, son of Feidlimid (*from whom* the Uí Fheilmeda are named), son of Enna Cennselach: namely, Eocho, Ailill, and Eogan, *from whom* comes Bec son of Eogain.

PAGE 157:—(xxiv) **Sliab Cua**, why is it so named? Not difficult. Cua the Big-headed, son of Brocshalach of the withered knees, was the foster-son of Boibli son of Buirche. A great cattle-plague came to Ireland in the time of Conall Cláranech, so that not a single heifer was found in Ireland except for one in Glenn Samaisce and one bull. These were held by Boibli. Every foster-son was sent in turn to guard them. When it came to the turn of Cua Big-headed to guard them, he betrayed them. He took them with him, made a cooking-pit <note>Original: *brothlaig*</note> for them, and ate them on the mountain. *Whence the poet said*: Cua Big-headed with the fair form, son of Brocshalach of the withered—

# Text of Extracts. [XII. xxv—xxviii

PAGE 160:—(xxv) 
a. **Mag Muirisci** *from which it is named*. Not difficult: a great sea-fish named Rosualt, which the sea cast onto the land there. Colum Cille used to reveal the secret of that animal to everyone: it made three spewings, and the height of each spewing was significant. One spewing was into the sea, with its tail held high, which caused the drowning of boats and ships and a slaughter of sea animals in that year. A second spewing was into the air, with its tail pointed down and the spew directed upward, which caused a slaughter of the winged creatures of the air in that year. Another spewing was onto the land, which rotted the land and caused a slaughter of men and cattle in that year. It is said that this creature appeared in the time of the Aeds and Colum Cille. *From which* Dallán [Forgaill] *sang*: "He read the secrets of the Rosualt among schools of scepters."

*Or*, it was a great abundance of sea-fish that happened there in the time of Garb Glúnraige, so that they filled the glens and slopes of the land on the side facing the sea.

*Or*, it may be that Muiresc, daughter of Ugaine Mór, was given that plain, and it was there that Muiresc died.

->A sea-fish the great sea cast up,<-
->whose name was the royal, great Rosualt:<-
->the deed was fierce, clear, and bright,<-
->which Colum Cille prophesied.<-

*Or*:

->An abundance of dead fish from a warm tide<-
->in the time of Gairréisc Glúnraige:<-
->the sea vomited forth thousands of offspring<-
->throughout the four lands of the Erna.<-

*Or*:

->If it is Muiresc the dark and predatory,<-
->the fierce daughter of the grandson of good Echu:<-
->it was a fame of cattle without a proper contract,<-
->she who obtained the plain by the great sea.<-

b. Mata of Muiresc of the men of Olnégmacht was the mother of the three sons of Ros: namely Finn, Cairbre, and Ailill. It is that Ailill whom the Connachta took as their king by right of his mother. That Muiresc was also the wife of Fer dá loch (who was Cairbre Cennderg), and she bore him sons: including Cet, Annlúan, Ailill, Moghcorb, Toiche, Finn, and Scannlán.

c. Macha, daughter of Aed Ruad son of Badarn and wife of Cimbáeth son of Finntan, was she who reared Ugaine Mór son of Echu Buadach. Cesair the Beautiful, daughter of the King of the French and wife of Ugaine Mór, was the mother of his three daughters: Aine, Aife, and Muiresc.

PAGE 163:—(xxvi) 
A.M. 2545. Rudraige son of Partholón was drowned in Loch Rudraige after the lake erupted over him, so that from him it is called Loch Rudraige.

PAGE 165:—(xxvii) 
a. **Benn Bairchi**, from what is it named? Not difficult: Bairche was the cowherd of Ross Ruadbuidhe. The peak was his herding seat, and he equally guarded every cow from Dún Sobairche to the Boyne; not one animal of them grazed a morsel more than another. From that comes Benn Bairchi, as was said:

->Bairche, the famous cowherd,<-
->belonged to the very strong Ross Ruad:<-
->great is the peak which no blow makes weak,<-
->his smooth herding seat.<-

b. *Alternatively*: Bennán son of Brecc killed Ibel son of Manannán there while going to his wife, whose name was Lecon daughter of Lodar. That is the reason Manannán let out three "sips" (sorrows) from his heart: Loch Ruide, Loch Cuan, and Loch Dachaech. Bennán was killed after that upon that peak, *from which* it is called **Benn Bennáin**.

c. A.D. 730. The sea cast a whale (a great beast) ashore in the province of Ulster, specifically at Boirche. Everyone in the vicinity came to see it because of its strangeness. When it was being butchered, three teeth of gold were found in its head, each weighing fifty ounces. Fiacha son of Aed Rón, King of Ulster, and Eochaid son of Bresail, lord of the Uí Echach, sent one of the teeth to Bangor, where it remained for a long time upon the altar of Bangor, visible to everyone in general.

PAGE 170 :—(xxviii) 
**Gáirech**, from what is it named? Not difficult: the "shout" (*gáir*) of the great battle being fought there in which Cúchulainn was killed.

*Or*, it may be from the shout that the youths of Emain Macha raised around Cúchulainn in his bed of blood, so that horses and chariots and weapons and racks crashed together in the mud of the ford, becoming like glowing metal in a smith's forge, seething and sparking because of the magnitude of the great outcry they made while mourning their comrade. *From which the poet says*: "A shout they made..."

...noble youths of Emain of Ulster of the red weapons, lamenting the bloody company; he shed blood upon true men.

PAGE 176:—(xxix) *a.* **Mag Raigne**, *from which it is named*. Raigne the Roman came from the lands of the Romans and Rome, with a spade upon his back, after clearing the channel at bright Tours in the lands of the Franks in three days. He feared that another similar task would be imposed upon him. Therefore, he fled until he reached Imlech Meccond. It was entirely a ridge of woods at that time, until he cleared it with his hoe and his spade. *As the poet says*: It is he who cleared the plain, Raigne the very strong Roman; when he went from Tours in the east, in flight and avoidance. *From which also the poet sang*: I have heard of a good man of companies, etc. *b.* A.D. 859. Renewal of the fair of Raighne by Cerbhall son of Dunghal <note>lord of Osraidhe</note>.

(xxx) **Tonn Chlidna**, *from which it is named*. Not difficult. Clidna, daughter of Genann son of Triun, came from the Hill of Two Wheels in Mag Mell of the Land of Promise with Iuchna Curly-hair to reach the Mac Óc. He played a trick upon her. He played music for her in the bronze boat in which she was, until she fell asleep. And he turned her sail back until she came around Ireland to the south to that place. It was then that the infinite sea-burst rose, which spread through the regions of the present world. For these were the three great tides of Ireland: the tide of Clidna, the tide of Ladrann, and the tide of Baile. But they did not rise at the same time <note>the middle tide was the tide of Ladrann</note>. The tide then surged high and divided across the land of Ireland, until it reached that boat and the girl sleeping in it upon the shore, so that beautiful Clidna daughter of Genann was drowned there. <note>From which comes</note> Tonn Chlidna. And also as Cáilte lamented at the same place in the time of Patrick, during the conversation they had about the *dindsenchas* of Ireland: "White-headed Clidna, lasting the deed," etc.

PAGE 179:—(xxxi) **Druim nAssail** is asked of me: why is the hill wave-bright? From the man who dwelt on its edge, from whom comes Assal son of Umór. And all the sons of Umór, what is their title there? What is their branch of kinship, except that they are of the Fomorian race? A man of those was high Assal, who settled upon the firm high ridge: in the middle of Munster of bright honor, above the territory of Mál son of Ugaine. One night Fergus mac Róig went to the house of Assal son of Umór. Assal welcomed him: "Welcome to you, if we may be happy." "Why," said Fergus, "why are you so? Why is your mind downcast?" "Tonight," said Assal, "is my betrayal; my death is in my vision." "I will not go inside," said Fergus, "it is not good for a guest to be heedless. Go, boy, over the ridge to the east; unyoke the chariot then." The chariot-ford of Fergus is there, south of the side of the hill. He settled there a short distance from the road; there was a man keeping watch. In the middle of the night a company came from the land named Spain. Before he could rise up—a true thing was heard—there were thirty spears in Fergus. Fergus took up his rages around the very red points: he killed thirty of them then, and he was left in his bed of blood. The hosts went away after that; they attacked the house of Assal there. They took the head of noble Assal from Ireland with them to Spain. Fergus was nursed for his many wounds in the house of Conchenn son of Dedat. Cúrúi came there to seek news, from the land of the Franks strongly. He complained of his trouble to him, Fergus to the prince of Mag Mis. They went, both of them, a long way to avenge it. The city of the king who took the head—the two strong men came around it. They smothered and killed around the king the huge and countless host. And they brought the two heads with them from Spain to the land of Ireland: the head of the very strong king from the east, and the head of Assal to Druim nAssail.

PAGE 182:—(xxxii) **Roeiriu** in Uí Muiredaig, etc. Roeiriu son of Senán son of Sétna, son of the king of Connacht, fell in a battle there against the Leinstermen and it is there he was buried, as others say. And Roeiriu daughter of Rónán, the royal poet of the king of Leinster; her father gave her the hill of Dagda in his land so that she inhabited it and was buried there. And from these the mound of Roeiriu is named, and they sing this song: "There is a hiding-place," etc.

Fáil, son of Inogach, son of Dacháir, with the children of Míl, the fierce and mighty, advanced to Banba <note>Ireland</note> of the green peaks. Their tools for their traditional crafts were the billhook, the axe, and the heavy oar. The axe was for cutting and strong destruction, and the billhook for clearing. Noble tools without pride, and oars for great rowing. They cleared three plains of equal fame; they possessed them through the shout of their naming: Mag Fea, which is not hidden from a woman; Mag Fera and Mag Femein. Each was set against the other without delay or regret, without the foolish intent that betrayed them in the field; an exchange of weapons and prayer. Mag Fea was not abandoned, though it was silent. Fea, wife of Néit, wife of the son of Indúi; a fair woman who was a beloved love, daughter of Elcmar of the generous laws. I have heard of the brightness of their appearance: two excellent, outstanding oxen, Fé and Men, by those names; from them comes the name of Mag Femein.

(xxxiv) **Sliab Bladma** [etc.] Bladma, or Blod, son of Cú, son of Cas of the famous small sword, killed the herdsman of Bregmáel, the smith of Cuirche son of Sníthe, king of the Uí Fuada <note>or king of Muaidhe</note>. He went afterward in his little boat until he settled at Irros Bladma. Ros Náir, however, was its name at first. He went from there into the mountain, *whence* <note>from which</note> it is called Sliab Bladma. Or it is Blad son of Breogon who died there, and from him was named *mons* <note>mountain</note> Bladma: Blod son of Cú, son of Cas of the famous small sword, killed the herdsman of fair Bregmáel; the smith of Cuirche son of Sníthe, he settled at the wood of the land of Náir. [Or they are sea-beasts, that is, reddish beasts are their names, and they used to be in the waters and on the dry lands, and it is they who cut down the trees; *whence* <note>from which</note> it is called the beast-abounding Sliab Bladma, and it was Ros Náir son of Edlecon *prius* <note>formerly</note>.]

PAGE 192:—(xxxv) **Maistiu** [etc.] Maistiu, that is, *mes-dú* <note>mast-place</note>, that is, a place or town in which there is mast <note>acorns or nuts</note>. *As it is said*, it was a forest in the time that was, *etc. Otherwise*, Maistiu daughter of Oengus son of Umór, whom Dáire Derg son of Eochaid Long-side brought from the territory of the assembly at the Fair of Oengus, until he met Grisban the artisan, daughter of Richis, in the middle of the plain. She took a longing for her <note>out of jealousy</note> and struck her with disfiguring charms so that she died before her because of it. Dáire cast a throw at Gris with a hero’s strong stone that he had, so that he made fragments of her head in the middle of the plain, and she lay in a bloody stream; so it has been Gris from then until now. Or Maistiu, daughter of Oengus son of Umór, was the woman-embroiderer of Oengus the Young <note>the Mac Óc</note>; it is she who first designed the shape of a cross in Ireland in the border of the breast-fringe of Oengus's tunic, for Oengus showed it to her in that place; *whence* <note>from which</note> Mag Maisten *is named*. Eamuin also, and Conall son of Oengus, and Maer, *from whom* comes Áth Maeri and Áth Mara today. And Maer and Maistiu died of grief for Conall the Slender, son of Oengus; *whence* <note>from which</note> Maistiu and Áth Mara.

PAGE 199:—(xxxvi) **Mag Life**, *from which it is named*. Not difficult. Life, daughter of Canann of the many-curded boat, went with Deltbanna son of Drucht, the cupbearer of Conaire the king of Tara. She asked Bodb of Femen for it. Because the plain over which she came was beautiful to her, she desired nothing but that it be named from her name. So Deltbanna distributed it to the men of Ireland so that that plain might be named from the name of his wife. *Whence the poet said*: Life, radiant, enough of fame, daughter of Canann of the hundred-curded boats; from her name the plain is called, from when she came to the land of Tara. [Or that Fea is the name, and *Lí* <note>beauty</note> comes from the thing that was beautiful to her of what she saw.]

PAGE 213:—(xxxvii) *a.* **Finnghlas** in Luachair Dedad, *from which it is named*. Not difficult. Bláthnat, daughter of Mend, king of the men of Falga, was the wife of Cúrúi. And she was the lover of Cú Chulainn, and it was she who made a tryst for Cú Chulainn with the men of Ulster together with him to come for her, and to take vengeance on him <note>Cúrúi</note> for the three cows of Iuchna and the cauldron that was taken at the siege of the men of Falga (that is, the Hebrides today), and to avenge the shaving of Cú Chulainn when Cúrúi shaved him with his sword and rubbed the dung of the cows around his head. She told him to come on Samhain night for her, and she would pour out the milk of those cows of Iuchna—that is, the three cows of Iuchna and their cauldron which Cúrúi brought with him. For it was for the cauldron the cows were milked, and its fill was milked from them. She then poured the milk of the three cows of Iuchna down the stream from the fortress to Tráig Lí, so that the stream was white, and so that the Ulstermen should come there and...

They captured the city and killed Cú Roí. *Whence the poet said*: Bláthnat, daughter of Mend, was slain; a slaughter of young ones in the glen. A great deed for a woman to betray her husband, for it was against him she intended it. *b.* Bláthnat, daughter of Conchobar, was the wife of Cú Roí son of Dáire. And Bláthnat, daughter of Mend, king of the men of Falga, was also his wife. *c.* Mórann of Man, daughter of Ir son of Uinnside—or perhaps Uinnside, sister of Eochaid Horse-mouth, was the mother of Cú Roí son of Dáire.

PAGE 226 :—(xxxviii) *a.* Adarca in Uí Failge [etc.]. Iuchna Horse-mouth, *who was also* Iuchna Fair-hair, a royal hospitaller who lived at Fafainn to the north and east in the hospitaller’s hollow. It was his custom to foster and raise the offspring of his house for a year, until his cattle loved him. When he died, his cattle gathered to him and remained for three days and three nights over his body. Because he did not return with them, each of them went toward another in Tuatha and they divided Iuchna with hornless cattle <note>anadarcaib</note> and joined in a struggle until they cast their horns, so that there were mounds of them in the Tuatha. From this they are called Adarca <note>Horns</note>. Then they moved to quench their thirst at the Boyne and dispersed to Almu until they died in their herds there, *and from which it is said* Almu. Almu, then, was the daughter of Becán the hospitaller, wife of Iuchna Fair-hair; she turned back after Iuchna’s death, following her herd to her father’s place, where she died of grief for Iuchna and for the loss of her cattle; *and from her Almu is named. Or thus:* Almu, "al-móin" <note>against the bog</note>, that is, against the bog to the west, *as it is said* "air-brí" <note>against the hill</note> against the Hill of Eile to the east. Or Almu, that is "ail mó," *id est* <note>that is</note> the rock over the bog or in the bog. Or "all mó" <note>great cliff</note>, or "ollam mó" <note>greatest scholar</note>. *b.* Aillenn [etc.]. Cremm the Great took the daughter of Lugaid, king of Leinster, by elopement. Her name was Aillenn. Aillbe was the name of her lapdog. Aillenn died of shame for her youth, and an apple tree grew through her grave. From this it is called the Apple-tree of Aillenn. Her lapdog died after her, and a yew tree grew through it. From this it is called the Yew of Baile, that is, Aillbe by metathesis <note>deilidin</note>. *As it is said*: The apple-tree of high Aillenn, the yew of Baile of the small estate; though they are brought from afar, ignorant people do not understand them. Art Mes-Telmann son of Sétna was the first who dug a rampart in Aillenn. Fiach, however, and Buirech and Ururus dug it finally. Buirech then threw a stone out of the ditch that remains in it, of which he said: "A stone there!" <note>ail ann</note> and that is the name it shall have. Its names are many thereafter, *as another said* [etc.].

PAGE 230:—(xxxix) *a.* The three Fothads; that is, they were three "fó-shuith" <note>good offspring</note>, that is, they were good foundations, for they were the first children of Fuinche. Or Fothad, that is "fotha-ithi" <note>foundation of food</note>, for Mac Niad conceived them secretly with Fuinche—she was Fuinche daughter of Nár son of Irmora. Or Fothad, that is "fothaidhi" <note>good thieves</note>, for every secret marriage is a theft <note>taidhe</note>. Wherefore the druid said: "Welcome the theft from which the three were thus born." From that, the name Fothad stuck to them. *b.* Fuinche of the three breasts, daughter of Firmora of the men of Cliach, was the mother of the three Fothads, and of Currach son of Cathair, and of Téite son of Mac Niad, *from whom* comes the Assembly of Téite. *c.* Why is Ard Fothaid so called? Not difficult. Fothad slept there for nine months to the sound of the Grouse of Boirche <note>circi Boirchi</note> while he was on an expedition. *Hence* Ard Fothaid: Fothad Airgthech, pure in movement, slept there with his vigorous spirit for the space of nine months—a clear deed—to the sound of the Grouse of Boirche. *d.* Eochaid Airgthech: it was by him that silver shields were first made in Ireland.

And from that also the poem was spoken: Tuag of the beautiful, wise, grey-green estuary, do you know its place-lore <note>dinnsenchas</note>? Do you know without mildness the history of white-hipped Tuag? . . . After being five years in the kingship of Ireland, Conall Collamrach son of Eterscél of Tara, son of Eochaid Ailtlethan, fell by the hand of Nia Segamain. 4887. XIII. *ibid.* :—(i) The Bann was small at one time, if there were anyone who remembered it; women and children used to leap across it before the fierce outburst of Lough Neagh. Eocho, son of the fair Mairid, son of a fitting King of Cashel: he fell in love in his strong land with his father’s high-wife, Aeiblenn. Aeiblenn, daughter of bright Guaire, from the great Brugh of the Mac ind Óc; it is from her, by our tradition, that Slieve Eibline is named. Eocho and the bright Aeiblenn avoided the wealth of Mairid: they escaped from the center of Cashel of the Cas to the Brugh of the fierce Mac ind Óc. The dear pair were not alone, having their herds of cattle: a thousand great men, as verses proclaim, unyoked without sorrow by the Boyne. **PAGE 234:**—(ii) Lough Neagh [etc.] Rib son of Mairid and Eocho son of Mairid came from the south out of Irluachair, the two of them on a migration, and they separated at Belach Dá Liag. One of them went eastward <gloss>ms. westward</gloss>, namely Eocho, until he settled at the Brugh of the Mac ind Óc. He <note>Midir or Aengus</note> came to them in the form of a hospitaller with his gelding in his hand and ordered them to leave, so that they would not be in the Brugh. They told him they had no power to carry the heavy load they had <gloss>ms. they had</gloss> without horses. "Put," said he, "all that the plain contains of your burdens and straps upon this gelding, and take it with you to the place where it lies down under it." They went from there until they reached Liathmuine. The gelding lay down with them there and passed its urine, making a well of it until it came over them; so that it is Lough Neagh—that is, Eocho the king and his horse's urine spread there. Rib himself, however, went around westward until he settled in Mag Finn; that land was the playing-field of Midir and the Mac ind Óc. Midir came to them in the same manner with a tethered horse, and they put their property upon it until he brought them to Mag nAirbthen, where the lake now is. The gelding lay down there and passed its urine so that it became a spring that burst over them. Rib was the name of the king. Rib was drowned. *Whence* Lough Ree and Lough Neagh *are named*: Aengus drowned noble Eocho through his horse's urine with swiftness; Midir came, the power followed them, until he drowned Rib in Mag Dairbthen. (iii) Lough Ree [etc.] Rib son of Mairid and Eochaid son of Mairid came from the south out of Irluachair on a migration, and they separated at Belach Dá Liag; and Eocho went to Brega to the Brugh of the Mac ind Óc and so on. Rib, however, went westward until he settled in Mag Finn, and that was the playing-field of Midir and Aengus. Midir came to them in the guise of a hospitaller with a tethered pack-horse in his hand and ordered them not to stay on his grazing-land. Rib <gloss>Rib</gloss> did not obey him. Then Midir brought three plagues upon them: their cows and their oxen in the first period, and their horses in the second period. And Midir came to them in the same manner with his horse tethered in his hand and commanded them to leave or he would kill them all. "We have nothing to carry our belongings with us," said Rib. "I have a horse here for you," said Midir, "that will carry all your goods. And in the place where it stops, its urine shall come forth; it shall carry no more, and its bridle must be left with it about its head; and you will be sorry if this is not so." Rib went on until he reached Mag nAirbthen, that is, the place where Lough Ree is. And the horse passed its urine and the horse performed its carrying and left its bridle. Then || the urine went down into the ground so that it was necessary to put a lid tightly over it; and Rib built his house around it and his bed above it. He was there for thirty years until it burst forth on the Monday night of Lughnasadh, so that Rib was drowned with his wife and his children and his people; and it spread over all Mag nAirbthen. *Whence* Lough Ree. That was one hundred and eleven years after the birth of Christ. **PAGE 237:**—(iv) A.D. 558. In this year the mermaid was captured, namely Líban, daughter of Eocho son of Mairid, on the shore of Ollarba in the net of Beoán son of Inle, the fisherman of Comgall of Bangor. (v) Líban, that is, the sea-birth, daughter of Eocho son of Mairid, son of Caireid, son of Bresal . . . son of Tigernmas, son of Fallach, son of...

Eithriel son of Iriel son of Eiremon [son of Milesius]. (vi) *a.* Sliab Mis, *from which it is named.* Mis, daughter of Mairid, sister of Eocho son of Mairid, remained behind after the migration when she went with Congainchnes son of Dedad. That mountain is the inheritance and patrimony on which her family and kin remained. Mis, the very clever daughter of Mairid, longed for it with its flowery borders. After her migration, without grief, the mountain was no longer associated with Congainchnes. *b.* Sliab Mis [etc.] Mis daughter of Mairid, wife of Coimigin Congainchnis son of Dedad. To her was given the mountain of Senach Garb son of Dedad as a marriage portion and for her residence with her husband after her migration, when Eocho and Rib, the two sons of Mairid, arrived (from whom Lough Neagh and Lough Ree are named). Thus, the mountain was the inheritance where Mis remained; hence, Sliab Mis. *Otherwise*, Sliab Mis—that is, the mountain of "ill-knowledge"—because of the ill-knowledge of the magical host found there by Fotla, Banba, and Eriu.

### XIV. PAGE 238 :—

(i) This is the history of the seed of Ir throughout Ireland. Ir was the *eighth son of Milesius. When the sons of Milesius came to Ireland, he died and was afterwards buried in Skellig. From him, a third of the royal race of Ireland was born. Ir, however, had one son, namely Eber.* Eber son of Ir, *who held Magh Lini and a fifth part of Ireland before all the Scots [Gaels]*. Eber had two sons, namely Artri and Ebric. Eber fell by the hand of Palap son of Eremon. Ebric son of Eber had two sons, namely Cermna and Sobairche. They were the first two kings of Ireland from the Ulstermen. By them the two forts were built, namely Dun Cermna and Dun Sobairche. Eocho son of Conmael in Munster killed Cermna in his fort, or *in battle*. Eocho Echchenn, king of the Fomorians, killed Sobairche. The descendants of Cermna and Sobairche are not recorded. Art son of Eber had one son, namely Setna, High King of Ireland. His son killed him, as *others say*, namely Fiacha Finscoithe. [However,] Rothechtaid son of Maine son of Oengus Ollmucada, of the seed of Eremon, killed Setna son of Art at Cruachan between the two hands of Fiacha Finscoithe, his own son. For that reason, Fiacha Finscoithe killed him in revenge for his honor. Ollam Fotla son of Fiacha Finscoithe son of Setna son of Art son of Eber son of Ir son of Milesius of Spain; it was he who first established the Feast of Tara and built the Wall of the Scholars at Tara. Ollam was forty years in the kingship of Ireland, and seven of his descendants held the kingship of Ireland without anyone else between them. Ollam had four sons, namely Cairpre, Finnachta, Slanoll, and Gede. Rudraige son of Sithri son of Dub son of Fomoir son of Argatmar son of Sirlam son of Finn son of Blatha son of Labraid son of Cairpre son of Ollam. Argatmar's grandson was Cimbaeth son of Fintan son of Argatmar. Aed Ruad son of Badurn son of Argatmar. Dithorba son of Dimman son of Argatmar; from him come the Kings and their progeny. These are the sons of Rudraige: Congal Claeringnech. The two sons of Congal: Uislenn (father of Ainle, Noeisen, and Ardan) and Cathbad the Druid. Bresal Bodibad *according to certain people; some say he was a Leinsterman*. Mac Rosa son of Rudraige, namely Fergus mac Rosa. Ferfiled son of Glas son of Ros. Celtchair son of Uithechair son of Fothad son of Ferfiled son of Glas. Fercheirtne the poet, son of Oengus Belderg. Iliach son of Loegaire Buadach son of Conad son of Iliach. Mal son of Rochride... Fergus son of Leite. Illann son of Fergus. Geirgenn father of... Cas, *whose son was Fachtna Fathach*. Briere son of Carbad son of Cas. Aithirne son of Athchlo. Eirrge Echbel. Twenty-five kings of the Ulstermen held the kingship of Ireland, besides the seven kings who took it from the Dal Fiatach. (ii) A.M. 4981. After being seventy years in the kingship of Ireland, Rudraige son of Sithrige [etc.] died in Airgetglinn. The third heifer was in Cliu Máil. *d.* **Oengus Olmucaidh**—that is, the "drinking of Mogaeth" was his—specifically Mogaeth the Great-drinker, son of Mofeibis; it is he who drank more ale than anyone else in his time. It was his daughter who was the wife of Fiacha Labrainne and the mother of Oengus Olmucaidh—that is, the drinking of Mogaeth. *e.* **Feidlim Foltlebar** (Feidlim the Long-haired) and **Aeife**, daughter of Ailill son of Mata of Muirisc, were the two wives of Laegaire Buadach. *f.* **Finnabair**, **Daruamna** (daughter of Conchobar), and **Bríbethach** were the three wives of Celtchar son of Uithechar.

PAGE 252:—(iv) *a.* **Róch**, daughter of Eochaid son of Coirpre, was the mother of Fergus son of Ros and Sualtam Sidhe. **Flidais**, daughter of Ailill the Black, son of Fidach, was the wife of Ailill the Fair, son of Domnall Dualbuide, and she was later the wife of Fergus. (v) **Uladh** [Ulster]—that is, *oll-sháith* (great satisfaction)—that is, a great satisfaction which they gave to the poets. Or *Ulaid*—that is, *oll-leth* (great half) of Ireland—they were such in war and in strife. Or *Ulaid*—that is, *uil-léith* (all grey)—that is, they had grey beards in the battle of the fair of Macha, for white wool was tied to their chins. Or *Ulaid*—that is, *uille léith* <gloss>the manuscript says "to the side"</gloss> they had in the battle. Or *Ulaid* is from **Ollom Fodla**, son of Fiacha Fínscothach, as it is said:

->Eocho Mumó, greater than every vow,<-
->King of Ireland, son of Mofeibis:<-
->From him is the name of Munster [Muma] out there,<-
->And the name of Ulster [Ulaid] from Ollom.<-

Or *Ulaid*—that is, *oll-letha* (great divisions)—because they took half of Ireland at first, of which it was said:

->The children of Fachtna, there is no neglect,<-
->Against every night of destructive battle:<-
->They are named from then until now,<-
->The Ulaid, since they were great and all-grey.<-

(vi) **Eochaid Múmhó**—that is, "mo-mo" (greater and greater)—meaning his deeds, his courage, and his power were greater than those of every other king.

### XV. PAGE 253 :—

(i) *a.* **Art Aenfir** [Art the Lone Man], from what does the name come? It is not difficult; because in the end Conn had no son but him, for **Connla** and **Crinna** fell by the hands of Eochaid Finn and Fiacha Suighde, as the poet said:

->The two brothers of Conn, without setting him aside,<-
->Eochaid Finn and Fiacha Suighde:<-
->They killed Connla and Crinna,<-
->The two sons of Conn, the two fair youths.<-

Art Aenfir was the name he took after his brothers were killed, because Eochaid Finn was a source of hatred to Art. Or, he was the only "choice son" that Conn had, because Crinna fell by the hands of Eochaid Finn and Fiacha, and Connla went on an adventure with a fairy woman to the mound of Bodaighe <gloss>as it is written</gloss> as that *Adventure of Connla* is told. As the poet said:

->From the death of Crinna by Eochaid,<-
->From the adventure of Connla, he went further:<-
->The beloved man went across the sea,<-
->From this, he was called Art Aenfir.<-

*b.* **Fiacha Suidghe**—that is, *soghuidhe* (easy to entreat)—because it was easy to intercede with him due to his gentleness. (ii) **Medb Lethderg**, daughter of Conán of Cualu of the Leinstermen, was the wife of Art Aenfir, son of Conn, and it is from her that **Ráith Medba** in Tara is named. **Echtach**, daughter of Urcaide the Smith, was the mother of Cormac grandson of Conn. She was also the wife of Lughna, the steward of the sons of Oengus son of Eochaid Finn (the enemy of Art), and she bore three sons to him. Another wife of Lugna was **Coinne Chíchech**, and she bore three sons to him, and from her the *Cenél Coinni* are named.

PAGE 256 :—(iii) **Cleitech**, from what is it named? It is not difficult; Cleitech son of Dedad, son of Sin, died there. Or *Cleitech*—that is, *cleithe ach* (the roof of sighs) of Ireland—because of the lamentation the men of Ireland made there when mourning Cormac son of Art. Or *cleithe tech* (the roof of the house) of Ireland was burned there over **Muirchertach mac Erca**.

### XVII. PAGE 258 :—

(i) **Belach Gabráin** [the Pass of Gabrán], etc. **Gabrán**, the hound of Failbe Flann, went on the track of **Lurgan**—that is, a pig that was in Druim Almaine. It did not find a place to stay with him until it went under the earth in the bog of Allen, so that it is called "Lurgan in the bog of Allen." Since the hound did not catch the quarry, and no quarry had ever escaped it before to its reddening or its warming <note>meaning to its wounding or its being hunted</note>, it turned back toward home until it died there on the pass. From this, it is called *Belach Gabráin*:

->Dear to me was the pure Gabrán,<-
->Who happened here on the track of Lurgan:<-
->No quarry ever escaped him over the heather,<-
->Except for one grey pig.<-

**A.D. 1510.** **O'Donnell** (Hugh son of Hugh Roe) went to Rome on a pilgrimage. While he was away, his followers and friends were in sorrow, grief, and low spirits after him. After recovering his health, he came to his home, and the churches and territories were joyful and delighted at his arrival. **1537.** O'Donnell (Hugh son of Hugh Roe) [etc.], Lord of Tyrconnell, Inishowen, Cenél Moain, Fermanagh, and Lower Connacht... his victory was never seen by his enemies, and he never retreated a single step before few or many... a man who did not allow the power of the English into his own country, for he bound peace and friendship with the King of England when he saw that the Irish did not give leadership to any one of themselves, but the people of kinship and mutual hospitality were in opposition to one another... a man who maintained his generosity according to what was right for the religious orders, the churches, the poets, and the learned men. The aforementioned O'Donnell (Hugh son of Hugh Roe) died on the 5th of July, specifically on a Thursday, in the monastery of Donegal, after entering the Franciscan habit, after weeping for his crimes and transgressions, and after repenting for his sins and offenses. PAGE 282:—(ii) **A.D. 1536.** The title of **O'Connor** was given to Tadhg Óg, son of Tadhg, son of Aodh, son of Toirdhealbhach Carrach O'Connor. He was the first person called O'Connor in Lower Connacht of the lineage of Brian Luighneach; for "son of Domhnall, son of Muirchertach" was the name of whoever held the leadership or power of that lineage until then. This change of name was made for the sake of honor and to distinguish him from the lords who came before him.

XX. PAGE 296:—(i) *a*. **A.D. 976.** Mathghamhain, son of Cinnéidigh, High King of all Ireland, was captured by Donnabhán, son of Cathal, lord of Uí Fidhgeinte, through treachery. He was delivered to Maolmuaidh, son of Bran, lord of Desmond, who killed him in violation of the protection of saints and righteous men. **977.** A battle was won by Brian, son of Cinnéidigh, against the foreigners of Limerick and Donnabhán, son of Cathal, in which the foreigners of Limerick were defeated and a great slaughter was made of them. The battle of Belach Lechta took place between Brian, son of Cinnéidigh, and Maolmuaidh, lord of Desmond; Maolmuaidh fell there, along with a slaughter of the men of Desmond. (ii) **A.D. 1014.** A conflict occurred among the Uí Eachach themselves, namely between Cian, son of Maolmuaidh, and Domhnall, son of Dubhdábhoireann, where Cian, Cathal, and Roghallach—the three sons of Maolmuaidh—fell, with a great slaughter around them.

PAGE 297:—(iii) *a*. **Brian Boru**: Béibionn, daughter of Eochaidh, son of Murchadh, son of Maonach (the king of West Connacht), was his mother. *As the poet said*:

> The son of Béibionn of the fragrant mouth, though his followers were few: he did not think to use the strength of his hand until he obtained the inheritance of Ireland.

Gormflaith "the Fair," daughter of Murchadh, son of Finn, King of Leinster, was the mother of Donnchadh, son of Brian Boru; of Sitric, son of Amlaíb Cuarán, king of the foreigners of Dublin; and of Conchobhair, son of Maelsechlainn, King of Ireland. Brian Boru, moreover, had six sons: Murchadh, Conchobhair, and Flann were the three from whom no descendants came. Mór, daughter of Eidhin, son of Cléireach, son of Edálach, son of Cumascach of the Uí Fiachrach Aidhne, was the mother of those three. *As the poet said*:

> Mór, daughter of beautiful Eidhin, was the mother of Murchadh of great beauty: his secret treasure was not forgotten; she bore three noble sons to Brian.

Understand that Béibionn, the mother of Brian, had two sisters: Caoineach and Creascha. From Caoineach come the Clann Chosgraigh (the people of Aodh of Cork), and from Creascha come the Clann Mhaoilruanaidh, as the poem says which begins: *Cianóg, daughter of Ciocarán*. It is this Gormflaith whom we mentioned before—the daughter of Murchadh, son of Finn—who leaped the three famous leaps, of which it was said:

> Three leaps Gormflaith leaped, which no woman shall leap until the end of time: a leap into Dublin, a leap into Tara, and a leap into Cashel of the stone fort above all.

For this Gormflaith was with Amlaíb Cuarán, who was called king of the foreigners of Dublin, until she bore Sitric, son of Amlaíb. She was with Maelsechlainn, King of Ireland, until she bore Conchobhair, son of Maelsechlainn. And she was with Brian Boru until she bore Donnchadh, son of Brian. It was from her that the dissension arose which started the Battle of Clontarf. *b*. **A.D. 1014.** A hosting by the foreigners and the Leinstermen into Meath and afterwards into Brega, where they plundered the sanctuary of Feichín and took many captives and countless cattle. A hosting by Brian, son of Cinnéidigh, son of Lorcán, King of Ireland, and by Maelsechlainn, son of Domhnall, King of Tara, to Dublin. The foreigners of Western Europe gathered against Brian and Maelsechlainn and brought ten hundred coats of mail with them. A brave battle was fought between them, the like of which was not found in that time, at Clontarf, specifically on the Friday before Easter. In that battle fell Brian, son of Cinnéidigh, High King of Ireland, in the eighty-eighth year of his age; Murchadh, son of Brian, royal heir of Ireland, in his sixty-third year; Toirdhealbhach, son of Murchadh, son of Brian; and Conaing, son of Donnchuan, a nephew to Brian [etc.]

**XXI. PAGE 306:—**(i) *a. How Mág Corainn is named. It is not difficult.* Corann was the harper of Diancecht, son of the Dagda, until he called one of the pigs of Drebrinne with his harp called *caelchéis*. It ran north with the strength of its bones. Then the warriors of Connacht and their pack of hounds ran <note>with the strength of running</note> after it as far as Céis Corainn. From this come Céis Chorainn and Mág gCorainn. Concerning this, the poet said: Corann, the skilled harper, son of the swift-judging Dagda: he called the pig with a cry of melody, through his harp to Céis Corainn. *b.* Corann [etc.]. It is not difficult. Corann was the harper of Diancecht, son of Echtach the striker, and the Tuatha Dé Danann gave him land for his harping in Mág Corainn, from which Corann is named. As for Céis Chorainn, however, when the pigs of Drebrinne were scattered, it happened that the fifth pig reached the *caelchéis* of Corann, and it was killed there. From this Céis Chorainn is named. *c.* Eile, daughter of Eochaidh and wife of Forgall, son of Matamuirsce of the men of Olnégmacht; and Dreibne, daughter of Eochaidh Feidlig, after whom the "pigs of Drebrinne" are named.

**XXII. PAGE 306 :—**(i) *a. Genealogy of the Dairine, that is, the seed of Lugaid son of Ith.*
Duach, son of Maicniadh, son of Maccon, son of Lugaid Laigde, son of Dáire Sírchrechtach, son of Lugaid, son of Ith, son of Breogoin. The five <note>read: six</note> sons of Dáire Sírchrechtach are: Lugaid Laigde, from whom are the Corco Láigde; Lugaid Cal, from whom are the Calraige <note>Bolcban the Briton was the mother of Lugaid Cal. Lasair, daughter of Laegaire son of Niall, was the wife of Lugaid Cal</note>; Lugaid Oircthe, from whom are the Corco Oircthe; Lugaid Laiges <note>from whom are the Laiges of Leinster</note>; Lugaid Corp <note>from whom are the Dál Mescorb of Leinster</note>; and Lugaid Coscaire, from whom are the Coscraige among the Déise, to whom belonged Danél son of Fathach. *b. Concerning the genealogy of the Corco Láide here first.* Lugaid Laighe, from whom are the Corco Laige, was the son of Dáire Sírdréchtach <note>or Doimthig</note>. This was another name for the elder Lugaid. He was the son of another Lugaid, namely Maccon. And Lugaid was the name of Dáire, if some of the poets speak truly. Macniadh was the usual name of Lugaid Laighe. Maccon had a distinguished son, namely Macniadh. Macniadh <note>son of Maccon</note> had good children, namely Aengus of the Bloody Spear and Duach. *c. Calraige, that is "cal-troige," the children of Lugaid Cal, for "troige" means children or kindred; or Calraige, that is the kingdom of Cal, namely Lugaid Cal.* (ii) Lugaid Laighe *et cetera*. This is the story that is remembered here, concerning the reason for the additional names given to the sons of Dáire Doimthig—namely the five <note>read: six</note> Lugaids—and what was the reason for the name Lugaid being given to every son of them. It is not difficult. It was in the prophecy that one of his sons would take the kingship of Ireland, and that his name would be Lugaid; therefore, the name Lugaid was given to every single one of his sons. Now, the Fair of Tailtiu was celebrated by Dáire, and his sons performed their horse-racing there. Dáire said to the druid: "Which son shall take the kingship after me?" "A golden fawn will come into the Fair," said the druid, "and the son who catches the fawn is the one who shall take the kingship after you." Afterward, the golden fawn arrived, and the men of Ireland went after it. The sons pursued it from there to Beinn Edair <note>Howth</note>, and a magical mist was set between them and the men of Ireland. The sons of Dáire followed it from there to Dál Mescorb in Leinster; Lugaid Laighe (that is, Macniadh) caught the fawn, and Lugaid <note>Coscaire</note> cut it up, so that from this he is called Lugaid Cosc. Then a great snow fell upon them, so that it was a struggle for them to hold their weapons. One of the sons went to look for a house. He found a large house there, with a great fire, and food and ale in abundance, with silver dishes and couches of white bronze, and a hideous hag within the house. "Young man, what do you seek?" she said. "I seek a bed until morning." And she said: "If you come into my bed tonight, you shall have it." The youth said he would not do it, and he went back to his brothers. "You have failed to obtain the sovereignty and the kingship," she said. The sons went into the house one after another. She asked one of the men what had happened to him. "A wild pig," said he, "and I ate it alone." "Lugaid Orc shall be your name among your kindred," she said. Then she asked another the same question. "Nothing happened to me," he said, "except that I slept." "That is sleepy," she said.

"Lugaid Cal shall be your name and that of your kindred." She then asked another man the same question. "A wild fawn escaped from me," he said. "Lugaid Laeghas shall be your name and that of your kindred," she said. She asked another man the same. "What the other men cast away from them is what I consumed," he said. "Lugaid Corb shall be your name," she said, "for what you have consumed is corrupt." Lugaid Laigde finally went into the house as well, and the hag said the same to him.
