The hag, however, went into the couch of white bronze, and Macniad followed her into the couch; and it seemed to him that the brightness of her face was like the sun rising in the month of May, and her fragrance seemed to him like a sweet-smelling herb-garden. He coupled with her after that, and she said to him: "Your journey is good, for I am the Sovereignty, and you shall take the sovereignty of Ireland." After that, they found new food and old ale, and drinking horns serving them alone, and he slept with the Sovereignty. Thus they were the next morning: without house or fire, but only a level, high plain, and their hounds tied to their spears. They went forward after that to the assembly of Tailtiu and told their adventure, and the men of Ireland dispersed from the assembly. From this they spoke of the six Lugads.

PAGE 311:—(iii) Gemlorg, daughter of Conchobar Abradruad and wife of Lugaid Lága; Glenn Gemluirg in Brega is named after her.

PAGE 312:—(iv) *a.* A.D. 186. The twenty-first year of Art, son of Conn of the Hundred Battles, in the kingship of Ireland. The battle of Cenn Febrat [was fought] by the sons of Oilill Olum and by the three Cairbres (the children of Conaire son of Mug Láma) against Dadera the druid, against Neimid son of Sroibchenn, and against the south of Ireland. In this place Neimid, king of the Erna of Munster, and Dadera, the jester of the Dairine, fell. Dadera fell by Eogan, son of Oilill. Neimid fell by Cairbre Rígfoda, son of Conaire, in revenge for his father, namely Conaire himself. Cairbre Musc wounded Lugaid (that is, Maccon) in his calf, so that he was lame thereafter. This is the reason for that nickname: because Lugaid was fond of a hound that was feeding its whelps in his foster-father's house, and he used to drink from the teat of the aforementioned hound, so that "Maccon" <note>Son of Hound</note> stuck to him. *b.* Maccon: that is, a hound that Oilill Olum had; Red Elóir was its name. When Maccon was an infant in Oilill's house, he used to creep toward it on all fours, and the hound would clasp him to its breast, and he could not be rescued from the hound without going to it.

PAGE 314:—(v) Mág Mucruime <note>etc.</note>. It is not difficult. Magical pigs came from the cave of Cruachan to Oilill and Medb, so that they destroyed corn and milk in every place they were; and the men of Ireland could not count them or gaze upon them in every place they were. Then Oilill and Medb came to arrange a hunt for them at Fraechmág, and hunted them to Belach na bFert. There Medb caught one of the pigs by the leg, but its skin was left in her hand, and they were counted after that in that place. *From which* comes Mág Muicríma <note>Plain of Pig-counting</note>.

(vi) Croichen Red-hand, the handmaid of Étain, was the mother of Medb, from whom Mág Cruachna is named; or Clófhionn was her mother also. Medb of Cruachan was the mother of the seven Maines, of Orlam son of Oilill, and of Finnabair; and she was the mother of the three sons of Fergus, namely Ciar, Corc, and Conmac; and she may have been the mother of Illann of the many feats, son of Fergus.

(vii) Ráth Cruachan <note>etc.</note>. It is not difficult. Cruachu or Croichenn Red-hand, the handmaid of Étain, went in elopement with Midir of Brí Léith from Fremainn, from the assembly of Aengus. Sinech of the fairy-mound of Cruachan was then a friend to Midir. He stopped there then, out of affection, to converse with her for nine periods of time. Then Étain thought that that fairy-mound belonged to Midir. "Is this your dwelling?" asked Étain. "It is," said Midir. "My own dwelling is closer to the sunrise than this," said Midir. "Question: what benefit is it to us to visit this fairy-mound and the plain?" asked Croichenn. "Your name shall be upon it in reward for your journey, O Croichenn," said Midir. Then Midir went to Brí Léith, so that there it was destroyed upon him [by] <meta>catchword: [la]</meta>

<summary>This page recounts the legendary origins of the six Lugads through their encounter with the personified Sovereignty of Ireland, the history of the Battle of Cenn Febrat, and the etiological myths of Maccon, Mág Mucruime, and Ráth Cruachan.</summary>

Eochaid airemain. This is the beginning of the "Wooing of Etáine" from the lore of the sites of Rath Cruachan. (viii) $a$. The Plain of Ai [etc.] Answer: Ai, son of Allghubha, was the twenty-fourth servant that the sons of Míl brought with them. It was he who requested of those fellow laborers that they should clear a plain for him. Thus, it was they who cleared the Plain of Ai for him in twenty-four hours, so that Ai requested it after they finished, in order that the ownership of that plain might be his and his name remain upon it. *Hence* the Plain of Ai *is so called*. $b$. Loch Néill—*whence is it named*? Answer: Niall, son of Enna Aignech, son of Oengus Tuirbech. He was the first leader of the outlaws of Ireland during the reign of Conall Chromderg, son of Labraid Luichet. He followed the trail of the pigs of Drebrinn when they went out from the fairy mound of Collomrach, until he found them in Daire Tarbgai. The pigs ran before them, past dogs and people, throughout the Plain of Ai, because the name of Enna Aignech's dog was Ai. As soon as they reached the lake—that is, the Lake of Enna Aignech's dog—Niall was drowned there with his dogs and his outlaws. *As the poet says*:

> Niall was drowned with hundreds of heads
> while following the trail of Drebrinn’s pigs;
> the strong tower was a master of deception,
> the leader of the outlaws of Ireland.

(ix) Moncha, daughter of Trethan son of Biced, was the wife of Eogan Mór, son of Oilill Ólom. <insert>PAGE 318:—</insert>(x) A.D. 195. After being thirty years in the kingship of Ireland, Art mac Chuinn of the Hundred Battles fell in the Battle of Mag Mucraime by Mac Con and his foreigners. Liogairne Lecanfhoda, son of Aengus Balbh, son of Echaid Finn Fuathnairt, laid hands on Art in that battle, having come in the army of Mac Con. A.D. 225. After being thirty years in the kingship of Ireland, Lugaid (that is, Mac Con), son of Maicniad, fell by the hand of Ferchis son of Coman the poet, after he had been expelled from Tara by Cormac grandson of Conn. (xi) $a$. Ailill Úlom was so named because there was neither skin nor flesh on his ear after it was stripped bare by Aine, daughter of Eogabal. Or *aulom*, from *aulo lom*, meaning "bare is his chariot-pole"—that is, he was a royal person without a protective covering because of his vigor. $b$. Echtach, daughter of Eimir, was the mother of Ailill Ólom. $c$. A.D. 234. In the eighth year of Cormac, Ailill Ólom son of Mog Nuadat died.

XXIII. <insert>PAGE 319:—</insert>(i) $a$. Eithne Thaebfhota, daughter of Catháir Mór, was the wife of Cormac grandson of Conn and the mother of Cairbre Lifechar. Or, she was truthfully the daughter of Dunlaing, king of Leinster, <gloss>[the manuscript says "most truthfully"]</gloss> as is found in uncorrupted books. [Or] it may be that Feidelm the bondwoman of the Leinstermen was his mother. Or it may be that she was Ciarnait, the bondwoman of Cormac, and that Eithne was a name for Ciarnait. $b$. Ciarnait was the daughter of the king of the Picts, whom the Ulstermen took by force in captivity over the sea and the great ocean. Cormac grandson of Conn heard of this and requested her from them, and she was brought to his house. She was the most beautiful and loveliest woman in the world during her time. She was in a relationship with Cormac, and his love for her was immense. Eithne the learned, daughter of Catháir Mór, heard that Ciarnait was with him and said that they could not both be with him at once. It was necessary to give her into Eithne's power. Eithne imposed slavery upon her, and that slavery was to grind nine measures of grain every day. It happened that Cormac and she were together in private so that he made her pregnant, and she was then unable to grind. Cormac took pity on her and brought a mill-wright over the sea, and a mill was built by him to spare Ciarnait. Regarding this the poet said:

> Ciarnat, bondwoman of just Cormac,
> fed many hundreds with her quern;
> nine measures each day she had to grind,
> it was no work for a single person.
> The noble king came upon her
> in his house while she was alone;
> he made her pregnant in private,
> after which she could not perform the grinding.
> The grandson of Conn took pity on her,
> he brought a mill-wright over the great wave;
> the first mill of Cormac son of Art
> was a help to Ciarnait.

(ii) $a$. Fergus Bód over Brega—that is, "fire over Brega." <insert>PAGE 329:—</insert>(iii) THE CLANS OF EBER in the half of Conn [the North]: THE GAILENGA in the east and the west. THE CIANNACHTA in the south and the north. THE LUIGNE in the east and the west, and the four DELBNA: Great Delbna and Little Delbna in Meath; Delbna Ethra in western Meath, and Delbna of the Land of Two Lakes in Connacht. The Gailenga and Ciannachta are the descendants of Tadg.

# Text of Extracts. [XXIII. iii

...son of Cian, son of Ailill Ólum [Finnchaem, daughter of Cerb and wife of Cian son of Ailill Ólum, was the mother of Tadg son of Cian]. Sadb, daughter of Conn of the Hundred Battles, was the mother of the seven sons of Ailill Ólum. Among these was Cian, the father of Tadg. These were the ones killed in the Battle of Mucrima by Lugaid mac Con and by Lugaid Lága, son of Mug Nuadat (who was their father's brother). It was Lugaid Lága who killed Art son of Conn in the Battle of Mucrima. Béinne Brit, moreover, was the one who killed Eogan son of Ailill, and Lugaid Lága killed him immediately in return. Mac Con had thirty hundred [three thousand] men from Munster, thirty hundred from Conn’s Half, and thirty hundred from the Britons along with the son of the King of the Britons, Béinne. They brought three sacks of battle-grains three times over the sea. Lugaid mac Con then took the kingship of Ireland; he was in the kingship for twenty-seven years until Cormac mac Airt expelled him. Cormac then took the kingship of Ireland until the power of the Ulaid rose against him and they expelled him into Connacht, after taking his hostages and after the Ulaid had prepared a feast for Cormac in the north of the plain of Mag Breg, where the servant of the King of the Ulaid held a candle under Cormac's hair and burned it severely.

The three sons of Imchad, son of Finnachta, son of Ogoman, son of Fiatach, were: Fergus Dubdétach [Black-toothed], Fergus Casfhiaclach [Crooked-toothed], and Fergus Foltlebor [Long-haired]. Cormac went to Tadg mac Céin so that Tadg might come with him to give battle to the Ulaid. "Give me land for it," said Tadg. "You shall be given," said Cormac, "as much as your chariot can circle until evening after the battle is won at Mag Breg." "I will accept that," said Tadg. "Go," said Tadg, "to Lugaid Lága and bring him with you to the battle, and I will reveal to you the town where you will find him sleeping." Cormac went and found him sleeping and turned the point of the spear toward his heart. "Who does this?" asked Lugaid. "Cormac is here," he said. "You have a claim on me," said Lugaid, "for it was I who killed your father." "My <term>éric</term> <note>blood-fine or compensation</note> for it," said Cormac, "is the head of a king in battle for you." "I will accept for Cormac the head of the King of the Ulaid, Fergus Dubdétach," said Lugaid. "I will give it," he replied.

The hosts went until they were at the Brug of the Mac ind Óc, and the Ulaid were at Crinna facing them. Tadg did not permit the battle to be joined until the following morning. They prepared early, but Cormac was not allowed into the battle; he stayed behind the battle in a ditch with his servant above him. Cormac put his royal clothing on the servant, and the servant stood in the likeness of Cormac. Lugaid brought a head with him and showed it to the servant. "It is not he," said the servant, "not the head of the king, but the head of his brother." Lugaid brought another head with him. "It is not he," said the servant, "but the head of his other brother." He brought the third head. "Is this it?" asked Lugaid. "It is," said the servant. Lugaid gave a blow to the servant and killed him, then he himself fell and a faint came over him. Tadg broke seven battles against the Ulaid that day until he reached Glais Nera beside Druim Inasclainn. *Regarding this, Flannacán sang*:

> Tadg son of Cian in the north at Ráth Cró,
> broke seven battles in a single day:
> Against the Ulaid with a swift course,
> from Crinna to Ard Céin.
> A battle in Airgetros of the marshes,
> a battle in Conach, fierce and wild:
> The battle of Crinna, though its fame is swift,
> the battle at Sithbi was a labor.
> The battle of Druim Fuait, a resounding sound,
> the battle of Carraic, hard with armed strife:
> Against the right of sword-wielding Conchobar,
> so that seven are thus counted.

Afterward, Tadg went in his chariot after three spears had passed through him, with a servant and the servant’s mother (who was of the Half of Mug) so that she might be a witness for him. However, a faint came upon Tadg every other hour until he reached Ath Cliath, and it was not yet evening even then. At that point, Tadg rose from his final faint and asked, "How far have we come, servant?" "We have come a great way," said the servant. "Have we brought Tara within our circle?" asked Tadg. "We have not," said the servant. Tadg struck him and killed him. *Regarding this, Cinaeth sang*:

> Upon the single stone at Ráth Cró,
> the falling of the three Ferguses:
> Which Cormac said clearly,
> "I will not hide its cost for its reward."
> Before Tadg the battle was broken,
> as was proclaimed by Cormac:
> Throughout six battles of sharp combat,
> from Crinna to Ard Céin.
> Tadg bound his contract after that,
> upon Cormac of the very bright laws:
> For his portion in Brega without betrayal,
> if he should survive...

...as in a great battle. Unless his charioteer had subdued them, they would have known his great deeds; the land would have belonged to Tara, and he would have driven the chariot again. Afterward, an ear of barley was placed by Cormac into one of his wounds, a worm into another wound, and a spear-point into another wound, so that the skin healed over them and he was in a wasting sickness for a year. Lugaid Lága went from him to fetch the skilled physician in Munster. The physician came with his three students until they heard the cry of the man as they approached the house. "What cry is this?" asked the physician. "A groan from a spear-point," said the first student. "What is this again?" asked the physician. "A groan from a living creature," said the second student. "What is this then," asked the physician at the third groan. "A groan from a point," said the third student. The physician performed his healing and opened the wounds, and hooks were placed over him. A coulter was then reddened in fire, and the physician made a thrust with it toward the man's belly, so that the ear of barley, the worm the size of a mouse, the spear-point, and everything else that was in there came out. 

Tadc went into Munster and prepared for battle against Cormac, but they made peace. Tadc, moreover, had two sons: Connla and Cormac. Cormac was the ancestor of the Ciannachta of the south and north, and the ancestor of the Éile of Munster. Cormac Gaileng was the ancestor of the Gailenga of the east and west, and of the Saithne. 

(iv) *a.* Cormac Gaileng, that is, "deceitful spear." *b.* <term>Gaileng</term>, that is, "false shame." Cormac Gaileng, son of Tadg, son of Cian, son of Ailill Ólum, took his father's spear to the badgers until they came out on his guarantee, and Cormac killed them. Then Tadg went to consume a feast after that at the house of Cormac Gaileng, and his nature was disgusted while drinking the feast, for he knew his honor had been violated by his son. Thus, that was the cause of Cormac's expulsion by Tadg; *whence he was named Gaileng*, that is, "shameful spear" or "dung on honor." *Elsewhere, he is named Cormac Gaileng for his habitation. c.* Cormac Gaileng, son of Tadc, because he took Tadc's spear to the badgers so that they came out on Tadc's honor. *Whence the Gailenga are named. I, however, think they came out then because they were forced by the immense heat of the igniting smoke, and it is no wonder if the heathens thought they were called out by the truth of that famous man. And after they came out, Cormac immediately killed them, and therefore he was made an exile by his father,* Tadg. *From this comes the proverb of that people.* Sciath, daughter of Lugaid son of Aengus Finn, son of Fergus Dubdétach, was the wife of Tadg son of Cian and the mother of Cormac Gaileng.

XXIV. PAGE 326:—(i) *a.* <term>Eocho Mugmedón</term>, that is, there was a swelling around his middle like the chest of a fat, fleshy man; the middle of a fat man. *Whence he is called Mugmedón.* *b.* Eochaid Mugmedón, that is, he had the middle of a slave (*mug*). His head resembled the king, but his middle resembled the slave, that is, Mungata. He was a noble young lord, that is, <term>Echtiger</term>n. Or *muine*, that is, he had a thick neck; *for muin means neck or throat.* *c.* A.D. 365, the eighth year of Eochaid Mugmedón, son of Muiredach Tírech, over Ireland, when he died in Tara. *d.* Muirenn, daughter of Fiachra in Munster, was the mother of Eochaid Mugmedón. 

(ii) *a.* Moingionn, daughter of Fidach, son of Ailill of the Érainn of Munster, sister of Crimthann, and Cairenn Chasdub (curly-black-haired), the mother of Niall of the Nine Hostages, were the two wives of Eochaid Mugmedón. [Eocho] was in his sleep when land was given to the brothers, and he was wandering. Then Bresal said, "That is weak (*tim*), O Eochaid." From that, "Timín" stuck to him.

Half a year in the kingship of Ireland for Nuada Necht, son of Sédna Sithbac; he fell in the battle of Cliach in Ui Dróna by the hand of Conaire Mór. *b.* Nuada Necht, that is, Nuada the beautiful, for *necht* is said to mean beautiful or bright.

XXVII. PAGE 343:—(i) *a.* A.M. 5192. One year for Conchobar Abradruad, son of Finn the poet, son of Ross Ruad, son of Fergus Fairrge, in the kingship of Ireland until he fell by the hand of Crimthann, son of Lugaid Riab nDerg. *b.* Conchobar Abradruad, that is, he possessed eyes with red lashes; for *mala* is called *abhra* <note>eyebrow or eyelash</note>. PAGE 352:—(ii) *A stag was killed* by Tadhg, son of Cian. Tadhg, son of Cian, *killed a stag*; by a stag *was killed* Tadhg, son of Cian, at Ros na Ríogh.

XXVIII. PAGE 359:—(i) Tuathal Techtmar, that is, it is he who first took their heads <note>possibly meaning their chiefs or territories</note> from the provinces of Ireland, namely the men of Meath. Or, it was because of the abundance of his possessions. Or, for the possessing <gloss>techtadh</gloss> of every good thing during his time in Ireland. Or, for the possessing of everyone in common by him; for he did not leave a small green sod in Ireland without the princely law. (ii) *a.* Fiacha Finnolaidh, that is, the majority of the cows of Ireland were white <gloss>finna</gloss> in his time. *b.* Eithne, daughter of the King of Scotland <term>Alban</term>, wife of Fiacha Finnolaidh, was the mother of Tuathal Techtmar. (iii) *a.* Feradach Fechtnach <note>the Fair-Fortunate</note>, that is, for the fortunateness of his reign, for in his time was the Collar of Morann. Eithne Emna, wife of Morann son of Máen—it was for her the collar was made. *b.* Nár Thuathchaech <note>the left-eyed</note>, daughter of Lotan of the Picts <term>Cruithentuaith</term>, wife of Crimthann Nia Náir, was the mother of Feradach Fechtnach. (iv) *a.* Crimthann Nia Náir [son of Lugaid Riab nDerg], that is, the champion of Nár. That is, Nár the left-eyed from the fairy mounds, or from the Picts, was his wife; she it was who took him on an adventure <term>echtra</term>. *b.* Béfina, daughter of Crimthann, wife of Finn son of Finnlogh, was the mother of Eochu Feidlech and Eochu Aireman. She was the mother of Ailill son of Finn; <note>the author adds: I do not know this part</note>. *c.* Clóann, daughter of Artech Uchtlethan, wife of Eochu Feidlech, was the mother of the three Fair Twins <gloss>Finn Emna</gloss> and of Clothru; and all four of them were born at one birth. Onga, another daughter of Artech, was the mother of Mumaine and Eithne. *d.* The three Fair Twins, namely Bres, Nár, and Lothar, the three sons of Eochu Feidlech; they are called the three Fair Twins because the wife of Eochu bore them at one birth; for even if two or three are born at once, they are called twins <gloss>emuin</gloss>. *e.* Clothru, daughter of Eochu Feidlech, was the mother of Lugaid Riab nDerg [son of the three Fair Twins], and she was also the mother of Crimthann son of Lugaid [Riab nDerg]. (v) *a.* Lugaid Riab nDerg <note>Lugaid of the Red Stripes</note>, that is, two red stripes were across him: a belt around his waist and a belt around his neck. His head resembled Nár, his chest resembled Bres, and from there down he resembled Lothar. *b.* Daréra, wife of Rumal king of Leinster <term>Laigen</term>, it was they who raised Lugaid Riab nDerg. Derbforgaill, daughter of the king of Lochlann, was the wife of Lugaid Riab nDerg. *c.* Rumal Dériar, that is, the king of Leinster; he was the first of the Leinstermen to hold territory from the Boyne to Buaighnech. He is called *Dériar* because he did the will of his god by his strength. And Derra his wife raised Lugaid Riab nDerg, and he was the foster-teacher of valor to Cúchulainn; therefore it is said that Cúchulainn was a foster-father to Lugaid. (vi) Fidir and Dáirine, two daughters of Tuathal Techtmar, were the two wives of Eochu Ainchenn, king of Leinster, and it was through them that the cattle-tribute <term>borama</term> was imposed upon the Leinstermen. (vii) *a.* Áine, daughter of Finn son of Cumall, was the mother of Eochaid Doimlén. Oilech, daughter of Ubthaire the Fair, king of Scotland, was the wife of Eochaid Doimlén and mother of the three Collas. *b.* Eochaid Doimlén, that is, a great ox in affliction <gloss>ro-dam ar lén</gloss>, because he did not attempt to take anything of Ireland, for Fiacha Sraiptine did not allow him. As the poet said: "Eochaid was a great ox of affliction in his time, without reaching any of Ireland; father of the three long-lived Collas, from whom the kings of Oirgialla descended." Or Eochaid [Doimlén], that is, *domus plena* <note>Latin: full house</note>, meaning he had a house full of hostages. *c.* Fiacha Sraiptine, that is, a stream <gloss>sraib</gloss> of fire was brought into his ships. Or he was raised in Ui Sraibtine in Connacht. Or indeed, showers of fire used to come in his time. Or *roibtine* means fierceness; Fiacha Roibtine, that is, Fiacha the Fierce. *d.* A.D. 276. Uaibtech was killed this year by the children of Cairbre Lifechar, namely Fiacha Sraibtine and Eochaid Doimlén.

PAGE 362:—(viii) Feidlimid Rechtada, that is, legal judgments <gloss>bretha rechta</gloss> used to serve him; for *talio* <note>lex talionis</note> was observed by him, namely *simile uindictum* <note>similar vengeance</note>, which is like-for-like punishment: an eye for an eye, a foot for a foot, a hand for a hand, and so forth. Because of the greatness to which legal judgments served him, he was called Feidlimid Rechtada <note>the Law-giver</note>. (ix) *a.* Bresal Beolach, that is, "vivid-hero" <gloss>beo-laech</gloss>, meaning a living warrior. Or it was because he had a large mouth <gloss>bél</gloss>. *b.* A.D. 435. PAGE 369:—(x) A.D. 241. The massacre of the maidens in the Sloping Trenches <gloss>claoinferta</gloss> at Tara <term>Temair</term> by Dúnlaing, son of Enna Niad, King of Leinster. Their number was thirty royal maidens, with a hundred maidens attending each one of them. Cormac slew twelve kings of the Leinstermen in single combats in revenge for that massacre, along with the binding of the Boruma tribute with its increase after Tuathal. (xi) A.D. 405. PAGE 374:—(xiv) Belach Conghlais [etc.] namely: Glas, the seventh son of Donn Desa, was a foster-son of Eterscél Mór, King of Ireland. Glas was reared at Tara and was the chief of the hounds for Eterscél and for Conaire. When his brothers went on a marauding expedition, he went with his hounds into the plain of Tara until they encountered a wild pig. He followed it southward to the pass of the swineherd <gloss>belach muccud</gloss>, and there the pig, the pack of hounds, and Glas perished. Hence the name Belach Conghlais <note>The Pass of Glas's Hounds</note>. The seven sons of Donn Desa were: Fer Gair for watching; Fer Lee for hearing; Fer ... for estimating; Lonma for buffoonery; Fer Rorogair for the bonds of a hero, that is, for the deeds of strong men; Fer Gel for single combats; and Fer for hound-management. As is said concerning their names, characters, and deeds in the *Duil Sluinnti Laigen* <note>The Book of the Naming of the Leinstermen</note>.

The wife of Aed sang <gloss>cecinit</gloss>:

> Dear were the three sides that I shall not hope to see again:
> The side of Tailltiu, the side of Tara, and the side of Aed, son of Ainmire.

<meta>This page transitions from the chronological annals of the early 8th century to a collection of translated extracts from various ancient manuscripts, focusing on the genealogy of Saint Kieran, the origins of the people of Ossory, and the etymological history of the name "Leinster."</meta>

<language>English</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>I. i—vi]</page-num>

## Translation of Extracts.

I. PAGE 1:—(i) Saint Kieran’s pedigree in ten generations to Angus *osrethi*: LL. 352 β, 357 : 8 (ii) “March 5: Kieran, bishop and confessor. He is of the race of Angus *osairge*, of the race of Labraid *loingsech* from whom "Leinster" is named, of the seed of Heremon. An ancient vellum book that we have quoted under "Bridget," February 1, states that in ethics and life Kieran resembled Pope Clement:” MD (iii) “Here begins the genealogy of ‘the seed of Bern’—that is, the men of Ossory—who (to go higher) are the seed of Bresal *brec*, son of Fiacha *fobhrec*, etc., as we have written in Leinster’s genealogies [Bresal *brec*’s pedigree in seventeen generations to Ugaine *mór*: LL. 378 a]. Now this Bresal had two sons: Lugaid, ancestor of Leinster; Connla *caemh*, of Ossory; yet the designation ‘Leinster’ is no more appropriate to clan-Lugaid than it is to clan-Connla. In the time of this Bresal *brec*, the first murrain was in Ireland, and it left there but three heifers, red ones: one in *Cliach*, one in *Line*, one in *Cuailgne* (from which comes the local name *Imlech fir aendartadha*) and, as some say, it is from the cattle-spoil then brought by Bresal into Ireland that *Bennchor*, ‘Bangor,’ in Ulidia is named. Laegaire *bern buadach*, whose mother was the daughter of Moghruith’s brother Delbaeth the magician, was the son of Crimthann *mór*; and Daire mac Dedadh’s daughter Cennait, who ‘kept Crimthann company,’ she was Angus’s mother [here nine generations to Bresal *brec* above]:” LL. 339 a (iv) “*Osraighe* ‘Ossory’ = *oséirghe* ‘deer-pace,’ that is, it was the pace of deer they showed in flight before the Decies when they vacated the country in which today the Decies are seated. Or again: *osraighe* = *osfhrìthe* [*osrithe*] ‘deer-waif,’ that is, it was among wild deer that Angus, progenitor of ‘Ossory,’ was picked up:” K. 4 : 1 (v) “*Laigin*, ‘Leinster,’ how is it so called? *Laigin* being essentially *lagain*, it is from the *lagain* or ‘broad spears’ which the Danes brought from over the seas when with Labraid *loingsech* they came here, their leader being the King of Denmark’s son Ernoll. From the time of this Labraid to this day, the Leinstermen are endowed with heroism, inspiring horror, fear, and terror; as the poet says: ‘Labraid *loingsech* (all-sufficient were his numbers), by whom Cobthach was slain at *Dinn rígh*, came with a spear-bearing host across the sea’s expanse, and from them the *Laigin* have their title. Previously *Tuaim Tenba* had been the name of that hill on which the massacre was committed; it has been *Dinn rígh* or ‘hill of kings’ ever since, from the slaughter of the princes there. Two hundred and forty strangers brought over spears with wide heads—from such these *lagain* or ‘broad spears,’ then introduced, the Leinstermen now have the name of *Laigin*:’” LL. 159 a (vi) “*Gailíon* and *Domhnann*, these two (as is told in the *táin bó Cuailgne*) are names for Leinster. Along with Labraid *loingsech* their protégé, there came to Ireland a band of *galls* or ‘strangers’ and sacked *Dinn rígh*, etc.; from whom are called the *Gailíon*, essentially *gall-líon* or ‘stranger-multitude,’ whose posterity for a long time endured in the land, witness *Dún gailíon* among the *dál Meisi corb*:” LL.

...that his brother’s sons, the three Collas, committed parricide; this crime separated the kingdom of Ireland from the clan of Eochaid. The circumstances of the murder were these: Fiacha *sraibhtine*, as we have said, was king in Tara and had an admirable son, Muiredach *tírech*, who was his lieutenant; for at that time it was the rule that the king himself did not go into battle, but his lieutenant went in his place. In his father’s place, then, Muiredach once went into Munster with a great army. The men of Munster gave him battle; he won it and brought away Munster’s hostages <note>pledges</note>. Meanwhile, Fiacha *sraibhtine* stayed at home in *Dubhcomar*, to the south of Tara, and had a host in the camp where he lay; his three nephews, the Collas, also had another host upon another hill; but the entire force belonged to Fiacha. When, therefore, news came that Muiredach had won the victory, everyone was saying: "Muiredach *tírech*—he is the future king of Ireland!" Then the three Collas said: "What shall we do? Fiacha actually holds the kingdom, and the people say that his son shall be king after him. Our best move is this: before Muiredach arrives, let us give battle to this old king, for this army of his that is here with us will desert him and join us; then, if the other one comes, we will give him battle as well." From one hill to the other, they sent a message to Fiacha, their father’s brother; and he was challenged to the fight by them, his brother’s sons. Fiacha had a magician named *Dubhcomair*, who said to the king: "I can obtain victory for you, but the situation stands like this: if you defeat them, you will commit parricide upon your brother’s sons, and you will indeed still be king, but none of your children will ever be king again; if they defeat you, parricide will be committed upon you, and from your lineage Ireland shall have a ruler for all time, but there shall never be a prince from the three Collas. You, therefore, choose," said the wizard. Fiacha answered: "Let me be defeated and let my descendants have the kingdom." "I too," said the magician, "will fall with you, and the battle shall continually bear my name;" which is why "the Battle of Dubhcomar" is that battle's title. Fiacha was duly slain in the battle; the Collas, with three hundred men, went to Scotland, fleeing from Muiredach, who assumed the royalty of Ireland. Because of their brave quality, the king of Scotland showed the Collas great affection, and they were in Scotland for three years; then they considered coming over to Ireland so that Muiredach might commit parricide upon them, so that the reproach resting on them (namely, their own parricide) might be lifted from them. So all three Collas, without either hound or *gilla* <note>attendant</note>, set out and reached Tara. The gatekeeper told Muiredach: "The three Collas are on the green; what shall be done with them?" "Open the liss <note>enclosure or ring-fort</note>," said Muiredach, "to see what they will do." The trio entered and stood in the middle of the royal house in Tara, and Muiredach said: "Do you have news?" One of them answered: "For you, no news can be more painful than what we have done: the slaughter of your father." "We know those tidings already." "Understand that we have not come to beg," the Collas said; and the king replied: "Do not worry about that; it shall not be avenged upon you. If you have come to have yourselves killed, it shall not succeed: I will not remove the infamy you have earned in that way." "That is a fine taunt for a coward to make," answered the Collas; to whom Muiredach replied: "Do not be so ill-tempered, and you shall have welcome and peace." For a long time afterward, they lived in good brotherhood, and the three Collas were the ones Muiredach had for his lieutenants in war; between

After a three-year exile in Scotland, the Collas return to Tara and are eventually reconciled with Fiacha's son, King Muiredach Tírech.</summary>

between whom and the king there was great mutual affection. Muiredach eventually said to them: ‘I see that they <note>our descendants respectively</note> have begun to increase and branch out greatly; it may be that after our time they will not live in peace; therefore, let us separate, and during my time, acquire a country of your own.’ The Collas asked: ‘What country do you, by your power, most readily assign to us, so that we may make swordland of it?’ (for there were no better warriors than the Collas). Muiredach said: ‘Attack Ulster; they are not kindly disposed toward us.’ But there, the warrior force was too great for the Collas; so they went to the men of Connacht and became their protégés, and the Connachtmen received them. Subsequently, Connacht came with them, seven battalions strong in total, and they were at the cairn of *Achadh lethderg* in Farney, in Ulster. From that cairn, they fought seven battles against Ulster, one daily until the end of a week: six being fought by Connacht and one by the Collas. Every single day Ulster was routed; the Collas’ battle was on the last day; there was no cowardly failure in fighting there; the battle was maintained for a summer’s day and night, until blood reached the shields; close by the cairn is *coll na nothar*, ‘Hazel of the Wounded.’ <note>In this last battle</note> Ulster gave way at the break of the second day; the slaughter lasted as far as Glenree. Then the others spent a week harrying Ulster, and they made swordland of the country in which are the *Mughdorna*, the *úi Chremthainn*, the *úi mac Uais*, and up to the Oriors. ‘Conn’s Half’ consists of the O’Neills of the North, the O’Neills of the South, the three Connachts, Oriel, and others:” LL. 332 : 3 (xix) a. “Cairbre, called *lifechair* because of the degree to which he loved *Liffe*; or *Liffe* was his mother; or she brought him up in *Liffe*:” K. 1 *b* : 2 *b.* “*Colla os*, from whom come the *úi mac Uais* and *úi Thuirtri*: a wild doe reared him. *Colla menn*, from whom come the *Mughdorna*: Mennet the Pictish woman and *Mughdorndubh* of Ulster brought him up, namely: Mennet, from whom come the *dál Mennet* in Mourne; as for *Mughdorndubh*, however, it is unknown where he is from, but he is assigned to Ulster. *Colla fochrích*, or *fochrí*, or *ochre*: and it was the artisan Crinna’s wife, *Eilech*, whom Eochaid *doimhlén* got with child in place of her husband, in consequence of which she bore Colla. <note>The paternity</note> she hid from her husband, and the boy was reared <note>by them both</note> until the end of twenty years. Through pride, therefore, once upon a time, Boann (well knowing the well’s power) said that there existed no hidden power able to mar her beauty, and so she visited the spring; three times she walked counter-clockwise <note>left-handed</note> around it; whereupon three volumes of water spouted forth over her and robbed her of a thigh, an arm, and one eye. Then, to hide her disgrace, she turned away and fled toward the sea, with the water following her to the estuary of the Boyne. Now, she was the mother of Angus, son of the Daghda. Or it stands thus: *Bó* is the name of a stream, the *Fionn* is a river of Slievegorey, and it is to their confluence <note>united waters</note> that the name of *Bóann* <note>*bófhionn*, pronounced *bó-ionn*</note> is given. *Book of Leinster 154 a.* (iii) “Whence the name *Sliabh Fuaid*? It was Fuad, son of Bile, son of Brige, son of Breogan, who, on the passage to Ireland, happened upon an island in the sea: *Inis Maighdena*, meaning *mó óghdéda*, that is *mór* (‘great’) + *ógh* (‘perfect’) + *diadha* (‘godly’). If anyone set the sole of his foot upon it, so long as he remained there, he would never tell a lie. Fuad therefore brought away from it a *fód* or ‘sod’ <note>genitive *fóid*, similar to *fuaid*</note>, and his judgment and equity were based upon it. For when a falsehood was uttered, the sod would turn its soil upward and its grass to the bottom; when truth was spoken, its grass turned upward. That sod is still in the mountain, and upon it landed the single grain that fell from Saint Patrick’s work-horse <note>garran</note>. For this reason, and because truth is maintained there, from that time to this it has been the resort of solemn elders. Alternatively: *Sliabh Fuaid* may have been named after Breogan’s son Fuad personally.” *Book of Ballymote 404 a.* PAGE 104:—(iv) “A.D. 447: The nineteenth year of Laeghaire, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages. ‘Secundinus,’ or *Sechnall, son of Ua Baird* and son of Saint Patrick’s sister Darerca, bishop of Armagh, was seventy years old when he resigned his spirit on November 27.” *Annals of the Four Masters.* PAGE 105:—(v) *a.* “Whence the name *Benn Edair* (‘the Hill of Howth’)? “Where does *mágh Femin* ‘Femen’s plain’ come from? Femen and Fera were two brothers, sons of Brath son of Deth: they had one iron mattock and one iron shovel between the two of them; while Femen was covering the earth, Fera would dig it up, and so on by turns [until they had cleared the plain], which is the origin of the names *mágh Femin* and *mágh Fera*:” LL. 168$\beta$

PAGE 112:—(xii) “Where does *fidh Gaibhli* ‘Feeguile’ come from? It was *Gabhal Glas*, son of *Ethadón*, son of Nuadha Silver-arm, who took away the Daghdha’s daughter Ainge’s bundle of twigs that she had gathered to make a tub from them. For any tub the Daghdha made, as long as the tide flowed, it never stopped leaking; but when the ebb set in, not a single drop came from it. From *belach fualascaigh* ‘the osier pass,’ Gabhal then made a throw with that bundle; it landed, and a wood [sprang up from it and] spread in every direction, which is the origin of *fidh Gaibhle* ‘wood of Gabhal.’ Or it may have been Gabhal *gháirechtach* ‘the boisterous,’ daughter of Goll *Glas* and wife of Orc mac Ingas, who was drowned in that river after her husband Ailill, son of Aedh *róin*, had been slain at *áth Oirc* or ‘Orc’s ford’; which gave the name to the Gabhal river and *áth Oirc* [on the same river]. Or again, the river may be called Gabhal from the *gabhlugbudh* [= *gabhalughudh* ‘forking’ from *gabhal* ‘a fork’] which it makes at the point of the two *cluains*: Clonsost and Clonmore:” LL. 159$\alpha$

PAGE 114:—(xiii) *a.* “Where does *Temhair luachra* ‘Tara of Luachair’ come from? It is derived from Temhair, daughter of Ith son of Breogon and wife of Heremon; both Tara of Bregia and every other Tara in Ireland are named after her as well. As for Luachair itself, until the time of Hugony’s sons or, as some say, even down to the birth of Conn of the Hundred Battles, it was a flowery plain; in fact, the Suir, Nore, and Barrow rivers had their source there, as well as lakes Riach and Lein in Luachair, and *bile toirthen* and *eóron* <note>ancient sacred trees</note> were seen there:” BB. 376$\beta$

*b.* “Where does *loch Léin* ‘Killarney’ come from? He used to make three showers fly from this anvil: one of water, one of fire, and one of pure crimson gems (the same thing that Nemannach also practiced when he hammered Conor mac Nessa’s goblets in the north), and hence the name *loch Léin*:” cited manuscript 379$\alpha$

PAGE 178:—(xxvi) a. "Where does *mágh muirisce* ('the plain of Murrisk') come from? It was a *muiriasc mór* or 'huge sea-fish,' such as is called a *rosualt* <note>perhaps a rorqual</note>, that the sea cast ashore. It was Columbkill who made it his practice to declare the mystery of this animal to all men, and it was this: it used to produce three vomits <note>in separate years</note>, and every one of them was directed upwards. That is, with its tail-flukes in the air, it would make one vomit into the sea; in that year, there was a swamping of currachs and barques, and a plague afflicted the creatures of the sea. With its hind end immersed, it would spew another vomit high into the air; in that year, death raged among the winged beings of the atmosphere. Yet a third vomit it would send over the land, making it all stink; in that year, destruction fell upon men and four-footed animals. It was in the time of the Aedhs and of Columbkill that this animal used to appear, which is why *Dallan forgaill* sang: 'Among the schools provided with libraries, you have read the mysteries of the *rosualt*.' Or: it was a *tóla muiréisc mhóir* ('an inundation of huge sea-fish') that happened in the time of *Garbh of Glúnraighe* and filled all the glens and hillsides of the land bordering the sea. (xxxi) "What is the origin of *tonn Chliodhna* ('Cleena’s Wave')? It was Genann mac Treon’s daughter Cleena who came with Iuchna *ciabainech* from *tulach dá roth*, out of *mágh mell* in the promised land, to seek the *Mac Óg*. He <note>Iuchna</note>, however, played a trick on her: in the metal ship in which she was, he played music for her until she slept; then he turned back and set a direct opposite course, rounded Ireland to the south, and reached the point named above <note>the spot where Cleena’s Wave is now</note>. (ii) "Lughaid *laeighde* etc. The tale which is here brought to mind <note>recorded</note> gives the origin of that superabundance of names <note>sobriquets</note> which distinguishes Daire *doimthech*'s sons, the six Lughaids. What, too, is the reason for which every one of them was called Lughaid? It was prophesied that of Daire's sons, a son should reign over Ireland and his name would be Lughaid; therefore, they each bore that name. Daire held the Convention of Taillte, and there his sons raced their horses; then their father said to his magician: 'Which son will succeed me?' The sorcerer answered: 'Into the meeting will come a fawn, bright with the color of gold; and the son that catches him is the one that shall succeed you.' In due course, the golden fawn arrived, and the men of Ireland went after him. From there even to Ben-Edar the six lads press him hard, and between them and all the rest <note>at last</note> a magic mist is interposed. From that point onward yet to *dál Mescorb* in Leinster, Daire's sons stick to him; there Lughaid *laeighe* collars the *laegh* or 'fawn' <note>whence the nickname</note>, another Lughaid does his *coscar* or 'breaking up,' and hence Lughaid *cosc* <note>or *coscaire* as before, 'the breaker up'</note>. Then a great snow pelts down on them, so that it was work for them to keep a hold of their weapons, and one of the lads goes off to seek a house. He found there a large house with a big fire, with food and liquor in plenty; silver dishes, bedsteads of white bronze, and <note>above all</note> a fearsome *cailleach* or 'hag' was in the mansion. 'Youth,' she said, 'what do you crave?'"

...whom immediately]. Cormac went to Teigue mac Cein, asking that he should come with him and give battle to Ulidia (Ulster), and Teigue said, "Give me land for it." Cormac replied: "There shall be given to you as much of *mágh Bregh* as your chariot shall encompass after the battle is won." Teigue said: "I will take it; you, therefore, go now to *Lughaidh Lágha* and bring him for the battle; I will reveal to you the place in which you shall find him asleep." Cormac went, found him so, and held the spear's point at his heart. "Who does this?" asked Lughaidh <note>roused</note>. "Cormac is here!" Lughaidh said: "I am in your debt; it was I that slew your father." "I require his *eric* <note>blood-fine</note>." "I offer you a king's head taken in battle." Cormac said: "I will accept the king of Ulidia's head: Fergus Blacktooth's." "I will give it," answered Lughaidh. The army marched and took position at the *Brú of Mac in óg*, with Ulidia lying ready for them at Crinna of *Cenn comair*; but Teigue did not allow the battle to be joined until the next morning. 

At daybreak they went to work; Cormac, however, was not allowed into the battle, but was hidden away in a trench well to the rear with his *gilla* <note>servant</note> standing over him; this servant he had dressed in his own armor, so that the *gilla* had the appearance of the king. Lughaidh brought a head and showed it to the *gilla*, who said: "That is not the king's head, but his brother's." He brought another head: "Nor is that," said the *gilla*, "but his other brother's." He brought a third head, and Lughaidh asked, "Is this it?" The other answered: "It is." Then Lughaidh dealt him a blow with it and killed him, while at the same time he himself fell down and fainted away. 

That day Teigue routed Ulidia seven times, as far as *glas Nera* near *druim Inesclainn*; concerning which Flannacán sang: "Teigue mac Cein at *Ráth chró* in the North <note>etc.</note>." Teigue now (after three spears had passed through him) got into his chariot and took with him a *gilla* whose mother was of "Mogh's Half," so that he above others should be a witness for him. Teigue had a succession of deep faints until at last he reached Dublin, and even then it was not yet evening <note>which, had the charioteer acted fairly, should have been long past</note>. Here he awoke from his last faint and inquired: "How far have we traveled, *gilla*?" "We have traveled a great deal," he answered. "Have we included Tara?" "We have not." Therefore Cinaeth sang: "Upon the one stone at *Ráth chró* <note>etc.</note>." 

Afterward, Cormac inserted a barley beard into one of Teigue's wounds, some kind of worm into another, and a spearhead into the third; the skin formed over these, and for a year the patient lay in a wasting sickness. *Lughaidh Lágha* went from him into Munster to fetch the expert physician; he came with his three pupils and, as they neared the house, they heard a man cry out. "What cry is this?" said the physician. "A groan caused by a *colg* <note>a beard of grain</note>," said the first pupil. "But what is this again?" the master asked. "A groan caused by a living creature," answered another pupil. "And this?" he asked at the third groan. "A groan caused by a weapon-point," said the third disciple. 

The physician treated him: he opened the wounds, and a set of bandages were passed over Teigue <note>to keep him in place</note>; then a coulter <note>plow-blade</note> was heated red in the fire, and the physician made a feint at the man's belly with it, causing the barley beard, the worm (the size of a mouse), the spearhead, and all other harmful things that were in him to come out. Teigue retired into Munster and prepared to make war upon Cormac, but they made peace. Now Teigue had two sons, Connla and Cormac: the former was the grandfather of the northern and southern Cianacht, as well as of the Ely of Munster; Cormac was the ancestor of the eastern and western Gaileanga, as well as of the *Saithne*: <note>From the Book of Leinster, LL. 328 β (iv) a.</note>

This was the cause of Cormac’s banishment by Teigue, and for this reason he was called *gaileang* = *gai* + *lang*, that is, ‘the one who defiled honor.’ Furthermore: because Cormac was surnamed *gaileang*, the term Gaileanga is used for his tribe:” *cod. cit.* 253 $\beta$ *c*. “Teigue’s son Cormac was called *gaileang* because he took his father’s spear to the badgers, and they came out on the faith of Teigue’s honor; hence the Gaileanga (though I, the writer, believe they emerged under the compulsion of the enormous smoke arising from a fire kindled by Cormac; yet it is not at all surprising if the heathens supposed them to come out because they were summoned on the faith of that famous man’s integrity). For this act, Cormac was exiled by his father Teigue, and from this came his nation’s common nickname:” LL. 329 : 3 *d*. “Sciath, daughter of Lughaid, son of Angus *fionn*, son of Fergus Blacktooth, wife of Teigue mac Cein, was the mother of Cormac Gaileang:”

Page 45, second to last line, 'the tokens [etc.]': Fifteen signs before the day of judgment. Jerome found in the books of the Hebrews <note>Possibly "the annals," though the original reads "animalibus"</note> fifteen signs for the fifteen days before the day of judgment, but whether those days will be continuous or interrupted he did not specify. On the first day, the sea will raise itself forty cubits above the height of the mountains, standing in its place like a wall. Second, it will descend so much that it can hardly be seen. Third, sea beasts appearing on the sea will give out roars up to heaven. Fourth, the sea and the waters will burn. Fifth, buildings will fall. Seventh, rocks will strike against one another. Eighth, a general earthquake will occur. Ninth, the earth will be leveled. Tenth, men will come out of caves and go about like madmen and will not be able to speak. Eleventh, the bones of the dead will rise and stand above their graves. Twelfth, the stars will fall. Thirteenth, the men living then will die, so that they may rise with the dead. Fourteenth, heaven and earth will burn along the surfaces of the earth and the air. Fifteenth, there will be a new heaven and a new earth and all shall rise; hence Gregory says in the homily on that gospel: there shall be signs and wonders, etc. . . (*Speculum Christianorum* containing many good things, Paris: Claude Jaumar, 1497, folio 46 b).

Page 46, line 3, after 'body' add: 'on that day, and in the place where there shall be neither opposition [dissension] nor ending;' line 12, *caire* of the manuscript is more likely to stand for *coire* 'cauldron' than for *cuire* 'band' or 'gang,' compare on the contrary *boile* (frequent in northern manuscripts) for *baile* 'town,' not for *buile* 'madness.' That a utensil of the kind is appropriate here, the following (told to me long ago, with much else, to lighten a mile or two of the road) will show: a beggar of the traditional sort on his rounds enters the parson's kitchen and, after seating himself, demands a meal as if by right; the servant girl conveys the message, and the parson, who is at dinner but forgets that it is Friday, sends down to the <term>duine bocht uasal</term> or 'poor gentleman' a cut from his joint. On theological grounds this is returned peremptorily, and the parson instructs the girl:—

> Beir sgéla uaim go dtí an nduine sin
> ós tu as deirionaighe bhí ag labhairt leis.
> Nach í an fheoil théidheann go hiffernn
> acht na croidhtheacha bhíos fallsa:

i.e., "Carry a message from me to that man (since you were the last one to speak with

The <term>bacach</term> <note>an Irish beggar</note> sends her back immediately with the stanza completed:—

> Beirse sgéla uaimse go dtí an ministir
>    ós duitse as usa labhairt leis.

i.e. “From *me* to the minister (since for *you* it is the most easy to have speech with him) do *you* convey the news that in Hell there’s a big cauldron and ministers are dancing in it [i.e., on the boil]!”

Such is *freagra an bhacaig ghaodhlaig ar an ministir* ‘the Irish beggar’s retort on the minister.’

i.e. “Discipline your father in good time; never suppose him to be better than yourself; a single well-spoken word, or one fraught with wit, never let such a thing issue from your mouth.”

P. 49, l. 25, ‘Thus Antichrist [etc.]’: Concerning the Antichrist. The Antichrist will be born in great Babylon to a prostitute of the tribe of Dan. He will be filled with the devil in his mother's womb; he will be nurtured in physical wickedness; he will rule the entire world. He will subjugate the whole human race to himself in four ways. First, he will attract the nobles to himself with riches which will flow to him in great abundance, because every hidden treasure will be revealed to him. Second, he will subject the common people to himself through terror, because he will rage with the greatest cruelty against the worshippers of God. Third, he will win over the clergy with wisdom and incredible eloquence, because he will know all arts and all scripture by heart. P. 50, l. 22, ‘to the sword’s edge’ literally ‘under mouth of sword,’ an idiom which hardly seems necessary to consider a Hebraism derived through the Latin scriptures, such as: *And Joshua put Amalek and his people to flight with the edge of the sword* (Exodus 17:13). Sometimes it is, like <term>dubh</term> ‘black,’ a mere intensive, compare Hiberno-English ‘the black North’ = ‘the very heart of the North’; ‘a black Tory,’ ‘a black Whig,’ and so on. Lastly: it is evident that the <term>cú ruadh</term> of p. 59, l. 16 (Irish p. 57, l. 1), stands neither in apposition nor as a parallel, but in contrast to the immediately preceding <term>sionnach</term> ‘fox’ (index C, under the word <term>coinfiadh</term>).

# Notes and Corrections.

'tabak'; line 31, *lith = leith* (just as *bith = beith, lis = leis*, etc.) represents the pronunciation of the northern half of Ireland: a peculiarity whose great age, along with many others (inflectional and phonetic) characterizing various districts, would be easy to demonstrate from manuscripts. Here, however, the much-criticized native speaker would have to be consulted, and purely scientific theorists would find themselves on slippery ground.

P. 79, line 25, for the literal ‘in,’ read rather ‘at’ *bruidhen Dáchoga* (‘Dachoga’s fort’), and understand it as ‘on the site of it,’ which was in West Meath; the tale bearing that title belongs to Conor mac Nessa’s cycle, dating to around 33 A.D.

P. 75, Irish text, line 10, read *marbadsom*; line 24 and following, the matter in [ ] is simply the result of scribal playfulness and is absolutely devoid of all interest, whether philological or phonetic—unless, indeed, one focuses on the single microscopic fact that *áirie* represents the northern pronunciation of *áirithe* without aspiration. Some passages of this kind are much longer and, where contextual help is little or nonexistent, constitute veritable puzzles; this one is a very mild affair, the only word left dubious (and that intentionally, through abbreviation) being *qur-*, where the hidden trick apparently is a play on *curadh* (see Index C, under the word *cur*) and *cú ruadh* as printed. Gillariach mac Teigue O’Clery (Harleian MS 5280), flourished around 1460, and Donall O’Davoren (Egerton MS 88) a century later, were experts at this game. Of the same kind is a feature in some pieces of (among others) Egerton MS 1782: the substitution of *i* for *a* in certain combinations specified in *Irische Texte* III. i, p. 234. There is no trace of dialect here; the reason for its existence lies in what Zimmer calls the ‘strongly expiratory accent,’ which can be traced back quite far and began fusing and erasing case-endings, etc., very early. Thus, in the scribe’s time and long before, the definite article *in* had in common speech become *an*; the preposition *i* became *a*; the scribe then (to amuse himself) reversed the process and in various instances wrote *i* for *a*. Here, scientists are humbly asked to believe that since Ireland has been Ireland, no man ever pronounced it that way—unless, perhaps, the Gael possessed some prototype of Dick Swiveller with his famous line: “is the old *min* <note>man</note> friendly?”

P. 76, Irish text, line 1, read *con toidecht = co dtoidecht*; where, as in so many cases (p. 81, l. 8), the interchange of *g* and *d* is merely phonetic, showing that the writer aspirated the letter. Thus, incorrect (or playful) scribes will write *a ghún* for *a dhún* (‘his fort’) or *a dhort* for *a ghort* (‘his field’), but not *a gún* for *a dún* (‘her fort’), nor *a dort* for *a gort* (‘her field’).

*ibid.*, line 15, there is no need to read the <term>nominative</term> *Senach*, but rather the <term>genitive</term> *Senaigh* for the manuscript's *Senaidh* (see the previous remark). Following *epscop* <note>bishop</note>, this genitive of the name (functioning like ‘*episcopus Johannis*’ for ‘*episcopus Johannes*’) is frequent in the Book of Leinster (LL.), etc. This is an extension of the idiom (much used by the people when speaking English) which produces *amadán fir* (‘a fool of a man’ = ‘a foolish fellow’), *togha marcaigh* (‘a choice of a horseman’ = ‘a choice horseman’), and so on; compare the familiar French phrases ‘*une drôle d’histoire*’ and ‘*farceur de Jacques*,’ etc.

P. 77, Irish text, line 24, read *scithlim*. Dermot’s vision mentioned above recalls Nebuchadnezzar’s in Daniel 4.

P. 79, Irish text, line 11, *a cinaidh = i gcinaidh*.

P. 81, Irish text, line 6, the manuscript reads *noeghoidechta*, which is a misspelling of *noeighedechta*; line 9, according to *Irische Texte* III, volume 1, page 223, *tar mo shárugad* is ‘an idiomatic phrase’; add this explanation: *sáraighim*, the fundamental concept of—

# Notes and Corrections.

Which means 'excess' (compare French '*excéder*'), means 'I override,' 'outrage,' or 'violate,' whether physically in any way or by disregarding another's rights and privileges; the verbal noun *sárughadh* or *sárachadh*, coupled with a possessive pronoun or dependent genitive, means such outraging, etc., of a person, sanctuary, or anything capable of being so treated. When, therefore, a person A cannot attain a given end without doing a *sárughadh* of some sort against person C, such necessary violence is conceived of as an obstacle in A's way; and, should he nevertheless persevere to success, he is said to do so *dar sárughadh C*, 'over [in spite of] violence to C,' where the simple preposition *dar* ('across') conveys the notion of overcoming, surpassing, or traversing—just as Leander did the Hellespont or a French sportsman does his '*banquette Irlandaise*' (see page 86, line antepenult). A common saying is: *ní féidir an seanfhocal do shárughadh*, which means "you cannot go beyond a proverb," or "it is not possible to beat a proverb."

# Notes and Corrections.

Page 131, Irish, line 28, *gid beg mór* ‘be it little or be it much,’ a very common omission of the disjunctive <note>the word "or"</note>; is Cormac’s example under the word *cel* (Calcutta edition, page 36): *gar cian co tís for ceal*—that is, “be it short or be it long until you shall go to Heaven”—of this kind? Also the last line of Finn’s ‘rhetoric’ in the house of Mael Mac Morna (*Féilire* of Angus the Culdee, edited by Stokes, page clxxiii above): *gar cian co ticfa*—that is, “be it short or be it long until he shall come?” Since these examples are identical on the face of them, their translations must also be the same; whereas those printed in the cited books not only differ, but each completely excludes the other: “a long old age until you shall go to Heaven” <note>a wish: Cormac</note>; “short is the time until he shall come” <note>a proposition: Angus</note>. 

Both, I think, are incorrect; but assuming for a moment that the first is sound (as stated in the note for that passage, cited edition page x), then the quotation ‘*serus redeas in coelum*’ <note>‘may you return late to heaven’</note> is, if not ‘a literal translation’ (O’Reilly following O’Flanagan), at least a relevant illustration. Except as a mere reference point for the word *cian*, the citation *bátar for* [etc.] in the cited note has no bearing on the matter, which is one of syntax, not of the words themselves; for of these, except for the verbal form *tís* for *ticfair*, every one is still used at the time of this writing and in its old sense (Index C under the words *cel*, *cian*). The true Horatian parallel to *gar cian* would be (with the order inverted) ‘*serius ocius*’ <note>‘sooner or later’</note>; while our *gid beg mór* (Irish in these groupings favoring the positive degree and Latin the comparative) has its equivalent in ‘*sit plus minus*’ <note>‘be it more or less’</note>, according to the context. Exactly the same as *cian gar* is *fad gairit*, page 139, line 36; *cian mór* (*céin máir*) and *gar beg* are different. But this does not exhaust the subject.

Page 134, Irish, line 18, for the manuscript reading *arbítin* read *ar bithin*, a nominal preposition meaning ‘because of’; at present (in Munster at least) it is *do [de] bhíthin*, with a dependent genitive as in the text and, before a verb, with *go*, such as: *do bhíthin go raibh* ‘because it was.’ Owing to the silencing of the aspirated *th*, the northern half of the country would comparatively lengthen the first *i*, and our scribe was prone to reproducing methods of pronunciation that were then, as they are now, alien to Mac Carthy-Riach’s territory of Carbery.

Page 135, Irish, lines 31, 35, read *díoghbaigh*.

Page 137, Irish, line 21, manuscript *bhunaid*; in view of this aspiration, it will be better to fill the gap thus: *d[amhsa crét í an chúis]*, and translate it as printed on page 150, second to last line.

Page 138, Irish, line 7, for *i bfiadh* the manuscript has *afiadh*, with the *f* dotted; line 17, read *dofaeth*, *cuill*; line 36, manuscript *duin* for *dún*, to the detriment of the meter, and the scribe knew this at least as well as I do; second to last line, for *so* read *ro*.

Page 151, line 40. Here we have the answer of Garadh’s children; in the translation add single quotation marks, and read: ‘by gentle Morna’s children shall fall the virile Fintan . ., Banbh, Sinna, Sciathbrec . ., and Finn More son of Cuan.’ But whether we should instead translate it as: ‘Banbh of the Shannon <note>Index B under the word *Sinna*</note>,’ or again ‘Sinna of the speckled shield,’ is perhaps not very easy to determine based on the merits of this one passage alone.

# Notes and Corrections.

Page 140, line 26, for the manuscript reading *ollarda*, written undoubtedly under the influence of *ollarba* (see Index B under the word), read *ollamda*, as also in the translation, page 154, line 27.

Page 141, Irish, line 14, read *résiu*; line 29, manuscript reading *treicibhsa*: there is no saying how far back this aspiration of the Old Irish B-future extends.

Page 146, Irish, line 6. We know that for several, and perhaps for many centuries, *ingnadh* or *iongnadh* (‘a wonder’) has not—except for the sake of the meter, whether universally in ‘classical’ verse or occasionally as needed in modern stressed measures—been pronounced as written. Instead, it is pronounced according to the speech of today: *íoghnadh* in the northern half of the country and *iughnadh* in Munster, produced by the natural tendency to simplify rapid pronunciation. Here our scribe, who writes *ignad*, appears rather to indicate the northern pronunciation as exemplified in these touching lines:—

->A n bríste sin Sheoin ní hiongna a bheith fann.<-
->bíonn san ló ar a thóin is san oidhche ar a cheann<-

which Goldsmith might have turned:—
> ‘Friend, never let it puzzle you, nor me,
> John’s smallclothes in such feeble plight to see;
> For they’re compelled a double debt to pay,
> A quilt by night, a pair of breeks by day.’

If they are read in the Munster fashion, the important internal assonance of *iongnadh* [*íoghnadh*] with *oidhche* is lost; the rest holds. In one of his playful marginal notes (Egerton 88), Donall O’Davoren writes *únadh* crudely and, phonetically speaking, correctly; but when, for example, the definite article is used (*an tiongnadh*, ‘the wonder’), the *i* asserts itself; see Index C under the word *eolas*.

*Ibid.*, *do théiged* [etc.] is not quite literally translated as ‘the stalk alone reached to Dermot’s knee’ (page 161, line 29), where one should read: ‘Dermot’s knee went into the stalk of each sprig of them’—that is, his leg from the knee down was contained within it (just as one might say four ‘goes into’ five), with a bit of the stalk remaining. In Ireland, we would say ‘used to go,’ which, as understood there, has a distinct force of its own; but the Irish habitual tenses (present and past) cannot always be expressed according to correct English usage.

Page 162, line 30, read ‘brooklime of the Flesk.’

Page 147, Irish, line 9, manuscript reading *nó go nosl-* with an *i* under the dash, which is placed as it appears in the type, not halfway up the *l*; a dash in the latter position either stands alone or has a letter written above it (never below it). The abbreviation certainly denotes the passive *oslaicthi* (not the active *oslaiced* as was hastily printed), and it has been translated as such (page 163, lines 2, 3). The description of this wonderful chain is rather obscure, and we do not have space to discuss it. By ‘locked,’ understand merely ‘fastened’ or ‘closed,’ not ‘padlocked.’

Page 148, Irish, line 22, for the manuscript reading *cennac* (with two strokes over the final *c*) and *isingl-* (with a dash at the middle of the *l*), read *cenn i cenn* and *isin glenn*; line 39, the manuscript reading *atáithe* (‘you are’) is written fancifully to represent the pronunciation of regions other than Munster, where alone (I imagine) this form is still in use, correctly pronounced *táthaoi* or *atáthaoi*; older spelling *táthái* or *atáthái*; compare *taoim* or *ataoim* (‘I am’), *taoir* or *ataoir*.

Page 155, Irish, line 28, *Sadhb* ‘Sabia,’ ‘Saby,’ ‘Sara,’ common enough down to the end of the 18th century, was pronounced ‘Sâw’ (consonantal *w*, not like the English ‘saw’) in the northern half; ‘Syve’ in Munster, as, for example, Brian Merriman writes: *a bfeiceann tu a Shadhb iriu luigheamh a ghéaga*. Here we have two ways of evading the guttural *dh*: (i) it becomes a *litera prolongationis* <note>letter of prolongation</note> to a short vowel (ii) it coalesces with the same and forms a diphthong; compare Scottish ‘nŏcht,’ English ‘nought’ pronounced to rhyme with ‘taught’ and, provincially, with ‘stout’; Scottish ‘lĭcht,’ English ‘light.’

Page 182, line 33, literally ‘for of you [all] not a fugitive shall escape alive.’

Page 168, Irish, line 22, delete [*d’*], which is superfluous; the idiom (see page 313, line 16) equals the less correct *gach ní a dtángais d’iarraidh*, or *dá iarraidh*, and they differ much as do: ‘the thing for which you came to ask,’ and ‘the thing which you came to ask for.’

Page 188, line 21, ‘manifest to view’ literally ‘without concealment,’ according to a usage (much wider in Irish than in English), which for emphasis expresses positives by the negation of their opposites, and vice versa, so that: ‘there will be many a dry eye after him,’ and (to a clumsy horseman) ‘many a good horse you never rode!’ are held more elegant than: ‘few will weep for him,’ and ‘you have not ridden many good horses.’ As for *cleith*, our forefathers’ wisdom says: *ní fhuil cleith ar an olc acht gan a dhéanamh* that is, “there is no concealment for evil but not to do it.”

Page 171, Irish, line 30, manuscript *ua mhéith macha* read *úi Mhéith macha*; line 33, manuscript *brug-si*.

Page 194, line 17, ‘what have you to offer’ literally ‘what have you for us.’

P. 219, l. 27 and following, a flagrant plagiarism from ‘The Battle of Moytura of the North.’

P. 197, Ir., l. 28, *colba chiuil*. In a limited number of words beginning with *s* followed by *ea, eo, eoi, iu, iui*, that letter when aspirated is pronounced as *ch* is in the same position—a peculiarity which modern scribes often reproduce this way: for *a Sheaáin* ‘O John,’ they write *a chSeaáin*; for *do shiubhal* ‘to walk,’ *do chsiubhal*; for *a sheol*, *a shiúl* ‘his sail’ (genitive *a sheoil, a shiúil*), *a chseol* etc. = *a cheol, a chiul* ‘his music,’ genitive *a cheoil, a chiuil*. And since *seol* or *siul* also means ‘bedstead,’ we have *colba chiuil* for *colba shiúil* explained. The mind would not be deceived, but the eye would enjoy a ridiculous combination (see note to Irish p. 92, line 13); had the genitive of *crann ciuil* ‘musical instrument’ appeared (Index C, under the word), it would undoubtedly have been written *croinn shiúil*, ‘a ship’s mast.’

P. 198, Ir., l. 15–16, here a dotted *f* represents *bhf*.

P. 199, Ir., l. 2, add a period (.) at the end; line 25, perhaps supply *doithber*.

P. 201, Ir., l. 1, manuscript *sin* for *sinn*, incorrectly; line 21, *tar romainn* is a concise construction including both *tar romat* (second person singular) and *ticmís romainn* (first person plural); *tar* (‘come thou’) is the present spoken form in Munster.

P. 202, Ir., l. 9, after *ocus* delete (]); line 31, *ionnrámh*, delete the accent; line 32, read *nó*.

This signifies the incredible efforts performed in surmounting adverse hills, mountains, and rocks with rapid speed; that part, which is also closest to health, signifies the infected blood of his own body. When these things were finished, the woman offers milk to be drunk.

# Notes and Corrections.

...drinking of wine) Noah lay asleep in his tent, completely naked. There came to him his son, whose name was ‘wicked Ham.’ He behaved such that he made a laughingstock of his father, and told his brothers (namely Japheth and Shem) how Noah was. So that they would not see their father’s shame, they came ‘with their backs toward him’ <note>that is, walking backward</note> and threw his garment over him. Soon after, Noah woke up, and it was revealed to him that Ham had mocked him; accordingly, he cursed him and blessed the other two. Ham, therefore, was the first who was cursed after the Deluge, and from him descended the ‘Wee-bodies’ <note>pigmies</note>, Fomores, ‘Goatheads’ <note>satyrs</note>, and every other deformed shape that human beings take. For this reason, too, extermination was inflicted on the Canaanites and their lands were given to the sons of Israel, namely as a sign of that same curse; for the Canaanites are of the seed of Ham. Such then is the origin of the Monstrosities <note>the species mentioned above</note>, which are not (as the Gaels relate) of Cain’s seed; for nothing of his seed survived the Flood, the very purpose of which was the drowning of Cain’s clan. Why, even all the clans of Seth (except for Noah with his three sons and their four wives) were drowned with them, as Moses mac Amra relates in Genesis of the Law; which Law God Himself gave to Moses on Mount Sinai, having written it with His own hand” (Rawlinson 486, folio 49 : 2; compare Lebor na hUidre 2 a).

Page 240, Irish, line 15, manuscript *coirpri* (Index C, under that entry); in the quatrains below, a few readings are doubtful.
Page 241, Irish, line 2, for *usa* read *tusa*.
Page 270, line 31, ‘copper’s resonance’ refers to timpan and harp strings made of copper wire.
Page 242, Irish, line 16, better *dá ndechsa*.
Page 243, Irish, line 32, for manuscript *gabar* read *gobar*.
Page 244, Irish, lines 16—22; page 246, lines 4—11, 20—24. We have here three more humorous passages of ancient flavor, of which the first records a little queen’s story, and the others relate certain witticisms of a pygmy king; and truly, it is no different than how that Vibius Crispus in Suetonius mocks Domitian the fly-catcher—and not so absurdly. However, out of the respect due to readers of a more serious character, we have preferred to mark such things with dots <note>in the English version, pages 277 etc.</note> rather than even translate them into Latin. The speech is clear to the natives; let those learned in foreign stocks digest it themselves, I pray, by leaning on dictionaries.
Page 245, Irish, line 34, for manuscript *na* [etc.] read *fern na hurbaidb?*
Page 276, lines 11 etc., ‘of which horse:’ an animal that would have suited the Shah exactly; in Maelbrighde’s beautiful Latin gospels (Harleian 1802), written at Armagh in 1139, a symbolic miniature gives an equally gaudy Lion of St. Mark.

# Notes and Corrections.

'of the red eyebrows,' who after a one-year reign was slain by Lughaid *riabhnderg's* son Crimthann, A.M. 5192. Conor was the son of Finn the poet, son of Ros *ruadh*, and was therefore the nephew of Fergus mac Roich of the *Táin*.

<margin>P. 363, Irish, l. 15, *dúthcha*</margin>
(by progressive assimilation for *dúithche*; see Index C under the entries *dabach* and *moch*) is the comparative of the adjective *dúthaigh*, meaning 'peculiar,' 'special,' 'natural to,' or 'own.' It is used (frequently in manuscripts and by word of mouth) primarily as a noun in the derived sense of 'country': "*Eire mo dhúthaigh*" 'Ireland my country,' says John Collins of Myross in his admirable version of Campbell's 'Exile.' As this meaning has completely prevailed over the original one, the latter is now expressed by the derivative masculine noun *dúthchas*: 'that which is naturally inherent in,' or, by virtue of that, 'incumbent on' someone. *Ba dhúthchas dó a dhéanamh* means 'it was natural for him to do it'; *ba dhúthchas dóibh a bhfuil ó Chorcaigh mhóir go Cinn tsáile* means 'nature to them was all that is from the city of Cork to Kinsale,' i.e., that area of the country was theirs by natural, hereditary, and indefeasible right. Here we have a noun used for an adjective, as is very common in Irish: *fuath liom é* 'he is a hatred <note>hateful</note> to me,' *grádh lem anam í* 'love to <note>beloved of</note> my soul she is,' where the adjectives *fuathmar*, *grádhach*, and *grádhmar* cannot be substituted. In the English spoken in Ireland, we say: "'it is a disgust to me," "'it is a weariness to me," etc.

<margin>P. 404, last line, 'kinder,'</margin>
is an idiom perhaps unfamiliar to English readers, but as common in Ireland now as it was when Dean Swift ridiculed it in his Dialogue devoted to Hiberno-Anglicisms. 'And kind father for him,' he says, meaning it was bred in him and to be expected of him. 'The cat has stolen the cream; whip her!' someone might say, and counsel for the cat might answer: 'surely it was natural for the creature; why did you leave it where she could get it!' compare the phrase 'a cat follows its kind.' In a negative sense <note>in mala parte</note>, 'kind mother for her' is equivalent to the French *elle chasse de race* <note>it runs in the family</note>. Here the Irish construction is: [it would not have been more natural for anyone else but you to come and drive this troublesome tribute away from the province of Leinster]. Synonyms include: *ba chinél*, *ba chinélta*, *ba dhú is ba dhual*, but especially *ba dhílis*, so that in our passage *ní dílse* can take the place of *ní dúthcha*. 'A kindly Scot' (a term applicable only by one Scot to another) is *albanach cinélta* or *dilis*, in the sense of the familiar French *pays* or *payse* <note>compatriot</note>, but referring to race rather than place.

<margin>P. 364, Irish, l. 1, here *nimh*</margin>
is not related to physical 'poison.' The people always translate it as 'venom,' and the adjective *nimhnech* as 'venomous,' as in: 'he put great venom into the stroke' (for example, in billiards); 'he put in great venom when approaching the fence'; where it merely denotes high energy or determination (not temperament) and is interchangeable with the equally common *fuinneamh* (see Index C under that word). In the famous song 'Jack and his Leather Breeches,' the hero says of the young lady (eventually his wife) who was smitten with him at sight on the racecourse: *is do chuir sí nimh a súl i gciumhais mo bhríste leathair*, i.e., "and the 'venom of her eyes' <note>her keenest glances</note> she fixed upon the waistband of my leather breeches." However, 'he had venom in for him this long time' means 'he had long held a grudge against him.'

<margin>ibid., lines 28 and following,</margin>
nothing is missing here.

<margin>P. 366, Irish, l. 41, example of *iongnadh*</margin>
pronounced as it is written: *cár bh'iongnadh duine dod cháil do thuitim i lár na haindeise*, i.e., "what wonder is it for a man of your character to fall into the depths of misery" (from a song by Uilliam dall of County Tipperary).

Page 368, Irish, third line from the bottom, in *tsechtmad*, note the gender observed with the ordinal.

Page 369, Irish, line 1, *tromlach* ('the weight,' 'the weighty part,' as people say for 'the bulk') is a derivative of *trom* 'heavy' using the same process that forms *crioslach* 'a limit,' *teghlach* 'household,' *tellach [tenlach]* 'hearth,' *mátharlach* 'womb,' *turlach* 'a lake dry in summer and wet in winter,' from *crios* 'girdle,' *tegh* 'house,' *teine* 'fire,' *máthair* 'mother,' and *tur* 'dry': see Zeuss² page 855, under the entry *-lach*; where *óclach* is not relevant, being (as is well understood today) a compound *óclaech*, still pronounced *óglách* (from which also comes *ógláchas*); like *macámh* for *macaemh* 'a youth,' and *cárthann* for *caerthann* 'the rowan-tree.' Note, by the way, that *chatlach inna fer* (in the same place) is literally η των ανδρων καθολικη (being made feminine instead of neuter to imitate 'universitas'), therefore it does not belong here; *cathlach*, *cathlachda* = 'catholic.'

Page 370, Irish, line 6, I have taken the Latin marginal note as referring to King Failghe's nickname *roth*; anywhere else in the sentence it would be a redundant statement.

Page 372, Irish, line 31, here the poem is inserted from the place to which he refers: LL. 47 β, last line.

Page 373, Irish, line 30, to *ghuidimse* add ([]).

Page 376, Irish, line 34, is *amlaid atchonnaic* <note>etc.</note>; here people would translate this frequently occurring idiom: "'it is the way he saw L. and U. was round the vat and they drinking it;" it is much used also where neither manner nor comparison is involved: *is amhlaidh do bhíos ag caitheamh mo phróinneach lá agus* — "'it is the way I was eating my dinner one day, and —," having much the same force as the popular French "'v'là-t-il pas qu'un jour je <note>etc.</note>'; it also explains reasons: 'why did you do it? it is the way he told me to do it' = 'c'est qu'il m'a dit de le faire,' 'it is as how he told me to do it.'

Page 413, line 17, 'full-grown men of war' is a guess.

Page 377, Irish, line 5, *clothaige in bar scélaib* i.e., "in your stories <note>in your record</note> is renown;" where *clothaige* is an abstract noun formed in the usual way from *clothach*, a derivative adjective of *cloth* 'fame' or 'victory': compare *faebraige* from *faebrach*, page 363, line 5; *fechtnaige* from *fechtnach*, page 395, line 6; *coscraige* from *coscrach*, page 397, line 16.

Page 416, line 24, 'the slaughter <note>etc.</note>' literally 'the slaughter <note>with</note> which your people are being slain is unendurable.'

Page 382, Irish, line 24, for <insert>cruai</insert>*d* read *rind*; line 25, for *di* read *dind* (Lec.).

Page 386, Irish, line 18, here (returning to the subject of the note for Irish page 131, line 28) we find *cian gairit co bráth* ‘be it long or be it short until Judgment Day’; again, *cian gairit ticfait náim ann* ‘...until saints shall come hither’: previously, page 365, the third line from the bottom; the same words: page 366, line 6; *cid mór laighet dobérasa do'n fhiur* ‘be it much or be it little you shall give to the man’: page 402, line 28; lastly, in Molling’s invocation we have the disjunctive expressed, *cid cian cid gairit ár techt . do spirut nár comaitecht* ‘whether far or whether near [long or short] our travel be, may your spirit be our convoy’: page 389, line 12.
