Page 423, line 22, ‘May you be [etc.].’ These lines, obscure in every way, seem to invoke frustration and impotence upon the Saint’s opponents: oaks do not bear rocks; waves are restless, dash themselves to spray, and subside; belfries are noisy and rise up, but the church is the power.

Page 391, Irish, line 18, read *atchonnaic*.

Page 392, Irish, the second to last line, read *saerchlannaibne*.

Page 395, Irish, lines 11 and following, *tiocfaidter ris, ret rath* (impersonal future); this use of *ticim* ‘I come’ with the prepositions *fri, ri, re*, is very frequent, meaning ‘oppose,’ ‘thwart,’ or ‘check’; in his Dialogue already referred to, Swift introduces the idiom: “I came against you there,” i.e., I was one too many for you, I spoiled your game.

Page 430, line 15, for ‘privily’ read ‘zealously,’ ‘with best endeavor’; line 35, ‘swimming’: Elizabeth’s commanders in Ireland reported that this skill was as common among the women as the men there, and that they were just as skillful.

Page 439, line 16, ‘I will [etc.]’ literally ‘this [accident] will [etc.]’; but evidently the text ought to be as rendered.

Page 444, line 35. ‘The Tonsure of Simon Magus,’ distinctive of the Celtic Church before she accepted the Roman rule, was a shaven strip of a certain width extending across the crown from one ear to the other.

Page 410, Irish, line 7, manuscript *námat*.

Page 447, line 22, ‘town,’ and line 26, ‘fort,’ literally ‘castle’ [*caistiall*]; but in Cuan’s day there was no such thing in Ireland, nor for a long time after.

Page 448, line 6, ‘sweet the sound [etc.],’ literally ‘beautiful is the sound of the watching party [wakers] around Cuan the Doubler’s head.’

Page 412, Irish, last line, *conndebairt* (see page 411, line 5) is typical of a whole class of ‘writings’ in which there is an apparent arbitrary doubling of a letter, but this is not the case: there is no such thing as *conn* for the conjunction *con*, and it never ought to be printed that way; but (to take our case) either as in the text, or *con ndebairt*. The scribe’s object is to satisfy etymology by writing the primary form *con*, and by *ndebairt* to indicate the pronunciation of his day (and ours) which, by transferring the *n*, made it *co ndebairt*.

Page 414, Irish, line 15, for *dó* read *do*; line 22, read *dobéram*.

->Translation of Extracts.<-

**I. v.** *Dinn righ* 'mound of kings,' otherwise *dumha Slainghe* 'tumulus of Slainghe' <note>son of Dela, who died there in the Year of the World 3267</note>, is just south of Leighlin-bridge on the Barrow, and the spot is still well known. Here, in the fort hitherto called *bruidhen tuama Tenbath*, Maen son of Olioll Aine (also known as Labraid *loingsech*), massacred King Cobthach, son of *Ugaine the Great*, along with thirty chiefs assembled there, in the Year of the World 4658. The earthen remains of this stronghold have a circumference of two hundred and thirty-seven yards at the base, are sixty-nine feet high from the level of the Barrow, and a hundred and thirty feet in diameter at the top <note>Annals of the Four Masters for that year, O'Donovan's notes</note>.

*ibid*., xiii. There is a curious legend of the Conaille, or descendants of Conall *cernach*:—Conaille Murtheimne do chlaind Chonaill chernaich dóib .i. dál Runtar ocus dál nImda i Cuailngiu ocus Glasraige .i. Glas ocus Runtar ocus Imda trí meic Chonaill chostomail. a ingen féin ruc dó na trí meic sain .i. Creidne banfhéinnid ingen Chonaill chostomail ammáthair. ba rí dana cóicid Chonchobair in Conall costomail. ba aithis imorro lais a ingen do breith nammac dó . bretha na meic uad in immull a fheraind ocus a cheiniuil. is móiti dana ra chuir uad ar ecla na rígna .i. a mná féin .i. Aife a hainm na rígna. bái dana cocad mór etir in rígain ocus Creidne. luid Creidne iar sain for ḟéinnidecht d'fogail for a hathair ocus for Aife. dobert a meic sechtar bunad a ceiniuil ar ulc rá nathair. trí nónbair di for longais . cúlmong fuirri . cuma no ḟhiched de muir ocus tír . secht mbliadna di for longais etir Eirinn ocus Albain. dogní iartain síd fria hathair ocus atbertside fria tré ḟháistini .i. in tír i rucait do meic bid acut ocus bid rit chlaind co bráth . ocus issed ón ro ḟíorad. Conall costomail mac Ḟianchada meic Oengusa .m. Gaith .m. Enbláith .m. Rochada .m. Iriéil ghlúnmair .m. Chonaill chernaig .m. Amairgin. Caulnia ocus Connluan emon ruc Lebarcham ingen Oe ocus Adairce do Choinchulainn is díob corco Caullainn ocus dál Cualni i Cruithniu—that is, "The Conallides, or the Conallic people of the Muirthemne region, are from the lineage of Conall *cernach* the 'triumphant,' of whom these specifically exist: 'Runtar's portion' [the Runtarides], 'Imda's portion' [the Imdaïdes] in the land of Cooley, and the 'Glasrigia' [the Glassides]; the three sons of Conall *costomail* 'the quarrelsome' were Glassius, Runtarus, and Imdaus. His own daughter bore these three to her father; namely, their mother was Creidne the female warrior, daughter of Conall *costomail*, king of Conchobar's province [Ulster]. Then, because the king considered it a disgrace that his own daughter had borne these boys to him, they were taken to the outer borders of his land..."

And as for their footmen, they have one sort who are armored in mail and bascinets; each of them having his weapon, called a spar, much like the Tower axe, and they are named Gallowglass; and for the most part, their boys carry three darts each for them, which darts they throw before they come to hand-to-hand combat. This sort of men are those who do not easily abandon the field, but withstand the brunt of battle until death. The other sort, called Kerns, are naked <note>unarmored</note> men, wearing only their shirts and small coats; and many times when they come to the skirmish, they are quite naked except for their shirts to hide their private parts; and these have darts and short bows. This sort of people are both hardy and active in searching woods or marshes <note>bogs</note>, where they are difficult to defeat" (Sta. Pa. Ir., Henry VIII, xi no. 2). 'The divine Spenser' (Edmund), who knew them, after bestowing some abuse on their ethics—which perfectly fits his own Elizabethans in Ireland (both masters and men) as well—says of the kern and gallowglass:—"Yet surely they are very valiant and hardy; for the most part, great endurers of cold, labor, hunger, and all hardship; very active and strong of hand, very swift of foot; very vigilant and circumspect in their enterprises, very present in perils, very great scorners of death" (View of the State of Ireland).

XX. iii *a*, l. 7, read 'that left no issue'; the three that did so were Teigue, Donough, and Donall (LL. 332 : 6, l. 16 below); modern criticism has rightly reduced Brian's age at death to seventy-three years, and his son Murrough's to fifty or even forty-three (IV M at the year 1013, O'Donovan's note g).

*ibid.*, l. 12, *muinter Aodha* ('people of Aedh') may mean either the clan of *O hAodha* (anglicized as O'Hea or Hayes in the South; Hay or Hughes in the North), or that of *Mac Aedha* (which should be anglicized as 'Mac Hea,' but is now always Mackay or Mac Hugh); *clann Choscraigh* was the tribe name of the latter (who were seated just east of Galway Bay); therefore, for 'O'Heas' read 'Mac Hughs.' These are of the race of Brian, son of *Eochaid m.m.* (previously, pp. 368, 373); the northern clan of *Mac Aodha* [*Mág Aodha* 'M'Gee'], from whom the late bishop of Peterborough descended, come from *Colla uais* (previously, II. xviii, xix *b*, xx *a*). In A.D. 1062, O'Conor (Hugh 'of the gapped spear'), King of Connacht, won a battle over the O'Flahertys of the West in which eighty men of the Mac Hughs fell on the losing side (IV M at that year, and O'Donovan's note a). The Scots say *Mac Aoidh*, 'M'Kay' or 'M'Coy.'

*ibid.*, l. 13, 'Ciocarán's daughter Cianóg.' ->An anonymous man composed this for O'Ciarmaic.<-

Tell me of the history of Aine, is there anyone here who remembers it:
the best hill that ever was, which stands over the wonderful land of Ireland.
Delightful is cold Knockainy, where many hosts used to gather:
great was their goal and their fame, concerning Aine and Eogabal.
Uainide and tall Eogabal, sons of very tall Donn of Uisnech:
Donn of Uisnech set out without restraint to seek a place throughout Ireland.
They went to the house of noble Nechtan, so that the druid might tell them:
where they would settle—a great task—to know it and to reveal it.
"Leap upon Nechtan with power," [he said], "mightily over your enemies:
to the ridge of the hazel-wood of the dykes, which is over the Mairtine of Munster.
Good is the place to which you go westward; it is the best over which the sun sets:
welcome to him who would reach it without blemish, if its clearing were achieved."
Five tribes were around the hill without sin, this is where they found fuel:
the Dilraige and Margraige, the Sibenraige and Callraige.
The Gargraige was the fifth tribe that was around the hill, no false word:
they went out, a fierce deed, to fight against the Tuatha Dé Danann.
"I will ward off," said fair Aine, "the five battles on your behalf:
and the fair hill shall be named after me, during the time of the seed of Eve and Adam."
"O daughter, it is a great task," said Uainide and Eogabal:
"to ward off the five battles rightly, unless magic should help you."
After that Aine went out and began shaping the five battles:
she routed them over the slopes of Luachra and scattered the ancient tribes.
They settle around the hill without fault and divide it into four:
the brave, fair men make four equal portions.
Uainide in the northern half, facing cold Uisnech:
and Fer Fí in the southern half, his house in the well-fitted cairn.
Eogabal in the western end, it has always been so:
and Aine in the eastern end; the hill is among friends.
Cacht was the queen of noble Eogabal, Emer was with Uainide of the struggle:
Red-cheeked Eiter was with Fer Fí, and Aine remained single.
Each one clears the wood from their portion, until the territory of the hill was smooth:
the name 'ridge of the hazel-wood' is taken from it, and the name of Aine stayed with it.

<vocab>S. Cuimin, Rún, Fiachna, Aine, Eogabal, Tuatha Dé Danann, Muman, Cnoc Aine, Uainide</vocab>

# Notes and Corrections.

A ine a hainm ó an ríg co bráth . itir gnáth ocus ingnáth :
mochen [thaebus] ris gach tan . is adba ríg is rígan
A ithesc gilla garbáin géir . aisti ro gab [Ci]ar [co céill] :
[ro gab] Cuan calma in fer . aisti rogab [uair] Fergel
[A isti ro] gab [Eogan] ard . ocus Amalgaid imard :
dochuala is ní m[isde in mod] . aisti do gab Eolchobor
[A g-sin a nanmann gan chol] . cach ríg d’an dual [in degchnoc] :
ocus a flaithes colleic . a fhírglain cháim a Chiairmeic
A Chiairmeic chliach a cliu Mháil . a ógláig oirdnide áin :
Aine fa deoid is ar tús . is dím dlegar a himthús

i.e. “Tell me the history of <term>Knockainy</term>—is there anyone here who remembers it? It was the best hill <note>at one time</note> that ever stood on Ireland’s wondrous land. Cool <term>Knockainy</term> is a pleasant hill, which many and various hosts once frequented; great was their triumph and their renown, along with <term>Aine</term> and with <term>Eogabal</term>. <term>Uainidhe</term> and tall <term>Eogabal</term> were sons of the noble <term>Donn of Uisnech</term>; whom <term>Donn of Uisnech</term> set in motion to go in search of a place <gloss>a settlement</gloss> somewhere in Ireland. They went to the honorable <term>Nechtan’s</term> house, so that the sorcerer, through his knowledge and power of revelation, might tell them where they must settle down. <term>Nechtan</term> then said to them with 'venom': 'By main strength, leap now across your enemies, even to the rampart-enclosed <term>Drom collchoille</term> that dominates the Munster tribes called the <term>Mairtine</term>. That is an excellent place to which you are traveling westward; from there, everything the sun shines upon seems most beautiful; I consider those happy who should reach it, and whose privilege it was to clear it.' Five tribes surely lived around the hill, and there they gathered their firewood: the <term>Dilraighe</term> and the <term>Margraighe</term>, the <term>Sibenraighe</term>, and the <term>Calraighe</term>. The <term>Gargraighe</term> were the fifth tribe around the hill, and this is no false statement; all of them (and it was a senseless act) turned out to give battle to the <term>Tuatha Dé Danann</term>. Fair-haired <term>Aine</term> said: 'I will relieve you of the pressure of those five battalions, and for as long as the descendants of Adam and Eve endure, let this charming hill take its name from me.' 'Girl, it is a huge task,' said <term>Uainidhe</term> and <term>Eogabal</term>, 'to successfully fend off those five armies, unless indeed magic comes to help against them.' Thereupon <term>Aine</term> goes forth and begins to work spells upon those five armies; she routs them through all the paths of <term>Luachair</term> and scatters the ancient tribes far and wide. <insert>She and her people</insert> then settle around the hill and divide it into quarters: the brave and gentle men make four equal portions of it. <term>Uainidhe</term> was to the north, directly facing chilly <term>Uisnech</term>; <term>Fer-fi</term> was to the south, with his dwelling in a handsome cairn. <term>Eogabal</term> was at the western end, and so it has always been; while <term>Aine</term> was at the eastern point, and thus the hill is shared among friends. <term>Cacht</term> was the queen of noble <term>Eogabal</term>; <term>Emer</term> was the queen of warlike <term>Uainidhe</term>; <term>Fer-fi</term> had red-cheeked <term>Eter</term>, and <term>Aine</term> lived a single life. Each cleared the wood from his own portion, so that the hill's enclosure was smooth; <term>Druim Collchoille</term> ('ridge of the hazel wood') was abolished, and <term>Aine’s</term> name has stuck to it <gloss>Cnoc Áine</gloss>. <term>Aine</term>, bestowed by the king, is its name forever, both in common and special use; oh, well for those who continually visit it: it is an abode of kings and queens!” (Eg. 92, f. 37 *b*).

<summary>This page recounts the legendary history of Cnoc Áine (Knockainy), explaining how the goddess Áine used magic to rout five local tribes and clear the hill for her kin. The text details the division of the hill into quarters among Áine, Eogabal, Uainidhe, and Fer-fi, marking the transition from its old name, Druim Collchoille, to Cnoc Áine.</summary>

<page-type>appendix</page-type>
<header>TO FACE PAGE 604.</header>

# SUPPLEMENTARY.

The anonymous verses given on translation page 575, and relevant to section XXII, were inserted to fill a space too small for the translation of the four concluding quatrains; it reads as follows (a few epithets and filler words omitted):

> “The utterance of keen *Gilla Garbháin* <note>or Garbhán’s keen gilla? that is, the poet</note> is that out of it proceeded *Ciar*; from there came *Cuan*, a valiant man, and from there too *Fergel* once upon a time. Out of the same *Eoghan* issued, and *Amalgaidh*; and so, as I have heard, did *Eolchobor*. There now undoubtedly you have the names of all the kings to whom the beautiful hill was ‘kind’; also the succession of their reigns, O *Ciarmhac* <note>my interrogator</note>. *Ciarmhac* of *Aine Cliach*, out of *Clí Máil*, O noble youth of rank: Knockany, from first to last, it is from me that its history is rightly required.”

Addressed to *Ó Ciarmhaic* (*Ciarmhac*), lord of *Aine Cliach*; whose name is Anglicized as ‘Kiarwick,’ ‘Kerwick,’ and (by false analogy) ‘Kirby’ or ‘Berwick.’ Of this lineage were my great friend, the late John Kirby of the Irish bar, and the Recorder of Cork (Berwick) who perished in the terrible railway disaster at Abergele.

Page 94 of the Irish text, second to last line, read *mac Lugach*; page 214, line 21, read *anuas*; page 233, line 16, read *can ingnadh* <note>modern *cá hingnadh*</note>.
Page 408 of the translation, line 7, translate *Ocha alachath* as ‘of Ocha (another battle)’; page 409, last line, for ‘bear it laboriously into,’ read ‘shoot it in.’

---

It is a pity that considerations of volume size prevented the translation of the numerous verses in section XXVIII, which are very distinctly ‘poetry’ as opposed to simple memory aids, and are fine specimens of very beautiful and spirited meters.

Several place-names missing from Index B were intended to appear in Index C under the heading of ‘Battles,’ and others.

<summary>This supplement provides a translation of quatrains concerning the kings of Knockany and the Ó Ciarmhaic lineage, alongside a list of textual corrections and notes on missing index entries.</summary>
